Consider three recent cases filed by consumers against large companies. John Feeney accused a computer manufacturer of charging tens of thousands of its customers an illegal $ 13 sales tax.Elizabeth Dean brought a class action against a private, for-profit vocational school for misleading its students about the costs and marketability of their degrees.ErnestineHawkins sued a bank after she was injured by an accident in its lobby.Anyone who has tracked the evolution of the U.S. civil justice system can predict what happened next. The businesses did not deny the plaintiffs' allegations or debunk their legal theories. Instead, they moved to compel arbitration.
The use of private dispute resolution as the first line of defense against consumer lawsuits has long been controversial. In 1925, Congress passed the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) to abolish common law rules that made it impossible to obtain specific performance of an agreement to arbitrate.The statute lay somewhat dormant until the 1980s, when the U.S. Supreme Court held that it preempts state law,governs statutory claims,and embodies a "liberal federal policy favoring arbitration."Countless firms added arbitration clauses to their contracts, making arbitration "a phenomenon that pervade[s] virtually every corner of the daily economy."Some Justices, business groups, and the defense bar applauded this development, arguing that arbitration's speed, flexibility, and affordability pave the way for customers to pursue claims.But other courts, plaintiffs' lawyers, and consumer advocates objected that abridged procedures thwart substantive rights, and that arbitrators--who, unlike judges, are paid by the case--are reluctant to rule against the repeat-playing firms that may select or veto them again in the future.
Since 2010, these issues have been thrust back into the spotlight. For decades, judges maintained the legitimacy of alternative dispute resolution by policing arbitration clauses for fairness.If a consumer proved that arbitral expenses or one-sided procedures thwarted her rights, a court would strike down all or part of the arbitration clause under the unconscionability doctrine.But in 2010, theCourt held inRent-A-Center, West, Inc. v. Jacksonthat drafters could bypass this layer of judicial review by delegating questions about the scope or validity of the arbitration clause to the arbitrator.By allowing private judges to decide these pivotal issues, the Court rejected concerns that they are biased against consumers. Similarly, until 2011, over a dozen jurisdictions refused to enforce class arbitration waivers when plaintiffs asserted numerous low-value claims.These judges reasoned that because small-dollar grievances will either be aggregated or abandoned, class arbitration waivers liberated firms from liability.However, inAT&T Mobility LLC v. ConcepcionandAmerican Express v. Italian Colors Restaurant(Italian Colors),the Court made class arbitration waivers bulletproof, placing the onus on customers to initiate their own arbitrations rather than ride the wake of class proceedings.
The cases from the first paragraph of this Article illustrate the profound impact of the Court's recent FAA jurisprudence. InFeeney, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court held thatConcepcionandItalian Colorsrequired each plaintiff to pursue their small-dollar lawsuits in individual arbitration.The state high court speculated that few customers would do so, and called this result "untenable," but felt bound to obey "a controlling statement of Federal law."
Similarly, inDean, the plaintiff urged a district judge in Tennessee to exempt her and the other former students from arbitration because they were buried in debt and could not afford to pay the arbitrator's fees.Yet the defendant's arbitration clause stated that its "scope or enforceability . . . shall be determined by the arbitrator, and not by a court."The judge reasoned that, as paradoxical as it sounds, underRent-A-Center, the issue of whether the plaintiffs should be arbitrating was for the arbitrator to decide.The court sent the matter to the private tribunal, but not before flying a red flag of protest:[T]his holding present[s] a serious fairness issue. . . . [T]he court is concerned that one or more of the named plaintiffs in this action will not be able to afford the out-of-pocket costs to arbitrate, even under conservative cost assumptions. Indeed, several of the plaintiffs have represented that they haveno income and no unencumbered assets whatsoever. . . . While required by the FAA, this result strikes the court as manifestly unjust and, perhaps, deserving of legislative attention.
[T]his holding present[s] a serious fairness issue. . . . [T]he court is concerned that one or more of the named plaintiffs in this action will not be able to afford the out-of-pocket costs to arbitrate, even under conservative cost assumptions. Indeed, several of the plaintiffs have represented that they haveno income and no unencumbered assets whatsoever. . . . While required by the FAA, this result strikes the court as manifestly unjust and, perhaps, deserving of legislative attention.
However, the Mississippi district court inHawkinshad no such misgivings. The plaintiff asserted that she could not be forced to arbitrate her tort claim because she had closed her account at the bank where she fell three years before the incident.She contended that there was no contract--and therefore no agreement to arbitrate--between her and the institution.The court held that this argument was irrelevant because the plaintiff's original deposit agreement provided that "[a]ny dispute regarding whether a particular controversy is subject to arbitration . . . shall be decided by the arbitrator(s)."The court sent the dispute to arbitration and defended this result:[T]he Supreme Court's decision[s] . . . might be regarded by some as creating a legal 'black hole' which inevitably sucks in disputes and sends them to arbitration . . . . [However,] while many plaintiffs seem to regard arbitration as the place where 'lawsuits go to die,' at least one empirical study of consumer arbitrations conducted by the American Arbitration Association found, among other things, that [c]onsumers won some relief in 53.3% of the cases they filed and recovered an average of $ 19,255.
[T]he Supreme Court's decision[s] . . . might be regarded by some as creating a legal 'black hole' which inevitably sucks in disputes and sends them to arbitration . . . . [However,] while many plaintiffs seem to regard arbitration as the place where 'lawsuits go to die,' at least one empirical study of consumer arbitrations conducted by the American Arbitration Association found, among other things, that [c]onsumers won some relief in 53.3% of the cases they filed and recovered an average of $ 19,255.
These opinions reveal that the Supreme Court's reading of the FAA inspires strong, divergent reactions. But they also highlight a flaw in the fabric of this debate. Both critics and proponents of the Court have only the dimmest sense of what actually happens in the extrajudicial forum. Are the many commentators who have condemnedConcepcionandItalian Colorscorrect that class arbitration waivers "deny a willing plaintiff any and all practical means of pursuing a claim"?Or is individual arbitration superior to the class action because it is faster, cheaper, and allows consumers to act pro se?Is the expansion of arbitral sovereignty inRent-A-Centerunwise because arbitrators favor repeatplayers?Or do private judges resolve cases in a "completely fair and impartial manner"?These are empirical questions about a system that does not lend itself to empirical inquiry.For example, the paper thatHawkinscites for the proposition that consumer plaintiffs hold their own in arbitration--a 2009 publication by the Searle Civil Justice Institute at Northwestern University School of Law (Searle Report)--predatesRent-A-Center, Concepcion, andItalian Colors.Even the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Arbitration Study (CFPB Study)--released as this Article was being edited--only analyzes arbitral awards from 2010 and 2011 in the financial service industry, and thus does not capture the full impact of the Court's game-changing decisions.
This Article shines fresh light on these issues by analyzing 4,839 cases filed by consumers with the American Arbitration Association (AAA) between July 2009 and December 2013. We reach three main conclusions. First, the eclipse of the consumer class action has affected the nature and volume of filings within the arbitral forum. AfterConcepcion, some plaintiffs' lawyers, whom we call "arbitration entrepreneurs,"have tried to overcome their inability to aggregate disputes by bringing scores of discrete proceedings against the same company. Nevertheless, they have been unable to prosecute enough matters to replicate the deterrent or compensatory functions of the traditional class action.
, we discover that consumers win--defined as recovering $ 1 or more--491 of the 1,407 arbitral awards (35%). Admittedly, fully arbitrated cases, like those that progress all the way to a judgment in court, may not be representative of all disputes.Thus, it would be unwise to use win rates as the springboard for bold policy prescriptions. Nevertheless, it is sobering that the consumers in our data prevailed less often than those in previous studies of AAA records.
, we show that repeat-player issues have acquired new urgency since the consumer arbitration revolution. Arbitral bias has become more important afterRent-A-Centeropened the door for arbitrators to determine whether an arbitration clause is unconscionable. After all, if private judges skew their rulings to serve their pecuniary needs, then it would be perverse to allow them to decide whether the arbitral process is fair. But less intuitively, we show thatConcepcionhas also raised the stakes in the repeat-player debate. Companies that once faced a single lawsuit brought by thousands of customers now find themselves embroiled in dozens of bilateral arbitrations. As a result, the Court's class arbitration opinions have bred a cadre of "high-level" and "super" repeat-playing defendants (collectively "extreme" repeat players).Our multivariate regression analyses demonstrate that these elite corporations outperform their one-shot counterparts on win rates and damage payments. Thus, to the extent that extreme repeat players owe their success to experience within the extrajudicial tribunal,Concepcionis more pernicious than believed: not only does it shield big companies from class action liability, but it allows them to dominate individual cases as well.
The Article contains three Parts. Part I sets the stage by describing how arbitration has displaced litigation as the primary method by which consumers resolve disputes against companies. It reveals that this massive shift has occurred even though courts, lawmakers, and scholars know very little about what transpires in the extrajudicial forum. Part II lays out our research methodology and offers descriptive statistics about win rates, damages, and arbitral costs. It then presents striking evidence that high-level and super repeat players are harder to beat and pay less in damages than one-shot firms. Part III sifts through potential explanations for our findings and discusses their normative significance.

questions.question: Whether the displacement of consumer class actions by individualized arbitration has changed the volume and character of consumer filings and whether individual arbitrations can reproduce the compensatory and deterrent functions formerly provided by class actions.
What are consumers' success rates and typical monetary recoveries in individual consumer arbitrations filed with a major arbitral provider during the study period?
Whether defendant firms that repeatedly appear in consumer arbitrations achieve systematically better outcomes (higher win rates and lower damage awards) than one-shot defendant firms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85ucololrev459!!ARTICLE: MASS ARBITRATION AND DEMOCRATIC LEGITIMACY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: MASS ARBITRATION AND DEMOCRATIC LEGITIMACY

shared_topics.topic: Effects of Supreme Court decisions (Concepcion, Italian Colors, Rent‑A‑Center) on consumer arbitration and class actions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses those rulings as a focal example of how the Court has expanded the FAA and made adhesive arbitration clauses broadly enforceable, arguing this transformation undermines democratic and contractual norms; Paper B studies the concrete post‑decision effects, documenting shifts in AAA filings, the decline of consumer class actions, and how firms and lawyers adapted to the new landscape.

shared_topics.topic: Consent and legitimacy of adhesive standard‑form arbitration clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques standard‑form arbitration provisions as non‑consensual fine print that degrades contractual assent and democratic legitimacy; Paper B investigates whether consumers in practice can meaningfully pursue claims under those clauses—considering costs, procedural barriers, and whether arbitration truly reflects voluntary consent.

shared_topics.topic: Delegation/separability doctrines letting arbitrators decide arbitrability and unconscionability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the separability doctrine and Rent‑A‑Center's delegation of threshold issues to arbitrators as a legal fiction that severs arbitration from ordinary consent and judicial oversight; Paper B examines Rent‑A‑Center empirically, showing how courts routinely send arbitrability or unconscionability questions to private tribunals and analyzing the consequences for consumer access and fairness.

shared_topics.topic: Repeat‑player advantage and asymmetry between corporations and consumers in arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns that mass arbitration empowers businesses to impose procedural rules and exploit structural advantages over individual adherents; Paper B provides empirical evidence that 'high‑level' and 'super' repeat‑playing defendants outperform one‑shot firms on win rates and damages, underscoring the practical significance of repeat‑player bias.

shared_topics.topic: Private arbitration's erosion of public enforcement and access to remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues mass arbitration lets private actors 'delete' rights granted by democratic law and displaces public law enforcement mechanisms; Paper B shows empirically that the eclipse of class actions and proliferation of individual arbitrations weakens collective deterrence and compensatory functions, reducing effective remedies for many consumers.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36loyuchilj535!!ARTICLE: Privatized "Justice"
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Privatized "Justice"

shared_topics.topic: Supreme Court expansion of the Federal Arbitration Act and preemption of state limits
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how recent Supreme Court decisions have read the FAA broadly—extending arbitration to statutory claims, state-court suits, and preempting state laws that would limit arbitration—transforming the enforceability of pre-dispute arbitration clauses against consumers.

shared_topics.topic: Class-action waivers' effect on consumer aggregation and access to relief for small-value claims
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with the consequences of class-action waivers (discussed via decisions like Concepcion and Italian Colors), arguing that such waivers block the economically viable aggregation of small claims and shift disputes from class litigation to individual arbitration, undermining deterrence and compensation.

shared_topics.topic: Adhesion contracts and consumer consent to pre-dispute arbitration clauses
shared_topics.justification: Both criticize the widespread use of mandatory arbitration terms in adhesion contracts—pointing out that consumers often do not knowingly consent to waive judicial remedies and that these clauses are routinely enforced despite imbalance in bargaining power.

shared_topics.topic: Procedural features of arbitration (fees, costs, appeals, and delegation clauses) and their impact on fairness
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on procedural aspects—arbitral fees, lack of appellate review, and 'delegation' clauses that assign threshold gateway questions to arbitrators—and examine how these features affect whether arbitration is truly a fair and accessible forum for consumers.

shared_topics.topic: Arbitral bias and repeat-player advantages favoring corporations
shared_topics.justification: Both raise concerns that arbitration can systematically disadvantage one-shot consumer claimants—Paper A empirically documents superior outcomes for repeat-playing corporate defendants, while Paper B argues more generally that privatized forums create structural incentives (and limited supervision) that may favor repeat participants.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88notredamelrev825!!ARTICLE: KILLING THEM WITH KINDNESS: EXAMINING "CONSUMER-FRIENDLY" ARBITRATION CLAUSES AFTER AT&T MOBILITY V. CONCEPCION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: KILLING THEM WITH KINDNESS: EXAMINING "CONSUMER-FRIENDLY" ARBITRATION CLAUSES AFTER AT&T MOBILITY V. CONCEPCION

shared_topics.topic: the impact of recent Supreme Court arbitration decisions (e.g., Concepcion, Rent-A-Center, Italian Colors, Amex) on enforceability doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how the Court's post-2010 decisions have reshaped the legal rules courts apply to consumer arbitration clauses — Paper A by tracing doctrinal options for responding to Concepcion and Amex and Paper B by treating Rent-A-Center/Concepcion/Italian Colors as the legal pivot whose real-world effects the authors empirically evaluate.

shared_topics.topic: cost-based "vindication of rights" challenges and the affordability of arbitration for consumers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on cost-based challenges as a doctrinal route to invalidate arbitration/class-waiver clauses when individual arbitration would be prohibitively expensive, while Paper B empirically probes whether arbitral costs and fee rules actually deter filings, affect who brings claims, and influence consumer recovery rates.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of class-action waivers on aggregation, deterrence, and the shift to individual arbitrations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how anti-aggregation features (class waivers) drive cost-based objections and how courts should treat clauses that foreclose collective litigation, and Paper B documents empirically that class-waiver enforcement has reduced class filings, spawned 'arbitration entrepreneurs' bringing many separate cases, and failed to replicate the deterrent/compensatory functions of class actions.

shared_topics.topic: how firms craft arbitration clauses (and related procedural features) and the real-world consequences for consumer outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys and interprets corporate responses—’consumer-friendly’ clause modifications like fee-shifting, bounties, and promises to cover costs—to survive judicial review, while Paper B assesses whether those contractual regimes and firm behavior translate into consumer wins, payment levels, and differential outcomes for repeat-defendant firms in AAA data.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57stanlrev1631!!2005 STANFORD LAW REVIEW SYMPOSIUM: THE CIVIL TRIAL: ADAPTATION AND ALTERNATIVES: SYMPOSIUM ARTICLE: Creeping Mandatory Arbitration: Is It Just?
compared_to.partner_title: 2005 STANFORD LAW REVIEW SYMPOSIUM: THE CIVIL TRIAL: ADAPTATION AND ALTERNATIVES: SYMPOSIUM ARTICLE: Creeping Mandatory Arbitration: Is It Just?

shared_topics.topic: mandatory arbitration imposed through standard-form contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the shift from voluntary, negotiated arbitration to arbitration clauses unilaterally imposed on consumers via form contracts, with Paper A documenting empirically how firms embedded arbitration clauses across consumer agreements and Paper B critiquing the broader phenomenon of 'creeping' mandatory arbitration imposed through everyday transactions.

shared_topics.topic: loss of access to collective litigation and effects on small-value claims
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how arbitration clauses and class-action waivers undermine the ability of consumers to pursue aggregated claims—Paper A empirically examines how Concepcion and Italian Colors reduced class procedures and forced individual filings, while Paper B warns that mandatory arbitration denies the average consumer meaningful access to court and collective remedies.

shared_topics.topic: procedural fairness and potential bias in arbitration (repeat-player problem)
shared_topics.justification: Both express concern that arbitration may be substantively unfair to consumers: Paper A provides empirical evidence that repeat-player firms fare better in AAA proceedings (suggesting arbitrator or structural bias), and Paper B raises normative critiques that mandatory arbitration can advantage powerful firms and leave vulnerable parties unprotected.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the judiciary and federal law in expanding arbitration's reach
shared_topics.justification: Both scrutinize how courts and the Federal Arbitration Act shape arbitration's enforceability—Paper A analyzes recent Supreme Court decisions that broaden arbitral sovereignty and limit judicial oversight, while Paper B critiques judicial encouragement of mandatory arbitration and the weakening of state protective power.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64smulrev3!!ARTICLE: Alternative Dispute Resolution
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Alternative Dispute Resolution

shared_topics.topic: arbitration and mediation as alternatives to litigation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically analyzes how consumer arbitration has displaced litigation for consumer claims and compares individual arbitration to class actions, while Paper B surveys the growing use of mediation and arbitration in Texas as alternative processes to resolve civil disputes.

shared_topics.topic: legal and statutory developments that shape ADR practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on federal law and Supreme Court decisions (FAA, Rent-A-Center, Concepcion, Italian Colors) that expanded arbitral enforcement, whereas Paper B examines the state-level legislative framework (the Texas Alternative Dispute Resolution Procedures Act) and recent developments that have driven ADR's institutional growth.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional growth and shifting role of ADR in the civil justice system
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the rapid expansion of consumer arbitration filings and the resulting change in how consumer claims are brought, and Paper B discusses the broader expansion and increasing influence of ADR (mediation, arbitration, collaborative law) in Texas practice.

shared_topics.topic: the role, behavior, and influence of neutrals/arbitrators and repeat actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates repeat-player effects and concerns that arbitrators might favor repeat-playing firms, while Paper B highlights the rising population of 'professional neutrals' and the implications of their expanding role in ADR processes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 96nclrev381!!ARTICLE: CONSPIRACY TO ARBITRATE (c) 2018 Christopher R. Leslie.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSPIRACY TO ARBITRATE (c) 2018 Christopher R. Leslie.

shared_topics.topic: effects of recent Supreme Court FAA decisions (e.g., Concepcion, Italian Colors, Rent-A-Center) on consumer access to relief and the arbitration landscape
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically assesses how those decisions changed filing patterns, win rates, and the feasibility of private enforcement; Paper B analyzes doctrinal developments from the same decisions and argues they incentivize firms to use arbitration clauses to shield themselves from litigation and statutory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: role and consequences of class-action waivers for aggregation, deterrence, and consumer recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the eclipse of consumer class actions, the rise of 'arbitration entrepreneurs,' and the inability of individual arbitrations to replicate class deterrence; Paper B treats class-action waivers as a central mechanism firms use in contracts to prevent class litigation and undermine collective enforcement of legal rights.

shared_topics.topic: firm advantages and industry-wide adoption of arbitration clauses, including coordinated strategies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uncovers a repeat-player effect where high-level and 'super' repeat-defendant firms obtain better outcomes and pay less in damages; Paper B examines how firms may achieve market-wide mandatory arbitration either independently or through illegal agreements ('conspiracies to arbitrate'), amplifying defendants' power across an industry.

shared_topics.topic: the judiciary's role in applying arbitration law (delegation clauses, compelled arbitration) and its implications for substantive rights and antitrust claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how courts' enforcement of delegation clauses and waivers (per Rent-A-Center and Concepcion) affects who decides arbitrability and can limit consumer access to court; Paper B criticizes courts for misreading the FAA—compelling arbitration of conspiracy-to-arbitrate and related antitrust claims—and argues these judicial practices protect conspirators and erode legal protections.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43pepplrev493!!ARTICLE: Innovation in Arbitration Law: The Case of Delaware
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Innovation in Arbitration Law: The Case of Delaware

shared_topics.topic: delegation of arbitrability and the allocation of judicial vs. arbitral authority
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Supreme Court's doctrinal shifts (e.g., Rent-A-Center) that permit parties to delegate threshold questions (scope, enforceability) to arbitrators and examines the consequences; Paper B analyzes statutory choices in the Delaware Rapid Arbitration Act and earlier schemes that deliberately limit or reassign court involvement, thereby engaging the same question of who decides arbitrability and how statutory design mediates that allocation.

shared_topics.topic: procedural design of arbitration (expedited timelines, fee rules, class-waiver effects) and implications for access to justice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically evaluates how procedural features—most notably class-arbitration waivers, fee burdens, and the move to many individual proceedings—affect consumers' ability to vindicate claims; Paper B dissects DRAA provisions (mandatory time limits, financial penalties for arbitrators, restricted court intervention, confidentiality) and warns of practical difficulties and fairness implications, engaging the same concern about how procedural rules shape access and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: federal-state interaction and state innovation in arbitration law under the FAA
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the Supreme Court's FAA jurisprudence and its preemptive impact on state-law policing of arbitration clauses, while Paper B investigates Delaware's recent statutory innovations and explicitly addresses the limits imposed by federal jurisdiction and FAA preemption, so both papers engage the tension between federal arbitration doctrine and state-level reform efforts.

shared_topics.topic: institutional incentives and repeat-player effects arising from arbitration governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides empirical evidence that high-level/super repeat-playing defendants fare better in AAA consumer arbitrations and raises concerns about arbitrator incentives and repeat-player bias; Paper B examines institutional design choices (who serves as arbitrator, sanctions for delay, appellate review) that shape arbitrator incentives and institutional behavior, linking statutory design to the same problem of how arbitration governance creates advantages for repeat actors.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nclrev1027!!Article: THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT AND TESTAMENTARY INSTRUMENTS*
compared_to.partner_title: Article: THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT AND TESTAMENTARY INSTRUMENTS*

shared_topics.topic: the Supreme Court's expansive reading of the Federal Arbitration Act and federal preemption of state law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how recent Supreme Court decisions have broadened the FAA's scope and preempted state rules—Paper A explores the implications of that expansion for probate courts and state regulation of wills and trusts, while Paper B traces the same doctrinal shift in the consumer context and studies its effects on litigation channels and forum choice.

shared_topics.topic: who decides arbitrability and the separability/delegation doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the separability/delegation doctrines that allow arbitration clauses (or arbitrators) to determine their own scope: Paper B focuses on Rent-A-Center's delegation to arbitrators in consumer disputes and its practical consequences, and Paper A examines how the separability doctrine would operate (or be limited) when arbitration clauses are embedded in testamentary instruments.

shared_topics.topic: whether arbitration undermines access to justice and individual rights (costs, class waivers, fairness concerns)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront normative concerns that arbitration can deny plaintiffs practical remedies—Paper B empirically examines win rates, the impact of class-action waivers and filing costs on consumers, while Paper A assesses comparable worries about deprivation of rights in probate and argues those concerns are attenuated or can be managed in the testamentary setting.

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope and application of the FAA to nontraditional or contract-adjacent settings
shared_topics.justification: Both articles probe the FAA's applicability beyond classic bilateral consumer or employment contracts—Paper B documents the pervasiveness of arbitration in consumer contracts and the effects of treating many adhesion terms as binding, whereas Paper A asks whether and how the FAA should (or does) reach arbitration clauses in non-contractual dispositive instruments like wills and trusts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52ucdavislrevonline73!!ARTICLE: Diminution Doctrine: Arbitration's First Amendment Problem
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Diminution Doctrine: Arbitration's First Amendment Problem

shared_topics.topic: how enforcement of arbitration clauses (class waivers, fees, etc.) limits consumers' access to courts and the right to petition
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically documents that class-action waivers, arbitration costs, and post-Concepcion filing patterns have reduced consumers' practical ability to pursue claims in court or aggregate small-value claims. Paper B develops a constitutional critique—via 'diminution doctrine'—arguing that FAA enforcement has eroded the Petition Clause guarantee of judicial access by channeling disputes into private arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: the public-interest harms from privatizing dispute resolution — especially loss of precedential development and judicial oversight
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how mass diversion of disputes into private arbitrations reduces public visibility of outcomes and changes deterrence and compensatory functions formerly served by class litigation. Paper B frames those same consequences constitutionally, arguing the FAA's privatization diminishes 'precedential currency' and meaningful judicial review protected by the right to petition.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of Supreme Court FAA jurisprudence (e.g., Concepcion, Rent-A-Center, Italian Colors) on the structure and fairness of consumer dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically studies the concrete effects of recent Supreme Court decisions—showing changes in filing volume, the rise of unilateral defendant repeat-players, win rates, and recoveries. Paper B targets that body of doctrine more abstractly, arguing that the Court's rulings expanding enforcement of arbitration agreements have deeper constitutional consequences for petition rights and the public role of courts.

shared_topics.topic: delegation of arbitrability to arbitrators and concerns about repeat-player bias and fairness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that Rent-A-Center-style delegation clauses shift threshold questions to arbitrators and shows empirically that repeat-playing firms fare better in arbitration, raising concerns about biased adjudicators. Paper B treats the delegation trend as part of the FAA's erosion of judicial functions, arguing that allowing private adjudicators to supplant courts undermines protections the Petition Clause was meant to secure.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26connlrev521!!ARTICLE: ARBITRABILITY IN RECENT FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS LEGISLATION: THE NEED FOR AMENDMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ARBITRABILITY IN RECENT FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS LEGISLATION: THE NEED FOR AMENDMENT

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of arbitration agreements for statutory civil‑rights and consumer claims under the Federal Arbitration Act
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the FAA (and the Supreme Court's Gilmer decision) brought civil‑rights statutes like the ADA and ADEA within the ambit of compulsory arbitration; Paper B examines how the same body of FAA jurisprudence (Rent‑A‑Center, Concepcion, Italian Colors) has been used to compel consumer statutory claims into arbitration and to limit judicial screening of arbitration clauses.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and fairness of arbitral procedures for protecting substantive statutory rights given asymmetric bargaining power
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that arbitration may be ill‑suited to vindicate important public civil‑rights mandates because of procedural limitations and unequal bargaining positions, advocating a de novo post‑arbitral trial; Paper B empirically studies whether consumer claimants fare poorly in arbitration—documenting lower win rates, costs barriers, and advantages enjoyed by repeat‑playing firms—thereby assessing the procedural fairness concerns in practice.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of Supreme Court arbitration doctrine on courts' ability to consider statutory policy and procedural safeguards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that Gilmer and subsequent doctrine curtailed courts' ability to refuse arbitration based on statutory policy, rendering congressional textual encouragement largely irrelevant; Paper B shows how later Supreme Court decisions (Rent‑A‑Center, Concepcion, Italian Colors) reshaped the terrain—delegating gateway issues to arbitrators and insulating class‑waivers—producing concrete changes in case disposition and access to aggregation mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legislative or regulatory responses to remedy harms from expanded arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for statutory amendment (e.g., explicit post‑arbitral de novo trials) to protect civil‑rights claimants, arguing legislative text should override or clarify FAA effects; Paper B documents empirical harms and gaps in knowledge and highlights calls for legislative attention and regulatory study (e.g., CFPB) as possible responses to problems revealed by the Court's arbitration rulings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 21cardozojconflictresol1!!ARTICLE: THE LIFE OF ARBITRATION LAW HAS BEEN EXPERIENCE, NOT LOGIC: GORSUCH, KAVANAUGH, AND THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE LIFE OF ARBITRATION LAW HAS BEEN EXPERIENCE, NOT LOGIC: GORSUCH, KAVANAUGH, AND THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT

shared_topics.topic: Supreme Court-driven transformation of the Federal Arbitration Act and its practical consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the Supreme Court has effectively rewritten the FAA through a pro-arbitration doctrinal regime (the 'strong federal policy favoring arbitration'), and Paper B examines the real-world consequences of that jurisprudential shift by analyzing how recent Supreme Court precedents altered the volume, nature, and outcomes of consumer arbitrations.

shared_topics.topic: Delegation of gateway arbitrability questions to arbitrators and the shrinking role of courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses doctrinal trends and specific decisions that reduce judicial gatekeeping over arbitrability (downsizing the court's role), and Paper B focuses empirically on Rent-A-Center and related rulings that delegate threshold questions (scope/validity) to arbitrators and the downstream effects of that delegation.

shared_topics.topic: Repeat-player dynamics and concerns about arbitrator impartiality and accountability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises normative and doctrinal worries about arbitrators' de facto lawmaking power, lack of public accountability, and calls for judicialization given potential biases, while Paper B provides empirical evidence that repeat-player defendants (and 'extreme' repeat players) fare better in AAA consumer arbitrations, implicating the same impartiality and accountability concerns.

shared_topics.topic: Impact of arbitration doctrine on consumer access to justice and ability to aggregate claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames arbitration law in terms of policy objectives and access/fairness trade-offs that courts manage through doctrine, and Paper B documents how decisions upholding class-waivers and arbitration clauses have reduced class aggregation, increased one-off arbitrations, raised cost barriers, and thereby impaired consumers' practical ability to pursue claims.

papers.node_id: 2006michstlrev235!!ARTICLE: ALTERING JUDICIAL REVIEW OF LABOR ARBITRATION AWARDS
papers.title: ARTICLE: ALTERING JUDICIAL REVIEW OF LABOR ARBITRATION AWARDS
papers.abstract:
The law surrounding judicial review of labor arbitration awards under Section 301 of the Labor-Management Relations Actis a well-established staple of American labor law jurisprudence.The law surrounding judicial review of commercial arbitration awards under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)is equally well-established.
Arbitration law is, of course, not limited to these two federal statutes. The FAA only applies to agreements involving interstate commerce.Section 301, which applies to most private-sector collective bargaining agreements, only applies to such contracts between private-sector employers and labor organizations involved in interstate commerce.Some forty-nine states have filled in this gap by enacting state arbitration statutes.
Arbitration, as used in this Article, is a private system of dispute resolution whereby the parties to a contract have consented to have their dispute finally resolved by a neutral arbitrator.It is important to distinguish voluntary arbitration, which this Article examines, from "compulsory arbitration" whereby parties are compelled to submit certain disputes to arbitration.This is because the law surrounding judicial review of compulsory arbitration decisions is much less deferential to the arbitrator's determination.It is also important to distinguish voluntary arbitration from other forms of arbitration such as "advisory arbitration" whereby the arbitrator does not have the authority to issue a final and binding award. The law surrounding advisory arbitration is quite different in that subsequent litigation over the merits of the dispute is still possible because the determination is only advisory.
This Article is primarily about whether the parties to a collective bargaining agreement which provides for arbitration of disputes, commonly referred to as grievances, can voluntary agree to alter the standard of judicial review to which any such labor arbitration decision would normally be subjected. In the context of commercial arbitration under the FAA, this issue has generated a significant amount of scholarly debate by academic commentatorsas well as a conflict in the federal circuits-- with somecourts even drawing a distinction between expanding judicial review and eliminating judicial review altogether.This issue has also generated conflicting state court decisions.Significantly, however, with one exception,the alteration of the standard of judicial review of labor arbitration awards in the private sector has not been addressed by scholarly commentators or by courts. The single judicial exception is a statement in dicta by Judge Posner of the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals.
Interestingly, none of the many courts that have addressed the legality of altering judicial review of commercial arbitration awards have discussed the parties' reasoning for wanting to alter the standard. However, in examining whether any change is legally permissible, it may be useful to understand the motivation of the parties for wanting to change the standard.
This author believes that sometimes parties to a collective bargaining agreement as well as parties to a commercial arbitration agreement may be interested in altering the standard of judicial review for some of the same reasons arbitration developed in the first place -- the need for a cost-efficient and speedy resolution of disputes. In such cases, the parties may be interested in lowering the standard of judicial review or perhaps even eliminating it in order to make any arbitration award rock solid.
However, where the stakes are especially high, some parties may see a need to impose a check on arbitration by altering the standard of review to make it more akin to litigation. The parties may be interested in the expertise of arbitrators and the speed of the process, but also want to reserve the right to appeal. After all, as the Supreme Court has recognized, arbitration is not designed to be a perfect system of justice.
The Supreme Court has not yet addressed whether the arbitration standard of judicial review may be altered. In fact, it has denied certiorari four times where the issue has been raised in the context of a commercial arbitration under the FAA.Given the amount of conflicting opinions that have been generated and the amount of scholarly debate, it is only a matter of time before the Supreme Court takes up this issue in the context of a labor or commercial arbitration. The issue may also arise in the context of employment arbitration, given the explosive use of employment arbitration since the Supreme Court's Gilmer v. Interstate/Johnson Lane Corp.decision in 1991.
Although there are a number of commercial cases addressing alteration of the standard of judicial review, the present state of the law does not provide any clear answer to the question whether the parties may contractually alter the standard of judicial review of a commercial arbitration decision. There is a tension between freedom of contract, which lies at the heart of arbitration law, and the need for judicial oversight in order to prevent abuse.
Both advocates who favor allowing judicial review of an arbitration decision to be altered and those who advocate against such alteration have good arguments. It appears that neither is completely right or completely wrong. In the end, courts will have to balance the parties' desires against the need to retain supervision over the arbitral process. This Article maintains that the parties should be able to alter the standard of judicial review so long as no fraud or bias activity is involved, and so long as the parties clearly and convincingly have expressed their intentions to do so.
Courts will also have to address this issue one day with respect to labor arbitration. This author submits that regardless of how the Supreme Court ultimately rules with respect to commercial arbitration under the FAA, an even more compelling case exists to allow parties to a collective bargaining agreement containing a labor arbitration provision to alter thestandard of judicial review. This is, principally, because labor arbitration is fundamentally different from commercial arbitration.
In contrast to the FAA, Section 301 is phrased broadly and does not set forth any procedural or substantive requirements for labor arbitrations, including the vacatur of labor arbitration awards. The law of labor-management relations compels the employer and employees to bargain in good faith in an effort to reach a collective bargaining agreement. Also, in labor-management relations, the parties deal with one another in an ongoing relationship, which will continue to exist long after the dispute in question is resolved.
Arbitration is a substitute for private litigation in the commercial context, but it is a substitute for industrial strife in the labor context. Finally, the parties to a collective bargaining agreement containing a labor arbitration provision can change the agreement during a subsequent phase of collective bargaining negotiations.
Before discussing alteration of judicial review in labor arbitration, this Article must first examine the FAA and the conflicting case law on whether parties may alter the judicial review standard under that statute and whether labor arbitration should receive different treatment from the courts than that received by commercial arbitration.

papers.node_id: 64smulrev3!!ARTICLE: Alternative Dispute Resolution
papers.title: ARTICLE: Alternative Dispute Resolution
papers.abstract:
THIS is the first issue in the distinguished sixty-year history of the Annual Survey of Texas Law to include a chapter on Alternative Dispute Resolution ("ADR"). The wisdom of the editors will strike the growing population of "professional neutrals" across Texas as confirmation of the expanding influence of mediation, arbitration, collaboration, and other innovative alternatives to our civil justice system. Recognition of the trend in our society to look for more efficient, more practical, and more relevant processes to resolve disputes comes on the heels of celebration of the twentieth anniversary of passage of the Alternative Dispute Resolution Procedures Act("Act" or "ADR statute") by the Texas Legislature in 1987. The Act precipitated the growth of ADR in Texas and caused Texas to become a leader in the then nascent ADR movement in the United States.
This article will address developments during the Survey period in mediation and arbitration, and will briefly summarize the status of the movement to promote "collaborative law" in our civil jurisprudence.

questions.question: Whether mediation and arbitration have recently expanded in use and influence within the state's civil justice system.
Whether collaborative law is gaining acceptance and being integrated into ordinary civil dispute resolution practice in the state.
Whether the growth of alternative dispute resolution methods has improved the efficiency, practicality, and perceived relevance of civil dispute resolution compared with traditional litigation.

papers.title: Article: Alternative Dispute Resolution
papers.abstract:
THIS is the first issue in the distinguished sixty-year history of the Annual Survey of Texas Law to include a chapter on Alternative Dispute Resolution ("ADR"). The wisdom of the editors will strike the growing population of "professional neutrals" across Texas as confirmation of the expanding influence of mediation, arbitration, collaboration, and other innovative alternatives to our civil justice system. Recognition of the trend in our society to look for more efficient, more practical, and more relevant processes to resolve disputes comes on the heels of celebration of the twentieth anniversary of passage of the Alternative Dispute Resolution Procedures Act("Act" or "ADR statute") by the Texas Legislature in 1987. The Act precipitated the growth of ADR in Texas and caused Texas to become a leader in the then nascent ADR movement in the United States.
This article will address developments during the Survey period in mediation and arbitration, and will briefly summarize the status of the movement to promote "collaborative law" in our civil jurisprudence.

questions.question: How have mediation and arbitration practices changed in the jurisdiction during the recent survey period, and what effects have those changes had on the operation, efficiency, and influence of the civil justice system?

To what extent is collaborative law being adopted as an alternative to traditional litigation, and how does its promotion affect dispute resolution outcomes (for example, accessibility, cost, and the roles of legal professionals)?

papers.node_id: 38hastingslj239!!ARTICLE: Alternative Dispute Resolution and the Public Interest: The Arbitration Experience.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Alternative Dispute Resolution and the Public Interest: The Arbitration Experience.
papers.abstract: In recent years, the legal profession has become increasingly enchanted with nonjudicial dispute resolution mechanisms: negotiation, conciliation, mediation, fact-finding, mini-trials, settlement, rent-a-judge, and arbitration, among others.Although most, if not all, of these devices have been with us for a long time, they have recently been applied in innovative ways to new types of cases and have generated widespread enthusiasm among lawyers, judges, legislators, and members of the general public.  The enthusiasm is not universally shared, however.  Professor Owen Fiss of the Yale University School of Law is a major critic of the alternative dispute resolution (ADR) movement.  Although the principal target of his 1984 article,Against Settlement,is, as its title suggests, settlement itself, the article also decries, albeit less explicitly, all processes that assist, induce, or compel parties to avoid judicial resolution of their legal disputes.  Indeed, Professor Fiss appears to treat settlement and ADR as roughly equivalent, or at least intimately related, concepts.

questions.question: Whether the increased use of alternative dispute resolution, especially arbitration, advances or undermines the public interest (for example, effects on transparency, accountability, and development of public norms).

Whether settlement-oriented ADR operates as a meaningful substitute for judicial resolution-i.e., whether ADR displaces court adjudication and what public-policy consequences flow from that displacement.

papers.node_id: 11cardozojconflictresol437!!ARTICLE: ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION IN REAL ESTATE MATTERS: THE NEW YORK EXPERIENCE*
papers.title: ARTICLE: ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION IN REAL ESTATE MATTERS: THE NEW YORK EXPERIENCE*
papers.abstract:
New York continues to experience an ever-increasing number of real estate disputes. In 2009, the New York State courts' caseload was approximately 4.7 million, the highest tally in the state's history.Contributing to the caseload was a 17% increase in statewide home foreclosure filings in 2009, part of an 84% increase in filings over the previous four years.
The increasing number of cases, in New York and all across the country, has led to a growing trend toward resolving disputes using alternative dispute resolution ("ADR"). States across the nation are enacting laws that require parties to attempt mediation before litigating over foreclosures. The 2008 New York State budget included twenty-five million dollars to provide services to homeowners who entered into a subprime or unconventional mortgage.Administered through the New York State Housing Trust Fund Corporation, the program has awarded sixty-four grants through February 2009. The grants include foreclosure-prevention,counseling, and mediation services in New York's sixty-two counties.
ADR is a technique to settle disputes outside a courtroom. There are a number of ways to use ADR in real estate cases. Anyone who has leased or purchased real estate can appreciate the potential for disputes and understand the need for parties to be protected against costly and time-consuming litigation. Real estate cases include residential and commercial landlord-and-tenant disputes, conflicts between cooperative boards and shareholders, and problems involving construction, leasing, subleasing, sales, broker-client relationships, broker-agent relationships, appraisals, foreclosures, property-management issues, real estate partnerships and other associations. When a dispute arises, commercial and not-for-profit ADR institutions can administer real estate related mediations and arbitrations on a regular and quick basis. The court system relies on those institutions to oversee court-ordered and court-promoted ADR. Some states, like New York, offer court-administered ADR if the dispute is appropriate, the parties agree (or, in some cases, whether or not the parties agree), and volunteer mediators and arbitrators are available. In New York, court-promoted ADR includes pilot programs like the New York City Civil Court mediation programs and the Supreme Court mortgage-foreclosure program.
This article is intended to provide an overview of the available ADR options in New York for individuals and those in the real estate industry and the advantages and disadvantages as compared to litigation. The first section examines the different forms of ADR available to the real estate consumer. The second notes the general advantages and disadvantages of these ADR processes. The third looks at the particular advantages of ADR in real estate cases. The fourth presents an overview of different ADR programs promoted in New York to resolve real estate disputes.
With no end in sight for the housing crisis and the overburdened courts' dockets, ADR provides an efficient, cost-effective method, not only to relieve the courts' dockets, but also to promote compromise between, and bring peace to, the parties.

questions.question: Whether using alternative dispute resolution (mediation, arbitration, and similar processes) reduces court caseloads, time to resolution, and costs for real estate disputes compared with traditional litigation.

Whether and in what ways alternative dispute resolution produces different outcomes - for example settlement rates, party satisfaction, perceived fairness, and enforceability - than litigation for parties in real estate conflicts.
How effective court-promoted and community ADR programs are at preventing foreclosures and resolving housing-related disputes during a housing or mortgage crisis.

papers.abstract:
WHEN parties need to resolve a dispute, they may often turn not only to the state-sanctioned method of dispute resolution -- trial before a court -- but also to alternatives, notably, to arbitration, abbreviated trial procedures, or mediation. Although particular methods of alternative dispute resolution (which will be referred to collectively as ADR) vary from one another, they share the feature that a third party is involved who offers an opinion or communicates information about the dispute to the disputants.In addition, the formality, length, and complexity of ADR are usually less than those of official proceedings.
Interest in ADR has grown over the years, and today utilization of ADR is widespread. Moreover, ADR is increasingly encouraged by courts and legislation; in various areas of dispute, plaintiffs and defendants are requiredto use ADR before they are given recourse to trial.Alternative dispute resolution is now part of the law school curriculum; casebooks on ADR have been published; and journals devoted to it have been established.Indeed, the group of lawyers, arbitrators, academics, and jurists fostering ADR has taken on some of the aspects of a social movement.
Why, exactly, is ADR employed? What are its advantages to private parties and to society? Should ADR be subsidized, provided, or mandated by the state? In examining these questions in this article, I apply the economic approach in that I assume that parties take rational account of the effects of ADR on the likely disposition of their disputes, and for clarity I consider stylized models of parties' behavior.I make a basic distinction in the analysis between ex ante agreements to employ ADR -- arrangements made before disputes arise -- and ex post resort to ADR -- use of ADR after disputes have arisen.
Ex ante ADR agreements are treated in Section I of this article. Here, ADR may be adopted because it is to the mutual benefit of the parties to a contract or to those who have some other relationship with each other. Three reasons why ADR may be mutually beneficial are discussed. First, ADR may lower the cost of resolving disputes or risk. Second, ADR may engender superior incentives through greater accuracy of result or other characteristics. Suppose, for instance, that substandard performance of a contract would be correctly assessed by expert arbitrators under ADR but not by courts. Then the parties to the contract might well prefer to adopt ADR because it would induce good performance, thereby raising the willingness of the promisee to pay for the contract. Third, ADR may result in improved incentives to engage in disputes or to refrain from that. For example, it may be that the number of disputes brought under the legal process would be excessive, dissipating substantial resources of the parties without instigating mutually desirable changes in behavior;thus an ADR agreement that would serve to limit the number of disputes would be advantageous.
Such benefits of ex ante ADR agreements cannot generally be obtained by means of ex post agreements to use ADR. Where courts are not able to ascertain substandard performance and this occurs, the parties will hardly have any reason at that point to adopt ADR -- it will be too late to induce good performance. The advantages of ex ante ADR agreements, combined with the frequent inability to secure them through ex post ADR agreements, explain why parties will often want to make ex ante ADR agreements.
Because ex ante ADR agreements made by knowledgeable parties raise their well-being, the agreements raise social welfare (in the absence of external effects). Thus, it is suggested that ex ante ADR agreements should ordinarily be enforced by the legal system.At the same time, there is no general call for ex ante ADR to be subsidized or otherwise aided by the state.
Ex post ADR agreements are considered in Section II of this article. Parties will tend to make ex post ADR agreements when, after a dispute arises, ADR would produce mutual gains. This can come about in two major ways: through promotion of settlement, and through reduction of dispute resolution costs. To determine how ADR functions in these respects, I append ADR to the standard economic model of litigation. Specifically, I assume that a potential plaintiff decides whether to sue, and if so, he either goes immediately to trial, agrees to a settlement, or engages in binding or nonbinding ADR. Alternative dispute resolution is assumed to be cheaper than trial and possibly to convey information about what would occur at trial. Two ADR regimes are studied: where the use of ADR is voluntary, and where nonbinding ADR is required before there can be a trial.I compare outcomes in these regimes with that where ADR is unavailable.
The main descriptive conclusions are readily summarized. First, the tendency to bring suit is not affected by ADR where its use is voluntary. A person will bring suit in the model only if he has a credible threat to proceed thereafter. If ADR is voluntary, the defendant can always refuse to engage in ADR, so that the plaintiff must be willing to go to trial to have a credible threat, which is exactly his situation in the absence ofADR. When, however, nonbinding ADR is required before trial, the situation is altered. For example, since ADR is cheaper than trial, it may be that a party who would not be willing to go to trial would be willing to engage in nonbinding ADR and thus to bring suit. But it may also be that the tendency to sue would be decreased because, to go to trial, a party must incur ADR costs plus trial costs rather than just the latter.
Second, given that suit has been brought, the availability of ADR tends to reduce the frequency of both trial and of immediate settlement. Being a kind of substitute for trial and being cheaper than trial, parties may elect ADR rather than go to trial. Similarly, parties may elect ADR rather than settle since ADR constitutes an inexpensive form of legal combat; the costs of ADR are lower than those of trial and may not be high enough to discourage the parties from use of ADR. It will be seen in the analysis that these conclusions, along with those concerning the election of binding versus nonbinding ADR, depend significantly on how well ADR predicts trial outcomes.
Following the descriptive analysis of ex post ADR, I consider its private and social value. I observe that the private value of ex post ADR does not incorporate its incentive effects on parties' behavior; only ex ante ADR agreements reflect incentive effects. Consequently, it is not clear in principle that even voluntary ex post ADR agreements enhance individuals' welfare, and there is no apparent basis for the state's requiring nonbinding ADR before trial. (Indeed, such mandatory ADR can have the perverse effect of increasing the cost of litigation, by adding another layer to it, without promoting settlement.) This raises questions about the general wisdom of public policies requiring or otherwise furthering use of ADR.

questions.question: Whether ex ante agreements to use alternative dispute resolution (ADR) improve private and social welfare by lowering dispute-resolution costs and by creating better performance and dispute-avoidance incentives between contracting parties.

Whether ex post use of ADR - when voluntary or when required before trial - affects parties' decisions to initiate lawsuits, the probability of settlement versus trial, and overall litigation costs, and whether mandatory pre-trial ADR is socially beneficial.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: JUDGING-LITE: HOW ARBITRATORS USE AND CREATE PRECEDENT*

shared_topics.topic: informational role of ADR/arbitration in predicting trial outcomes and shaping settlement decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models ADR as a cheaper mechanism that can convey information about likely trial outcomes and thus alter the incidence of settlement and trial; Paper B empirically examines whether arbitrators' reasoned awards and citation practices supply precedent and legal signals that similarly inform parties about probable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering via arbitration as a substitute for public courts and its effect on the supply and development of precedent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how ex ante and ex post ADR agreements shift dispute resolution out of courts and considers the social-welfare implications of private resolution, while Paper B investigates whether arbitration produces usable precedent or instead diminishes the publicly available body of law when disputes leave the judicial system.

shared_topics.topic: policy questions about mandating ADR and the appropriate degree of judicial oversight or enforcement of arbitral processes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether ex ante ADR agreements should be enforced and questions mandates such as required nonbinding ADR before trial, and Paper B addresses the limited formal judicial review of awards and whether judges should treat arbitral decisions as persuasive precedent or otherwise engage with them.

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of ADR/arbitration on parties' behavior (performance, suit filing, and rights vindication)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models how ex ante ADR can create incentives for better performance and how ADR availability affects plaintiffs' decisions to sue or settle; Paper B explores whether arbitrators' use (or non-use) of precedent and possible institutional biases influence parties' incentives to pursue arbitration and the effectiveness of arbitration in vindicating statutory or contractual rights.

shared_topics.topic: effects of mandatory or pre‑dispute ADR/arbitration clauses on access to court and collective relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how ex ante mandates to arbitrate and class‑action bans shift disputes out of public courts and block collective actions, reducing claimant access and publicity; Paper B analyzes ex ante ADR agreements and mandatory (pre‑trial) ADR regimes, modeling how such requirements change the propensity to sue and the availability of trial as a backstop.

shared_topics.topic: costs and efficiency tradeoffs of ADR versus litigation and their impact on who can obtain relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper B treats lower cost as a principal economic rationale for ADR and models how cheaper ADR alters settlement and trial frequency, while Paper A emphasizes how filing fees, legal costs, and privatized ADR providers deter one‑shot or low‑resource litigants from pursuing claims, thereby shaping access to justice.

shared_topics.topic: incentive and distributional effects of ADR for repeat players versus one‑shot litigants
shared_topics.justification: Paper B discusses how ex ante ADR can create incentives (e.g., better performance via expert arbitrators) and how information from ADR affects dispute behavior, whereas Paper A theorizes and documents how repeat players leverage procedural design (including ADR) to structure favorable processes that disadvantage one‑shot litigants.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and legal treatment of ADR agreements and their systemic consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that ex ante ADR agreements typically should be enforced and studies the welfare implications of enforcing or mandating ADR, while Paper A examines judicial enforcement of arbitration and confidentiality clauses, class‑action waivers, and how courts and doctrine have reshaped dispute resolution by giving effect to private ADR arrangements.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when private ex ante ADR agreements should be enforced or can substitute for courts and whether the state should mandate or subsidize ADR; Paper B critiques reliance on self-deregulation and argues that market actors require public law enforcement to prevent abuse, engaging the same question of how much dispute resolution should be left to private mechanisms versus the state.

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of dispute‑resolution and regulatory regimes on parties' behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how ex ante ADR can create performance incentives (and how ex post ADR lacks those effects), while Paper B contends that deregulatory policies create perverse incentives for corporate misconduct (e.g., Enron), with both papers focusing on how institutional design shapes actors' incentives.

shared_topics.topic: normative assessment of mandatory versus voluntary dispute‑resolution or deregulation policies

shared_topics.topic: how institutional design affects the incidence and social cost of disputes or market misconduct

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IS THERE A FLIGHT FROM ARBITRATION?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides a formal economic account of why parties adopt ADR ex ante or ex post—emphasizing cost reduction, improved accuracy, and incentive effects—while Paper B empirically investigates why franchisors and franchisees do or do not use arbitration clauses, showing how cost, perceived fairness, and appealability shape those choices.

shared_topics.topic: how ADR/arbitration affects litigation behavior (filings, settlements, trial frequency)

papers.node_id: 81denvulrev597!!ARTICLE: Alternative Dispute Resolution: The Federal Arbitration Act and Resolving Disputes in Arbitration Versus a Court Proceeding
papers.title: ARTICLE: Alternative Dispute Resolution: The Federal Arbitration Act and Resolving Disputes in Arbitration Versus a Court Proceeding
papers.abstract:
Almost everyone enters into an agreement to arbitrate, whether aware of it or not. Arbitration clauses are now the standard method for resolving disputes in many consumer contracts, such as insurance, medical, and broker contracts. Standard arbitration agreements pose the quintessential question: when a dispute arises, and a person's competency to enter into the contract as a whole is challenged, is the arbitration agreement embedded within the contract enforceable?
With the passage of the Federal Arbitration Act ("FAA" or "Act") in 1925,along with the federal government's power and authority to enforce the FAA, comes an emergent issue of determining when arbitration, rather than a court proceeding, must be used to resolve a dispute.Due to arbitration provisions becoming more common in consumer contracts, many contract disputes, and accordingly many court opinions, will be based on the enforceability of arbitration agreements in years to come.In fact, conflicting court decisions resolving arbitration agreements have been abundant since the enactment of the Act, and courts are still trying to reach a consistent pattern of uniformity to enforce arbitration provisions.
The FAA establishes in Title 9 of the United States Code, Section 2, that "a written provision in any maritime transaction or a contract evidencing a transaction involving commerce to settle by arbitration a controversy thereafter arising . . . shall be valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract."Additionally, Section 4 states that if a contract with an arbitration provision has been entered into, and the "making" of the arbitration agreement is not at issue, the court shall order the parties to proceed to arbitration.Thus, many issues arise when an arbitration provision is placed in a contract because the agreement to arbitrate is made "valid, irrevocable, and enforceable," by federal statute, which can only become unenforceable under the same theories as a contract may become unenforceable under contract law.Since the adoption of the FAA, arbitration agreements are increasingly used in resolving disputes that arise out of the contract as a whole, which undoubtedly favors businesses over consumers.
This survey paperexplores the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals opinion in Spahr v. Secco,where the court decided that a mental capacity claim challenging the validity of a contract containing an arbitration agreement should be resolved in a court proceeding instead of arbitration.Prior to Spahr, the Tenth Circuit had not addressed this issue.Other circuits, however, have decided cases similar to Spahr.Although the outcome in Spahr is different from the outcome other circuits reached in similar cases,the holding in Spahr is likely to have important implications on future court decisions because Spahr readily provides a logical, fair, and rational method of evaluating the enforceability of arbitration agreements.
If Spahr is appealed to the United States Supreme Court, however, the Tenth Circuit's holding in Spahr may be reversed because the Supreme Court will likely want to maintain uniformity in court decisions pursuant to the Prima Paint rationale.In contrast, if the Court can findsufficient public policy reasons to support Spahr,the Court may alter their Prima Paint decision and create a new standard for arbitration agreements that combine the Prima Paint and Spahr rationales. Should this occur, arbitration will undergo a change for the better because the decision in Spahr adds a logical and fair method of interpreting the FAA that gives arbitration agreements their intended effect.Thus, combining the Prima Paint and Spahr rationale will provide an enhanced method of evaluating arbitration agreements that is both rational and maintains the national legislative goals of favoring arbitration.
Part I of this survey examines the background of the FAA by looking at its history and formation, as well as relevant FAA provisions. Part II of this survey analyzes the Tenth Circuit's recent decision in Spahr v. U.S. Bancorp Investments, Inc., where the Tenth Circuit held the arbitration provision unenforceable. Part III of this survey examines other recent circuit court rulings in similar arbitration cases. Finally, this paper takes the position that Spahr properly held a mental capacity challenge to a contract containing an arbitration agreement goes to the "making" of the arbitration agreement, and thus should be determined in a court proceeding.

papers.title: ARTICLE: AN ANALYSIS OF HOME WARRANTY CONTRACTS
papers.abstract:
The question of whether a home warrantycontract is a wise financial decision for the typical homeowner is a debatable one in the realm of personal finance.With a general rise in housing prices and the housing market in the United States the past couple of years,the sale of home warranties reportedly rose eight percent from 2014 to 2015.Despite the reported rise in the number of issued home warranty contracts in the United States, home warranty companies have been subject to complaintsand many home warranty contractsoften include exclusions.
An unexplored area of the literature concerning home warranty contracts is an analysis of the types of contractual provisions that are actually found in home warranty contracts. This article comprehensively examines the contractual provisions of the standard contracts of seventeen different home warranty companies to compare and contrast contractual provisions.As discussed in Part II, almost all of the standard contracts limit home warranty coverage to residential property only, and a number of the contracts not only exclude commercial property, but property utilized in situations such as day care facilities and the homes of fraternities and sororities. Part III discusses the typical coverage grants - in most cases, the standard coverage included within a home warranty contract is an air conditioning system, heating system, electrical system, and often included kitchen appliances. Many home warranty contracts also include additional coverage options which can be purchased outside of the standard contract price, such as pools, spas, and septic tanks.
Part IV examines the common exclusions and limitation of liability provisions found in standard home warranty contracts. Home warranty contracts commonly include a provision stating that the home warranty company has the sole right to determine whether a covered item will be repaired, replaced, or whether a cash settlement will be offered in lieu of repair or replacement.Home warranty contracts also often include a provision excluding primary coverage or coverage altogether in the event there is coverage for the covered item under an existing warranty or contract.In addition, home warranty agreements often include exclusions for hazardous substances, force majeure events, acts of nature, and other occurrences as well as an overall monetary limitation per contract period.
Part V of this article analyzes the various waiver of damages provisions found in almost all home warranty contracts. Generally, home warranty contracts often include a waiver of tort, and a waiver of special, punitive and consequential damages.A number of home warranty contracts also contain class action waiver provisions, class arbitration waiver provisions, arbitration clauses, choice of law clauses, and/or choice of forum clauses.Finally, Part VI of this article examines several other miscellaneous provisions which have appeared in various home warranty contracts.

questions.question: What types of coverage, optional add-ons, and explicit exclusions are typically included in standard home warranty contracts?

Whether and how standard home warranty contracts limit the seller's liability and consumers' monetary recovery (for example through caps on payouts, company control over repair vs. cash settlement, or waivers of certain categories of damages)?

Whether and how standard home warranty contracts restrict consumers' access to dispute resolution and remedies (for example by imposing individual arbitration, class-action waivers, or choice-of-law/forum provisions)?
