papers.title: ARTICLE: MASS ARBITRATION AND DEMOCRATIC LEGITIMACY
papers.abstract:
In 1902, in The Kensington,the United States Supreme Court invalidated a liability disclaimer on a steamship ticket.Although the defendant had destroyed the passengers' luggage, it argued that the "small but legible type" on the ticket limited its legal responsibility to 250 francs.The Court disagreed. For one, the Court noted that the defendant did not call this "exceptional stipulation[]" to the plaintiffs' attention.Moreover, the Court reasoned that the plaintiffs' lack of consent was apparent from the provision itself, which was so "unjust" that it would "be deemed as wanting in the element of voluntary assent."Three years later, the same Justices would constitutionalize freedom of contract in Lochner v. New Yorkwhen they held that a state law capping bakers' work hours violated the doctrine of economic substantive due process.However, the laissez-faire zealotry that animated Lochner did not extend to self-serving, pre-printed forms. In fact, the Court in The Kensington took pains to avoid calling the text on the ticket a "contract."
This chasm between standard forms and bargained-for deals persisted as the decades passed. By the middle of thetwentieth century, there was burgeoning consensus that adhesion "contract" was an oxymoron: non-negotiable fine print did not reflect the parties' agreement in any meaningful sense.In an influential article, Arthur Allen Leff argued that the paperwork spawned by consumer transactions was as much a "thing" as the underlying goods, and thus deserved the same pervasive regulation.Other scholars and judges saw a deeper problem. In their eyes, mass contracting, which bound numerous adherents in lockstep, was "the exercise of unofficial government."David Slawson drew upon administrative law to argue that standard form terms - like rules promulgated by unelected bureaucrats - were democratically illegitimate.Cases like Henningsen v. Bloomfield Motors, Inc.sounded similar concerns and subjected adhesion contracts to searching oversight.And in 1975, the Iowa Supreme Court opined that enforcing a draconian clause in an insurance policy might be unconstitutional:
The concept that persons must obey public laws enacted by their own representatives does not offend a fundamental sense of justice: an inherent element of assent pervades the process. But the inevitable result of enforcing all provisions of the adhesion contract … would be an abdication of judicial responsibility in face of basic unfairness and a recognition that persons' rights shall be controlled by private lawmakers without the consent, express or implied, of those affected.
But then the pendulum swung violently in the other direction. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, voices in thenascent field of law and economics challenged the idea that one-sided, adhesive provisions are "unfair."Reversing the polarity of Leff's "contract as thing" analogy, these commentators argued that "harsh" clauses are no different than low-quality goods: they may be less favorable to adherents, but they are also less expensive.Because drafters in competitive markets must disgorge their savings through lower prices and higher wages, it is entirely possible that most consumers and employees would actually prefer onerous but cheaper terms.In addition, these scholars argued that drafters must cater to adherents' interests, even if most adherents ignore the fine print. So long as some adherents compare rival forms, drafters - who cannot distinguish these elite "shoppers" from the uninformed masses - must offer everyone the same ideal terms.
This sunny view of adhesion contracts sparked the "contract procedure" revolution.In 1991, the Court held that a forum-selection clause benefited not just the cruise line that had drafted it (by limiting its litigation costs), but passengers (who paid "reduced fares").Citing similar rhetoric, the Court expanded the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA),summarily rejecting any claim that adhesive arbitration provisions are non-consensual.Lower courts enforced arbitration clausesthat drafters had placed at the bottom of their shipping boxesor inserted in their customers' monthly bills.Banks, credit card issuers, retailers, franchisors, software licensors, computer manufacturers, communications companies, technology startups, brokerages, gyms, hospitals, and nursing homes began to lace their standard forms with dispute resolution provisions.Instead of expressly stripping adherents of substantive rights, these companies tried to achieve that goal indirectly by rewriting procedural rules.
The stakes in this debate have only risen in the last two years as the Court has decided a series of controversial cases about the intersection of arbitration and class actions.In sharp contrast to The Kensington's disapproval of liability-limiting fine print, the Court recently held in AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcionthat judges must enforce adhesive class arbitration waivers - denying consumers the ability to band together in a class action - even if small-value consumer protection claims will "slip through the legal system."Then, in June 2013, the Court took this approach to the next step in American Express Co. v. Italian Colors Restaurant (Amex),requiring plaintiffs to arbitrate federal antitrust claims on a bilateral basis even though the cost of doing so would eclipse any individual plaintiff's potential recovery.More than ever, the Court seems steeled against the argument that form contracts are non-consensual. Indeed, as Justice Scalia casually observed in Concepcion, "the times in which consumer contracts were anything other than adhesive are long past."
Against this backdrop, Margaret Jane Radin's Boilerplate is a welcome attempt to rekindle radical skepticism of masscontracting.Radin organizes her dense and sprawling masterpiece around two central claims. First, she argues that the widespread use of standard forms causes "normative degradation" - the erosion of contract law's bedrock requirement of consent. Second, and more provocatively, she echoes leftist courts and scholars from the 1970s and argues that the lockstep use of standard forms permits private actors to override the public laws and thus causes "democratic degradation." To cure these maladies, she outlines a novel legal standard that links the validity of fine print to: (1) the quality of the adherent's assent, (2) the nature of the rights affected, and (3) the provision's frequency of use (pp. 155-58).
In this book review, I argue that the pervasiveness of arbitration clauses in consumer and employment contracts vividly illustrates the wear on democratic ideals that Radin describes. To be sure, accusations of democratic illegitimacy are usually the province of public law, where federal judges invalidate and interpret legislation, and bureaucrats enjoy broad discretion to add their own gloss to statutes.But the core objection to these practices - that they permit unelected officials to rewrite the legislative blueprint- has a shadowy analogue in mass arbitration. Companies invoke the FAA to alter procedural rules on a massive scale.The issue of whether adhesive arbitration provisions are consensual is hotly contested. Yet, no matter one's view of fine print generally, the Court's separability doctrine - a legal fiction that allows arbitrators to decide the very question of whether an arbitration clause is valid - drives a wedge between arbitration and contractual consent.Finally, after years of denying that arbitration affects substantive rights, the Court is now shunting plaintiffs to an extrajudicial forum even when there is no dispute that doing so will deprive them of any remedy. Thus, through the expedient of printed or electronic words, corporations do precisely what Radin says: they "delete rights that are granted through democratic processes" (p. 16).
A few qualifications are in order. First, Boilerplate is aboutadhesion contracts generally, not just arbitration. Radin discusses a rogue's gallery of terms, from warranty disclaimers to exculpatory clauses to end-user license agreements. Also, one of her oeuvre's greatest strengths is its breadth. Radin displays her fluency in economics, philosophy, political science, and psychology, and discusses the role of advocates, agencies, disclosure, international law, emerging technology, and non-governmental organizations. Yet a veritable contracts All-Star team has already canvassed these aspects of Boilerplate in book reviews,symposia,and blog posts.Thus, I will leave these issues for others. In addition, I am interested in the uneasy relationship between mass arbitration and democratic governance because I have struggled with it in previous articles.And narrowing my focus stays true to the heart of Radin's work. Boilerplate mirrors the larger debate over form contracts in the way that it is pulled back, again and again, to the thorny entanglement of fine print and procedural rules.
,acknowledge that arbitration jurisprudence may seem like particularly inhospitable terrain for Radin's democratic degradation thesis. After all, the FAA is a federalstatute designed to foster arbitration.How is it undemocratic for businesses to accept Congress's invitation and funnel disputes outside of the court system?The answer is that the FAA's current musculature is a product of the Court, not Congress. In 1925, lawmakers passed a procedural rule for federal courts that placed arbitration agreements "upon the same footing as other contracts" by making them specifically enforceable.Today, the statute governs in state court,preempts state law,extends to the outer limits of the Commerce power,applies to employment contractsand federal statutory claims,deems arbitration clauses to be separable from the agreements in which they are embedded,overrides class action rights,and fills contractual gaps with pro-business default rules.Although a few of these developments have flickers of support in the FAA's text and legislative history,nobody seriously contends that the Court has been faithfully divining Congress's wishes.Indeed, even sitting Justices have voted to expand the FAA while conceding that they were "abandoning all pretense of ascertaining congressional intent" and "building instead, case by case, an edifice of [our] own creation."Thus, the modern FAA - the one that has transformed the arbitration clause into a kind of covenant that runs with economic activity - lacks an authentic democratic pedigree.
This book review contains two Parts. Part I summarizes Boilerplate and explains why it is essential reading for anyone interested in contract law's intractable problem. Part II takesthe torch from Radin and uses the FAA as a case study in democratic degradation. Focusing on Concepcion and its recently-decided sister case, Amex, it shows how the FAA allows private parties to amend the public laws.

papers.node_id: 6jempiricallegalstud768!!ARTICLE: Measuring the Value of Class and Collective Action Employment Settlements: A Preliminary Assessment
papers.title: ARTICLE: Measuring the Value of Class and Collective Action Employment Settlements: A Preliminary Assessment
papers.abstract:
There has been an ongoing debate in the literature on the relative merits of arbitration, individual litigation, and class action litigation in providing adequate remedies for disputes arising out of the employment relationship. For the last decade and a half, the debate centered on whether arbitration provides a fair forum for plaintiffs, despite the relativeinformality of the process, the employer's ability to tailor procedures, and the claimed propensity of arbitrators to curry the favor of repeat-player employers. The empirical literature to date has not borne out these criticisms. Almost without exception, the studies find that employment arbitration is quicker, less costly, and results in a win-loss rate that is no different than in litigation. Median awards are somewhat lower (perhaps due to the fact that low-value claims are more likely to proceed to hearing in the more informal process of arbitration).
With the introduction by employers of express provisions in employment arbitration agreements purportedly barring class action claims,the debate has shifted to the relative merits of individual arbitration versus class action litigation or class-wide arbitration of employment claims. Proponents of class action litigation make two empirical arguments for the superiority of their preferred mode of dispute resolution over individual arbitration. First, it is maintained, class actions or class-wide arbitration are likely to do a better job of providing compensation for claimants (and thus deterring employer wrongdoing) because by aggregating claims in a single proceeding, the employer will not be able to benefit from the costs to claimants as a group of delay and relitigating underlying liability in individual proceedings. Second, it is further argued, class actions provide the only practicable vehicle for obtaining redress of certain low-value claims, which, if required to be asserted on an individual basis, would never be championed, thus allowing the employer to escape with impunity. Thus, plaintiffs' advocates argue, with some support in the courts,that there should be a nearly blanket rule banning agreements precluding class action treatment for certain types of employment claims.
Unfortunately, very little empirical work has been done to test either of these propositions. We begin in this article the process of bringing some facts to light on potential recoveries in employment class actions. This is intended as a preliminary assessment, to stimulate further research.
For this study, we assembled a data set of major employment settlements reached since 1993. (The number of settlements per year in our sample is depicted in Table 1.) Employment claims include those arising under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII), the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA) and other federal and state anti-discrimination laws, the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) and similar state wage-hour laws, and the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA).
Our essential finding is that, contrary to assumptions of some academic commentators and courts, mean individual potential recoveries and (with the exception of certain ERISA and state/federal off-the-clock claims) median potential individual recoveries are not negative-value amounts. One therefore cannot assume as a prima facie matter that such claims would not be pursued by individual employees, whether in arbitration or litigation. Much, of course, depends on institutional design--the costs of access to the forum, the delay factor, and whether attorney representation is required. Class treatment arguably reduces access costs and provides a mechanism for funding legal counsel but does so in a manner that, through aggregation of claims, may reduce the value of individual claims and entail a considerable loss of party autonomy. We hope to provoke additional empirical research on whether class actions do a better job at providing compensation, both as to amount (net of costs) and time from claim to recovery, than individual arbitration, and whether any such difference outweighs the loss of party autonomy inherent in class adjudication.

Are expected individual recoveries from employment claims large enough that claimants would pursue them individually absent class aggregation (i.e., are many claims economically infeasible to bring individually)?

papers.title: ARTICLE: MISGUIDED FAIRNESS? REGULATING ARBITRATION BY STATUTE: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE OF DECLINING AWARD FINALITY
papers.abstract:
A. Overview: Historical and Structural Flawsin the Federal Arbitration Act
Congress created a policy that favors arbitration by enacting the U.S. Arbitration Act (USAA), now called the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA).FAA proponents convinced Congress that the law was needed to end judicial hostility to arbitration.This view was exaggerated,grounded in two English precedents from the 1700sthat some American courts followed.English and American courts were not hardened opponents to arbitration. Many rulings preserved the autonomy of arbitration.
When lawmakers passed the FAA in 1925, they never learned that an English statute of 1697 authorized judicial enforcement of arbitration awards.Congress did not appreciate that as early as the 1600s, English sentiment favored arbitration because court litigation wasted time and money.Lawmakers overlooked Lord Mansfield's pivotal use of his court's authority in the 1700s to foster commercial arbitration.
These oversights would be academic but for the fact that Congress patterned the FAA after New York's arbitration law,and NewYork based its legislation on English law.Somehow, Congress lost perspective of the American replication of English law. Amusingly, FAA sponsors acted as though they pioneered protection of arbitration from intrusive court review.
If the FAA was founded on historically faulty grounds - specifically, if the judicial hostility thesis was flawed eighty years ago - why does this problem matter today? Ironically, the FAA retarded the development of common law standards that were deferential to arbitration. Paradoxically, the FAA set into motion current state legislation that is leading to much greater vacatur of arbitration awards.
For this Article, I collected and analyzed employment arbitrations that were challenged by a losing party. My database contains 426 federal and state court rulings from 1975-2007 that confirmed or vacated awards. These courts acquired jurisdiction of arbitrator rulings because the FAA oddly allows parties to choose a federal or state forum, including the respective reviewing standards.Magnifying this anomaly, the FAA sets forth specific and narrow standards for federal court review of contested awards,but allows states to enact their own judicial review standards.For many years, state arbitration laws mirrored the FAA. In a key finding, however, my research shows that this parallelism is breaking down.
This is because states are enacting more intrusive reviewing standards.My data suggest that the Revised Uniform Arbitration Act (RUAA),a model law that expert commissioners drafted in 2000, plays a role in this development. The RUAA was largely motivated by disturbing trends in the 1990s that raised questions about the fairness of arbitration. The growing use of mandatory arbitration fueled this concern.In the workplace, employers implemented arbitration procedures to enhance their advantage over individuals. They shifted large forum costs to employees,designated inconvenient venues,placed arbitrary remedial limits on arbitrator powers,shortened time bars to file claims,and selected arbitrators without employee input.RUAA Commissioners stated in their prefatory note that their "new provisions are intended to reflect developments in arbitration law and to insure that the process is a fair one."
My research does not assess whether post-RUAA arbitrations are more fair, but my statistical analysis shows a pernicious trend for arbitral finality - a finding that would surprise and chagrin the FAA Congress. Recall that lawmakers wanted minimal court interference with arbitration. My data from federal courts would reassure them. District judges confirmed 92.7% of these arbitrator decisions.But state trial judges confirmed only 78.8% of awards.This difference is statistically significant. The analysis for appellate courts produced a similar result - an 87.7% confirmation rate at the federal level, but only a 71.4% level for state courts.
These results raise serious concerns because (a) there is now a measurable degree of judicial hostility to arbitration in state courts, (b) federal and state courts do not provide uniform or even similar results, (c) the FAA may be contributing to forum shopping for the enforcement of arbitration awards, and (d) the increased level of judicial reversal of arbitration awards portends more time-consuming and expensive litigation - and relitigation - of disputes, notwithstanding an underlying agreement by parties to resolve disputes with a final and binding award.
conclude that these worrisome trends and possibilities are structurally rooted in the history and text of the FAA. Left alone, courts can be more trusted than state legislatures to preserve the finality of the arbitration process. But courts are increasingly subservient to state arbitration statutes that elevate arbitral fairness over finality. In the short term, higher rates of vacatur may mollify critics and skeptics who call attention to particularly unfair arbitration practices.But Isuggest that the trend line for vacatur implies serious costs for disputing parties. More arbitration proceedings are becoming lengthy and costly preludes to final disposition by courts. This implies that long queues at American courts will grow as parties lose confidence in arbitral finality.

papers.abstract:
Several recent cases have narrowed the grounds for judicial review of arbitration awards by removing the doctrine of manifest disregard as a possible ground for vacatur.In the aftermath of these decisions, authorities are divided over the effect that these rulings will have on the efficacy of the arbitration process and the incentives that they will provide to parties considering arbitration as a possible method of dispute resolution. Both academics and practitioners have suggested that these developments will cause companies to review and possibly change their contractual arbitration agreements,but why and how? InHall Street Associates, L.L.C. v. Mattel, Inc., the Supreme Court noted that amici for each of the opposing parties came to differing conclusions on this issue: one claimed that parties willflee from arbitration without the option of expanded review, while the other asserted that parties avoid arbitration because of expanded review.Both practitioners and academics seem to think that the recent developments will cause firms to avoid arbitration because of the high risk of proceeding without the safety net of judicial review;however, it has also been suggested that the existence of manifest disregard as a ground for judicial review will "discourage the selection of the United States as an arbitral situs" in an international arbitration situation, thereby suggesting that expanded review is unattractive to parties.
As a result of this divide, this Note explores the possible effects of the elimination of manifest disregard onex antedecision making of the contracting parties and of the market as a whole. This Note begins in Part II by providing a brief history of judicial review, vacatur, and modification of arbitration rulings. Next, Part III contains an analysis of common factors that influence a party's decision when deciding whether to arbitrate in light of the courts' new, more narrow grounds for review. Finally, Part IV concludes that the mixed effects resulting from the abrogation of manifest disregard will cause minimal change in the practices of individuals and have even less effect over the market as a whole.

papers.node_id: 62sclrev407!!ARTICLE: Much Ado About Nothing: The Future of Manifest Disregard After Hall Street
papers.title: ARTICLE: Much Ado About Nothing: The Future of Manifest Disregard After Hall Street
papers.authors: Mylinda K. Sims; Richard A. Bales
papers.abstract:
Human errors can have significant effects. Take, for example, game two of the 2009 American League Division Series between the Minnesota Twins andthe New York Yankees.Umpire Phil Cuzzi called "a fly ball [hit] down the left-field line" as foul.However, the ball hit off the fielder's glove, landed fair, and then "bounced into the stands for what should have been a ground-rule double."The press labeled Cuzzi's call "[a] truly awful call that might have cost the Twins a victory on the road in their series with the Yankees."Decisions such as this have fueled a debate regarding instant replay in Major League Baseball.
While individuals press for expanded review on the baseball diamond in the major leagues,the arbitration community also wrestles with the issue of expanded review. In particular the arbitration community struggles with whether the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) contains exclusive standards of review or if nonstatutory standards remain viable after the Supreme Court's 2008 decision in Hall Street Associates v. Mattel, Inc.
Section 10 of the FAA contains a list of bases on which a court can vacate an arbitrational award.Lower courts have long stated but seldom have held that these bases are nonexclusive.Courts have found that they may vacate an award on nonstatutory grounds in narrow circumstances, such as manifest disregard of the law.In Hall Street, the Supreme Court created doubt as to whether nonstatutory standards are still applicable when it stated that the grounds for vacatur are "exclusive" to those stated in the FAA.Some courts have interpreted this language to eliminate all nonstatutory grounds for vacatur.In contrast, other courts have interpreted it merely to limit the use of nonstatutory grounds.Thus, the circuit courts are split as to whether nonstatutory standards of review such as manifest disregard of the law survive the Supreme Court's decision in Hall Street.
This Article argues that the FAA standards are not exclusive, and that while the standard of manifest disregard of the law survives, it should be replaced withthe standard of manifest disregard of the agreement. Under the doctrine of manifest disregard of the agreement, a court may vacate an arbitration award only if the award fails to "draw[] its essence" from the construction of the contract.By contrast, under manifest disregard of the law, a court may base vacatur on an arbitrator's acknowledgment and disregard of a legal principle.Part II.A will provide an overview of arbitration and of the standards of review established through the FAA and the judicially-created nonstatutory grounds for review. Part II.B will discuss the doctrine of manifest disregard of the law. Part II.C will discuss the doctrine of manifest disregard of the agreement. Part III will provide an overview of the United States Supreme Court decision in Hall Street regarding the doctrine of manifest disregard of the law and recent Supreme Court developments. Part IV will provide an overview of the circuit court split resulting after Hall Street. Part V.A will discuss whether manifest disregard of the law survives Hall Street and will present possible solutions to resolve the circuit split. Part V.B will propose an exchange of manifest disregard of the law for manifest disregard of the agreement.

papers.node_id: 70rutgersulrev401!!ARTICLE: Murphy Oil and Norris LaGuardia to the Rescue: Preserving Employee Rights to Concerted Dispute Resolution in an Era of Mandatory Individual Arbitration
papers.title: ARTICLE: Murphy Oil and Norris LaGuardia to the Rescue: Preserving Employee Rights to Concerted Dispute Resolution in an Era of Mandatory Individual Arbitration
papers.authors: Timothy P. Glynn; Charles A. Sullivan
papers.abstract:
In 2012, the National Labor Relations Board (the NLRB or "Board") held in In re D.R. Horton, Inc.,that employers may not compel employees to sign mandatory arbitration agreements waiving their National Labor Relations Act (NLRA)right to concerted pursuit of legal redress of employment claims.It did not strike down arbitration as such; rather, it mandated that any agreements required of covered workers leave open an avenue for collective pursuit of claims, either in arbitration or through the court system.The Board noted, but did not stress, that a similar result would follow under the Norris LaGuardia Act.In 2013, we weighed in on the issue in an article in the Alabama Law Review,arguing essentially that, under either statute, arbitration clauses prohibiting employees from all avenues for collective pursuit of legal relief - whether in court or in arbitration - were unenforceable.
Neither the Board nor we had much success initially, with the Fifth Circuit's rejection of the argument in its review of Horton, whichcontained a dismissive footnote about our efforts.And, for the most part, other federal courts refused to follow Horton as well.
But the Board persevered, reiterating and elucidating its position in Murphy Oil USA, Inc.And although the Board's position in Murphy Oil was again rejected by the Fifth Circuit,two circuits recently rode to the rescue: the Ninth in Morris v. Ernst & Young, LLP,and thein Lewis v. Epic Systems Corp.The resultant circuit split led to the Supreme Court's grant of certiorari in all three cases, which are slated to be heard this upcoming Term. Since the Court granted review, the Sixth Circuit has joined the Ninth and Seventh Circuits in agreement with the Board's position in Murphy Oil.
The final resolution of this question will turn on two principal propositions from the Board's decisions in Horton and Murphy Oil. The first is that employees' rights to engage in concerted activity for mutual activity guaranteed in Section 7 of the NLRA and its precursor Section 2 of the Norris-LaGuardia Actinclude the right to concerted legal redress, whether through the judicial process or arbitration.The second is that nothing in the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)changes this result. Because almost nothing has happened since we published our article that calls the first proposition into question, we can disposeof it fairly quickly here. We will delve more deeply into the second point, since it has proven more contested, and the dispositive role of the Norris-LaGuardia Act has, until now, been underappreciated.

questions.question: Whether workers' rights to engage in concerted activity include a protected right to pursue employment-related legal claims collectively (either in court or in arbitration).

Whether the policy and law favoring enforcement of arbitration agreements prevents or preempts those concerted-activity protections, making mandatory individual-only arbitration clauses barring collective legal redress enforceable.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83notredamelrev551!!ARTICLE: MISGUIDED FAIRNESS? REGULATING ARBITRATION BY STATUTE: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE OF DECLINING AWARD FINALITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: MISGUIDED FAIRNESS? REGULATING ARBITRATION BY STATUTE: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE OF DECLINING AWARD FINALITY

shared_topics.topic: whether and how the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) yields to or preempts other legal protections (NLRA, Norris–LaGuardia, and state arbitration statutes)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A litigates and theorizes that statutory labor protections (Section 7 of the NLRA and the Norris–LaGuardia Act) preserve employees' right to concerted legal redress and that the FAA should not nullify those rights; Paper B analyzes the FAA's historical text and structure and shows how its interaction with state arbitration laws (and model reforms like the RUAA) produces divergent legal outcomes, raising the same question of the FAA's limits and interaction with other statutes.

shared_topics.topic: the legality and practical effects of mandatory employment arbitration clauses that bar collective/class or concerted proceedings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on NLRB decisions and circuit splits about whether employers can require arbitration clauses that prohibit collective pursuit of claims, arguing such waivers are unenforceable; Paper B documents employer use of mandatory arbitration in the workplace, describes the procedural and remedial terms that disadvantage employees, and links those practices to statutory and judicial responses—both engage the legal status and consequences of mandatory employment arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts in defining arbitration's reach, including judicial review, vacatur rates, circuit splits, and forum shopping
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts circuit-level disagreement and impending Supreme Court review over enforceability of collective-waiver provisions, illustrating how courts shape arbitration doctrine; Paper B provides empirical evidence that federal and state courts vary substantially in vacating or confirming awards, leading to forum shopping and reduced arbitral finality—both examine how judicial treatment determines arbitration's practical enforceability and finality.

papers.node_id: 56ambuslj815!!ARTICLE: New Battles and Battlegrounds for Mandatory Arbitration After Epic Systems, New Prime, and Lamps Plus
papers.title: ARTICLE: New Battles and Battlegrounds for Mandatory Arbitration After Epic Systems, New Prime, and Lamps Plus
papers.abstract:
Workers and consumers are increasingly required to waive their right to go to court when they sign employment contracts.Employers may insist not only on arbitration, but also onindividualor bilateral arbitration, thereby prohibiting class actions or other methods of cooperation between workers to address workplace grievances.Arbitration is often a suitable, fair, and expeditious means of resolving employment disputes. Nevertheless, most employees have little bargaining power in negotiating the arbitration agreement or any meaningful choice in deciding whether or not to accept such agreements.
Businesses frequently favor arbitration because this method of resolution is less expensive, less time consuming, and confidential.They also are concerned with prohibiting expensive class action suits.However, from an employee or consumer perspective,mandatory arbitration may seem unfair.Not only does the individual surrender her right to a jury trial, but she also is prevented from joining forces with similarly situated employees or consumers.An individual may forego arbitration and thus any recovery for an alleged violation of rights because the amount of money involved in a single claim is not worth the cost of retaining an attorney.Employees may also forego solo arbitration because they fear retaliation by employers.Moreover, studies show that employers are more likely to prevail in arbitration because arbitrators are keen to retain their business.Mandatory arbitration is an important issue because more than half of private sector nonunion workers are subject to mandatory arbitration.In addition, low wage workers are the most likely to be subject to mandatory arbitration.
Several U.S. Supreme Court decisions have had a strong impact on the rise of mandatory arbitration provisions. Over the past few decades,the Court, often by a narrow majority, has interpreted the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) in a manner that establishes a strong policy of enforcing arbitration provisions as written.The FAA, passed in 1925, was intended to overcome judicial hostility to arbitration provisions.Some have argued that the FAA was designed to apply only to the enforcement of arbitration agreements between merchants and that the Act was never intended to apply to agreements involving consumers or employees.Nevertheless, the Supreme Court has held that arbitration provisions in both consumer contracts and employment contracts areenforceable.The Court's proarbitration stance has undoubtedly encouraged employers to use arbitration provisions more frequently. As the use of mandatory individual arbitration provisions increased, workers challenged their use, stating that the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) guarantees a right to band together to enforce their rights.But in a 2018 decision, the Supreme Court held that even this protection guaranteed by a federal statute did not trump the FAA.
In the 2018 and 2019 terms, the U.S. Supreme Court decided three cases involving arbitration agreements.InEpic Systems v. Lewis, the Court held that employers may include class action waivers in predispute arbitration agreements.The Court found that the public policy in favor of enforcing arbitration embodied in the FAA overrides any concern that mandating individual arbitration interferes with employees' rights to engage in concerted activity for mutual aid or protection under the NLRA.The Court insisted that the FAA envisions individual arbitration because it provides distinct advantages in terms of cost and time efficiencies, and avoids the morass of classactions.InLamps Plus, Inc. v. Varela, the Court held that a court cannot order parties to class arbitration if the arbitration provision was ambiguous about the availability of class arbitration.The Court rejected a neutral state contract law interpretation that would construe any ambiguity against the employer-drafter. The Court determined that the FAA, not state contract law principles, resolved any ambiguity in favor of individual arbitration.TheEpic SystemsandLamps Plusdecisions continued the Court's proemployer interpretation of the FAA.These two cases demonstrate that the Court is unwilling to use the FAA's saving clause to preserve an employee's right to collective action. The Court's insistence that the FAA takes precedence over provisions of another federal statute and state contract law indicates its commitment to enforcing arbitration provisions as written.
The third case,New Prime Inc. v. Oliveira, provided some clarification about who is exempted from the FAA's coverage.In a previous landmark case,Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams, the Court interpreted the FAA narrowly to cover most employees engaged in interstate commerce and to exclude from the Act's coverage only transportation workers engagedin interstate commerce.InNew Prime, the Court held that the transportation worker exemption applies to independent contractors as well as to employees. Thus, withNew Prime, transportation workers will escape the consequences ofEpic Systemsas the decision makes it clear that employers cannot require transportation workers to waive their right to class action.
The Court's decisions in these three cases resolved long-running disputes about the breadth of the FAA. Nevertheless, in the aftermath ofEpic Systems, Lamps Plus, andNew Prime, several questions remain unanswered, and new questions are emerging. The viability of state laws and interpretations that seek to give workers and consumers more leverage is shaky as the Court's slim majority appears intent on crafting arguments to uphold individual arbitration provisions at all costs.Nevertheless, state courts and legislatures continue to seek ways to protect workers and consumers who are disadvantaged by mandatory individual arbitration provisions. California persists in allowing representative suits under its Private Attorney General's Act (PAGA), and state courts continue to consider traditional contract defenses, such as lack of mutual assent and unconscionability, as arguments to bypass onerous arbitration provisions.Moreover, even though the NLRA proved not to be a savior of workers' rights for mutual aid and protection, the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) continues to object to arbitration provisions that insist on worker confidentiality where those provisions infringe upon substantive section 7 rights.Additionally, theNew Primedecision will reinvigorate the battle over what it means to be "engaged in interstate commerce" to qualify for the FAA's transportation worker exemption. Employers will undoubtedly argue that transportation workers may be forced to arbitrate under state law provisions that do not exempt them. The role of state law in such agreements will raise new issues about preemption.
This article first briefly summarizes the conclusions and reasoning of the Supreme Court inEpic SystemsandLamps Plus. Part II considers avenues that lower courts are still pursuing in the wake ofEpic SystemsandLamps Plusto preserve workers' rights to collective action. After a summary of theNew Primedecision, Part III demonstrates the diverging approaches that courts are taking to determine who qualifies as a transportation worker for the FAA's section 1 exemption. The article concludes that despite the attempts of state courts and state legislation to ensure that workers and consumers are able to effectively vindicate their rights, the Court is likely to strike down state statutes and decisions that carve out exceptions to arbitration. We advocate that Congress should amend the FAA to resolve the inequality of bargaining power between employers and employees and preserve the rights of employees to act together to redress workplace disputes.

questions.question: Whether mandatory individual arbitration clauses and class-action waivers reduce workers' and consumers' ability to vindicate their rights and obtain collective or representative relief.
Whether judicial enforcement of arbitration agreements preempts or undermines state-law and statutory efforts to preserve collective or representative remedies for workers and consumers.
Which categories of workers should be exempt from enforcement of mandatory arbitration based on the nature of their work's connection to interstate commerce, and how should that exemption be defined?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92nwulrev1!!ARTICLE: PUNITIVE DAMAGES AND THE CONSUMERIZATION OF ARBITRATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE DAMAGES AND THE CONSUMERIZATION OF ARBITRATION

shared_topics.topic: the Federal Arbitration Act's preemption of state law and the Supreme Court's pro‑arbitration interpretations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how the FAA and recent Supreme Court decisions displaced state law limits on arbitration (e.g., restricting punitive damages), and Paper B analyzes the Court's recent rulings (Epic Systems, Lamps Plus, New Prime) that enforce arbitration provisions and constrain state-law or statutory exceptions.

shared_topics.topic: the expansion of arbitration from merchant-to-merchant disputes to consumers, investors, and employees (the 'consumerization' of arbitration) and its consequences for noncommercial parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents arbitration's shift into consumer and investor contexts and the attendant loss of public‑forum protections, while Paper B documents the parallel expansion into employment relations and how mandatory arbitration affects workers' ability to vindicate rights.

shared_topics.topic: limitations on remedial avenues in arbitration (caps or prohibitions on remedies that reduce effective relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on efforts to bar or cap punitive/exemplary damages in arbitration (including NASD proposals), and Paper B shows how class‑action waivers and individual arbitration requirements prevent collective relief and often make small claims unviable.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and institutional or contractual governance of arbitration versus public policy and oversight
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines industry governance (e.g., NASD rules, industry‑sponsored arbitration) and contractual choice‑of‑law strategies that shape remedies and arbitrator authority, and Paper B examines employer‑drafted arbitration clauses and institutional practices that structure dispute resolution to favor businesses.

shared_topics.topic: state legislative and judicial responses to arbitration (choice‑of‑law clauses, unconscionability, and other defenses) and the resulting preemption tensions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses attempts to use choice‑of‑law clauses and state protections to limit arbitration remedies and how federal preemption undermines those strategies, while Paper B surveys state statutes (like PAGA), contract‑defense doctrines, and divergent state‑court approaches that seek to preserve collective or substantive rights despite federal preemption.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49arizlrev69!!ARTICLE:Arbitration and the Individuation Critique
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Arbitration and the Individuation Critique

shared_topics.topic: aggregation versus individuation of claims (class arbitration and class-action waivers)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze whether arbitration necessarily forces individualized proceedings or can and should accommodate aggregated relief: Paper A explores the potential and mechanics of class arbitration and informal aggregation, while Paper B examines how class-action waivers and recent Supreme Court rulings (Epic Systems, Lamps Plus) have curtailed collective proceedings in employment arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetry between repeat-player businesses and one-shot consumers/workers
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with the concern that businesses enjoy repeat-player advantages while consumers and employees are one-shotters lacking bargaining power: Paper A frames this as Galanter’s repeat-player critique of individuation, and Paper B documents employees’ limited ability to negotiate mandatory arbitration and the resulting enforcement imbalances.

shared_topics.topic: specific arbitration contract terms that limit remedies or collective action (e.g., confidentiality, punitive-damage limits, class waivers)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers scrutinize particular contract provisions that individuate disputes and restrict relief—Paper A catalogs such terms and questions how widespread they are and how they operate in practice, while Paper B focuses on class waivers and confidentiality clauses as mechanisms that prevent collective enforcement and reduce workers’ remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of external institutions and law on arbitration practice (ADR providers, courts, and statutes)
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how non-party institutions shape arbitration outcomes: Paper A assesses the role of ADR providers (AAA, JAMS) and their due-process standards in moderating arbitration’s effects, and Paper B surveys judicial (Supreme Court) interpretations of the FAA, the NLRB, state laws (like PAGA), and statutory exemptions that determine arbitration’s scope.

shared_topics.topic: reform and policy responses to address fairness and access to collective remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both propose or evaluate remedies to the perceived shortcomings of mandatory individual arbitration—Paper A suggests ADR-provider policy reforms and mechanisms to foster aggregation and repeat-player counsel, while Paper B discusses legislative fixes (amending the FAA), state-law strategies, and other doctrinal avenues to preserve collective enforcement rights.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63fordhamlrev1499!!SYMPOSIUM: NEW YORK STOCK EXCHANGE, INC. SYMPOSIUM ON ARBITRATION IN THE SECURITIES INDUSTRY
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: NEW YORK STOCK EXCHANGE, INC. SYMPOSIUM ON ARBITRATION IN THE SECURITIES INDUSTRY

shared_topics.topic: arbitration as an alternative to court litigation—tradeoff between speed/cost and access to justice
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze arbitration as a faster, less expensive substitute for courthouse litigation (Paper A in the securities context; Paper B in employment/consumer contexts) while stressing the risk that those efficiencies can come at the cost of delayed or denied relief and diminished access to justice for claimants.

shared_topics.topic: mandatory or effectively compelled arbitration and unequal bargaining power of claimants
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how disputes are channeled into arbitration—Paper A noting the growing use of arbitration to resolve securities disputes involving the investing public, and Paper B documenting widespread mandatory predispute arbitration clauses for workers and consumers—and both express concern that parties (investors, employees, consumers) often lack meaningful choice or bargaining power in accepting those agreements.

shared_topics.topic: procedural fairness, arbitrator neutrality, and potential bias
shared_topics.justification: Each paper worries about the fairness and legitimacy of arbitration procedures: Paper A emphasizes arbitration must be fair in fact and appearance to maintain confidence, and Paper B documents empirical and doctrinal concerns that arbitrators and arbitral processes may favor repeat business (employers/businesses) and thus disadvantage claimants.

shared_topics.topic: impact of arbitration practices on public confidence and legitimacy of the underlying industry/institutions
shared_topics.justification: Both works tie arbitration’s legitimacy to broader public trust—Paper A links fair arbitration to investor confidence and healthy securities markets, while Paper B links mandatory arbitration practices (and limitations on collective redress) to diminished ability of consumers and workers to vindicate rights and to erode confidence in institutions that regulate workplace and marketplace disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92nwulrev99!!ARTICLE: PUNITIVE DAMAGES AND THE PUBLIC INTEREST MODEL OF SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A RESPONSE TO PROFESSOR STIPANOWICH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE DAMAGES AND THE PUBLIC INTEREST MODEL OF SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A RESPONSE TO PROFESSOR STIPANOWICH

shared_topics.topic: arbitration's role in serving or undermining the public interest
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how mandatory individual arbitration and class-action waivers affect collective enforcement of labor and consumer rights and calls for legislative intervention to protect public welfare; Paper B centers on whether limits on punitive damages in securities arbitration serve or impede the 'public interest' role of arbitration as a surrogate forum for protecting investors and deterring misconduct.

shared_topics.topic: limits on remedies and procedural constraints in arbitration and their effects on access to justice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how class-action bans, confidentiality provisions, and individual arbitration reduce practical recovery and deter claims by low-value or retaliatory-sensitive plaintiffs; Paper B debates punitive-damages caps and internal appellate review as procedural/instrumental limits that change deterrence, compensation, and the ability of claimants to vindicate rights in arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: institutional governance of arbitration (statutes, courts, and industry rules shaping outcomes)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how the Federal Arbitration Act, Supreme Court decisions (Epic Systems, Lamps Plus, New Prime), the NLRB, and state laws interact to define arbitration's scope; Paper B analyzes industry governance through NASD and SICA proposals, task force recommendations, and internal appellate mechanisms that set arbitration policy in the securities context.

shared_topics.topic: concerns about fairness and unequal bargaining power in arbitration agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the imbalance between employers/businesses and individual employees/consumers in consenting to arbitration clauses and the resulting inequities; Paper B engages with fairness trade-offs in proposed punitive-damage limits and whether contractual or industry-imposed caps undermine claimants' ability to obtain just relief in arbitration.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 131yaleljf742!!ARTICLE: Arbitration Asymmetries in Class Actions
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Arbitration Asymmetries in Class Actions

shared_topics.topic: effect of mandatory arbitration and class‑action waivers on workers' ability to pursue collective or class relief
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how arbitration clauses and express class‑action waivers prevent aggregation of individual claims and thereby undercut class litigation or collective remedies—Paper A by showing how 'arbitration asymmetries' defeat class certification, and Paper B by tracing Supreme Court decisions (Epic Systems, Lamps Plus) that uphold individual arbitration and class waivers.

shared_topics.topic: who can challenge the enforceability of arbitration agreements and by what means (contract defenses, unconscionability, mutual assent)
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss substantive defenses and doctrinal routes for contesting arbitration provisions—Paper A stresses class‑wide challenges to the validity of arbitration agreements asserted against absent class members, while Paper B surveys state‑law contract defenses (lack of assent, unconscionability), PAGA and other avenues lower courts use to resist enforced arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: procedural and justiciability questions about resolving arbitrability for absent class members (timing and forum of adjudication)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with when and by whom arbitrability should be decided in class contexts—Paper A argues courts may and should adjudicate asserted arbitration rights at class certification (or after certification) without Article III or Rule 23 problems, and Paper B examines the post‑Epic/Lamps Plus landscape where lower courts craft different procedural approaches to preserve or displace collective relief.

shared_topics.topic: employer incentives, strategic uses of arbitration clauses, and the need for doctrinal or legislative responses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers highlight that employers draft and deploy arbitration provisions to avoid class exposure and that the law currently favors defendants; Paper A documents how defendants can manufacture asymmetries to defeat certification, and Paper B describes courts' pro‑arbitration rulings, state responses, NLRB involvement, and advocates for Congressional reform to address bargaining‑power imbalances.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 86marqlrev1!!ARTICLE: OPENING PANDORA'S BOX: CIRCUIT CITY V. ADAMS AND THE ENFORCEABILITY OF COMPULSORY, PROSPECTIVE ARBITRATION AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: OPENING PANDORA'S BOX: CIRCUIT CITY V. ADAMS AND THE ENFORCEABILITY OF COMPULSORY, PROSPECTIVE ARBITRATION AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of compulsory/prospective arbitration agreements in employment
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how the FAA and Supreme Court decisions determine whether employers can compel employees to arbitrate disputes (Paper A through an in-depth reading of Circuit City and its limits, Paper B by situating Circuit City among later decisions like Epic Systems and Lamps Plus that broaden enforcement).

shared_topics.topic: the FAA section 1 transportation-worker exemption and its scope
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss the statutory exemption for 'contracts of employment of ... workers engaged in interstate commerce' — Paper A examines Circuit City's narrow reading limiting the exemption to transportation workers, while Paper B traces subsequent litigation (including New Prime) and ongoing disputes about who qualifies for the exemption.

shared_topics.topic: conflict and preemption between the FAA and other federal statutes (e.g., NLRA, Civil Rights Act)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question whether arbitration under the FAA displaces or conflicts with rights created by other federal laws — Paper A highlights unresolved tensions with federal statutory rights (citing Alexander and concerns about statutory claims), and Paper B analyzes how the Court has treated NLRA and other statutory protections in Epic Systems and related cases.

shared_topics.topic: limits on arbitration clauses’ scope and contract-defenses (class waivers, unconscionability, mutual assent)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address what restrictions remain on arbitration provisions — Paper A notes Circuit City left open questions about permissible clause provisions and bargaining conditions, while Paper B surveys doctrinal developments (class-action waivers, ambiguity over class arbitration in Lamps Plus) and state-law defenses like unconscionability and lack of mutual assent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62sclrev407!!ARTICLE: Much Ado About Nothing: The Future of Manifest Disregard After Hall Street
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Much Ado About Nothing: The Future of Manifest Disregard After Hall Street

shared_topics.topic: how Supreme Court precedents reshape the availability of judicial review and defenses under the FAA
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the effect of Hall Street on lower-court vacatur standards and whether Hall Street's language forecloses nonstatutory review; Paper B examines how recent Supreme Court decisions (Epic Systems, Lamps Plus, New Prime) have constrained judicial and statutory avenues for limiting mandatory arbitration and strengthened enforcement of arbitration clauses.

shared_topics.topic: whether judicially‑created doctrines or state‑law contract defenses remain available to limit enforcement of arbitration agreements or awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that a judicial doctrine (manifest disregard) should survive Hall Street in a revised form (manifest disregard of the agreement); Paper B surveys how state courts and agencies invoke traditional contract defenses (unconscionability, mutual assent), statutory devices (PAGA), or agency objections to resist or bypass FAA enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: divergent lower‑court approaches and circuit splits in applying the FAA
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents a circuit split over whether nonstatutory vacatur grounds (like manifest disregard) survive Hall Street; Paper B highlights divergent approaches by courts to the FAA's Section 1 transportation exemption and to state-law attempts to preserve collective or class remedies after Supreme Court rulings.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and scope of specific FAA provisions (textual limits and exemptions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on interpreting FAA vacatur grounds (Section 10) and the exclusivity of statutory bases for vacatur, while Paper B focuses on interpreting the FAA's coverage and exemptions (e.g., Section 1 transportation-worker exemption) and the FAA's interplay with the saving clause and state law — both engage substantively with how particular FAA provisions should be read and applied.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 8cardozojconflictresol1!!ARTICLE: THE PROPRIETY OF EXPANDED JUDICIAL REVIEW UNDER THE FAA: ACHIEVING A BALANCE BETWEEN ENFORCING PARTIES' AGREEMENTS ACCORDING TO THEIR TERMS AND MAINTAINING ARBITRAL EFFICIENCY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PROPRIETY OF EXPANDED JUDICIAL REVIEW UNDER THE FAA: ACHIEVING A BALANCE BETWEEN ENFORCING PARTIES' AGREEMENTS ACCORDING TO THEIR TERMS AND MAINTAINING ARBITRAL EFFICIENCY

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and purposes of the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts read and apply the FAA: Paper A examines Supreme Court decisions (Epic Systems, Lamps Plus, New Prime) that interpret the FAA to favor enforcement of arbitration provisions, while Paper B closely reads sections 9–11 and the FAA's legislative history to evaluate the statute's purposes (notably enforcing agreements and promoting arbitral efficiency).

shared_topics.topic: the tension between enforcing arbitration agreements as written and protecting other legal or public-policy interests
shared_topics.justification: Both works confront conflicts between strict enforcement of arbitration clauses and competing values — Paper A focuses on how enforcement can undermine workers' collective rights and access to remedies (NLRA, PAGA, unconscionability), whereas Paper B examines courts' reluctance to allow contractual expansion of judicial review when doing so would undermine arbitral efficiency or other FAA objectives.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts, precedents, and circuit splits in shaping arbitration doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both articles survey and critique judicial decisionmaking: Paper A catalogs key Supreme Court rulings that have shifted the arbitration landscape and discusses divergent lower‑court responses, and Paper B maps circuit and district court splits over expanded vacatur clauses and urges Supreme Court guidance (including a proposed framework) to resolve the disuniformity.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how non‑FAA rules (statutory exemptions, state law, or private contract terms) can modify or escape FAA governance
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with the question of limits on the FAA—Paper A considers statutory and state‑law attempts to carve out exceptions (e.g., the section 1 transportation exemption, NLRA claims, California PAGA, contract defenses), while Paper B investigates whether parties can contractually expand or limit the FAA's judicial‑review provisions and how courts should treat those clauses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113pennstlrev1343!!Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Judicial Approbation in Building the Civilization of Arbitration
compared_to.partner_title: Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Judicial Approbation in Building the Civilization of Arbitration

shared_topics.topic: judicial role in shaping arbitration law and practice
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts — especially high courts — have been decisive in developing arbitration doctrine: Paper A compares national high courts (England, France, U.S.) in fashioning pro- or anti-arbitration policies, while Paper B chronicles recent U.S. Supreme Court rulings (Epic Systems, Lamps Plus, New Prime) that have materially reshaped arbitration practice.

shared_topics.topic: judicial enforcement and the scope of arbitration agreements (arbitrability, class waivers, exemptions)
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage substantively with what courts will enforce: Paper A treats judicial decisions on arbitrability, arbitrator powers, and award enforcement as the true test of a jurisdiction's commitment to arbitration, and Paper B examines courts' enforcement of FAA-based arbitration clauses, including class-action waivers and statutory exemptions like the transportation-worker carveout.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between statutory/regulatory endorsements and judicial interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers highlight the gap between legislative or treaty endorsements of arbitration and their real-world effect as determined by courts: Paper A contrasts formal ratification (New York Convention, UNCITRAL Model Law) with judicial implementation, while Paper B explores how the FAA, NLRA, state statutes, and preemption doctrines are interpreted by courts to expand or limit arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: tension between pro-arbitration policy and other legal/public-policy values (access to justice, cohesion of substantive law)
shared_topics.justification: Both examine conflicts between a judicially or legislatively promoted arbitration policy and competing legal values: Paper A discusses courts defending substantive-law coherence or promoting arbitration for commercial welfare, and Paper B analyzes how enforcement of mandatory individual arbitration can clash with employees' collective rights, access to remedies, and state public-policy protections.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70stjohnslrev539!!ARTICLE: CLAIM PRECLUSION AND REFORMATION OF CONTRACTS: NEW YORK CPLR 3002(d)
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CLAIM PRECLUSION AND REFORMATION OF CONTRACTS: NEW YORK CPLR 3002(d)

shared_topics.topic: tension between strict enforcement of written agreements and equitable contract remedies (reformation, estoppel, unconscionability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the FAA and recent Supreme Court decisions enforce arbitration clauses 'as written' and displace equitable contract defenses, while Paper B critiques CPLR 3002(d) and illustrates (via Kwiatkowski) how reformation and estoppel can provide relief when strict enforcement of a written contract yields injustice.

shared_topics.topic: how statutes and judicial decisions reshape the availability of post-judgment or alternative remedies for contract claimants
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how federal statutes (FAA) and Supreme Court rulings preempt or limit state-law remedies and collective remedies for workers, and Paper B examines a state statute that alters the preclusive effect of a judgment to allow a second action for contract reformation.

shared_topics.topic: safeguarding disadvantaged or asymmetrically bargaining parties from harsh enforcement of form contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on low‑wage workers and consumers who lack bargaining power and may be unable to vindicate rights under mandatory arbitration clauses, while Paper B shows how an illiterate insured was disadvantaged by strict enforcement and discusses statutory reform intended to protect such parties.

shared_topics.topic: judicial rules for interpreting ambiguous contract language and the role of contra proferentem/contractual interpretation doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses Lamps Plus and the Court's rejection of state contract-law interpretations (including resolving ambiguities against the drafter) in arbitration clauses, and Paper B recounts case law and doctrines (estoppel, reading requirements) about when courts will construe or reform written contract terms under particular factual circumstances.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 15cardozojconflictresol777!!ARTICLE: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY OF ARBITRATORS ACTING AS MEDIATORS IN CHINA
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY OF ARBITRATORS ACTING AS MEDIATORS IN CHINA

shared_topics.topic: arbitrator impartiality and bias arising from incentives or dual roles
shared_topics.justification: Paper A cites empirical studies and doctrinal concerns that arbitrators may favor repeat business from employers (producing pro-employer outcomes), while Paper B empirically and theoretically investigates how an arbitrator’s dual role as mediator can compromise impartiality if confidential mediation information or settlement-facilitation creates bias when arbitration resumes.

shared_topics.topic: confidentiality and ex parte communications undermining procedural fairness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights arbitration’s confidentiality and sealed procedures as blocking collective exposure of rights-violations and deterring enforcement, and Paper B analyzes how caucusing and confidential disclosures in arb‑med produce ex parte communications that can deprive a party of the chance to rebut evidence, raising due‑process concerns.

shared_topics.topic: the efficiency/settlement facilitation versus access to justice tradeoff
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes arbitration’s cost and speed advantages but argues those same features can prevent meaningful recovery, collective redress, and deter claims; Paper B explores whether and how arbitrators’ active settlement facilitation increases settlement rates and efficiency while potentially impairing adjudicative fairness and parties’ candor.

shared_topics.topic: limits of party autonomy and unequal bargaining power in selecting arbitration procedures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on mandatory, employer‑drafted arbitration clauses imposed on workers and consumers with little choice, questioning whether consent legitimates arbitral procedure; Paper B treats party freedom to adopt arb‑med as a justification for combined roles but also notes how anticipated reversion to arbitrator may distort parties’ willingness to participate candidly, revealing practical limits to meaningful consent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42wmmarylrev1!!ARTICLE: AS MANDATORY BINDING ARBITRATION MEETS THE CLASS ACTION, WILL THE CLASS ACTION SURVIVE?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AS MANDATORY BINDING ARBITRATION MEETS THE CLASS ACTION, WILL THE CLASS ACTION SURVIVE?

shared_topics.topic: use of mandatory arbitration clauses and class‑action waivers as a strategy to evade class litigation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how corporations deploy predispute arbitration provisions that expressly bar class actions (or require bilateral arbitration) as a deliberate technique to prevent class certification and thereby avoid collective litigation and related liability exposure.

shared_topics.topic: effect of individual arbitration on access to collective remedies and private enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine how requiring one‑on‑one arbitration undermines plaintiffs’ and workers’ ability to vindicate low‑value or widespread claims — reducing recoveries, deterring enforcement, and eliminating the deterrent and compensatory functions of class litigation.
