compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ARBITRATION PROVISIONS: LITTLE DARLINGS AND LITTLE MONSTERS

shared_topics.topic: scope and coverage of the Federal Arbitration Act (Sections 1 and 2) and how courts should interpret it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the FAA's pro‑arbitration structure and Supreme Court expansion of its reach, arguing Congress intended arbitration agreements to be treated as 'pre‑approved'; Paper B focuses on Section 1/Section 2 interpretation (Circuit City) and the Court's narrowing of the Section 1 exclusion for employment contracts and the doctrinal reasoning used to reach that result.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of arbitration agreements in the employment context
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the rise of arbitration clauses in employment contracts and debates whether courts may refuse to enforce one‑sided employment arbitration provisions; Paper B directly addresses the enforceability of compulsory, prospective arbitration agreements in private employment contracts and the implications of Circuit City for such clauses.

shared_topics.topic: applicability of state‑law defenses (e.g., unconscionability) and the limits of judicial review of arbitration clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should not apply unconscionability to arbitration provisions and distinguishes it from other state defenses like fraud and duress; Paper B notes that the Supreme Court's Circuit City decision leaves unresolved questions about permissible scope, bargaining conditions, and when state or federal doctrines can invalidate arbitration agreements.

shared_topics.topic: who should police or policeability of arbitration terms — courts versus arbitrators
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the question of whether, if courts are precluded from applying unconscionability, arbitrators are competent to police arbitration provisions; Paper B observes that Circuit City settles coverage but provides no guidance on enforcement mechanisms or negotiating conditions, prompting inquiry into which fora (courts or arbitrators) should police arbitration clauses.

shared_topics.topic: whether arbitration is a preferable forum to federal litigation for statutory claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that modern securities arbitration can be more investor‑friendly than federal court given restrictive judicial readings of federal remedies, while Paper B considers case law (Gilmer, Alexander, Circuit City) and whether arbitration procedures can or should displace employees' and claimants' access to federal statutory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: public‑policy implications of expanding compulsory or mandatory arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises macro questions about whether securities arbitration's evolution is socially desirable and what public policy tradeoffs the next decade will present; Paper B interrogates the policy consequences of Circuit City's narrowing of FAA exemptions and the broader implications of enforcing compulsory, prospective arbitration clauses.

shared_topics.topic: consent, bargaining conditions, and fairness of compulsory arbitration clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's micro perspective examines the parties' experience — cost, access, and fairness — in arbitration agreements between brokers and customers, while Paper B probes the permissible scope, required bargaining conditions, and fairness constraints for enforceable arbitration agreements in employment and related contexts.

papers.node_id: 15cardozojconflictresol623!!ARTICLE: OPENING THE FLOODGATES OF SMALL CUSTOMER CLAIMS IN FINRA ARBITRATION: FINRA V. CHARLES SCHWAB & CO., INC.
papers.title: ARTICLE: OPENING THE FLOODGATES OF SMALL CUSTOMER CLAIMS IN FINRA ARBITRATION: FINRA V. CHARLES SCHWAB & CO., INC.
papers.abstract:
When the Supreme Court held over twenty-five years ago that customers could be compelled to arbitrate their federal securities claims against their brokers,the vast majority of financial firms in the U.S. inserted pre-dispute arbitration provisions ("PDAAs") in agreements with their customers requiring them to arbitrate anyclaims arising out of their brokerage relationship.Since Sheerson/Am. Express, Inc. v. McMahon, investor advocacy groups, scholars, and legislators have called for Congressional action to eliminate mandatory arbitration in securities cases,but the closest Congress has come to such elimination has been to punt this issue to the Securities and Exchange Commission ("SEC"),which has not yet acted. Instead, building upon the development of a uniform securitiesarbitration code and other reforms that pre-dated McMahon,the SEC has prodded self-regulatory organizations ("SROs") to make significant reforms to its arbitration rules that have improved the arbitration process to make it fairer to investors.
Today, nearly all customer disputes are resolved through arbitration before the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority ("FINRA"),the largest arbitral forum for the resolution of securities disputes between member firms and their customers.Under the regulatory oversight of the SEC, FINRA has established a uniform, streamlined set of rules for the arbitration of customer disputes designed to provide fairness, procedural protections, and access to remedies customers would otherwise be able to obtain incourt.Fundamental to the regulatory oversight of its dispute resolution system, efficiency, and fairness to customers, is the requirement that all FINRA members who choose to use PDAAs (a nearly universal choice) are prohibited from limiting or abrogating any of the procedural and substantive remedies otherwise available to customers.
One of those remedies is the availability of a judicial forum for customers to bring or participate in a class action. Since 1992, the SROs have included provisions (now embodied in FINRA's Code of Arbitration Procedures for Customer Disputes [the "Customer Code"]), precluding representative actions in arbitration and further providing that members may not compel arbitration of any claim subject to a judicial class action unless that claim is removed from the class action.In its adopting release, the SEC agreed with the NASD that "class actions are better handled by the courts and that investors should have access to the courts to resolve class actions efficiently."
Thus, the financial industry understood that it could not place judicial class action waivers in their customer agreements without running afoul of SRO conduct rules.However, in October 2011, emboldened by the Supreme Court's decision in AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion,Charles Schwab & Co., Inc. ("Schwab") amended nearly seven million customer agreements to include a waiver of customers' rights to bring judicial class actions and, further, to preclude consolidation of customer claims in arbitration.In short, Schwab's waiver provision required that customers bring their claims, if any, in arbitration solely on an individual basis.
Predictably, FINRA's Department of Enforcement ("Enforcement") filed an enforcement action claiming violations of its member conduct rules prohibiting its members from inserting language in their PDAAs that limit customers' rights under FINRA's forum rules, including the ability to file judicial claims not otherwise prohibited by FINRA, i.e., class actions.The Office of Hearing Officers ("the Panel") agreed with Enforcement that Schwab had, in fact, violated the conduct rules as alleged, but refused to enforce the rules prohibiting waiver of class actions reasoning that, under the U.S. Supreme Court's recent decision in Concepcion, the conduct rules were unenforceable under the Federal Arbitration Act ("FAA").
Aside from the Panel's stunning refusal to enforce FINRA's Conduct Rules,the Schwab OHO Decision is fundamentally flawed because it all but ignores the member agreement between FINRA and Schwab and, instead, focuses on the agreement between Schwab and its customers - which was not directly being challenged. This is a significant, critical distinction between the Schwab enforcement proceeding and cases where the judicial class action waiver is directly being challenged by the customer or consumer subject to the waiver, as presented by Concepcion and the Supreme Court's most recent case on this issue, American Express Co. v. Italian Colors Restaurant.In contrast to those cases, the customers subject to the PDAA in Schwab's agreement were not challenging or resisting its enforcement. Instead, FINRA broughtan action to enforce its own member agreement with Schwab (which is itself an arbitration agreement), under which Schwab agreed to certain restrictions in exchange for the benefit of membership. By elevating Schwab's customer agreement over its member agreement with FINRA, the Panel's ruling is actually inconsistent with the FAA and Supreme Court precedent requiring strict enforcement of the parties' arbitration agreements.
The Schwab OHO Decision immediately reignited calls for a ban on mandatory pre-dispute arbitration provisions in consumer and investor contracts.The case is being closely watched by the financial industry, and will likely end up before a Supreme Court that is increasingly hostile to judicial class actions and has all but closed the door on the effective vindication doctrine with its most recent decision in Italian Colors.But the regulatory and contextual differences between Schwab and the Supreme Court line of cases provide hope that FINRA's conduct rules prohibiting class action waivers will stand as enforceable and, therefore, remain in the standard PDAA found in customer agreements with their brokers.
Should the Schwab decision ultimately stand,however, the consequences to smaller claim investors could be devastating given the line of cases from Concepcion to Italian Colors. Many investorswill be left with the choice of pursuing their claims pro se through a complex arbitral system or abandoning them altogether.This unfortunate result will add pressure on the SEC to exercise its authority under Dodd-Frank to limit or bar the use of mandatory PDAAs which, as explained below, may be counterproductive to the goal of fair and efficient resolution of investor claims.
Part II of this Article will provide a brief background of the regulatory framework governing the brokerage industry and its use of PDAAs in agreements with customers, and FINRA's limitations on judicial class action waivers. Part III will set forth the facts setting up the conflict between FINRA and Schwab and examine the Schwab OHO Decision. The reasons why the Schwab OHO Decision is flawed and should ultimately be reversed are set forth in Part IV of this Article. Finally, Part V will explore the consequences to investors with small claims should judicial class action waivers ultimately be held enforceable in securities cases, and alternative proposals FINRA can explore to provide avenues for the efficient resolution of investors' claims.

questions.question: Are a regulator's membership rules that bar contractual waivers of judicial class actions in customer agreements legally enforceable against member firms that insert such waivers into pre-dispute arbitration clauses?

If judicial class-action waivers in customer contracts are held enforceable (mandating individual arbitration), how will that affect small-value investors' ability to vindicate claims and obtain remedies?
What regulatory or procedural alternatives could preserve efficient access to relief for small claimants if class-action waivers in customer arbitration agreements are upheld?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93denvlrevonline111!!ARTICLE: COLORADO'S SECOND RENAISSANCE: ADOPTING THE UNCITRALMODEL LAW ON INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COLORADO'S SECOND RENAISSANCE: ADOPTING THE UNCITRALMODEL LAW ON INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION

shared_topics.topic: how statutory, regulatory, and institutional frameworks determine the enforceability of arbitration agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the Federal Arbitration Act, SEC oversight, and FINRA conduct rules interact to determine whether customer arbitration clauses and class-action waivers are enforceable; Paper B examines how a state's adoption of the UNCITRAL Model Law would change the statutory/regulatory regime governing enforceability and recognition of international commercial arbitration in Colorado.

shared_topics.topic: tension between access to judicial forums and arbitration as a dispute-resolution mechanism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the consequences of class-action waivers and mandatory pre-dispute arbitration for investors' ability to pursue judicial remedies, especially small-claims plaintiffs; Paper B considers how modernizing arbitration law (via the Model Law) affects parties' forum choices, predictability, and access to neutral dispute-resolution for cross-border commercial disputes.

shared_topics.topic: the use of legal reform to advance broader policy objectives (fairness, efficiency, and economic development)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses FINRA and SEC rule changes and potential legislative responses aimed at making arbitration fairer and preserving investor remedies; Paper B advocates adopting the Model Law as a legal reform to make Colorado more trade-friendly, efficient, and attractive to international business.

shared_topics.topic: conflicts between competing agreements or legal instruments and which governs arbitration proceedings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the conflict between Schwab's customer PDAA and FINRA's member agreement/rules and which agreement should control enforcement; Paper B addresses harmonization issues between state arbitration statutes and international instruments (the Model Law), i.e., which legal instrument governs international commercial arbitration in the state.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92texlrev2177!!Symposium: Steps Toward Evidence-Based IP: The Essential Role of Courts for Supporting Innovation
compared_to.partner_title: Symposium: Steps Toward Evidence-Based IP: The Essential Role of Courts for Supporting Innovation

shared_topics.topic: choice between arbitration and judicial forum for resolving commercial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that contracting parties in innovation contexts increasingly carve out rights to proceed in court (rather than arbitrate) for IP-related claims, while Paper B analyzes a dispute over whether broker-customer pre‑dispute arbitration agreements can bar access to courts (and class actions) for securities claims.

shared_topics.topic: when and why parties preserve access to specific judicial remedies (e.g., injunctions, class relief) instead of relying on arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows parties reserve court access to obtain injunctive relief and protect IP/confidentiality rights that arbitration may poorly protect; Paper B focuses on access to judicial class actions and the consequences if arbitration clauses (or waivers) eliminate that remedy for investors.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private arbitration clauses and external regulatory or institutional constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how contracts and arbitration interact with broader legal institutions and the continuing essential role of courts for innovation, while Paper B analyzes the tension between firm-customer arbitration clauses and FINRA/SEC member‑rules (and FAA precedent) controlling whether such waivers are enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: practical consequences of routinizing arbitration for parties with weaker enforcement leverage (innovators or small claimants)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues innovators often need courts because private self-help and arbitration can be inadequate to protect nascent IP and enforce vague innovation contracts, and Paper B warns that enforcing class‑action waivers in arbitration would leave small investors unable to vindicate claims, effectively denying relief.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57stanlrev1593!!2005 STANFORD LAW REVIEW SYMPOSIUM: THE CIVIL TRIAL: ADAPTATION AND ALTERNATIVES: SYMPOSIUM ARTICLE: ADR and the Cost of Compulsion
compared_to.partner_title: 2005 STANFORD LAW REVIEW SYMPOSIUM: THE CIVIL TRIAL: ADAPTATION AND ALTERNATIVES: SYMPOSIUM ARTICLE: ADR and the Cost of Compulsion

shared_topics.topic: risks of mandatory pre-dispute arbitration/compulsory ADR
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the consequences when broker customers are forced into individual arbitration (the Schwab dispute) and how that compulsory forum choice can close off judicial remedies; Paper B is a broad critique of compulsory ADR (both private and court‑annexed), cataloguing harms that arise when ADR is required rather than voluntarily chosen.

shared_topics.topic: use of adhesion contracting to insert arbitration and class‑action waivers that curtail statutory or collective remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents Schwab's mass insertion of a judicial class‑action waiver into customer PDAAs and the conflict with FINRA rules designed to preserve access to class litigation; Paper B warns that adhesion drafters will use arbitration clauses and related terms to short‑circuit legislation or even extinguish claims.

shared_topics.topic: harms to small/weak claimants and access to justice (pressure to abandon claims, pro se arbitration)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how enforcement of class‑action waivers would leave small investors unable to aggregate claims and likely to proceed pro se or forgo relief; Paper B analyzes how compulsory ADR tends to disadvantage the weak, increases settlement pressure, and can fail to satisfy parties' sense of justice.

shared_topics.topic: tension between regulatory protections and federal arbitration law/court precedent, and the need for reforms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the conflict between FINRA/SEC member‑protection rules and Supreme Court/FAA precedent (e.g., Concepcion, Italian Colors) and explores regulatory responses and alternative dispute‑resolution designs; Paper B argues against compulsion and proposes intermediate reforms (transparency, provider diversity, respect for rule of law) to make ADR fairer when used.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 87ucinlrev1167!!ARTICLE: EPIC SYSTEMS CORP. V. LEWIS: INDIVIDUAL ARBITRATION AND THE FUTURE OF TITLE VII DISPARATE IMPACT AND PATTERN-OR-PRACTICE CLASS ACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EPIC SYSTEMS CORP. V. LEWIS: INDIVIDUAL ARBITRATION AND THE FUTURE OF TITLE VII DISPARATE IMPACT AND PATTERN-OR-PRACTICE CLASS ACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how the FAA and Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Concepcion/Italian Colors in Paper A; Epic Systems in Paper B) govern the enforceability of PDAAs that include class-action waivers, debating whether and when such waivers must be enforced against customers or employees.

shared_topics.topic: whether other federal statutes or regulatory rules can override or invalidate arbitration/class-waiver provisions
shared_topics.justification: Each article examines the tension between the FAA and another legal regime — FINRA/SEC conduct rules and the member agreement in Paper A, and the NLRA/Title VII statutory framework in Paper B — asking whether those statutes or rules provide a basis to void or limit arbitration waivers.

shared_topics.topic: impact of mandatory individual arbitration and class-waivers on access to collective remedies and vindication of statutory rights
shared_topics.justification: Both papers evaluate the practical and doctrinal consequences of enforcing individual-only arbitration (for small-investor claims in Paper A; for disparate-impact or pattern-or-practice employment claims in Paper B), focusing on whether class or collective litigation is necessary to vindicate rights effectively.

shared_topics.topic: the authority and limits of administrative or regulatory bodies to challenge or shape arbitration agreements
shared_topics.justification: Each work engages with the role and power of non-judicial actors — FINRA's enforcement and member-rule regime in Paper A, and the NLRB's prior position and its judicial deference issues in Paper B — in attempting to regulate or nullify arbitration clauses and class waivers.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 34flastulrev99!!ARTICLE: STATUTORY MISCONSTRUCTION: HOW THE SUPREME COURT CREATED A FEDERAL ARBITRATION LAW NEVER ENACTED BY CONGRESS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: STATUTORY MISCONSTRUCTION: HOW THE SUPREME COURT CREATED A FEDERAL ARBITRATION LAW NEVER ENACTED BY CONGRESS

shared_topics.topic: Supreme Court expansion of the Federal Arbitration Act and its doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates FINRA v. Schwab in the line of Supreme Court decisions (e.g., Concepcion, Italian Colors) that have strengthened FAA-based enforcement of arbitration clauses, and Paper B traces how Supreme Court interpretive choices (Prima Paint, Southland, Moses Cone, Buckeye) transformed the 1925 FAA into a far-reaching federal arbitration regime.

shared_topics.topic: Enforceability of class‑action and representative‑action waivers in arbitration clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Schwab's insertion of judicial class‑action waivers and FINRA's claim that those waivers violate its forum rules, while Paper B explains how the Court's construction of the FAA has enabled enforcement of broad arbitration clauses (including waivers that foreclose class or collective remedies) against consumers and employees.

shared_topics.topic: Conflict between arbitration enforcement and regulatory or statutory protective rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the clash between FINRA/SEC membership and forum rules restricting class‑action waivers and the FAA‑based judicial rulings that may render those rules unenforceable, and Paper B documents how the FAA has been judicially construed to preempt state law and constrain regulatory efforts to protect consumers, workers, and small claimants.

shared_topics.topic: Effects of mandatory pre‑dispute arbitration on access to courts and remedies for small claimants/consumers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores the practical consequences for small investors if class waivers and compulsory individual arbitration are upheld (e.g., pro se arbitration or abandoned claims), and Paper B critiques the FAA's expansion for stripping citizens of jury rights and collective statutory remedies, thereby reducing effective access to enforcement mechanisms for individuals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016uilllrev371!!ARTICLE: THE DAY DOCTRINE DIED: PRIVATE ARBITRATION AND THE END OF LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DAY DOCTRINE DIED: PRIVATE ARBITRATION AND THE END OF LAW

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses containing judicial class-action waivers under the FAA and Supreme Court precedent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Schwab enforcement dispute in light of FAA preemption and Supreme Court decisions like AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion and American Express v. Italian Colors, while Paper B traces the doctrinal evolution in the Supreme Court that produced enforceability of class bans and their nationwide deployment.

shared_topics.topic: effect of class-action bans on small-dollar claimants' access to remedies (investors, consumers, employees)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the practical consequences for small investor claimants if judicial class-action waivers are upheld (pro se arbitration or abandonment), and Paper B shows at scale how class bans make small-dollar consumer and employee claims virtually uncollectible and foreclose aggregate relief.

shared_topics.topic: tension between industry/regulatory forum rules (e.g., FINRA/SEC/SRO rules) and federal arbitration law/judicial rulings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the clash between FINRA's member conduct rules prohibiting class-waiver clauses and federal arbitration doctrine as applied by an OHO decision, while Paper B examines how judicial expansion of the FAA has undercut other institutional mechanisms that once constrained arbitration's reach.

shared_topics.topic: removal of disputes from public courts into confidential, one-on-one arbitration and the resulting erosion of public-law development and transparency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that FINRA and the SEC historically favored courts for class litigation and worries Schwab's waivers will channel investor disputes into arbitration, and Paper B argues broadly that widespread enforceability of arbitration clauses with class bans shifts whole categories of claims out of the public common-law system, freezing doctrinal development and reducing transparency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50uclalrev143!!ARTICLE:When Is Cost an Unlawful Barrier to Alternative Dispute Resolution? The Ever Green Tree of Mandatory Employment Arbitration
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:When Is Cost an Unlawful Barrier to Alternative Dispute Resolution? The Ever Green Tree of Mandatory Employment Arbitration

shared_topics.topic: validity of mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses that bar access to the judicial forum
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze whether pre-dispute mandatory arbitration provisions (PDAAs) that prohibit resort to courts—including waivers of judicial class actions—are legally enforceable and how enforcement interacts with statutory and regulatory frameworks (Paper A through FINRA/SEC and FAA tensions; Paper B through employment agreements that remove judicial access).

shared_topics.topic: whether arbitration costs or terms unlawfully prevent vindication of statutory rights (the "effective vindication" issue)
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the question whether arbitration becomes an unlawful barrier when its costs or structural terms (e.g., fee-shifting, high filing costs, bans on representative actions) make enforcement of statutory claims impracticable, with Paper A citing Italian Colors and consequences for small investor claims and Paper B describing prohibitive costs that defeat anti-discrimination remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of class-action/representative-action waivers and bans on consolidation on low-value claimants' ability to obtain relief
shared_topics.justification: Both papers show concern that clauses forbidding class/collective relief or consolidation (or compelling individualized arbitration) disproportionately strip small-value claimants—investors or employees—of effective remedies, thereby incentivizing abandonment of meritorious claims.

shared_topics.topic: the role of regulators and adjudicators in policing arbitration terms and protecting access to remedies

papers.node_id: 104michlrev373!!ARTICLE: OPTING OUT OF LIABILITY: THE FORTHCOMING, NEAR-TOTAL DEMISE OF THE MODERN CLASS ACTION
papers.title: ARTICLE: OPTING OUT OF LIABILITY: THE FORTHCOMING, NEAR-TOTAL DEMISE OF THE MODERN CLASS ACTION
papers.abstract:
In recent years, there have been hundreds of academic articles and scores of books written about class action litigation.The law reviews abound with doctrinal critiques, letters to Congress, moralist manifestos, and economists' prescriptions for optimized class action rules. Reading it all, one would certainly think that abusive class action litigation is running amok in the United States.
On the doctrinal front, for example, Professor Martin Redish raises the objection that much of contemporary class action litigation is, in reality, a "lawyer-driven" hunt for bounty and that, when a court in such a case applies Rule 23 procedures to a substantive federal statute, it is effectively grafting a qui tam provision onto a law that contains no such remedy. Redish would have courts hold that Rule 23 may not be applied to lawyer-driven suits, lest it conflict with the remedial scheme of the substantive congressional enactment upon which the suit is based. Alternatively, he would settle for legislation banning the widespread scourge of lawyer-driven class actions.
From the moralist corner, Professor Charles Wolfram raises the somewhat less nuanced objection that plaintiffs' lawyers are, well, immoral. Professor Wolfram's attack focuses on the "low state of ethical practice in class actions" and the "sell-out lawyers who, for millions in fees, are willingto sign away the rights of tens of thousands of faceless and lawyerless class members."The moralistspurport to be pessimistic about "reform" efforts so long as a "sizable number of lawyers . . . are attracted to the big-money rewards of morally compromised (but legal) professional work."
Law and economics, of course, has had a field day criticizing class actions. Economic analysis has led some scholars to conclude that the agency costs inherent in "entrepreneurial litigation" (that's law and economics for lawyer-driven suits) produce inefficiencies that can only be addressed by a free market for legal claims, in which attorneys may purchase outright the claims of class members.Related scholarship focuses on auctioning the lead counsel position in class actions,on the problems of collusion between plaintiffs' lawyers and defendants,on the concomitant problems of self-dealing by class counsel,or on the supposedly outsized leverage that class certification gives even the most baseless of class claims.Indeed, economicanalysis has been brought to bear on virtually every imaginable issue related to class action litigation, prompting innumerable proposals for "reform."
It is, I think, overly dramatic to say that all of this scholarship misses the point. And yet, almost universally, the staggering heap of academic reform proposals ignores a fundamental and transformative point: in the ongoing and ever-mutating battle between plaintiffs' lawyers and the protectors of corporate interests, the corporate guys are winning. And they are winning because they have developed a new set of tools powerful enough to imperil the very viability of class actions in many -- actually, most -- areas of the law. In fact, I believe it is likely that, with a handful of exceptions, class actions will soon be virtually extinct.
Two factors guide this prediction: the demise of mass tort class actions and the rise of contractual class action waivers. First, as recently as ten years ago, a significant percentage of all class actions were tort cases; by most accounts, almost twenty percent.Since that time, the mass tort class action has met a fate similar to that of the Dodo bird. The latter was last seen on the island of Mauritius in 1680; the former has rarely been glimpsed since the issuance of broad class decertification opinions by federal appellate courts in asbestos, tobacco, and product liability cases in the 1980s and 1990s.
, and more significantly, the vast majority of the remaining class actions are based on some sort of contractual relationship. Virtually all consumer class actions, for example, arise out of some form of contract (adhesive or otherwise), just as employment discrimination class actions arise out of employment contracts. Federal antitrust class actions necessarily grow out of contracts (indeed, standing rules require as much), and the same is true for class actions relating to insurance benefits, ERISA plans, mutual funds, franchise agreements, and an endless variety of other matters.
All of these contract-based class actions are, I believe, on their way to Mauritius. Corporate caretakers have concocted an antigen, in the form of the class action waiver provision, that travels through contractual relationships and dooms the class action device. Where class actions are based on some sort of contractual relationship, this toxin is quite lethal. Developed in the late 1990s by marketers for one of the arbitral bodies,among others,the waiver works in tandem with standard arbitration provisions to ensure that any claim against the corporate defendant may be asserted only in a one-on-one, nonaggregated arbitral proceeding. More virulent strains of theclause force the would-be plaintiff to waive even her right to be represented as a passive, or absent, class member in the event some other injured person manages to commence a class proceeding.
These provisions, which I term "collective action waivers,"still face important judicial challenges, which have the potential to significantly limit their scope. The first round of attempts by plaintiffs' lawyers to invalidate collective action waivers was rooted in state law unconscionability doctrine and allegations that the waivers were inconsistent with substantive federal statutes.These arguments have met with failure everywhere except California, which has proven hospitable to the unconscionability challenge.
The plaintiffs' lawyers, however, are not going down without a fight and are beginning to bring second-wave challenges to collective action waivers, which are subtler and more surgical than the broad state-law unconscionability attack. For example, creative plaintiffs' lawyers are arguing that the collective action waiver's implicit prohibition against cost-spreading across multiple claimants precludes plaintiffs from vindicating federal statutory rights in complex matters that would be expensive to litigate, at least where each plaintiff has relatively little at stake.On this theory, the anti-cost-spreading feature should be treated no differently than mandatory cost-splitting provisions, which current doctrine holds invalid where they would preclude the exercise of federal statutory rights.The coercive imposition of collective action waivers by parties with market power has also been challenged under the Sherman Act.It remains to be seen how much traction these second-wave challenges will find in combating the collective action waivers. Certainly, the scope of these challenges is more limited than the broad first-wave challenges.
Assuming the collective action waiver emerges more or less unscathed from the current round of judicial challenges, it is only a matter of time before these waivers metastasize throughout the body of corporate America and bar the majority of class actions as we know them. It is true that, to date, the collective action waiver has likely had only minimal penetration;early adopters include financial services companies, telephone and Internet firms, and a handful of other aggressive firms with a keen interest in avoiding class action liability. But I regard it as inevitable that firms will ultimately act in their economic best interests, and those interests dictate that virtually all companies will opt out of exposure to class action liability. Why wouldn't they?Once the waivers gain broader acceptance and recognition, it will become malpractice for corporate counsel not to include such clauses in consumer and other class-action-prone contracts.
Ultimately, owing to new technologies and the emphatic judicial embrace of arbitration over the past twenty years, there are few areas of class action law to which the collective action waiver will not extend. Technology has vastly broadened traditional notions of contract and acceptance. Any transaction that may be cemented with the click of a mouse is susceptible to a class action waiver.Judicial preferences for arbitration, meanwhile, have led courts to an unprecedented solicitude for unilateral "envelope-stuffer" amendments of adhesion contracts -- for example, the unread notice stuffed in a consumer's monthly bill stating that, by continuing to use her credit card, or her telephone, she agrees to arbitrate any dispute that may arise.Increasingly, these unilateral notices are taking the form of mass emails, or even website postings, which have been held to support the imposition of arbitration provisions and even collective action waivers.
One seemingly contract-free bastion of class action practice is securities fraud litigation -- specifically, the paradigmatic Rule 10b-5 case where the plaintiff has purchased shares of the defendant issuer on the secondary market. Without a contractual relationship between the plaintiff and the issuing company, it would appear that there is no way for the issuer to impose an arbitration clause or a class action waiver. And yet even these actions may be susceptible to the waivers: Is it not possible for a class action waiver to be effected by some form of publication notice -- perhaps coupled with actual notice to all the exchanges and brokerage houses, and legends on stock certificates -- so as to allow securities issuers also to opt out of class action exposure? Might courts not develop a doctrine that the waiver "travels with the stock"? Would such a rule be any more astonishing than the other developments here on our legal Mauritius?
In the end, I do not think the real story of the contemporary class action is adequately told by the doctrinalists, the law and economics scholars or -- certainly -- by the moralists. I think an accurate appreciation of the present and future of class action litigation requires a heavy dollop of legal realism. One needs to appreciate the evolutionary arms race that is afoot between entrenched corporate interests and entrepreneurial plaintiffs' lawyers. Scholars and members of Congress are largely preoccupied with fine-tuning the rules governing the class action. Corporate lawyers, meanwhile, have plotted its demise.
My own view is that class actions -- warts and all -- do far more good than harm. I take it as beyond dispute that the threat of class action liability plays a vital role in deterring corporate wrongdoing. And while one might argue -- as many scholars do -- that class actions in contemporary practice may tend tooverdeter, or that agency costs hamper the effectiveness of the class action device, I am aware of no serious argument that we should ditch class actions in their entirety. Everyone seems to agree that sound public policy requires collective litigation be available for small-claim plaintiffs who would not have the incentive or resources to remedy harms or deter wrongdoing in one-on-one proceedings.
In any event, class actions have to exist if we want to fix them. If companies may render themselves impervious to the class action procedure simply by checking a box that says "I do not wish to be exposed to class actions," then -- ultimately -- all of the scholarly reform proposals will have been for naught. Accordingly, I would add to the heap of reform offeringsmy own proposed amendment to Rule 23, which would simply provide that the procedures set forth in the rule may not be waived by a standard-form adhesion contract.
But I am not holding my breath. Instead, I offer a dismal prediction of the near-total demise of the modern class action, organized as follows:

questions.question: Whether the widespread use of contractual collective-action waivers (often coupled with mandatory individual arbitration) will substantially reduce or effectively eliminate class action litigation as a mechanism for aggregating small claims across many areas of law.
Whether courts and other legal responses can meaningfully limit the enforceability or spread of contractual waivers of collective litigation and thereby preserve access to aggregated remedies.
Whether the displacement of class actions by individual arbitration and waivers undermines deterrence of corporate wrongdoing and access to remedies for plaintiffs with small stakes.

papers.node_id: 44textechlrev281!!ARTICLE: OUTSOURCING AMERICAN CIVIL JUSTICE: MANDATORY ARBITRATION CLAUSES IN CONSUMER AND EMPLOYMENT CONTRACTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: OUTSOURCING AMERICAN CIVIL JUSTICE: MANDATORY ARBITRATION CLAUSES IN CONSUMER AND EMPLOYMENT CONTRACTS
papers.authors: Judge Craig Smith; Judge Eric V. Moye
papers.abstract:
The Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial is vanishing before our very eyes.Many sources point to the increased reliance upon alternative dispute resolution, and mandatory arbitration specifically, as an explanation for this trend.As practicing attorneys, we never paid much attention to the increasing impact arbitration was having on our civil justice system. Since taking the bench, however, we have witnessed an alarming increase in the use of contract clauses mandating arbitration as a mechanism to take the resolution of civil conflicts away from citizen-juries and place it instead into the hands of professional arbitrators. The practical effect of enforcing these provisions is a paradigmatic shift in our civil justice system-no longer is it based upon the fundamental right of trial by jury. A person cannot open a bank account, obtain a credit card, buy a car, or use a cell phone without contracting away the Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial.In reality, a person must yield his or her very access to the courts in order to meaningfully participate in our modern society.Slowly but surely, the widespread enforcement of mandatory arbitration clauses has chipped away at the basic tenets of contract law and of the fundamental freedoms upon which our nation was founded: the right to a jury trial in civil cases.
In this Article, we focus our criticism on the use of mandatory arbitration clauses in consumer and employment agreements, not in contracts between entities operating at arm's-length.We recognize the ostensible benefits that arbitration brings to agreements between parties of equal bargaining power. These include, inter alia, confidentiality, expediency, and cost efficiency.While this alternative forum may serve the purpose of judicial efficiency, the hidden deleterious effects associated with its use in resolving disputes between parties of unequal bargaining power drastically outweigh its value.
We discuss the gradual transition away from our traditional, jury-based civil justice system to a privatized system of conflict resolution, with focus onthe U.S. Supreme Court's expansive interpretation of the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA). Part I of this Article recognizes the Seventh Amendment right to a trial in civil cases and sets the stage for mandatory arbitration's erosion of this constitutional right. Part II traces the evolution of case law interpreting the FAA and the development of the Court's current policy favoring arbitration. Part III addresses the current state of this area's jurisprudence as established by two recent Supreme Court decisions: AT&T Mobility, L.L.C. v. Concepcion and Rent-A-Center, West, Inc. v. Jackson.Part IV identifies problems posed by the use of arbitration in other than arm's-length transactions, emphasizing its restriction on individual access to our civil justice system, vis-a-vis the Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial. We submit that, in these types of transactions, the current policy endorsing blanket enforcement of agreements to arbitrate should cease. Instead, courts should adopt a national policy returning to constitutional protection and disfavoring mandated arbitration and contracts of adhesion. Part V discusses the various legislative proposals that would restrict or eliminate arbitration in consumer and employment contracts. Finally, Part VI suggests that Congress implement legislation to protect relationships between parties of unequal bargaining power from the harmful consequences of a national policy favoring arbitration.
. The Seventh Amendment Right to a Trial by Jury
The right to trial by jury is the only right that received the attention of the Framers of the Constitution in two separate amendments to the Bill of Rights.Many scholars and practitioners have noted, and some with alarm, the increased use of contract clauses mandating arbitration as the mechanism to take decisions related to the rights of competing parties away from citizen-juries and place them instead into the hands of professional arbiters.Some commentators, as well as a number of jurists, have even suggested that the increased requirement of arbitration cannot coexist with the constitutionally guaranteed right to trial by jury.
A number of guarantees that were considered fundamental by the Framers of the United States Constitution were not included in that document's original drafts. These guarantees were thought to be indispensable to the essence of the Republic, and as such, were placed within the Bill of Rights prior to the Constitution's ratification.
In Adamson v. California, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the Fifth Amendment protection against self-incrimination was not so fundamental as toapply to state prosecutions.Notably, the Justices differed over the incorporation of the Bill of Rights to the individual states.The Court's analysis turned on the notion of the fundamental nature of the rights as enumerated.Writing for the Court, Justice Miller provided the following guidance as gleaned from earlier Supreme Court precedent: the only way the Bill of Rights protection could be applied in state court would be if it were "implicit in the concept of ordered liberty."In other words, a right must be so basic-so fundamental-that no system could be considered truly just without providing for such a right. The guarantees of speech, free exercise of religion, and security in persons and homes were considered directly fundamental.Rights of the criminally accused have been similarly characterized.The Magna Carta notwithstanding, however, the right to trial by jury in a civil case has not been determined to be so fundamental.
In Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Co. v. City of Chicago in 1897, the Supreme Court for the first time held as fundamental a specific provision of the Bill of Rights, the Just Compensation Clause of the Fifth Amendment, through the due process guarantees of the Fourteenth Amendment and thereby made the same applicable to the individual states.In Malloy v. Hogan, the Court specifically rejected the notion that the Fourteenth Amendment applied to the states "only a 'watered-down, subjective version of the individual guarantees of the Bill of Rights.'"Thereafter, through the first half of the twentieth century, constitutional jurisprudence struggled with the question of the rights secured by the first eight amendments to the Constitution and their applicability to the states.For the most part, the answer came to be, occasionally begrudgingly: "Yes, they are fundamental."Hence, as the incorporation of the Bill of Rights continued throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, a majority of the Court determined many rights to be fundamental and therefore guaranteed to all citizens of the United States.

papers.node_id: 40textechlrev37!!ARTICLE: OVERVIEW OF ARBITRATION CLAUSES IN CONSUMER FINANCIAL SERVICES CONTRACTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: OVERVIEW OF ARBITRATION CLAUSES IN CONSUMER FINANCIAL SERVICES CONTRACTS
papers.abstract:
Agreements to arbitrate are commonly incorporated into consumer contracts.One noted practitioner cites two Supreme Court opinions, Allied-Bruce Terminix Cos. v. Dobson and Doctor's Associates, Inc. v. Casarotto, for "creat[ing] a sea change in the way that consumer arbitration would be viewed."This trend has had a significant impact on consumer financial services contracts.A study found that among all types of consumer contracts, arbitration provisions appear most frequently in financial services contracts-69.2% of agreements in the credit card, banking, investment, accounting, and tax consulting fields have arbitration clauses.The same study found that seventeen out of the eighteen consumer contracts for homeowner's insurance, renter's insurance, auto insurance, and health insurance contained arbitration clauses.Thus, when faced with consumer litigation, financial services companies often seek to enforce these agreements and send the dispute to arbitration, which may be more efficient than litigating in court and can offer other benefits.
Yet, merely having an arbitration provision in the contract is only the first step to achieving the goal of sending the dispute to arbitration.In recent years, courts in some states have been hesitant to enforce arbitration clauses in consumer disputes for a wide variety of reasons.Companies or individuals drafting and seeking to enforce such agreements, therefore, need to be aware of the issues that have caused courts to not enforce agreements to arbitrate.
