shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes and criticizes the Supreme Court's decision in Epic Systems upholding class/collective-action waivers under the FAA, and Paper B examines how class-action waivers operate in practice and how courts treat arbitration rights in aggregate litigation contexts.

shared_topics.topic: standards for waiver and revival of the right to arbitrate (litigation conduct, prejudice, futility)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B is devoted to the doctrinal tests courts apply to determine when a party has waived or can revive arbitration rights (including prejudice and futility considerations), and Paper A engages this issue insofar as class/collective waivers and compelled individual arbitration raise questions about when arbitration obligations should be enforced or treated as effectively waived.

shared_topics.topic: tension between the FAA's pro‑arbitration policy and statutory or equitable protections for collective employee action (e.g., NLRA §7)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the conflict between the FAA and NLRA Section 7 rights to engage in concerted activity, arguing Epic Systems misread that tension, while Paper B discusses how the FAA's policy influences courts' willingness to enforce or revive arbitration rights against competing fairness or statutory concerns in class/aggregate settings.

shared_topics.topic: impact of arbitration and waiver doctrines on access to remedies and enforcement of employment (and other) rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how class/collective-action waivers can undercut enforcement of the FLSA and other worker-protection laws by precluding effective aggregation, and Paper B highlights the economic and practical consequences when arbitration rights are found waived or when waiver standards in class actions create uncertainty about claim resolution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6jempiricallegalstud768!!ARTICLE: Measuring the Value of Class and Collective Action Employment Settlements: A Preliminary Assessment
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Measuring the Value of Class and Collective Action Employment Settlements: A Preliminary Assessment

shared_topics.topic: effect and enforceability of class-action waivers in employment arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines employers' express arbitration provisions barring class actions and the debate over whether such waivers deny adequate relief to employees, while Paper B analyzes how courts treat class-action waivers in doctrinal waiver/revival disputes and the special complexities that aggregate litigation poses for enforcing arbitration rights.

shared_topics.topic: whether aggregation is necessary to obtain redress for low‑value employment claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically questions the assumption that low‑value employment claims are economically infeasible to pursue individually and therefore require class treatment, and Paper B addresses how aggregate‑action doctrines (including futility and revival) and waiver rulings affect the practical availability of aggregate remedies for such claims.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrines and standards that determine when arbitration rights are lost or restored
shared_topics.justification: Paper B maps and critiques the varying jurisdictional standards for waiver and revival of the right to arbitrate, and Paper A engages with the role courts have played (and assumptions courts make) about arbitration versus class litigation when deciding whether arbitration clauses should be enforced in employment disputes.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs among aggregation, party autonomy, litigation costs/delay, and deterrence in employment disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes the institutional tradeoffs—aggregation can lower access costs and fund counsel but reduces individual autonomy and may change recoveries—while Paper B frames waiver/revival and fairness doctrines as judicial mechanisms that mediate those tradeoffs by determining whether parties must litigate collectively or may be forced into individual arbitration.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63fordhamlrev1499!!SYMPOSIUM: NEW YORK STOCK EXCHANGE, INC. SYMPOSIUM ON ARBITRATION IN THE SECURITIES INDUSTRY
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: NEW YORK STOCK EXCHANGE, INC. SYMPOSIUM ON ARBITRATION IN THE SECURITIES INDUSTRY

shared_topics.topic: arbitration as a faster, economical alternative to court litigation in securities and related disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that securities disputes are increasingly channeled into arbitration because court litigation is expensive and slow and arbitration promises speed and economy; Paper B documents the broader trend—driven by FAA jurisprudence and Supreme Court decisions—toward resolving consumer, commercial, securities and employment disputes through arbitration rather than through courts.

shared_topics.topic: the requirement that arbitration procedures be fair in fact and appearance to preserve legitimacy and access to justice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that arbitration must be fair both substantively and visually or its popularity will wane and investor confidence suffer; Paper B treats fairness as a central consideration in waiver and revival doctrines—examining prejudice, futility, and equitable factors courts use when deciding whether arbitration rights were relinquished or should be reinstated.

shared_topics.topic: the strain placed on arbitration by complex financial products and aggregate/class litigation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that increased public participation and increasingly complex products (ADRs, derivatives, limited partnerships) have driven more disputes into arbitration; Paper B analyzes how class actions and aggregate litigation complicate enforcement of arbitration agreements—creating futility, waiver, and revival issues that courts resolve in varied and sometimes inconsistent ways.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:Intrastate Choice of Applicable Law in the UCC

shared_topics.topic: limits of party autonomy to contractually determine the governing legal regime
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether parties can, by agreement, select a different Article or jurisdiction's version of the UCC to govern a transaction that takes place entirely within one state; Paper B analyzes the enforceability and limits of arbitration agreements and when courts will refuse to honor or will revive those agreed dispute-resolution mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: variation among jurisdictions and the resulting unpredictability in enforcement of contractual dispute rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on differences in state enactments of the UCC and how choice-of-law or local enactment can lead to different applicable rules even for intrastate transactions, while Paper B surveys divergent state and federal standards for waiver and revival of arbitration rights that produce inconsistent outcomes across fora.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial doctrines and public policy in overriding, interpreting, or reviving contractual rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts apply the UCC and may be constrained or guided by other choice-of-law principles and statutory provisions when determining applicable law, and Paper B examines how courts invoke doctrines like prejudice, futility, fairness, and the federal policy favoring arbitration to find waiver or to revive previously waived arbitral rights.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IS ADJUDICATION A PUBLIC GOOD? "OVERCROWDED COURTS" AND THE PRIVATE SECTOR ALTERNATIVE OF ARBITRATION

shared_topics.topic: how judicial doctrines and court decisions influence the availability and enforcement of arbitration rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes doctrinal standards (waiver, revival, futility) that courts apply to determine when arbitration rights are lost or restored and how Supreme Court decisions expanded the FAA's reach; Paper B considers how policy choices (e.g., user fees, allocation of court resources) and court practices impact whether arbitration is used as an alternative and how access to adjudication is structured.

shared_topics.topic: fairness and distributional concerns about who gets access to subsidized adjudication versus private arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames waiver and revival doctrines in terms of fairness to parties (including putative class members) and the consequences of denying arbitration or reviving it; Paper B treats court subsidies and proposed user-fee regimes as questions of fairness about which disputants should receive taxpayer-funded adjudication versus pay for private arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: judicial role in enforcing, reviewing, and reviving arbitral rights and awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether and to what extent courts must provide judicial review or supervision of arbitral awards (including confirmation/enforcement) under due process, and critiques judicial deference; Paper B examines the circumstances and standards under which courts will find waiver of arbitration, decline to compel arbitration, or later revive the right to arbitrate, i.e., when and how courts intervene in the availability of arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: procedural fairness and protective standards governing access to arbitration (due process, waiver, prejudice, futility)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames arbitration disputes in terms of procedural due process (Matthews balancing) and the need for safeguards like review to prevent erroneous deprivations, while Paper B focuses on fairness‑based doctrines—waiver, prejudice, futility, and revival—that govern when parties lose or regain the procedural right to arbitrate.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes competence-competence, separability, and the First Options 'clear and unmistakable' delegation doctrine—i.e., when parties can vest arbitrators with final authority to decide their own jurisdiction. shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats consent-related doctrines (separability/prima paint, 'core' consent issues) and how parties may contractually allocate decisionmaking about jurisdiction; Paper B examines when a party's litigation conduct constitutes waiver of the right to arbitrate and when that right may be revived—both focus on how agreement language and party behavior alter whether arbitration can be enforced.

shared_topics.topic: timing of judicial intervention and the effect of precedent/FAA policy on arbitration rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers timing (when courts may intervene before or after tribunal constitution) and relies on Supreme Court precedents shaping competence-competence; Paper B traces how Supreme Court decisions and FAA policy influence evolving doctrines (waiver, revival, futility), and both discuss the temporal point at which courts should defer to or reclaim jurisdiction over arbitration issues.

papers.node_id: 43vandlrev1199!!ARTICLE: Securities Arbitration After McMahon, Rodriguez, and the New Rules: Can Investors' Rights Really Be Protected?
papers.title: ARTICLE: Securities Arbitration After McMahon, Rodriguez, and the New Rules: Can Investors' Rights Really Be Protected?
papers.abstract:
Securities arbitrationis now ascendant as a favored device for resolving disputes between broker-dealers and their customers, and much of this recent status derives from a series of United States Supreme Court decisions.Culminating inShearson/American Express, Inc. v. McMahonandRodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/American Express, Inc.,these decisions have ended the reign of certain restrictive judicial decisions that previously governed the availability of arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA or Arbitration Act).Accordingly, such developments presage a greatly expanded use of arbitration as a future means of resolving disputes between broker-dealers and customers.Indeed, since the Supreme Court placed its imprimaturon the arbitration process, the arbitral forum already has become the likely, and in some instances the mandated,situs of deliberative proceedings on such conflicts.Logically, the focus of the debate and inquiry on the general subject of brokerage agreement dispute resolution must turn to the nature of this specific process.
Given the prominence that securities arbitration is likely to enjoy in the future, probing questions must be asked now regarding the effectiveness, basic fairness, and even legality of the procedures that effectuate it.  Underscoring the importance of such inquiry are certain basic facts about securities arbitration in America today.  First, this dispute resolution process is most often administered by organizations affiliated with, and indeed part of, the securities industry; and second, the process is predictably preferred by that industry to traditional litigation.Unquestionably, then, the inquiry must begin by addressing the circumstances under which a customer elects or agrees to have disputes resolved through arbitration, and continue through the hearing, final award, and any subsequent judicial challenges.  The following questions also should be posed in the interest of assuring both integrity and effectivenessin the resolution of conflicts through this important vehicle.
Does the brokerage agreement contain an adequate disclosure mechanism that not only will highlight the existence of a predispute arbitration clause in an agreement but also explain its effect to prospective brokerage firm customers?Further, even when such a mechanism is instituted, should there be an express prohibition against the current practice in many brokerage firms of interposing mandatory arbitration clauses as conditions precedent to opening certain types of trading accounts?
Do sufficient and reliable means exist for notifying customers of the available options and proper procedures when disputes arise?In the event the arbitration vehicle is chosen or required, do the options include the possibility of proceeding in nonindustry sponsored arbitral forums such as the American Arbitration Association (AAA)?Should they?  Is there an effective and convenient process for acquiring information and documents for case preparation prior to the arbitration hearing?Within the context of the hearing, do the arbitration rules provide the requisite accommodation between the need for flexibility (in the interest of economy, convenience, and ascertainment of truth)on the one hand, and definiteness, thoroughness, and decorum, on the other?Additionally, are there effective means of balancing the competing but important policies of avoiding arbitrator conflicts of interest, and retaining arbitrators with sufficient experience to understand the complex workings of the capital markets and the market regulatory system, brokerage firm operations and procedures, and the ever expanding panoply of investment devices?
Additional questions arise with respect to the application of legal theories underlying claims brought to arbitration.  To what extent, for example, do the arbitrators understand the pertinent legal theories?  Even if they understand these theories, do they actively apply them?  Is anything lost if the theories are not applied specifically and knowledgeably?  That is, should the arbitrators' judgments based on what is "fair," "just," or merely "sensible" be a sufficient basis for an award?  Should written opinions accompany arbitration awards, and would such opinions serve the public interest?  More specifically, would written opinions provide guidance to the securities industry and its current and prospective customers concerning what are proper brokerage and customer-investor standards of conduct?  Would such opinions generate a known and coherent body of jurisprudence in the field and specify the basis of the decision to facilitate subsequent judicial review of awards in proper instances?  Are large, complex cases more deserving of strict applications of law, and perhaps more juridical evidentiary processes?  How might such processes be implemented?  In this regard, should some matters be referred by arbitration panels to the courts, and if so, what standards should apply for referring appropriate cases?
The questions set out above are among the more critical ones that have generated extensive discussions by the Securities and ExchangeCommission (SEC or Commission);securities industry organizations such as the Securities Industry Conference on Arbitration (SICA), the Securities Industry Association (SIA), and the self-regulatory organizations (SROs);and various other organizations.  These discussions have culminated in the recent approval by the SEC of substantial revisions to the previous regulatory scheme for arbitration of customer brokerage disputes in industry sponsored arbitration forums.This Article is intended as a contribution to the ongoing attempts at improving the arbitration process.  The discussion will concentrate mainly on the new rules and recent decisional law; additionally, however, treatment will be accorded subjects not necessarily raised in those rules and decisions.
This Article has four main theses.  First, because the Supreme Court has skewed the avenues of choice for resolving disputes between broker-dealers and customers decidedly in favor of securities arbitration, the arbitration system -- most particularly those systems conducted by the securities industry itself -- must sustain a heavy burden to create and effectuate an absolutely fair, efficient, and economical process.  Second, the new arbitration rules, as well as the enthusiasm and resolve with which the industry approached these revisions of the prior rules, bespeak a significantly improved regime that is capable of meeting that burden.  Third, even this new regime can be improved, and in the important, over-arching interests of investor protection,investor confidence, and the integrity of capital markets, additional revisions such as the ones suggested in this Article should be considered carefully.  And fourth, the industry, the SEC, and the public must continue to monitor and evaluate the securities arbitration process.
Part II of this Article explores the historical development of securities arbitration, initially analyzing its statutory underpinnings and the evolution of applicable case law, and then explaining the complex, interactive regulatory roles of the SROs and the SEC in the arbitration process.  The dynamic interplay of economic, judicial, legislative, and regulatory forces in recent years has imposed upon securities arbitration the daunting burden of protecting the rights of investors and their confidence in the capital markets without inhibiting the process of national economic growth through rigorous investment and finance activities.
Part III discusses issues that are crucial to the improvement of arbitration procedures and their administration and sets forth specific recommendations.  The recommendations focus primarily on the need, in certain instances, for a prohibition against mandatory arbitration clauses; the desirability of allowing investors to choose to arbitrate before the American Arbitration Association; the importance of certain additional protections against arbitrator conflicts of interest; and the need to develop rules governing the conduct of complex cases, including the referral of cases to the courts.

questions.question: Whether the securities arbitration process, particularly when administered by industry-affiliated organizations, adequately protects investors' rights and delivers fair, efficient, and legitimate dispute outcomes compared with alternative dispute forums.
Whether mandatory predispute arbitration clauses in brokerage agreements systematically disadvantage customers and should be prohibited or restricted to preserve access to justice.

Whether procedural reforms-such as greater forum choice, enhanced disclosure of arbitration clauses, stronger safeguards against arbitrator conflicts of interest, requirements for reasoned awards, and tailored rules for complex cases-would measurably improve investor protection and confidence in the arbitration system.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27seattleulrev659!!ARTICLE:Contractual Stipulation for Judicial Review and Discovery in United States-Japan Arbitration Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Contractual Stipulation for Judicial Review and Discovery in United States-Japan Arbitration Contracts

shared_topics.topic: limited scope of judicial review of arbitral awards and remedies for errors of law or fact
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how statutory and case law severely constrain judicial review of arbitrators' legal and factual determinations—Paper A in the context of securities arbitration and recent Supreme Court decisions, and Paper B in U.S.–Japan transnational arbitration—each proposing contractual or regulatory measures to expand or ameliorate review in appropriate cases.

shared_topics.topic: restrictive discovery rules and evidentiary control in arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Both articles criticize arbitration’s curtailed discovery and flexible evidentiary practices as threats to fair adjudication—Paper A questions whether industry rules provide adequate pre-hearing access to information, and Paper B recommends drafting discovery schemes into arbitration agreements to address limited discovery in U.S. and Japanese practice.

shared_topics.topic: the fairness and enforceability of predispute/mandatory arbitration clauses and informed consent
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with whether parties truly consent to arbitration and how predispute clauses should be disclosed or limited—Paper A examines mandatory arbitration clauses in brokerage accounts and disclosure mechanisms for investors, while Paper B warns transnational parties (especially those lacking counsel) may unwittingly bind themselves to arbitration terms that disadvantage them.

shared_topics.topic: arbitrator authority, neutrality, conflicts of interest, and decisionmaking standards
shared_topics.justification: Both papers question the arbitral decisionmaker’s powers and governance—Paper A focuses on conflicts of interest in industry-sponsored panels and the need for rules to ensure experienced but impartial arbitrators, while Paper B documents arbitrators’ near-unchecked discretion to admit evidence, misapply law, or reach idiosyncratic outcomes and urges contractual or legal safeguards.

shared_topics.topic: tailoring procedural safeguards for complex or high‑stakes disputes (including referral to courts or special rules)
shared_topics.justification: Both authors argue that more elaborate procedural protections are warranted in large or complex cases—Paper A advocates rules for complex securities disputes and possible referral standards to courts, and Paper B suggests parties can (and should) contract for expanded discovery and judicial review in particularly important transnational contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2012michstlrev1103!!ARTICLE: WHAT'S LEFT TO REMEDY WAGE THEFT? HOW ARBITRATION MANDATES THAT BAR CLASS ACTIONS IMPACT LOW-WAGE WORKERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHAT'S LEFT TO REMEDY WAGE THEFT? HOW ARBITRATION MANDATES THAT BAR CLASS ACTIONS IMPACT LOW-WAGE WORKERS

shared_topics.topic: effects of mandatory arbitration clauses on access to remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how pre-dispute mandatory arbitration clauses imposed by stronger parties (broker-dealers in Paper A; employers in Paper B) restrict claimants' ability to vindicate statutory or contractual rights, with Paper A questioning prohibitions on mandatory clauses in brokerage agreements and Paper B showing how class-waivers and individual arbitration make recovery for low-wage workers practically impossible.

shared_topics.topic: forum choice and the suitability of arbitral forums versus alternatives
shared_topics.justification: Both articles question whether the chosen arbitral forum is appropriate — Paper A critiques industry-sponsored forums and advocates allowing non‑industry fora like the AAA or court referral for some matters, while Paper B critiques private arbitration as an ill‑fitting forum for low-wage wage‑and‑hour claims and proposes alternative venues (worker centers, unions, specialized courts).

shared_topics.topic: procedural rules (aggregation, complexity, and handling of complex/collective claims) shaping substantive rights
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how procedural features of arbitration (e.g., prohibitions on class or collective proceedings in Paper B; need for special procedures or court referral for large/complex securities cases in Paper A) determine whether claimants can effectively aggregate claims, obtain full relief, or have complex cases adjudicated with adequate legal process.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private arbitration regimes and public enforcement/regulatory oversight
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the relationship between private arbitration and public enforcement: Paper A emphasizes the SEC and SROs' regulatory role over securities arbitration and the need for continued oversight, while Paper B documents weak public enforcement of wage laws and shows how mandatory arbitration compounds under‑enforcement by agencies like Departments of Labor.

shared_topics.topic: proposals for institutional or rule reforms to make arbitration fairer for vulnerable claimants
shared_topics.justification: Both propose concrete reforms to address perceived inequities — Paper A recommends banning some mandatory clauses, stronger conflict‑of‑interest rules, allowing alternative fora, and special rules for complex cases, while Paper B offers paths including regulatory strategies, collective‑claim mechanisms, and forum redesign (unions, worker centers, specialized courts) to restore remedy access for low‑wage workers.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105minnlrev619!!ARTICLE: The Arbitration Rules: Procedural Rulemaking by Arbitration Providers
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Arbitration Rules: Procedural Rulemaking by Arbitration Providers

shared_topics.topic: arbitration providers' procedural rulemaking that changes parties' rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how an arbitration administrator (NAM) adopted an internal rule that functionally eliminated class arbitration for parties who selected that provider, and Paper B analyzes how securities-industry and SRO arbitration rules (and recent revisions approved by the SEC) materially shape procedures and outcomes in investor–broker disputes.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of mandatory predispute arbitration clauses and the adequacy of consent/notice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how standard-form arbitration clauses combined with a provider's silent-rule can wipe out class remedies without claimant awareness, and Paper B interrogates brokerage agreements' predispute arbitration clauses, calling for better disclosure and even prohibitions where arbitration is imposed as a condition of account opening.

shared_topics.topic: industry-sponsored arbitration and risk of provider/arbitrator bias or conflict of interest
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that a private arbitration administrator made a consequential rule change outside public view, raising concerns about private actors controlling dispute rules, while Paper B expressly critiques securities arbitration forums run by industry-affiliated organizations and urges stronger protections against arbitrator conflicts of interest and industry capture.

shared_topics.topic: procedural fairness and pre-hearing safeguards (notice, discovery, case management)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how a hidden procedural rule deprived claimants of the collective forum needed to vindicate rights, implicating fairness and notice, and Paper B systematically questions whether arbitration rules provide adequate disclosure, notice, access to documents, and case-management procedures (especially in complex cases) to ensure fair outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between arbitration processes and court oversight or referral (reviewability and forum boundaries)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Supreme Court FAA doctrine (Lamps Plus) and state contract principles with private-provider rules that limit class arbitration, implicating the boundaries between arbitration and judicial protection, while Paper B discusses written opinions, referral of complex matters to courts, and standards to facilitate judicial review of arbitration awards.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of mandatory arbitration clauses for statutory claims
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze recent judicial developments that expand enforcement of predispute arbitration agreements to resolve statutory rights — Paper A critiques the Supreme Court's Pyett/Circuit City line allowing CBAs or employer conditions to mandate arbitration of discrimination claims, while Paper B examines McMahon/Rodriguez and related FAA jurisprudence that firmly channels securities claims into arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: procedural fairness and adequacy of arbitral procedures (discovery, representation, evidentiary standards, written opinions)
shared_topics.justification: Both articles probe whether arbitration processes provide adequate procedural protections: Paper A compares grievance arbitration under CBAs (union representation, no forum costs) to litigation and employer-imposed systems, and Paper B evaluates discovery, evidentiary rigor, need for written opinions, and tailored rules for complex securities cases.

shared_topics.topic: repeat-player dynamics and arbitrator impartiality/conflicts of interest
shared_topics.justification: Each paper raises concerns about power imbalances and arbitrator incentives in private adjudication: Paper A discusses how unions and employers as repeat players (and arbitrators' need to stay acceptable to parties) affect labor arbitration, and Paper B focuses on industry-administered securities forums, potential arbitrator conflicts, and the need for safeguards against biased panels.

shared_topics.topic: access to justice and the impact of arbitration on enforcement of public rights
shared_topics.justification: Both works assess whether arbitration expands or constrains claimants' ability to vindicate public statutory rights — Paper A investigates whether CBA arbitration improves access for low-wage workers compared with tribunals (using Canadian experience), while Paper B questions whether arbitration adequately protects investors' rights and confidence in the capital markets.

shared_topics.topic: role of public regulation, courts, and reform in shaping arbitration systems
shared_topics.justification: Each article considers the role of external oversight and possible reforms: Paper A situates the debate in statutory and case-law regimes (Gardner‑Denver, Pyett) and looks to comparative institutional responses (HRTO in Canada), while Paper B analyzes SEC rule changes, SRO roles, and advocates rule reforms and continued regulatory monitoring of securities arbitration.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64alalrev1013!!ARTICLE: HORTON HATCHES THE EGG: CONCERTED ACTION INCLUDES CONCERTED DISPUTE RESOLUTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HORTON HATCHES THE EGG: CONCERTED ACTION INCLUDES CONCERTED DISPUTE RESOLUTION

shared_topics.topic: how the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) interacts with and can be displaced by sector-specific federal protections
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze tension between the FAA's strong policy favoring enforcement of arbitration clauses and later federal statutes or regulatory schemes that protect party rights — Paper A examines how Supreme Court FAA jurisprudence reshaped securities arbitration and the SEC/SRO role, while Paper B argues that the FAA cannot be allowed to invalidate statutory labor protections (NLA/NLRA) that preserve employees' concerted rights.

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability and legitimacy of mandatory predispute arbitration clauses that limit collective or forum options
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with whether employers/broker-dealers can require mandatory arbitration as a precondition of relationship entry and whether such clauses that preclude class, collective, or alternative forum procedures should be enforced or prohibited — Paper A recommends reconsidering or banning mandatory brokerage arbitration in some contexts, and Paper B contends that clauses waiving concerted/class remedies are invalid under federal labor law.

shared_topics.topic: requirements for clear disclosure and express contractual language about what arbitration clauses do to parties' rights
shared_topics.justification: Both papers stress that arbitration agreements must be explicit and accompanied by adequate disclosures: Paper A calls for mechanisms that highlight predispute arbitration clauses and explain their effects to investors, while Paper B emphasizes that arbitration clauses must clearly state how collective claims may be pursued (or else be void for unreasonably restricting NLRA rights).

shared_topics.topic: design and procedural rules of arbitral forums to protect vulnerable parties' ability to obtain meaningful relief
shared_topics.justification: Both debate how arbitral procedure and forum administration affect fairness — Paper A focuses on industry-sponsored versus neutral forums, arbitrator conflicts, discovery and complex-case rules, and written opinions, and Paper B focuses on whether arbitration can or must accommodate collective adjudication (e.g., joint/collective arbitration) so that employees retain effective concerted remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83nyulrev1420!!ARTICLE: THE UNCONSCIONABILITY GAME: STRATEGIC JUDGING AND THE EVOLUTION OF FEDERAL ARBITRATION LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE UNCONSCIONABILITY GAME: STRATEGIC JUDGING AND THE EVOLUTION OF FEDERAL ARBITRATION LAW

shared_topics.topic: the Supreme Court-driven expansion of the Federal Arbitration Act and its consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how a series of Supreme Court decisions have firmly endorsed arbitration and transformed the FAA’s scope, creating pushback in lower courts; Paper B traces that same doctrinal shift (McMahon, Rodriguez, Shearson) and assesses its practical consequences for the rise of securities arbitration between broker-dealers and customers.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for policing or limiting enforcement of predispute arbitration clauses (e.g., unconscionability, regulatory prohibitions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how state contract doctrines like unconscionability operate as the remaining judicial channel to invalidate arbitration agreements and how lower courts may manipulate those doctrines; Paper B examines parallel tools — regulatory rules, possible prohibitions on mandatory clauses, and procedural safeguards — as means to constrain or condition enforceability in the securities-arbitration context.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of decisionmaking authority and forum choice between courts and arbitrators (including industry-sponsored vs. neutral forums)

papers.node_id: 79kylj347!!ARTICLE: Securities Arbitration Appeal: An Oxymoron No Longer?
papers.title: ARTICLE: Securities Arbitration Appeal: An Oxymoron No Longer?
papers.abstract:
Appealing a tribunal's decision has been likened to putting "the dice into the box for another throw."Although this notion conjures up a subjective image of the process, the right of appeal has been for centuries an essential element in ensuring the fairness of our civil litigation system.
That system has been under an increasingly comprehensive attack by critics, who argue that it is too cumbersome, burdensome, time consuming, formalistic, and expensive.Many of those same critics aggressively promote the arbitration process in its place, hailing arbitration as having none of the aforementioned problems, while having many virtues.Recent U.S. Supreme Court decisionsupholding the arbitrability of claims under Section 10(b) (and Rule 10b-5 promulgated thereunder) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934and Section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933have provided a great deal of momentum for the shifting of a multitude of civil disputes into the forum of arbitration.
This article does not attempt to evaluate or comment on the relative merits of this trend.Rather, it examines what would seem to be a logical outgrowth of it.  With the arbitration process coming to be relied upon more and more, it is in fact becoming more like the civil litigation system it was designed to replace.
Part I of this Article examines the statutory bases for judicial review of arbitration claims.Part II explores the common law development of the "manifest disregard" standard of review.Part III then examines three reasons for active judicial review of securities arbitration decisions.

questions.question: Whether courts should permit robust appellate or judicial review of arbitration awards in securities disputes.
Whether the growing reliance on arbitration for securities claims has made arbitration sufficiently like ordinary civil litigation to justify expanded judicial oversight.
What legal bases and policy justifications support different scopes of judicial review of arbitration decisions in securities disputes (i.e., how much review is appropriate and why).

papers.node_id: 92nwulrev69!!ARTICLE: SECURITIES ARBITRATION IN THE PUBLIC INTEREST: THE ROLE OF PUNITIVE DAMAGES
papers.title: ARTICLE: SECURITIES ARBITRATION IN THE PUBLIC INTEREST: THE ROLE OF PUNITIVE DAMAGES
papers.abstract:
In January of 1996, the Securities Arbitration Task Force of the National Association of Securities Dealers, Inc. (Task Force) submitted its Task Force Report, "Securities Arbitration Reform,"to the NASD Board of Governors. The Task Force Report contained more than 170 recommendations for improvement of the securities arbitration system administered by the NASD, a self-regulatory organization (SRO) charged with assisting the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in administering the federal securities laws.Although the Task Force found the NASD securities arbitration system to be "a relatively efficient, fair, and less costly system for resolution of disputes,"it expressed its belief that many areas existed for improvement of the system.The Task Force's goal was to strengthen a securities arbitration system that operates in the interests of the public, including both investors and members of the securities industry.
The most controversial recommendations contained in the Task Force Report related to punitive damages. Two specific proposals, that "punitive damages remain available in NASD arbitration"and that punitive damages awards be "limited to the lesser of two times compensatory damages or $ 750,000,"have drawn the most attention.
A related and important additional punitive damage recommendation is that "punitive damages be available in arbitration in each state where they would be available in court for the same claims."This recommendation would have the effect of reversing the law in the state of New York, where courts have determined that punitive damages are not available in arbitration.
Some members of the securities industry have contended that punitive damages should not be awarded at all in arbitration or have offered suggestions for a more restrictive approach to punitive damages awards.In contrast, others have vigorously criticized the recommendation to cap punitive damages. This issue of the Northwestern University Law Review contains such a critique by Professor Thomas J. Stipanowich.Professor Constantine N. Katsoris has also recently written on the subject.Professors Stipanowich and Katsoris both are highly critical of the proposal to cap punitive damages. Their views are of particular interest because they are, or have been, members of the Securities Industry Conference on Arbitration (SICA).
No one who has followed the debate about punitive damages in securities arbitration during the last ten years will be at all surprised by the vehemence with which views are presented on the subject. As the Task Force Report emphasized: "No subject has generated more widespread controversy or resulted in more polarization between investor and broker-dealer communities than the appropriateness of punitive damages in securities arbitration."
This article asserts that a reformed arbitration system operated by the NASD, subject to supervision by the SEC, accomplishes the goal of securities arbitration in the public interest. In support of that conclusion, the article reviews the background of the Task Force Report, discusses the NASD eligibility rule, predispute arbitration agreements, the role of choice, and punitive damages, and defends the Task Force recommendations regarding punitive damages.

questions.question: Whether allowing punitive damages in securities-industry arbitration, and imposing limits (caps) on those awards, affects the arbitration system's fairness, deterrence, and ability to serve the public interest.
Whether arbitration should mirror court practice on punitive damages across states - i.e., whether punitive damages in arbitration ought to be available wherever they would be available in court.

Whether a reformed, self-regulatory securities arbitration system, subject to federal supervision, provides an efficient, fair, and public-interest-serving forum for resolving investor-industry disputes.

papers.node_id: 25fordhamurblj193!!ARTICLE: SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A CLINICAL EXPERIMENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A CLINICAL EXPERIMENT
papers.abstract:
Disputes between the securities industry and its customers are generally resolved in arbitration, which is designed to be simpler, cheaper, and faster than courtroom litigation.Such arbitrations between brokers and customers have been held at the New York Stock Exchange since 1872.Thereafter, other securities industry self-regulatory organizations ("SROs") have also provided a forum for the arbitration of such disputes. However, before 1978, the var ious SROs had differing rules governing such arbitrations.
In 1977, the Securities Industry Conference on Arbitration ("SICA") was created to develop a Uniform Code of Arbitration ("Uniform Code") to be used by all the SROs.The Uniform Code was largely in place at all the participating SROs by 1980.After the adoption of the Uniform Code, SRO arbitrations grewsteadily from 830 in 1980to 7271 in.Moreover, before 1987, these arbitrations were largely voluntary on the part of the public. Yet after the United States Supreme Court's decision in Shearson/American Express, Inc. v. McMahon,they generally became mandatory.
In 1988, the first full year after McMahon, SRO arbitrations more than doubled from the year preceding McMahon. In addi tion to the increase in the number of SRO arbitrations, McMahon brought into arbitration more difficult cases, such as those involv ing violations of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organiza tion Act,the Securities Act of 1933,and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934,as well as employment and discrimination cases.At that point, arbitration began to look more like the courtroom through the introduction of expanded discovery re quests, more frequent prehearing conferences, and other proce dures intended to provide safeguards to ensure a fair and complete hearing.Understandably, these additional safeguards raised the costs of arbitration with the result that investors with small claims often found it difficult to obtain counsel to represent them. This often resulted either in the hiring of persons who were not attor neys, or the claimants simply representing themselves, pro se.
This Article discusses the use of non-attorneys in representing such clients, as well as pro se representation by such claimants. It then describes the efforts of the Securities and Exchange Commis sion ("SEC") to ensure that such claimants have access to ade quate and effective representation through the use of law school clinics. Finally, this Article raises numerous issues that must be considered before establishing such clinics, and concludes thatproper planning and adjustment is necessary for a successful clinical program.

papers.title: ARTICLE: Securities Arbitration: Issues of Interest
papers.abstract:
Let me begin by expressing my great personal regard for Dean Seligman, as well as the esteemed panel. This is a tough group to come before and call into question proposed changes to the securities arbitration process conducted by the National Association of Securities Dealers, Inc. ("NASD") and the other self-regulatory organizations, especially since Joel asked that we keep our remarks brief. Yet, I will not despair in the face of such overwhelming adversity. After all, I know something about securities arbitration. In a past life, I served on between five and ten New York Stock Exchange ("NYSE") panels pitting customers against their brokers and firms.
Customers, brokers, and firms won some and lost some on my panels. We did not award any punitive damages. The customers generally had honorable complaints and asserted them well. The brokers and firms also generally acquitted themselves in an honorable and professional manner. I believe that justice was served by those panels. Even if you could prove to me today that we were not right on a particular claim, I would continue to believe that all parties had a fair chance to be heard by an impartial panel. I am proud of my service.
It is not surprising therefore that I support arbitration for customer complaints. No doubt the process could be improved, and many of the TaskForce's recommendations would do just that.Nevertheless, I will focus on two issues where I may disagree with my fellow panelists: (1) the merits of a proposed punitive damages cap, and (2) the appropriateness of mandatory arbitration for employment discrimination claims.

questions.question: Whether imposing a cap on punitive damages in securities arbitration is justified and how such a cap affects compensation, deterrence, and fairness for claimants and respondents

Whether mandatory arbitration of employment discrimination claims is appropriate - i.e., how requiring arbitration (rather than access to court) impacts fairness, remedial outcomes, and enforcement of anti-discrimination protections

papers.node_id: 58bclrev1355!!ARTICLE: SHARING ECONOMY INEQUALITY: HOW THE ADOPTION OF CLASS ACTION WAIVERS IN THE SHARING ECONOMY PRESENTS A THREAT TO RACIAL DISCRIMINATION CLAIMS
papers.title: ARTICLE: SHARING ECONOMY INEQUALITY: HOW THE ADOPTION OF CLASS ACTION WAIVERS IN THE SHARING ECONOMY PRESENTS A THREAT TO RACIAL DISCRIMINATION CLAIMS
papers.abstract:
In March 2015, Gregory Selden, an African-American man, planned a weekend trip to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.Selden opted to use Airbnb, an online marketplace that connects homeowners with travelers seeking accommodations, to book his lodging.He browsed the listings, found a room listed as "available" for his desired dates, and contacted the host.The host, Paul, responded that despite the information on Airbnb, the room was not vacant on Selden's desired dates.Later that afternoon, Selden continued his search for travel accommodations on Airbnb and noticed something strange: the room he was rejected from earlier was still listed as "available."The odd circumstances surrounding the room's availability, combined with the fact that he included a picture of his face on his Airbnb profile, led Selden to believe that he mayhave been racially discriminated against.To test his hypothesis, he created two imitation accounts with white sounding names and profile pictures of white people.Using the imitation accounts, Selden again contacted Paul and requested the same room for the same dates--Paul immediately accepted the faux requests.
Shortly after his discovery, Selden filed a class-action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against Airbnb on behalf of himself and other African-Americans who had allegedly been discriminated against on Airbnb.He alleged that Airbnb violated Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Fair Housing Act of 1968, andThe district court, however, granted Airbnb's motion to compel arbitration, finding that the court lacked jurisdiction over Selden's substantive claim.The judge explained that the court could not hear the case because Selden agreed to Airbnb's terms of service when he created his account, which included an individual arbitration clause.Thus, not only was Selden precluded from a jury trial, but he was also barred from pursuing a class action claim.
Gregory Selden's failed attempt to bring forth a class-action claim highlights a troubling trend within the sharing economy: individual arbitration clauses found in terms of service agreements have made it nearly impossible todevelop effective racial discrimination claims against powerful companies such as Uber, Airbnb, and Lyft.The sharing economy purportedly creates pluralistic platforms where people can collaborate to buy and sell goods and services; however, racial discrimination has prevented minorities from having a fair opportunity to engage in this market.Lawyers and legal scholars are developing theories on how "marketplace" companies such as Airbnb could be found liable under existing law and are proposing ways in which regulations could be reformed.While such theories are maturing, these efforts may never be addressed by a court due to the widespread adoption of mandatory arbitration clauses in the sharing economy.
Mandatory arbitration clauses, which are often coupled with a class action waiver, present a unique and troubling challenge to racial discrimination due to clashing legal standards.An arbitration clause with a class action waiver requiresthat a plaintiff assert his or her claims individually.Racial discrimination cases, however, often require the resources and systemic relief that accompany a class action lawsuit.Thus, attempts to unearth systemic, racial discrimination issues in the sharing economy are held hostage at the hands of arbitration agreements that include class action waivers.As the sharing economy becomes increasingly pervasive in the lives of consumers, cases like Gregory Selden's will only become more common.
This Note examines Airbnb as a case study to explore the setbacks created by the omnipresence of individual arbitration clauses within the sharing economy.Part I of this Note discusses the emergence of the sharing economy, and discrimination in the sharing economy sphere.Part II provides a background of arbitration law and class action waivers, and explores why such clauses are popular in the sharing economy.Part III of this Note shifts to civil rights law and explains the strong tie between civil rights and class action claims.Further, it argues that the waivers in arbitration agreements pose a threat to minorities.Part IVof this Note argues despite the courts' unwillingness to limit class action waivers, Congress should pass legislation with a contrary congressional command to the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), or a federal agency should promulgate regulations banning class action waivers in the civil rights realm.

papers.node_id: 35ambuslj515!!ARTICLE: SHIFTING ATTORNEY'S FEES IN LITIGATION ATTACKING COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION AWARDS: A DISINCENTIVE FOR MERITLESS MOTIONS FOR CORRECTION, MODIFICATION OR VACATUR
papers.title: ARTICLE: SHIFTING ATTORNEY'S FEES IN LITIGATION ATTACKING COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION AWARDS: A DISINCENTIVE FOR MERITLESS MOTIONS FOR CORRECTION, MODIFICATION OR VACATUR
papers.authors: William H. Daughtrey; Donnie L. Kidd
papers.abstract:
"Contracts to arbitrate are not to be avoided by allowing one party to ignore the contract and resort to the courts. Such a course could lead to prolonged litigation, one of the very risks the parties, by contracting for arbitration, sought to eliminate."
Commercial arbitration has increased in popularity and use over the past decade as the business community has begun to realize the allure of arbitration proceedings.Instead of submitting claims to a prolonged and potentially expensive suit in the civil court system, contractingparties have opted to submit their claims to binding arbitration.The desirability of arbitration is obvious: the process is expedient, relaxes the formal rules of the judiciary, allows the parties to structure the proceedings and choose a convenient forum, and usually reduces the cost of dispute resolution.By simply including a contractual clause that submits claims to binding arbitration, the parties seek to avoid the cost and delay of civil litigation for existing or future disputes. Although the statutory authority enforcing arbitration awards varies among jurisdictions, these statutes are generally similar and ensure judicial recognition and enforcement of awards granted to the parties as the final resolution of their legal controversy.
After an arbitration panel issues an award on a claim the parties have agreed to arbitrate, a civil court may not alter that determination except under narrow limitations.A court may vacate or modify a final arbitration award only when the party challenging the award can demonstrate that the award was obtained by fraud or that the arbitrator was partial, exceeded his authority, improperly conducted the proceedings, or exhibited a manifest disregard of the applicable law.Otherwise, the court is bound to construe all doubts in favor of arbitration and confirm the award as it stands.
Although the grounds for seeking a modification or vacation of an award are exceedingly narrow and rarely successful, parties disgruntled with an award nevertheless do challenge a final award and require theopposing party to defend the determination in court.The result is sometimes a protracted trek through the court system to defend a "final" award against claims that are often without merit.If the parties agreed to submit to binding alternative dispute resolution, then such post-arbitration litigation is offensive to arbitration's goals of speed, efficiency, and cost containment.
While arbitration is not a perfect procedure for dispute resolution and may require some judicial review, parties' abuse of court review cannot continue if the use of commercial arbitration is to increase. If arbitration is to provide a final determination of claims rather than a prelude to extended litigation, then a disincentive must exist to discourage disgruntled parties from challenging proper and final arbitration awards. While some courts have already begun to sanction parties entering baseless motions for vacation, modification, or correction of awards,these decisions are few to date.
After an inquiry into the goals of alternative dispute resolution and a presentation of post-arbitration litigation abuses, the proposal here will be to amend existing arbitration statutes to permit the courts to award attorney's fees and costs against parties who file meritless motions for vacatur of final awards. While the American Rule holds the parties responsible for their own attorney's fees, the special purpose of arbitration may serve to provide a qualification to this rule in order tomeet the intended goals of alternative dispute resolution.Additionally, the interpretations of minority jurisdictions that have awarded attorney's fees provide additional support for the position advanced in this article.A mechanism that will award fees and costs against baseless claims should serve to reform the arbitration process by promoting the desired finality of commercial arbitration awards without denying judicial review of awards in the proper instances.

questions.question: Does permitting courts to award attorney's fees and costs against parties who file meritless post-arbitration motions to overturn, modify, or correct awards deter frivolous challenges and preserve arbitration's goals of finality, speed, and cost savings?
Is it legally and policy-wise justifiable to create an exception to the default rule that each party bears its own legal fees by allowing fee-shifting for baseless challenges to arbitration awards?
Would a fee-shifting regime aimed at discouraging meritless challenges risk chilling meritorious judicial review or otherwise unduly restrict access to court review of arbitration awards?

papers.title: ARTICLE: SICA: THE FIRST TWENTY YEARS
papers.abstract:
. The Evolution of the Arbitration Rules Presently in Effect at the Various Self-Regulatory Organizations(SROs)
The resolution of customers' securities disputes by arbitration can be traced back to 1871 at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).Since that time numerous other self-regulatory organizations (SROs) have established arbitration programs for the resolution of such disputes.
To fully understand the rules presently governing arbitration at SRO forums, and elsewhere, we must look at the development of the present system. We must explore the judicial developments that have channeled such disputes into arbitrationand also examine legislative attempts to alter or influence the process of securities arbitration.Finally, we must look at the establishment and impact of the Securities Industry Conference on Arbitration (SICA) over the past twenty years,the SRO's participation in the process, the oversight role of the Securities and Exchange Commission(SEC or Commission), and the alternative forum offered by the American Arbitration Association (AAA) in this area.
Securities arbitration is a vast topic concerning various issues, many of which could be the subject of their own article. This article is an overview of the area which, by necessity, must be brief and concise, and unfortunately cannot fully explore and develop each of these issues. Accordingly, the coverage is intended to be broad and to express the views of litigants from both sides of the spectrum. On the other hand, the author does, from time to time, express his personal opinions based upon his experiences andobservations as an arbitrator and a Public Member of SICA as to what is necessary to preserve the public's trust in the integrity of the SRO arbitration process. Absent such trust, securities arbitration cannot remain the basically mandatory system that it is today.

questions.question: How have arbitration rules and procedures at self-regulatory securities organizations evolved over the past twenty years in response to judicial, legislative, and institutional developments?

To what extent have the creation and activities of the Securities Industry Conference on Arbitration (SICA), SRO participation, regulatory oversight, and alternative arbitration forums influenced the administration, fairness, and public legitimacy of securities arbitration?
What reforms or procedural safeguards are necessary to preserve or restore public trust in the integrity of a mandatory securities arbitration system?

papers.node_id: 65amulrev307!!ARTICLE: SPEAK NOW OR HOLD YOUR PEACE: PREARBITRATION EXPRESS WAIVERS OF EVIDENT-PARTIALITY CHALLENGES
papers.title: ARTICLE: SPEAK NOW OR HOLD YOUR PEACE: PREARBITRATION EXPRESS WAIVERS OF EVIDENT-PARTIALITY CHALLENGES
papers.abstract:
One of the few ways a losing party can challenge the result of an arbitration in an American courtis to argue that the arbitrator displayed "evident partiality" that tainted the arbitration.Evident partiality essentially means that either the arbitrator was actually biased in favor of a party, or there were facts unknown to the parties that could make an objective observer think the arbitrator was biased.
Beyond that essence, however, courts and theorists are and have long been deeply divided about the content and the application of the doctrine of evident partiality, offering different formulations of the evident-partiality test and reaching conflicting results in similar cases.At the same time, judicial reduction of alternative avenues to challenge arbitration awards, such as "manifest disregard" of law orfacts,has increased pressure on the fractured evident-partiality doctrine. "Manifest disregard" refers to the judicially-crafted doctrine allowing vacatur of an award based on the "manifest disregard" of facts or law by the arbitral panel.With greater frequency, disappointed losing parties mount evident-partiality challenges as their best hope for overturning an award. As a result, before an arbitration, parties face significant uncertainty and the unattractive possibility of extended, expensive post-arbitration litigation of an evident-partiality challenge.
While courts and scholars wrestle with defining and rationalizing evident partiality, this Article recommends a different approach: Parties can use express, prearbitrationwaivers of evident-partiality objections to reduce uncertainty and increase efficiency by foreclosing a large number of the most inefficient type of evident-partiality challenges. The Article's core argument is that concerned parties can use waivers to avoid the muddle of current evident-partiality doctrine. At the same time, courts should enforce these waivers as consistent with arbitration's fundamental principles of consensual dispute resolution and procedural efficiency.
After this introduction, Part II gives background about the doctrine of evident partiality, explaining its origins and purposes, and describing the workings of the pre-arbitration disclosure process and post-award judicial evident-partiality challenges. It then introduces the problem caused by current and enduring uncertainties about the content and application of the evident-partiality doctrine, combined with the increased pressure placed on the doctrine's disuniformities by the judicial elimination or narrowing of other avenues to challenge arbitral awards, such as "manifest disregard."
Part III argues that litigants ought to use, and judges ought to enforce, express waivers of evident-partiality objections as a way to avoid the problems created by the current disarray in and pressure on the doctrine. This Part first explains how an express-waiver procedure would work, and focuses on express waivers that would bar evident-partiality challenges based on relationships that are somehow disclosed by the arbitrator prior to the arbitration. It then explains the practical virtues of express waivers to parties by showing how they can greatly reduce the problems and uncertainties created by the current fractures in evident-partiality doctrine. Finally, it offers a theoretical argument for judicial enforcement of these waivers that is rooted in arbitration's fundamental principles of mutual consent and procedural efficiency. This argument is connected to recent Supreme Court jurisprudence in other areas of arbitration law that emphasizes parties' ability and flexibility to determine by consent the procedures that will govern their arbitration.
Part IV addresses potential objections to the use and enforcement of express, pre-arbitration waivers of evident partiality challenges. Among the objections addressed are arguments that enforcing express waivers would create bad incentives for arbitrators to be less than forthcoming in their disclosures, conflict with arbitration statutes or arbitral rules, and worsen the unfairness caused by binding arbitration agreements in consumer and employment law. This Article argues that the proposal is consistent with arbitration statutes and rules. If properly limited to challenges based on disclosed relationships, the proposal has minimal potential for sanctioning fraud or unfairness and would allow the parties a fair amount of flexibility to determine the scope of waivers for themselves. Furthermore, general concerns about the unfairness of certain kinds of arbitration are not a good reason to refuse to enforce the proposed waivers because the current disorder in evident-partiality doctrine is not a good safety valve for unfairness in particular types of arbitration agreements.

questions.question: Whether parties to an arbitration may validly use pre-dispute, express waivers to foreclose post-award challenges alleging arbitrator bias or apparent bias (based on relationships disclosed before the arbitration), and whether courts should enforce those waivers as a matter of law and policy.

Whether enforcing such pre-arbitration waivers would meaningfully increase procedural efficiency and certainty without creating unacceptable risks (for example, incentivizing nondisclosure by arbitrators or producing unfair outcomes for certain categories of parties).

papers.node_id: 10cardozojconflictresol509!!ARTICLE: STATE REGULATION OF ARBITRATION PROCEEDINGS: JUDICIAL REVIEW OF ARBITRATION AWARDS BY STATE COURTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: STATE REGULATION OF ARBITRATION PROCEEDINGS: JUDICIAL REVIEW OF ARBITRATION AWARDS BY STATE COURTS
papers.abstract:
The thesis of this Article can be stated simply and concisely: States possess the power to adopt standards for the conduct of arbitration proceedings and review of arbitration awards that are significantly different from federal law standards.The majorobjective of this Article is to explore the most important possibilities for reform of arbitration law and practice at the state level. State law standards will be of increasing importance in the reformation of arbitration practice. This Article focuses on the standards of review of arbitration awards employed by state courts, because the power to vacate an arbitration award is the sanction for defective arbitration proceedings. Many of my examples are drawn from Texas, where I have been teaching contracts and arbitration for many years, and from the Fifth Circuit--about which I have written at length.
The idea of states serving as laboratories for testing alternative approaches to perceived problems is too well known to require amplification here. Suffice it to say that potential improvements in the arbitration process are better tried initially at the state rather than the federal level, due to lower degree of risk if a change is deemed not to be successful. Over time, other jurisdictions can examine what has been tried in various states, and adopt (perhaps in revised form) those ideas that proved sound.
In view of the dramatically expanded role of arbitration in the American legal system during the last quarter century, and the numerous concerns about these developments, expanding state court review of arbitration awards offers a promising route for those who believe that arbitration needs to be checked--both in the sense of limiting arbitration and in quality control of arbitral awards. For this heresy, I expect to become a pariah among persons associated with the organized arbitration community, which consistently opposesany suggestion that courts do anything with respect to arbitration awards other than confirm them.
States can adopt standards of review that are more restrictive or less restrictive than those found in federal law. However, the possibilities for different state standards are not symmetrical. Federal law allows only for very limited judicial review of arbitration awards, so there is little room for a state to select a narrower level of review. The sole notable example is the unwillingness of some states to recognize manifest disregard of the law as a non-statutory ground for vacating an arbitration award.By contrast, there is a vast potential scope for expanding the regulation of arbitrators and arbitration awards under state law.
Most cases that are subject to the Federal Arbitration Act ("FAA") are heard in state, rather than federal, courts.Indeed, this fact is an important rationale for writing this Article, and is central to its relevance. While the FAA establishes substantive federal law regarding arbitration agreements, the Act does not create an independent basis for federal court jurisdiction.Some other basis must be found to invoke federal jurisdiction--usually diversity jurisdiction, subject to a minimum amount in controversy (currently $ 75,000).The dollar limitation on diversity jurisdiction is important because many consumer and employment arbitration proceedings involve lesser dollar amounts. Attempts to argue that section 10 of the FAA provides an independent basis for federal jurisdiction to review arbitration awards have met with uniform rejection by the federal courts.
The law of a particular state may become applicable to an arbitration proceeding in two very different ways. The primary focusof this Article is on state court proceedings that are governed by the law of the jurisdiction where a post-arbitration challenge is heard. In addition, a choice of law provision will serve to make the law of the specified state determinative. That choice of law is controlling in any federal or state court. Although a general choice of law clause will not serve to invoke the arbitration law of a state, a clearly expressed desire to contract out of the FAA and into the arbitration law of a named state is permitted, indeed required, by the FAA.As the United States Supreme Court has framed the matter: "The legislative history of the Act establishes that the purpose behind its passage was to ensure judicial enforcement of privately made agreements to arbitrate."The FAA does not require contracting parties to arbitrate pursuant to any particular set of rules, and that includes FAA rules.
This article proceeds on the assumption that its readers are generally familiar with American arbitration law and practice. One of the pleasures of publishing in a specialty journal is that the author can assume that the readers have a basic knowledge about the subject matter. This permits the author to assert that the United States Supreme Court strongly favors arbitration, and similarly uncontroversial propositions, without a lengthy explanation or a blizzard of footnotes that offers supporting evidence.
Part II of this Article presents a brief review of state and federal law standards for judicial review of arbitration awards. This body of law was already well established, although not codified, during the nineteenth century. Despite the vast changes in general arbitration law since that time--e.g., enforcement of executory arbitration agreements, statutory claims subject to arbitration, and the consumerization of arbitration--the law regarding judicial review of arbitration awards remains largely unchanged. With the enactment of the FAA at the national level, and the enactment of the Uniform Arbitration Act ("UAA") by most states (either the 1955 or 2000 version), the statutory grounds for vacating arbitration awards are largely identical throughout the country.
A necessary precursor to the discussion of state law standards regarding arbitrators and arbitration awards is the consideration (and refutation) of arguments that state arbitration law initiatives are preempted by federal law, as explicated in decisions of the United States Supreme Court. The power to expand review of arbitration awards under state law, whether based on statutory orcommon law developments, is considerable. Short of a large scale refusal to enforce arbitration awards, state standards for judicial review are not subject to FAA preemption.
After disposing of the canard that the FAA, supplemented by the arbitration jurisprudence of the United States Supreme Court, stands as a barrier to state law standards for review of arbitration awards, we turn to the central topic of the Article: State standards for judicial review of arbitration awards, and related state regulatory law. As with most rules, the ultimate occasion for enforcement may be a judicial proceeding but widespread compliance usually precludes the need for judicial action. For example, material violations of arbitrator disclosure rules can ultimately result in the vacatur of an arbitration award, but the preferred result (and far more common outcome) is that arbitrators comply with these rules and avoid any risk of an award being vacated.
The discussion of state law regulation of the arbitration process is a potentially vast topic, and no attempt at completeness is contemplated. Indeed, the discussion begins with a set of transactional assumptions designed to assume away a wide variety of potential arbitration issues. Largely, as a matter of self-discipline, I have adopted the "Top Ten" approach made famous by David Letterman, and limit my discussion to ten important state law arbitration process reforms. However, no attempt is made at rank ordering these topics, or the proposed reforms.

Whether federal arbitration policy and federal court doctrines constrain or preempt state efforts to regulate arbitration and broaden judicial review of arbitral awards.

papers.title: ARTICLE: STATUTORY MISCONSTRUCTION: HOW THE SUPREME COURT CREATED A FEDERAL ARBITRATION LAW NEVER ENACTED BY CONGRESS
papers.abstract:
This Article will focus on how a simple procedural statute enacted to require enforcement of arbitration agreements in federal court has become unrecognizable as the law Congress adopted in 1925. Today, as a result of judicial construction, the Federal Arbitration Act(FAA) reaches much further and imposes itself on a far greater proportion of our citizens than was ever envisioned in 1925. The FAA as interpreted affects statutory rights, consumer rights, and employee rights, as well as state police powers to protect those rights.Today's statute-which has been construed to preempt state law,eliminate the requirement of consent to arbitration,permit arbitration ofstatutory rights,and remove the jury trial right from citizens without their knowledge or consent-is a statute that would not likely have commanded a single vote in the 1925 Congress.
What processes and methods have enabled the judiciary to create a law never enacted by Congress? This Article will examine the interpretive methods the judiciary, particularly the Supreme Court, has used in major cases that have defined the FAA, as well as the effect of the choices it has made. Part II will examine the context of the FAA, including the drafting and political history, to see how its proponents and members of Congress understood the Act, which was adopted virtually without opposition. Part III will explore how Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkinsand Guaranty Trust Co. of New York v. Yorkproduced a dilemma that caused the first major misstep in interpreting the FAA. This misstep occurred in Prima Paint Corp. v. Flood & Conklin Manufacturing Co.,when the Supreme Court incorrectly asserted that the 1925 Congress relied exclusively upon the Commerce Clause as the underlying power for enacting the FAA. Part IV will examine how that misstep led to even greater missteps in two subsequent cases, Moses H. Cone Memorial Hospital v. Mercury Construction Corp.and Southland Corp. v. Keating.In those cases, the Supreme Court recast a procedural statute that was applicable only in federal court into a substantive statute applicable in both state and federal courts. Part V will follow the increasing expansion of the statute, which the Court interpreted not only to cover statutory claims, an area never anticipated by the enacting Congress, but also to cover worker agreements, which had been expressly excluded by Congress in 1925.Finally, the major misconstructions which took place in Prima Paint and Southland have recently been reconfirmed by the Court in its February 2006 decision, Buckeye Check Cashing, Inc. v. Cardegna.Moreover, the Buckeye Court expanded the holding in Prima Paint by finding that an arbitratorrather than a court should decide a claim that a contract is void for illegality.
The Article concludes that the different interpretive methods the Court used to construct the current statute failed to cabin judicial discretion to legislate and resulted in a complete rewriting of the statute. The statute's new architecture has had a substantial impact on our legal system. The FAA created by the Supreme Court in the last twenty-five years reflects judicial policy preferences reminiscent of the policies prevailing at the beginning of the last century, including laissez-faire economics and an antipathy to state laws and regulations favoring individuals, consumers, and small businesses.
