papers.node_id: 96washlrev1389!!ARTICLE: STRUCTURAL BARRIERS TO INCLUSION IN ARBITRATOR POOLS
papers.title: ARTICLE: STRUCTURAL BARRIERS TO INCLUSION IN ARBITRATOR POOLS
papers.abstract:
Forums that host mandatory consumer arbitration are increasingly facing pressure for failing to maintain diverse arbitrator rosters.For example, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), a quasi-governmental self-regulatory organization that is overseen by the U.S.Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and hosts the largest securities arbitration forum in the country,has come under fire for maintaining a roster that critics claim is overwhelmingly white and male.Nearly all disputes between an investor and stockbroker are subject to mandatory arbitration in the FINRA Dispute Resolution Services forum.The near mandatory nature of the FINRA arbitration forum, coupled with its transparency and public accountability, position the forum as a unique case study for evaluating arbitrator pool diversity and instituting measurable change.In 2014, the Public Investor Advocate Bar Association (PIABA), a bar association whose members represent investors in claims against stockbrokers in the FINRA forum,issued a report on the composition of FINRA's arbitrator roster, concluding that the FINRA roster was insufficiently diverse.The PIABA Report found that of the 5,375 arbitrators then in FINRA's pool, 80% were male.PIABA found that the average arbitrator age was sixty-seven and that 40% of the roster was over the age of seventy.The PIABA Report asserted that FINRA's claims that it maintained a diverse arbitrator roster were incorrect.PIABA further criticized FINRA for failing to take any measures to quantify diversity within its arbitrator roster while simultaneously claiming that the roster was diverse.
Since the 2014 PIABA Report, in response to scholarly and internalrecommendations,FINRA has increased transparency with regard to its arbitrator pool demographics,an action that may permit the assessment of FINRA's diversification efforts and potentially serve as a model for other arbitration forums.FINRA now maintains a webpage listing Dispute Resolution Service's efforts to ensure its arbitrator pool is inclusive.FINRA conducts a voluntary annual survey of its arbitrator pool to obtain information on the race, ethnicity, gender, age, and LGBTQ identity of its arbitrators and shares aggregate demographic information with the public.These actions to highlight efforts to diversify the roster - both in outreach and measurable change - indicate a greater degree of transparency within FINRA than other arbitral forums.Moreover, these efforts suggest a commitment to ensuring that investors have access to an arbitrator pool that is diverse.Accordingly, to the extent FINRA's transparency permits analysis of inclusion, FINRA's work may serve as model for other mandatory arbitration forums.
Approximately five years after it had been criticized for its own lack of diversity, FINRA responded to publicity surrounding entrepreneur and rapper Shawn Carter's (also known as Jay-Z) challenge to the American Arbitration Association (AAA) as an arbitration forum because AAAlacked sufficient Black arbitrators on its roster.FINRA suggested that its arbitrator roster exhibited more overall diversity than the AAA and that Carter would not have levied a similar challenge in the FINRA forum.FINRA's Office of Dispute Resolution Director said that "arbitrator diversity has been his "absolute number-one priority' since taking on his role on December 1, 2014," soon after the October 2014 publication of the PIABA Report.By capitalizing on press generated by Carter's fame,FINRA highlighted the work it had done to diversify its own arbitrator roster, but that does not mean that we should accept FINRA's claim that its roster is diverse at face value.Indeed, not all agree that FINRA's arbitrator roster has sufficiently diversified since PIABA's 2014 report.
FINRA's assertions that its roster has changed are subject to study, with some limitations, from publicly available information.While it is not possible to identify each arbitrator currently in FINRA's arbitrator pool, let alone that arbitrator's age, race, ethnicity, gender, or LGBTQidentity,it is possible to measure whether new arbitrators are being chosen to serve and actually decide smaller investors' disputes.This Article assesses - to the extent possible via FINRA's voluntary transparency - the results of FINRA's recent arbitrator recruitment gains.Limiting the inquiry to publicly available information released by FINRA is intentional. This Article fits into a broader research agenda assessing whether the information publicly released by FINRA in the name of transparency is meaningful.It also serves to inform other arbitration forums about how providing transparency can assist external evaluation of diversification and inclusion efforts and potentially increase public trust.
FINRA's assertions that it has increased the diversity of its roster since 2014 cannot be wholly assessed, because FINRA does not publicly release the names and individual demographic details of the members of its arbitration roster.However, FINRA does release decisions in its arbitration cases.These awards provide sufficient information to determine whether arbitrators who joined after 2014 - when FINRA faced criticism for a lack of diversity and began releasing arbitrator demographic information showing an overall more diverse pool - serveas the sole arbitrators deciding the smallest customer disputes.
Every FINRA arbitration that results in a decision by an arbitrator is published in a publicly available database maintained on FINRA's website.Each award must include, among other uniform information, the name(s) of the arbitrator(s) issuing the award.Thus, it is possible to determine whether FINRA's addition of more arbitrators reflective of the population has led to any change in who is presiding over smaller investor claims. This Article tests the hypothesis that structural barriers within FINRA's arbitrator selection process make it difficult for a new entrant to the FINRA public arbitrator roster to be selected as an arbitrator in small claim proceedings filed against a stockbroker. Thus, the Article assesses inclusion - whether new entrants to FINRA's arbitrator pool preside over smaller cases as the sole arbitrator.
Part I analyzes the historic roots of securities arbitration, identifying the fair resolution of smaller consumer claims as the most important focus in creating a uniform, and now mandatory, dispute resolution system to ensure trust in the markets. If consumers did not believe they could fairly and efficiently resolve their disputes, they would not trust the securities markets. The unique oversight and accountability of FINRA's forum thus sets it apart from other mandatory arbitration forums, making it an interesting case study due to the possibility of constituent-and regulator-led change. Part II explores the historic lack of diversity in the financial industry and examines how lack of representation within it undermines consumer trust and confidence, raising significant questions about the legitimacy of a mandatory system that does not represent all investors. The Part ends with a discussion of recent industry sentiment supporting greater inclusion and the need to assess whether public statements arereflected in subsequent action, adding additional reasons why FINRA may be well positioned as a member of the financial industry to supplement diversity and inclusion measures in its arbitration forum. Part III examines the FINRA arbitrator pool and selection process and identifies structural barriers preventing the inclusion of newer arbitrator entrants in the pool for smaller claims. These barriers are examined because they may undermine FINRA's goal of ensuring diverse arbitrator options for a subset of disputes in which consumer trust is most necessary to foster confidence in the securities markets - smaller claims. Part IV details the results of an empirical study designed to evaluate the impact of the newly identified structural barriers to inclusion. It concludes that despite limitations with the available public data, new arbitrator entrants are a small proportion of the arbitrators hearing smaller customer claims in the FINRA forum and that public customers are not obtaining the benefit of FINRA's recent arbitrator pool diversification efforts. The Article concludes with a discussion of recommendations, including providing greater transparency to more fully assess an arbitral forum's inclusivity and eliminating known barriers that make it difficult for new entrants to serve as arbitrators. Though FINRA's accountability to the public and SEC oversight may more readily lead to changes in its mandatory arbitration forum, the lessons learned from studying the increased transparency of the FINRA forum can inform interventions necessary to ensure diversity and inclusion in other arbitration forums.

papers.node_id: 17upajbusl573!!ARTICLE: Take It or Leave It: Unconscionability of Mandatory Pre-Dispute Arbitration Agreements in the Securities Industry
papers.title: ARTICLE: Take It or Leave It: Unconscionability of Mandatory Pre-Dispute Arbitration Agreements in the Securities Industry
papers.abstract:
"Counsel's argument that the parties voluntarily agreed to arbitration and that the process saves money is also disingenuous… . Individuals have no recourse but to agree to an arbitration clause. Further, since the individuals seldom win and are forced to reimburse costs and attorney fees, the only ones saving money are large institutions like the claimant."
The pervasive use of mandatory pre-dispute arbitration agreements ("PDAAs") in the securities industry is a relatively new phenomenon. Beginning in the 1980s, the Supreme Court announced that federal statutory rights, specifically claims arising under the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act"), are subject to arbitration unless Congress has evinced a contrary intent.An overwhelming majority of retail brokerage and many investment advisory agreements include language requiring all disputes between the customer and broker-dealer/investment adviser be resolved through arbitration- most often with Financial Industry RegulatoryAuthority ("FINRA") Dispute Resolution. Thus, only in rare instances can an investor open a brokerage or investment advisory account without agreeing to submit to mandatory pre-dispute arbitration.
This Article begins by discussing the jurisprudence of mandatory PDAAs in the securities industry, including the legality of forcing investors to waive access to class action lawsuits. The Article then transitions into a discussion of the arguments against the use of mandatory PDAAs, including the Supreme Court invention of a "pro-arbitration" policy and the adhesive nature of brokerage and advisory contracts. The Article then argues that mandatory PDAAs are per se unconscionable because they require investors to involuntarily waive certain constitutional rights and provide narrow appellate avenues that effectively preclude judicial review of arbitral awards. The Article concludes by providing an example of a mandatory PDAA reflecting the current legal regime governing arbitration and possible solutions for policy-makers - the most appropriate of which is to prohibit the use of mandatory PDAAs in the securities industry.
This topic is timely, especially since FINRA recently enforced a $ 500,000 fine on Charles Schwab & Co. for using a mandatory PDAA in contravention of FINRA rules. There has also been heightened Congressional interest in the issue, evidenced by a bill proposed by Representative Keith Ellison in the House of Representatives in 2013and a recent Senate Financial Committee report citing mandatory pre-dispute arbitration agreements as a critical issue for the SEC to investigate.
The use of mandatory arbitration agreements has harmed thousands of investors over the past twenty years. A June 2007 study of more than 14,000 FINRA arbitration awards over a ten-year period (1995 - 2004) found that investors with significant claims suing major brokerage firms could expect to recover only twelve percent of the amount claimed.In a2008 survey of over 3,000 individuals who participated in an arbitration (e.g., investors, advisors, attorneys), seventy-one percent of investors were dissatisfied with the outcome of the arbitration.Even with these chilling figures, it is important to note that arbitration is a proper dispute resolution process for some investors; however, individual investors should be permitted to make that choice.
. Jurisprudence of Mandatory Pre-Dispute Arbitration Agreements in the Securities Industry
Even though the pervasive use of mandatory PDAAs has only arisen in the last thirty years, the issue of the legality of mandatory PDAAs stretches back to the 1950s. This Section will demonstrate the Supreme Court's evolution on the issue of mandatory PDAAs, illustrate the current view of the Supreme Court on how these agreements are enforced, and analyze recent developments concerning the use of class action waivers in mandatory PDAAs.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central empirical question of the symposium as whether arbitration is indeed worse for individual claimants and discusses courts' competing empirical assumptions about claimant success; Paper B argues that mandatory pre-dispute arbitration agreements in the securities industry involuntarily deprive investors of constitutional and judicial remedies and thus harm access to justice.

shared_topics.topic: empirical comparison of arbitration versus litigation outcomes (win rates, award sizes, recoveries)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys and calls for stronger empirical study of whether claimants win more or less often and receive higher or lower awards in arbitration versus litigation and highlights selection/filtering problems in such comparisons; Paper B cites empirical studies (e.g., FINRA awards analysis, participant surveys) showing low investor recoveries and high dissatisfaction with arbitral outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: unconscionability and doctrinal arguments over enforceability of mandatory arbitration provisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reviews the legal debate over whether mandatory arbitration clauses are unconscionable and how courts rely (often weakly) on empirical claims in Armendariz and Oblix decisions; Paper B develops a doctrinal argument that mandatory PDAAs in the securities context are per se unconscionable because they force waivers of rights and limit judicial review.

shared_topics.topic: use of arbitration clauses to preclude class actions or aggregate claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights empirical work (Eisenberg et al.) suggesting firms deploy arbitration clauses more in consumer contracts possibly to bar class claims and flags class arbitration as an important empirical puzzle; Paper B specifically addresses the legality and effects of forcing investors to waive access to class action lawsuits in brokerage and advisory contracts.

shared_topics.topic: policy, regulatory and reform responses to pervasive mandatory arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses policy implications and suggests remedies like minimal due process safeguards and encourages empirical evidence to inform legal decisions; Paper B surveys regulatory developments (FINRA fine, Congressional interest), criticizes the Supreme Court's pro-arbitration stance, and proposes prohibiting mandatory PDAAs in the securities industry.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50setonhalllrev707!!ARTICLE: Corporate Hostility to Arbitration
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Corporate Hostility to Arbitration

shared_topics.topic: scope and expansion of FAA preemption over state efforts to regulate arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the Supreme Court has expanded the Federal Arbitration Act's preemptive reach to invalidate state laws and doctrines that limit or regulate arbitration, and Paper B critiques the Court's pro-arbitration jurisprudence as it applies to mandatory pre-dispute arbitration agreements in the securities industry.

shared_topics.topic: use of mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses in adhesion (take-it-or-leave-it) contracts and their fairness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that arbitration clauses are often non‑negotiable adhesion terms drafted by corporations to their advantage, and Paper B documents the pervasive, effectively mandatory use of PDAAs in brokerage and advisory contracts and argues those terms are unconscionable.

shared_topics.topic: class-action/aggregate litigation waivers and their impact on claimants' ability to vindicate rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights corporate inclusion of bans on aggregate litigation or class actions as a method of disadvantaging individuals in arbitration, while Paper B examines the legality and harmful effects of forcing investors to waive access to class actions in securities disputes.

shared_topics.topic: empirical and doctrinal concerns about arbitration's effectiveness for claimants (access to justice, recoveries, secrecy, limited review)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contractual terms (shortened statutes of limitations, secrecy, etc.) can make arbitration ineffective for individuals, and Paper B brings empirical evidence of low investor recoveries and dissatisfaction, and critiques the narrow appellate review of arbitral awards.

shared_topics.topic: regulatory and policy remedies for abusive mandatory arbitration (state laws, industry rules, prohibitions, and narrowing preemption)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes adjusting FAA preemption doctrine to allow state law carve-outs and preserve democratic accountability, and Paper B surveys policy options (including FINRA enforcement, Congressional action, and a proposed ban on mandatory PDAAs in securities) to address abuses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71valrev1305!!ARTICLE: THE SECOND ARBITRATION TRILOGY: THE FEDERALIZATION OF ARBITRATION LAW.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SECOND ARBITRATION TRILOGY: THE FEDERALIZATION OF ARBITRATION LAW.

shared_topics.topic: Supreme Court expansion of the Federal Arbitration Act and the resulting pro‑arbitration federal policy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces and analyzes the Supreme Court Trilogy (Moses Cone, Southland, Dean Witter) and Prima Paint as the constitutional and doctrinal basis for federalizing arbitration law; Paper B traces the Court's post‑1980s decisions applying that federal arbitration jurisprudence to securities statutes and shows how that jurisprudence enabled widespread mandatory arbitration in the securities industry.

shared_topics.topic: Conflict between the FAA and state/regulatory law — preemption of state‑law defenses and public‑policy exceptions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how the FAA and the Supreme Court's readings preempt traditional state‑law defenses (e.g., public‑policy exceptions, UCC §2‑207 treatments, municipal employee arbitration limits); Paper B engages the same preemption/tension by examining whether doctrines like unconscionability, contractual adhesion principles, FINRA rules, or statutory protections can limit or invalidate mandatory pre‑dispute arbitration agreements.

shared_topics.topic: Enforceability of mandatory pre‑dispute arbitration agreements and consent/adhesion concerns
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents state courts' historical resistance to enforcing certain arbitration clauses and how federal law has changed that enforcement landscape; Paper B directly analyzes mandatory PDAAs in brokerage/advisory contracts as adhesive terms, arguing they are effectively involuntary and often unconscionable in the securities context.

shared_topics.topic: Consequences of arbitration enforcement for access to judicial remedies, including class actions and appellate review
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how federal arbitration rules shift disputes out of state courts and constrict state‑law remedies, while Paper B examines concrete consequences in the securities world—class action waivers, limited appellate review of arbitral awards, and empirical evidence that arbitration reduces investor recoveries.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 128harvlrev907!!ARTICLE: NOTES DEFERENCE AND THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT: THE NLRB'S DETERMINATION OF SUBSTANTIVE STATUTORY RIGHTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: NOTES DEFERENCE AND THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT: THE NLRB'S DETERMINATION OF SUBSTANTIVE STATUTORY RIGHTS

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of arbitration agreements that bar class or collective proceedings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the NLRB's D.R. Horton holding that employer arbitration clauses prohibiting collective legal action violate the NLRA, while Paper B examines the legality and practical effects of class-action waivers in mandatory pre-dispute arbitration agreements in the securities industry.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between the Federal Arbitration Act and other federal statutes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the tension between the FAA and the NLRA and whether the FAA permits enforcement of agreements that waive NLRA-protected concerted rights, while Paper B interrogates how the FAA and Supreme Court pro-arbitration doctrine have been applied to claims under the Securities Act and Exchange Act.

shared_topics.topic: whether arbitration clauses effectuate impermissible waivers of substantive statutory or constitutional rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that collective legal action is a substantive NLRA right that cannot be waived by arbitration clauses, and Paper B contends that mandatory PDAAs force investors to involuntarily waive statutory and constitutional protections and narrow judicial review of awards.

shared_topics.topic: the role of administrative agencies and courts in regulating or reviewing arbitration agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Chevron deference to the NLRB's interpretation of the NLRA when evaluating arbitration waivers, and Paper B engages with agency oversight and enforcement (FINRA, SEC) and the judicial enforcement of arbitration regimes governing securities disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104kylj699!!ARTICLE: Arbitrating Ballot Battles?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Arbitrating Ballot Battles?

shared_topics.topic: use of arbitration (including pre-dispute agreements) to resolve disputes traditionally handled by courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes using pre-election arbitration agreements (and considers arbitration as an alternative or supplement to courts/specialized election tribunals) to resolve ballot-counting disputes, while Paper B analyzes the widespread use of mandatory pre-dispute arbitration agreements in the securities industry and whether arbitration should displace court adjudication of investor claims.

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy and fairness concerns about arbitration clauses (voluntariness, adhesion, and impartiality)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers substantively engage with whether arbitration agreements are fair and legitimate in their contexts: Paper A explores whether arbitration can produce greater fairness and predictability in contested elections and discusses critiques, and Paper B focuses on the adhesive/mandatory nature of brokerage PDAAs and argues such clauses are unconscionable and biased against individual investors.

shared_topics.topic: tension between arbitration's finality/predictability and access to judicial review or rights protections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights arbitration's potential to provide finality and predictability as benefits in election disputes, while Paper B emphasizes how mandatory arbitration narrows appellate avenues, can require waiver of statutory or constitutional protections, and effectively limits judicial oversight—both papers thus engage the tradeoff between finality and preserving access to courts/rights.

shared_topics.topic: policy and institutional design responses to regulate or limit arbitration in specific sectors
shared_topics.justification: Each article offers or evaluates institutional solutions: Paper A advances the design of pre-election arbitration agreements and discusses specialized election courts as alternatives or complements, and Paper B surveys legal/regulatory remedies (FINRA enforcement, proposed legislation, prohibiting mandatory PDAAs) to address perceived harms from mandatory arbitration in the securities industry.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nclrev1091!!Article: JUDGING-LITE: HOW ARBITRATORS USE AND CREATE PRECEDENT*
compared_to.partner_title: Article: JUDGING-LITE: HOW ARBITRATORS USE AND CREATE PRECEDENT*

shared_topics.topic: the functioning and quality of securities arbitration (reasoned awards, ad hoc decision-making, and consequences for investors)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the securities arbitration system created by mandatory PDAAs and documents poor investor recoveries and dissatisfaction; Paper B includes securities arbitration in its dataset and finds that securities awards often lack reasoned explanations and appear ad hoc, linking that quality problem to harmful consequences for parties.

shared_topics.topic: mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses and their effects on access to courts and enforcement of statutory/constitutional rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on mandatory PDAAs in brokerage/advisory contracts and argues they force investors to waive important rights and foreclose litigation options; Paper B studies mandatory arbitration regimes (consumers/employees/statutory claims) and assesses how mandatory forums influence whether statutory rights are meaningfully vindicated and how arbitrators apply precedent.

shared_topics.topic: limited judicial review of arbitral awards and implications for precedent and public law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that PDAAs provide narrow appellate avenues that effectively preclude judicial review of arbitral awards, undermining legal oversight; Paper B analyzes the formal limits on judicial review, the risk that arbitration reduces the supply of public precedent, and the potential for judges to treat arbitral awards as persuasive authority.

shared_topics.topic: how bargaining power and adhesive contract design shape arbitration terms and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the adhesive nature of brokerage and advisory contracts that compel investors to accept mandatory arbitration and skew outcomes toward institutions; Paper B highlights that arbitration regimes and arbitrators' practices reflect the preferences of the party that can dictate terms, raising concerns that power imbalances produce business-favoring procedures and results.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2005byulrev1!!Article: Arbitration and State Action
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Arbitration and State Action

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of mandatory pre-dispute arbitration agreements and limits on judicial review
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts and legal doctrines determine the enforceability of mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses — Paper A through a doctrinal critique (unconscionability, class‑action waivers, and the Supreme Court's pro‑arbitration posture) in the securities context, and Paper B by examining whether judicial enforcement of contractual arbitration (and subsequent enforcement of awards) can be constrained or treated as state action.

shared_topics.topic: whether agency-initiated or SRO-mandated arbitration in securities constitutes state action
shared_topics.justification: Both articles engage the question of state action where regulators and self‑regulatory organizations (FINRA/SROs) require or operate arbitration forums — Paper A documents the prevalence and regulatory context (FINRA, SEC) of mandatory PDAAs, and Paper B directly argues that agency‑initiated/SRO‑mandated arbitration can amount to state action with constitutional implications.

shared_topics.topic: impact of adhesion and bargaining-power asymmetries on fairness of arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Both works discuss how adhesive contracts and one‑shot versus repeat‑player dynamics affect fairness — Paper A foregrounds investor coercion, low recovery rates, and unconscionability in brokerage/advisory contracts, while Paper B highlights critics' concerns that streamlined, confidential arbitration procedures disadvantage parties with less bargaining power (employees/consumers/investors).

shared_topics.topic: using constitutional doctrines (due process/equal protection) to challenge arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider attempts to invoke constitutional protections against arbitration: Paper B develops and critiques theories that arbitration should meet procedural due process and equal protection if treated as state action, and Paper A addresses arguments that mandatory PDAAs force investors to waive constitutional rights and foreclose meaningful judicial review.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62brooklynlrev1335!!SYMPOSIUM: SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A DECADE AFTER McMAHON: CONTRACT THEORY AND SECURITIES ARBITRATION: WHITHER CONSENT? (c) 1996 Richard E. Speidel. All Rights Reserved.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A DECADE AFTER McMAHON: CONTRACT THEORY AND SECURITIES ARBITRATION: WHITHER CONSENT? (c) 1996 Richard E. Speidel. All Rights Reserved.

shared_topics.topic: whether investor 'consent' to pre-dispute arbitration is genuine or effectively mandatory/adhesive
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate whether arbitration clauses in brokerage and advisory contracts represent real, voluntary consent or are contracts of adhesion that force investors to waive forum choice; Paper A frames this as the erosion of consent after McMahon and the Ruder Report, and Paper B argues PDAAs operate as involuntary waivers that are practically mandatory for retail investors.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of Supreme Court/Federal Arbitration Act jurisprudence (e.g., McMahon) on the arbitrability of securities statutory claims
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how the FAA and Supreme Court decisions—especially McMahon—have created a strong pro‑arbitration enforcement regime that pushes federal and state securities claims into arbitration unless Congress or clear statutory language excludes them, and they assess the consequences of that jurisprudence for investor protection and forum access.

shared_topics.topic: limits on enforceability of arbitration clauses: validity defenses (unconscionability, fraud, duress), class‑action waivers, and scope of judicial review
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage substantively with defenses to enforcement under the FAA's 'savings clause' (unconscionability, fraud, duress), critique class‑action waivers in PDAAs, and discuss the narrowness of judicial review of arbitral awards (including doctrines like 'manifest disregard'), questioning whether these limits adequately protect investors.

shared_topics.topic: the need for regulatory or legislative responses (SEC, SROs/FINRA, Congress) to address fairness in securities arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider policy remedies—Paper A debates revitalizing consent versus a stronger public‑law model with more aggressive SEC/SRO oversight, while Paper B points to FINRA enforcement, Congressional proposals, and potential prohibitions on mandatory PDAAs as solutions to perceived unfairness.

papers.node_id: 74smulrev59!!ARTICLE: Taxing Employers for Imposing Mandatory Arbitration, Class Action Waiver, and Nondisclosure of Dispute Provisions
papers.title: ARTICLE: Taxing Employers for Imposing Mandatory Arbitration, Class Action Waiver, and Nondisclosure of Dispute Provisions
papers.abstract:
BEST Wishes Kevin" was piped in frosting below an American flag.Navy Reserve Lieutenant Commander Kevin Ziober attached a picture of the cake that his employer bought him to written testimony that he submitted to the House Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law.
In 2012, Ziober, then a manager at federal contractor BLB Resources, "received official orders from the Navy to deploy to Afghanistan for 12 months."Publicly, his employer hosted a surprise party with decorations, gifts, and the caketo thank Ziober for his service.Privately, and on the same day as the party, his employer - in violation of the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act - fired Ziober and told him that his job would not wait for his return from active duty.As Ziober describes,
Around 4:45 that same afternoon, I was summoned to a meeting.... I was fired on the spot and told that my position would not be waiting for me upon my return from active duty.
The shock of learning that I was being terminated from my job on the eve of my deployment to a combat zone created an unimaginable amount of concern and anxiety about how I would support myself and my family when I returned home. In the course of a few hours, I went from feeling supported, proud, and focused on serving my country, to feeling embarrassed, confused, and concerned about the well-being of my loved ones.

questions.question: Whether imposing a tax or financial penalty on employers who require employees to accept mandatory individual arbitration, class-action waivers, or nondisclosure-of-dispute provisions reduces employers' use of those provisions.

Whether taxing employers for imposing such dispute-limiting provisions meaningfully improves employees' access to remedies and collective enforcement (and thus employee welfare and deterrence of employer misconduct) compared with the status quo.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 89stjohnslrev1079!!ARTICLE: PRIVATE SOLUTIONS TO GLOBAL CRISES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PRIVATE SOLUTIONS TO GLOBAL CRISES

shared_topics.topic: use of mandatory or private arbitration to replace judicial adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how arbitration and private tribunals are increasingly used instead of national courts to resolve cross-border human rights and tort claims, and Paper B examines employers' use of mandatory arbitration clauses to divert employee disputes away from courts and limit judicial access.

shared_topics.topic: arbitration and related provisions as mechanisms that can shield corporations/employers from liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that arbitration can enable multinational corporations to avoid traditional liability in domestic courts for human rights abuses, while Paper B documents how mandatory arbitration, class-action waivers, and nondisclosure terms protect employers from collective or public litigation and reduce victims' remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contractual provisions (arbitration clauses, class‑action waivers, nondisclosure) in structuring dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on contracts and international agreements that create arbitration-based accountability regimes for MNCs, and Paper B centers on employer-imposed contractual terms—arbitration agreements, waivers, and NDAs—that determine how individual disputes are adjudicated and whether they can proceed collectively or publicly.

shared_topics.topic: confidentiality, procedural fairness, and power asymmetries in private dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights arbitration's private and confidential character and critiques assumptions that it always favors business interests, while Paper B engages with nondisclosure and secrecy provisions and their effects on procedural fairness and the power imbalance between employers and individual employees.

shared_topics.topic: policy and regulatory responses to the proliferation of arbitration-based dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys how international organizations and agreements are adopting arbitration as a means to enforce corporate responsibility, and Paper B proposes legislative or fiscal interventions (e.g., taxing employers who impose arbitration/waiver/NDAs) as a response to private dispute resolution practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18gastulrev927!!ARTICLE: TILTING THE JUSTICE SYSTEM: FROM ADR AS IDEALISTIC MOVEMENT TO A SEGMENTED MARKET IN DISPUTE RESOLUTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TILTING THE JUSTICE SYSTEM: FROM ADR AS IDEALISTIC MOVEMENT TO A SEGMENTED MARKET IN DISPUTE RESOLUTION

shared_topics.topic: employer-imposed mandatory arbitration clauses (take-it-or-leave-it contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A targets employer-imposed mandatory arbitration as a practice to be deterred (proposing taxation of employers who impose such clauses), and Paper B analyzes the rise of take-it-or-leave-it mandatory arbitration in employment/consumer contracts and the normative and doctrinal challenges it poses.

shared_topics.topic: class-action waivers and their effect on collective enforcement of rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly addresses class-action waivers as a contractual tool employers use to block collective claims, while Paper B considers the interaction between ADR and the new wave of large class actions and how private dispute mechanisms reshape the availability and form of collective remedies.

shared_topics.topic: how ADR practices (arbitration/mediation) affect access to statutory rights and procedural fairness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links mandatory ADR and nondisclosure provisions to impediments in enforcing statutory protections (e.g., employment rights), and Paper B critiques mandatory ADR on grounds of fairness and its impact on enforcement of statutory regimes (securities, anti-discrimination, antitrust), debating whether to infuse more legal due process into ADR.

shared_topics.topic: segmentation of the justice system and power asymmetries between repeat players/elite and ordinary employees/one-shotters
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats employer-driven contractual dispute rules as tools that shift dispute resolution power toward employers, and Paper B develops a theory of a segmented, hierarchical justice system where elites and repeat players access tailor-made ADR while ordinary litigants face lower-end, settlement-focused processes.

shared_topics.topic: use of nondisclosure/confidentiality to hide disputes and limit public accountability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A targets nondisclosure-of-dispute provisions as mechanisms employers use to silence claimants, and Paper B documents how elite private settlements and ADR can be kept 'secret from the general public,' reducing transparency and public scrutiny of legal claims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62brooklynlrev1459!!SYMPOSIUM: SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A DECADE AFTER McMAHON: TOWARD CHANGING MODELS OF SECURITIES ARBITRATION (c) 1996 Edward Brunet. All Rights Reserved.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A DECADE AFTER McMAHON: TOWARD CHANGING MODELS OF SECURITIES ARBITRATION (c) 1996 Edward Brunet. All Rights Reserved.

shared_topics.topic: use of mandatory or contractually imposed arbitration clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the shift toward a 'contract model' of arbitration where parties adopt and customize arbitration clauses (including binding arbitration), and Paper B examines employers imposing mandatory arbitration, class‑action waivers, and nondisclosure provisions on employees as contractual conditions of employment.

shared_topics.topic: procedural design of arbitration and access to remedies (discovery, written opinions, class relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the 'judicialization' of securities arbitration—greater discovery, early appointment of arbitrators, and issuing opinions—while Paper B focuses on how mandatory arbitration, class‑action waivers, and nondisclosure limit procedural avenues and collective remedies for employees.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries and the effects of unequal bargaining power on dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the move to customized arbitration clauses to market forces and party intent (implying strategic drafting by repeat players), whereas Paper B presents employer–employee power imbalances that result in imposed dispute‑resolution terms that disadvantage individual workers.

shared_topics.topic: public regulation and policy responses to private arbitration practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses NASD Task Force recommendations and voluntary institutional reforms to securities arbitration, and Paper B describes legislative and regulatory approaches (including proposals to tax employers) and congressional testimony aimed at curbing or changing mandatory arbitration and nondisclosure practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 8nevlj385!!SYMPOSIUM - RETHINKING THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT: AN EXAMINATION OF WHETHER AND HOW THE STATUTE SHOULD BE AMENDED: ARTICLE:Preserving the Federal Arbitration Act by Reining in Judicial Expansion and Mandatory Use
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM - RETHINKING THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT: AN EXAMINATION OF WHETHER AND HOW THE STATUTE SHOULD BE AMENDED: ARTICLE:Preserving the Federal Arbitration Act by Reining in Judicial Expansion and Mandatory Use

shared_topics.topic: mandatory pre-dispute employment arbitration as a barrier to employees' access to courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the FAA and judicial interpretations enable mandatory arbitration clauses in employment contracts that divert disputes out of court, and Paper B centers on employers imposing mandatory arbitration on employees (illustrated by the Ziober case) and the harms that practice creates for worker access to judicial remedies.

shared_topics.topic: class-action waivers in arbitration agreements and their impact on collective relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the troubling rise of arbitration provisions that ban class actions and effectively foreclose collective claims, and Paper B's title and focus explicitly target class-action waivers imposed by employers as part of mandatory dispute provisions.

shared_topics.topic: legislative and policy responses to mandatory arbitration (including federal statutes and alternative remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates proposed federal reforms such as the Arbitration Fairness Act and state-law efforts (RUAA) to limit FAA-driven preemption, while Paper B proposes or discusses using policy tools (e.g., taxing employers) as a regulatory response to employers' use of mandatory arbitration, nondisclosure, and class-waiver provisions.

shared_topics.topic: confidentiality and nondisclosure of dispute resolution outcomes and their implications for transparency and public accountability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns that private arbitration and arbitrators' control of arbitrability can keep processes and outcomes out of public view, and Paper B explicitly addresses nondisclosure provisions as part of employer-imposed dispute terms that silence workers and obscure misconduct.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev831!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:CONTRACT AND CONFLICT MANAGEMENT
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:CONTRACT AND CONFLICT MANAGEMENT

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and legal treatment of arbitration/ADR clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how federal law (especially the FAA) and court decisions shape the enforceability and judicial treatment of contract-based dispute resolution; Paper B focuses on employers' imposition of mandatory arbitration, class-waiver, and nondisclosure provisions and the legal/policy debate over treating such clauses as binding in employment contexts.

shared_topics.topic: adhesion contracts and disparities in bargaining power harming employees/consumers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights concerns about private justice under adhesion boilerplate and examples where unequal bargaining power produces unfair arbitration schemes; Paper B documents an employment setting where an employer imposed dispute rules on a worker and situates such mandatory dispute provisions in the context of employer-employee power imbalances.

shared_topics.topic: access to courts, remedies, and the substantive consequences of substituting private dispute resolution for litigation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates how ADR provisions can substitute for court adjudication, affect remedies, confidentiality, and delay, and how courts should treat interveners' outcomes; Paper B engages with how mandatory arbitration, class waivers, and nondisclosure can block or alter employees' ability to vindicate rights and obtain public remedies.

shared_topics.topic: policy and regulatory responses to private dispute resolution (legislation, judicial oversight, and alternative deterrents)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys the range of responses—industry policing, legislation, judicial oversight, agency regulation—to problematic ADR clauses; Paper B proposes or examines a policy response (taxing employers) as a tool to discourage mandatory arbitration, class-waiver, and nondisclosure practices in employment.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 119yaleljonline1!!ARTICLE: The Mess of Manifest Disregard
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Mess of Manifest Disregard

shared_topics.topic: judicial oversight and enforceability of arbitration agreements/awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques employers' use of mandatory arbitration, class waivers, and nondisclosure provisions as mechanisms that shift disputes out of courts and limit judicial remedies; Paper B analyzes whether courts retain meaningful power to police arbitral outcomes—specifically whether the 'manifest disregard' vacatur doctrine survives Hall Street—thereby engaging the same question of how and when judicial review of arbitration is available.

shared_topics.topic: how arbitration regimes affect employees' access to remedies and public adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and attacks employer practices (mandatory arbitration, NDAs, class waivers) that restrict employees from pursuing claims in public courts or as class actions; Paper B's examination of vacatur standards and finality concerns speaks to the practical consequences for litigants (including employees) of limited avenues for correcting erroneous or law-defying arbitral awards.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal uncertainty and policy responses to arbitration's limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper B highlights circuit splits and doctrinal uncertainty after Hall Street about the scope of vacatur doctrines, while Paper A considers policy interventions (e.g., taxing employers who impose certain arbitration terms) as a legislative response to perceived unfairness and the unclear legal landscape surrounding employment arbitration.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 108geolj855!!ARTICLE: Discrimination, Mandatory Arbitration, and Courts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Discrimination, Mandatory Arbitration, and Courts

shared_topics.topic: employer-imposed mandatory arbitration clauses in employment contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A targets employer use of mandatory arbitration (and related class-waiver and nondisclosure provisions) as a practice to be deterred (proposing a tax) and illustrates harms with an employee story; Paper B directly analyzes mandatory arbitration as a mechanism for resolving employment disputes, focusing on its interaction with discrimination claims and court access.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of arbitration/class-action waivers and nondisclosure provisions on employees' ability to vindicate discrimination and statutory rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents an employee harm in the employment context and links it to the broader problem of private dispute-resolution and secrecy (arguing for policy intervention), while Paper B examines how mandatory arbitration affects victims of discrimination and their ability to obtain relief through courts.

shared_topics.topic: legal and policy responses to employer dispute-resolution provisions (doctrinal and regulatory remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a regulatory/policy remedy (taxing employers who impose arbitration, waivers, nondisclosure) to change employer incentives, and Paper B engages with the legal/doctrinal role of courts in policing or accommodating arbitration in discrimination cases, i.e., how institutions respond to these employer practices.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE IRONY OF SECURITIES ARBITRATION TODAY: WHY DO BROKERAGE FIRMS NEED JUDICIAL PROTECTION?

shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine how brokerage firms or employers impose mandatory arbitration in customer or employment contracts to move claims away from courts (and juries) and thereby limit recoverable remedies and damages available to individual claimants.

shared_topics.topic: how legal and policy actors determine the enforceability and social consequences of arbitration terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Supreme Court decisions that made securities arbitration enforceable, while Paper B considers legislative/policy responses (e.g., taxation or lawmaking) to employer-imposed arbitration and related provisions, so both assess how courts and policymakers shape arbitration's reach and effects.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries and fairness concerns when private dispute provisions constrain statutory or common-law claims

papers.title: Article: The "Gateway" Problem in International Commercial Arbitration
papers.abstract:
Participants in international commercial arbitration have long recognized the need to maintain arbitration as an effective and therefore attractivealternative to litigation,while still ensuring that its use is predicated on the consent of the parties and that the resulting awards command respect.A priori, at least, all participants - parties, counsel, arbitrators, arbitral institutions - have an interest in ensuring that arbitration delivers the various advantages associated with it, notably speed, economy, informality, technical expertise, and avoidance of national fora, while producing awards that withstand judicial challenge and otherwise enjoy legitimacy.
National courts play a potentially important policing role in this regard. Most jurisdictions have committed their courts to do all that is reasonably necessary to support the arbitral process. Among the ways courts do so is by ensuring that arbitral proceedings are initiated and pursued in a timely and effective manner. But those same courts are commonly asked by a party resisting arbitration to intervene at the very outset to declare that a prospective arbitration lacks an adequate basis in party consent. No legal system that permits the arbitration of at least some disputes (and most do) is immune to the possibility that its courts will become engaged in an inquiry of that sort at the very threshold of arbitration. Each must decide how, at this early stage, to promote arbitration as an effective alternative to litigation, while at the same time ensuring that any order issued by a court compelling arbitration is supported by a valid and enforceable agreement to arbitrate. The challenge consists of identifying those issues that courts - in the interest of striking the proper balance between these two objectives - properly address at what is increasingly known, in common U.S. parlance, as the "gateway" of arbitration. This "gateway" problem is the focus of the present Article.
For purposes of this Article, I consider an arbitral regime to be effective to the extent that it operates to promote the procedural advantages I posited earlier - speed, economy, informality, technical expertise, and avoidance of national fora. While legitimacy might be defined in many different ways, I consider an arbitral regime to be legitimate (or to enjoy legitimacy) to the extent that the parties who were compelled to arbitrate rather than litigate, andwill be bound by the resulting arbitral award, consented to step outside the ordinary court system in favor of an arbitral tribunal as their dispute resolution forum.
Legal systems differ in their responses to the challenge of reconciling efficacy and legitimacy in arbitration, and even in the extent to which they acknowledge that the challenge exists and try to articulate a framework of analysis for addressing it. This Article proceeds on the premise that legal systems have a serious enough interest in properly reconciling the values of efficacy and legitimacy to warrant their developing an adequate framework of analysis, as well as articulating that framework in a clear, coherent, and workable fashion.
In the United States, Congress has largely ignored the challenge of reconciling efficacy and legitimacy in arbitration, as have the states even when establishing statutory regimes to govern arbitration conducted in their territory.The matter has accordingly fallen to the courts. In this Article, I reexamine the jurisprudence that American courts have developed, increasingly under the leadership of the U.S. Supreme Court, to address the fundamental tension between arbitration's efficacy and legitimacy interests that exists at the very threshold of arbitration. The exercise has come to consist largely of demarcating "gateway" issues (i.e., issues that a court entertains at the threshold to ensure that the entire process has a foundation in party consent) from "non-gateway" issues (i.e., issues that arbitral tribunals, not courts, must be allowed to address initially, if arbitration is to be an effective mode of dispute resolution).
This Article proceeds as follows. Part II briefly sketches the settings in which courts may be asked to conduct the early policing with which this Article is concerned. Part III identifies the terminological confusion that has hampered clear thinking on the subject, and proposes a coherent vocabulary for overcoming it. Part IV then explores critically the conceptual devices that courts and commentators have traditionally employed in sorting through the issues. In so doing, it demonstrates that the two notions most widely reliedupon for this purpose - Kompetenz-Kompetenz and separability - are unequal to the task, and explains why. A critical understanding of U.S. law in this regard is aided by comparing it to models - the French and German - that claim to have devised simple and workable formulae for reconciling efficacy and legitimacy interests at the outset of the arbitral process. That discussion will show how the often proclaimed universality of Kompetenz-Kompetenz and separability is in fact misleading.
Against this background, Part V traces how recent U.S. case law has progressively pursued a more nuanced balance between efficacy and legitimacy than the traditional conceptual tools tended to yield. The courts have achieved this result, not by erecting a single comprehensive framework of analysis, but rather through a series of pragmatic adjustments to the received wisdom associated with Kompetenz-Kompetenz and separability. I conclude that they have developed a suitably complex body of case law that ordinarily reaches sound results. But I am equally certain that, in doing so, they have failed adequately to rationalize the case law.The disparate strands of analysis - each of which is basically sound - have combined to produce a needlessly confusing case law to the detriment of clarity, coherence, and workability.I suggest that the case law can and should be recast, and that the central feature of that recasting must be a serious and frank confrontation of the underlying tradeoff between arbitration's efficacy and legitimacy interests. This Article is thus both descriptive and normative in outlook.

questions.question: How should courts decide, at the threshold of arbitration, which disputes about the existence and scope of party consent they will resolve themselves versus leave for arbitral tribunals, so as to preserve arbitration's procedural advantages (speed, economy, informality, expertise, avoidance of national courts) while ensuring legitimacy through genuine party consent?

Do prevailing judicial approaches to these threshold "gateway" issues adequately reconcile arbitration's competing interests in efficacy and legitimacy, or do they produce inconsistent, unclear results that require a clearer, reworked analytical framework?

papers.node_id: 53urichlrev1339!!ARTICLE: THE "VANISHING TRIAL": ARBITRATING WRONGFUL DEATH
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE "VANISHING TRIAL": ARBITRATING WRONGFUL DEATH
papers.authors: The Hon Victoria A. B. Willis Judson R. Peverall
papers.abstract:
Wrongful death arbitration represents the latest chapter in a seemingly endless arbitration saga in American courts. Over the past four decades, the United States Supreme Court has radically transformed the 1925 Federal Arbitration Act ("FAA") from its meek origins as a procedural device available only in federal courts into an imposing body of substantive law preempting state-court power over a large class of claims.Consequently, the judiciary has elevated arbitration clauses to "super contracts," replete with special rules favoring enforcement in areas of the formerly unenforceable.In the last decade, courts relying on the federal policy favoring arbitration have begun compelling arbitration of an entirely new line of cases - from those involving employee fatalities to the wrongful deaths of nursing home residents.
Although wrongful death arbitration appears to be spreading apace throughout the nation, the power of courts to compel arbitration in this area remains an unsettled question. Federal and state courts have consistently opposed one another in deciding whether a wrongful death claim constitutes an arbitrable dispute.Moreover, while a handful of commentators have bemoanedthe marriage of arbitration and wrongful death liability as fundamentally unfair,a close reading of the literature on wrongful death arbitration suggests that no commentator thus far has offered a complete, coherent, and convincing account of the power of courts to compel arbitration of wrongful death claims.
This article presents a new interpretation of wrongful death arbitration that critiques and refines judicial developments in this area by recharting the history and structure of these two legal doctrines: arbitration and wrongful death liability. Careful analysis will show that courts lack the power to compel arbitration of wrongful death claims. By consigning wrongful death litigants to arbitration when they never agreed to it, courts erode the substantive rights at play in a wrongful death action and distort its core deterrence objectives that have historically been the very tool for correcting public wrongs against society. Setting forth a comprehensive interpretation of wrongful death arbitration that rediscovers and reclarifies the principles behind wrongful death liability, this article intends to show that, instead of protecting rights and deterring misconduct, wrongful death arbitration has closed the door to public atrocities and, at the same time, abandoned the very protections wrongful death liability aims to defend.
Part I studies the early twentieth century assent of arbitration and the modern decline of civil trial litigation. This part links this historical development to wrongful death litigation and explains the theoretical approaches courts have used to compel arbitration in this area.
Part II then turns to the history of wrongful death liability in an attempt to recover the twin theories of corrective justice and deterrence inhering within its doctrinal structure. What gave rise to the original wrongful death statutes in Anglo-American law, as we shall see, was the widespread nineteenth century belief that property rights were paramount to human liberty.Wrongful death liability, both at common law and in its mid-nineteenthcentury statutory incarnation, served to protect the property loss of a family member - or "beneficiary"- upon the death of a spouse or child. Only husbands and fathers could originally recover for property losses upon the death of a servant, wife or child; however, as time moved forward, states passed the first wrongful death statutes in order to extend these property protections to women and children alike.This part concludes by exploring the contemporary treatment of wrongful death liability by showing that a twenty-nine-state majority now views wrongful death liability as a deterrence device designed to prevent future encroachments upon familial property rights.
Part III draws several lessons from this history. First, it shows that courts directly violate the rights of a beneficiary by placing a decedent's arbitration agreement above a beneficiary's property interests. This article argues that wrongful death liability is, and always has been, a tool for family members to recover losses in property, not to enforce rights held by the decedent. Finally, this part explains that the ability of arbitration to limit punitive damage claims, coupled with a growing lack of public precedent and relaxed procedural safeguards, stifle the basic deterrent purpose behind wrongful death liability.
When properly understood, arbitration should not stand as a bar to the courtroom for wrongful death claimants. Rather, it wasoriginally understood to be, often has been, and can become once again a contractual alternative to litigation for those parties consenting to its terms. If wrongful death litigation seems perverse today, it is only because our jurisprudence has imposed arbitration onto wrongful death liability, forcing nonconsenting family members to litigate their claims in ways they never saw fit.

questions.question: Can courts compel private arbitration to resolve claims brought by a deceased person's family members when those family members themselves did not agree to arbitration?

Does forcing post-death family claims into private arbitration undermine the surviving beneficiaries' substantive interests (for example, their property-based recovery) by limiting available remedies and procedural protections?
Does treating these post-death claims as arbitrable reduce the public deterrence and precedent-setting functions that resolving such disputes in public courts normally provides?

papers.node_id: 45yalejintll227!!ARTICLE: The Adjudication Business
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Adjudication Business
papers.abstract:
The business of providing adjudication services for international commercial disputes--whether through courts, arbitration, or alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms--is a growth industry. London and New York have long been go-to forums for international commercial litigation in court.The traditional top choices for arbitral seats include London, Paris, New York,and Geneva, homes to "the oldest and most popular arbitral institutions."Reflecting the commonly cited refrain that most international commercial disputes go to arbitration, there has also been growth and innovation in arbitration centers and in arbitration-friendly domestic laws.
A recent phenomenon has disrupted this traditional picture. States around the world are establishing international commercial courts: English-language-friendly domestic courts specializing in international commercial disputes. In the past sixteen years, Dubai (2004), Qatar (2009), Singapore (2015), Abu Dhabi (2015), Kazakhstan (2018), and China (2018) have all opened specialized courts focusing on international commercial disputes.Since the Brexit vote in 2015, this phenomenon has also appeared in Europe: Germany,France,the Netherlands,Belgium,and Switzerlandhave all either recently opened or considered plans to open new courts or court branches specifically dedicated to international commercial disputes. Other countries are alsocontemplating opening new international commercial courts or judicial divisions dedicated to international commercial disputes.
International commercial courts are not international courts. They are domestic courts whose subject matter jurisdiction is limited to, or focuses on, international commercial disputes. These courts add to, and are intended to complement, their home States' international commercial dispute resolution offerings. These States do not embrace litigationinsteadof arbitration; rather, they simultaneously have "litigation-friendly" international commercial courts and "arbitration-friendly" legal regimes that are favorably inclined toward arbitration clauses and deferential in their recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards.These courts present themselves as innovative, cost effective, and responsive to typical criticisms of courts. For example, they often have experienced foreign jurists or other experts as judges, incorporate ADR, and allow parties to opt-out of regular domestic law procedures, resulting in courts that offer something of a hybrid of litigation and arbitration.
Scholars, mostly outside the United States, are beginning to notice these courts. Several articles describe some subset of these new courts and discuss theircapacity to compete with arbitrationor with the London Commercial Court.More recently, entire volumes have been devoted to exploring the inner workings of these courts and speculating about their ability to attract cases.
This Article takes on the received narrative that competition with arbitration to provide the best dispute resolution mechanism has been the primary driving force behind the creation of these courts. It argues that this narrative is mistaken and incomplete.
To the extent that competition is driving the creation of these courts, the competitive forces at work may not be entirely positive or efficient. Moreover, there are explanations for these courts beyond competition: the proliferation of international commercial courts is also a result of particular domestic political economies and other forces. Studying these courts and the forces driving their creation can generate important insights into critical debates about courts, international commercial dispute resolution, and the relationship between courts and arbitration.
This Article offers four main contributions. The first is descriptive: the Article offers a typology of international commercial courts that tracks what appear to be the primary reasons why these courts have come to be.
Second, this Article seeks to correct and shape the current conversation about international commercial courts as an emerging source of positive, efficient competition with arbitration. Long before the rise of international commercial courts, scholars have argued and assumed that competition for forum selection in contracts is an efficient competitive force. That is, such competition is supposed to drive a "race to the top" for tribunals to develop the best, mostefficient procedures to resolve disputes.The nascent literature on the rise of international commercial courts likewise often relies on these assumptions as a jumping-off point, describing international commercial courts as competing with arbitration by combining the best of both worlds (litigation and arbitration).
This account is incomplete. These courts emerge not from some idealistic desire to perfect courts, but from a confluence of different local and international forces. Some courts have appeared because localities want to become new legal hubs for dispute resolution--providing not only new courts, but a forum hospitable to litigation, arbitration, and other forms of ADR (not necessarily focused on generating substantive law).Singapore, for example, recently created an international commercial court to complement its rising prominence in arbitration and as a regional economic hub.Some international commercial courts can emerge as aspiring litigation destinations without a parallel emphasis on arbitration or other kinds of ADR, as appears to be the case in Amsterdam, for example.Other locations, such as Dubai, Qatar, and Kazakhstan, have created special economic zones and view courts with dispute resolution expertise as an integral part of attracting investment and capital to those zones.Finally, China's aim seems keyed to exercising control over Belt and Road disputes,although it may have broader, longer-term goals as well.
It is important to pay attention to the driving forces behind international commercial courts because these goals will likely shape the courts' development. Moreover, over time, these courts' success may be judged domestically by metrics tied to these driving goals. These metrics will lead to decisions about, for example, whether governments will continue to fund the courts. Investment-minded courts will be deemed a success if they help expand investment; aspiring litigation destinations will be judged by the size of their dockets; China may judge its new court by its global influence or by other metrics.
It is possible that achieving these results might coincide with positive perceptions of the courts' quality, fairness, or cost-effectiveness. But it might not. Instead, courts might achieve these results in other ways, such as by cateringto certain constituencies or by expanding their jurisdiction. As the scholarship on corporate law has shown, probing the "race to the top" analogy reveals a more complicated picture than first appears.While there is much to celebrate about the innovation of international commercial courts, these complicated dynamics also recommend watching them closely to see how they develop. A goal of this Article is to begin a line of scholarship that celebrates these courts' potential and helps avoid their worst outcomes.
International commercial courts also offer insight into a second, related theme in scholarship about the relationship between arbitration and litigation. U.S. courts often portray arbitration and litigation as stark alternatives, with the former as parties' favorite for resolving disputes arising out of international commercial contracts. As I have argued elsewhere, this dichotomy is overblown.The new international commercial courts both bolster this argument and challenge the conventional story in a new way. For example, international commercial courts often borrow procedural devices, like party-driven design and confidentiality, that are typically thought to be characteristics distinguishing arbitration from litigation. These courts therefore explode assumptions about inherent differences between arbitration and litigation and undermine assumptions commonly made by U.S. courts that being pro-arbitration requires being hostile to litigation.
Finally, international commercial courts offer an important perspective on scholarly debates about whether parties really do prefer arbitration, as is widely assumed. The increased supply of international courts suggests that there may be a demand for them, frustrating accounts that arbitration has replaced litigation as the dispute resolution mechanism of choice in international commercial contracts. On the other hand, supply does not prove demand. If it turns out that these courts attract few cases over time, that study, too, could inform understandings of what parties want from dispute resolution and what courts are capable of.
Part I provides a background understanding of the differences between courts, commercial courts, and international commercial courts. Part II canvases the recent growth of international commercial courts around the globe. It sets forth a typology for understanding the emergence of these courts based on the forces driving their creation. Part III discusses the importance of this changing adjudication business landscape for understanding the law market and other forces that may be driving the rise of international commercial courts. Part IV investigates these courts' lessons for scholarship about the relationship between litigation and arbitration and parties' preferences. Part V celebrates the potentialof international commercial courts but also warns against the dangers of them catering excessively to either State or private interests.
