shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Brady and related decisions holding that where an arbitration agreement conflicts with AAA rules, the parties' agreement controls and the arbitrator must enforce it; Paper B engages the same issue through Stolt‑Nielsen and Concepcion, analyzing how courts limit arbitrators' power to adopt procedures (e.g., class arbitration) not consented to by the parties.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between party-crafted/ad hoc arbitration procedures and arbitration‑sponsoring organizations' rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes conflicts that arise when parties adopt, modify, or rely on AAA (or other institutional) rules and the legal consequences of those divergences; Paper B treats private dispute‑resolution providers' rules and practices as a key locus for reform and experimentation, recognizing similar tensions between party autonomy and institutional rule sets.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of judicial precedent and federal doctrine on arbitration procedure and party remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines Brady and comparable case law across jurisdictions to explain how courts resolve rule/agreement inconsistencies and the practical effects for practitioners, while Paper B traces Supreme Court federalization (FAA preemption, Concepcion, Stolt‑Nielsen) and discusses how those doctrines constrain state regulation and shape what procedural options (and reforms) remain available to parties and providers.

papers.node_id: 59nyulrev443!!ARTICLE: THE FORMALIZATION OF INFORMAL LAW: ARBITRATION BEFORE THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION.
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE FORMALIZATION OF INFORMAL LAW: ARBITRATION BEFORE THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION.
papers.abstract:
Zephaniah Swift, a Connecticut jurist of the early republic, described arbitration as "an amicable and neighbourly mode of settling personal controversies."Arbitrators, he wrote, "are not tied down to the same strictness, formality and precision as court of law.  Whilethey have greater latitude in the mode of proceeding than courts of law, they have ampler powers to do compleat and perfect justice between the parties in the decision of the matters in dispute."Yet, even as he sang its praises, Swift treated arbitration as an appendage to the legal system rather than as an integral part of it.  In a two-volume treatise, he gave arbitration only eleven pages alongside selfdefense and self-help.  Such has been the fate of arbitration in legal scholarship generally.
It is an unfortunate fate, and an undeserved one.  Long before Swift wrote, arbitration played a significant role in resolving the disputes of people who preferred not to go to law.  Unlike litigation, arbitration was inexpensive, expeditious, and private.  Above all, it was, as Swift recognized, "neighbourly" -- uniquely tied to and shaped by the communities in which it functioned.  The community ties were an essential part of arbitration.Without them, arbitration would nothave been the popular and effective alternative to formal legal process that it was.
Although we customarily think of arbitration as nonlegal in nature, the relationship between arbitration and the legal system has always been strong.  It became stronger in early America as the communities that had nurtured arbitration grew less communal.  In time, the legal system appropriated arbitration to itself and turned it into a formal process that differed little from legal adjudication.  The transformation was particularly clear in Connecticut, where it was part of a general pattern of legal change in America before the Revolution, the contours of which we are only beginning to appreciate.
This Article, then, is a study of arbitration and legal change.  It begins with a brief description of English arbitration practice at the time Connecticut was settled.  It then discusses the three principal stages in the transformation of arbitration in Connecticut by focusing on changes in how people submitted their disputes to arbitration.  Not coincidentally, these changes reflected shifts in the social and economic structure of the colony.  One has to look closely to see social and economic change reflected in matters of technical legal form.  But if one does, the view is well worth the effort.

papers.node_id: 64umiamilrev89!!Article: The Future of 28 U.S.C. § 1782: The Continued Advance of American-Style Discovery in International Commercial Arbitration
papers.title: Article: The Future of 28 U.S.C. § 1782: The Continued Advance of American-Style Discovery in International Commercial Arbitration
papers.abstract:
Likely the most salient, significant, and uniquely American contribution to private procedural international law is embodied in(a).This statute boldly authorizes the use of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure - specifically, the rules governing the discovery of documents and information in U.S. federal courts- to assist a "foreign tribunal" or "investigation" (preaction) with securing documents or deposition testimony from persons or entities present (not limited to residents) in the United States.
Adherence to § 1782(a) in the context of international commercialarbitration reconfigures the procedural law applicable to an arbitral proceeding as to the gathering of documents and information by parties, and even the very commencement of the proceeding. Post-Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.and its progeny, an "interested person" is vested with authority to prosecute a § 1782(a) petition in a federal district court in the United States prior to actually filing and serving a request for arbitration, so long as the filing of such arbitral proceeding is "in reasonable contemplation."Thus, the arbitration, which now as a matter of law constitutes a "foreign or international tribunal,"need not even be pending before a prospective respondent finds itself with a binding normative legal obligation to respond to "discovery," as opposed to the mere gathering or taking of evidence, pursuant to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.Intel and its progeny divest prospective institutional arbitral centers from even engaging in the most rudimentary arbitration case-management exercise of administering the gathering of evidence. Similarly, this extraordinary doctrinal development in private procedural international law divests arbitral tribunals of all authority concerning the applicable standard, the conduct, the admissibility, the nature, and the character of the disclosure and exchange of documents and information between parties and nonparties to an arbitral proceeding.
Irrespective of whether § 1782 is deemed a positive doctrinaldevelopment in both U.S. (domestic) and international arbitral proceedings, there are numerous paradigms in which risk-assessment models suggest that a party to a transaction would be decisively and materially disadvantaged should a dispute arise precipitating the invocation of an arbitration clause and, consequently, the possible filing of a § 1782 petition by the adverse party.
The most common scenario where a party to an arbitral proceeding would be disadvantaged if § 1782 applications were filed with U.S. federal district courts is the common case where the seat of the arbitration is located outside the United States and its territories, and the respondent to a § 1782 petition has headquarters, affiliates, asset managers, agents, representatives, bank accounts, or past transactions in the United States that fall within the ambit ofConversely, the petitioner is typically a non-U.S. entity with no ties whatsoever to the United States, other than the event giving rise to the arbitration that is now characterized as a proceeding in a foreign or international tribunal for purposes of § 1782(a). Consonant with this scenario, the respondent is meaningfully exposed in contrast to the petitioner, who has assets and contacts beyond the jurisdiction of federal district courts. A permutation of this equally treacherous and unilateral paragon occurs in the context of discovery in aid of execution of an arbitral award even before the award itself has been formally, if not substantively, reduced to an official, court-issued judgment. Moreover, it remains far from clear whether incorporating language in the arbitral clause would proscribe recourse to § 1782(a). It is equally opaque whether agreement on the United States as the arbitral seat, so as to attempt to render the tribunal "nonforeign" for purposes of § 1782, also would obviate the statute's application.
Intel and its scant progeny, to date, have yet to address these novel issues. Two methodologies, both strategically and tactically executed at the negotiating stage of the arbitration clause, do suggest themselves as possible defenses to the application of § 1782. This article seeks to explore the doctrinal consequences that may affect enforcement of an arbitration award arising from an arbitral tribunal's refusal to consider evidence obtained pursuant to § 1782 and in accordance with Article V of the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (the New York Convention)or consonant with the doctrine of manifest disregard of the law. In so endeavoring, this article shall necessarily trace the contours of the doctrine of manifest disregard of thelaw and submit to sustained and reasoned examination of the jurisprudence attendant to the proscription of § 1782.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LAW IN DISARRAY: JUDICIAL STANDARDS FOR VACATUR OF COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION AWARDS

shared_topics.topic: implications for the viability, character, and enforcement of commercial arbitration as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EVOLVING ISSUES IN REINSURANCE DISPUTES: THE POWER OF ARBITRATORS

papers.node_id: 84ucinlrev1221!!ARTICLE: The Future of Judicial Policing in Consumer Contracting
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Future of Judicial Policing in Consumer Contracting
papers.abstract:
In the Anglo-American common law of contracts, judicially-created doctrines have developed over the decades to ensure certain aspects of fundamental fairness in the bargaining process. These doctrines are generally grounded in the nature and quality of the assent given by a party in an inferior bargaining position, whether that inferior bargaining position results from individual weaknesses or systemic, institutional disparities in bargaining power. When one party suffers from substantially impaired bargaining power, courts will scrutinize the transaction for over-reaching or unfairness - "bargaining naughtiness" - on the part of the dominant party. This tradition is embodied in the contract doctrines of capacity, duress, undue influence, unconscionability, and fraud, among others. However, the efficacy of these doctrines has recently been brought into serious question by the rise of mandatory arbitration clauses in consumer contracts, and the favor shown for such clauses by the courts including, most recently, the United States Supreme Court.
In the early twentieth century, commentators and commercial entities were increasingly aware of the value of alternative dispute resolution techniques such as arbitration and the advantages of such techniques over the cost and delay characteristic of litigation. However, the state of the law in 1906was little changed from that in 1609.Courts still overwhelmingly followed the lead of Lord Cokeand Blackstonein holding that an executory agreementto arbitrate would not be enforced by the courts, because the deprivation of jurisdiction that it entailed was against sound public policy.Courts, wary of loss of control anddistrustful of non-legally trained arbitrators, more often than not refused to enforce provisions freely agreed to by commercially contracting parties for arbitration rather than litigation of disputes arising out of their agreements.
This reticence on the part of courts created several problems for a developing commercial law system. First, it deprived the judicial system of the relief from crowded dockets that arbitration could offer.Second, it deprived commercial actors of the benefits of speed, cost, and informality offered by the arbitral forum.Finally, and most problematically, it meant that perfectly valid expressions of contractual assent were being systematically ignored and refused enforcement by the courts whose ostensible purpose was to enforce those expressions of assent.In 1925, Congress stepped into the field with the United States Arbitration Act (now the Federal Arbitration Act or FAA).The FAA was intended by Congress to "even the playing field" for arbitrationby instructing federal courts to treat an agreement to arbitrate disputes in the same manner as any other lawful agreement between the parties.The FAA represents the first step towards the modern judicial policy in favor of arbitration.
In the eighty years since the passage of the FAA, the landscape of contract dispute resolution has changed dramatically. Most contracting today bears little resemblance to the arms-length bargaining envisioned by the early proponents of the FAA,still assumed by most contract doctrine, and still taught as the paradigm in most law schools. Instead, contracts of adhesion have proliferated,bringing lower transactioncosts and increased efficiency,but minimizing the opportunity for individuals and consumers to meaningfully affect the terms on which they do business with sellers, creditors, and other commercial actors. Substantive contract law has struggled to keep pace with this substitution of adhesion for bargainingand has often failed to do so successfully.Together with this decrease in opportunities for meaningful bargaining has come an explosion of arbitration.Courts, encouraged by the adoption of the FAA by Congress and the Uniform Arbitration Act by the states,have authorized the use of arbitration as a means for resolving future disputes in virtually every aspect of modern contracts.
Recent judicial expansion of the scope of arbitration threatens to elevate the value of arbitration over the values and principles of contract law from which it arose.Although a fundamental principle of arbitration law is that arbitration is a creature of contract,and that no one should be compelled to give up his right to litigate claims in favor of arbitration absent assent to do so,this is exactly the state of affairs produced by the Supreme Court in its most recent consumer arbitrationopinions.
This Article will analyze the relationship between assent and arbitration, and show how recent precedent elevates the latter over the former. Part I will provide an overview of the history of the FAA leading up to and including the landmark 1967 Supreme Court case Prima Paint v. Flood & Conklin Mfg. Co.,which enshrined the so-called separability doctrine in federal substantive law. Part II will discuss the confusion created in the lower courts by Prima Paint, as the courts struggled to reconcile the concepts of assent and policing of the bargaining process with the new federal doctrine. Part III will discuss the Supreme Court's 2006 opinion in Buckeye Check Cashing v. Cardegnaand its rejection of lower court compromises in favor of a strict pro-arbitration doctrine. Part IV will demonstrate why Buckeye cannot solve the conflicts generated by Prima Paint and its separability doctrine, and why the Buckeye decision forces the lower courts to either continue the search for a workable rule or accept the undermining of the moral foundations of contract law. Finally, Part V will conclude with recommendations for legislative, judicial, and strategic responses to Buckeye, in order to minimize the damage done to the law of contract and arbitration by this shortsighted decision.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 14lewisclarklrev905!!SYMPOSIUM: THE SUPREME COURT AND ARBITRATION: THE SUPREME COURT AND ARBITRATION: CONTRACTING AROUND HALL STREET
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE SUPREME COURT AND ARBITRATION: THE SUPREME COURT AND ARBITRATION: CONTRACTING AROUND HALL STREET

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and exclusivity of the Federal Arbitration Act's remedial provisions (e.g., vacatur/confirmation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the FAA's historical development and Supreme Court rulings (Prima Paint, Buckeye) that expand federal arbitration doctrine, while Paper B analyzes Hall Street's holding that the FAA sets 'exclusive' statutory grounds for vacatur and the limits that decision imposes on altering those grounds.

shared_topics.topic: how Supreme Court arbitration decisions reshape traditional contract-law policing of assent and fairness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that recent Supreme Court arbitration opinions elevate arbitration over contract doctrines (capacity, unconscionability, duress) and undermine judicial policing of bargaining, and Paper B situates Hall Street within that jurisprudential arc, examining its practical effect on parties' ability to preserve judicial protections.

shared_topics.topic: the permissible scope of judicial review over arbitration agreements and awards (separability, vacatur, confirmation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the separability doctrine and how it insulates arbitration clauses from contract defenses, reducing judicial oversight of consent, while Paper B focuses on limits to post-award judicial review (expanded-review provisions) and the enforceability of contractual mechanisms to broaden review.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between federal arbitration law and state law or alternative enforcement routes
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly considers whether parties can rely on state statutory/common law to obtain expanded review after Hall Street, and Paper A likewise discusses the role of the Uniform Arbitration Act, state responses, and recommends legislative/judicial strategies to mitigate federal arbitration rulings, showing both engage with federal-state tensions.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of contractual modifications to arbitration procedures/remedies and implications for party autonomy (especially in adhesion settings)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B evaluates whether parties can contract for expanded judicial review or otherwise 'contract around' Hall Street, while Paper A examines how mandatory arbitration clauses in consumer adhesion contracts and pro-arbitration precedent limit meaningful assent and the ability of parties to retain litigation rights.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43pepplrev493!!ARTICLE: Innovation in Arbitration Law: The Case of Delaware
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Innovation in Arbitration Law: The Case of Delaware

shared_topics.topic: federal-state interaction over arbitration law and the limits of state innovation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how the Federal Arbitration Act and federal court doctrine constrain or shape state-level arbitration rules: Paper A traces how the FAA and Supreme Court decisions created a strong federal pro-arbitration regime, and Paper B examines how that regime and federal jurisdictional rules limit — but do not entirely prevent — state experimentation such as Delaware's statutory innovations.

shared_topics.topic: the proper boundary between arbitration autonomy and judicial/public oversight
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the tension between treating arbitration as an autonomous, contract-based forum and preserving court supervision or public access: Paper A criticizes recent jurisprudence that elevates arbitration over traditional judicial policing of contracts, while Paper B discusses Delaware measures that limit court involvement and a confidential judge-run arbitration scheme that was struck down for violating public-access principles.

shared_topics.topic: how arbitration affects policing of bargaining fairness and protections for weaker parties
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider the implications of arbitration for substantive fairness in contracting: Paper A focuses on how mandatory arbitration undermines doctrines (e.g., unconscionability, duress) meant to protect parties with inferior bargaining power, and Paper B raises related concerns by analyzing procedural rules (time limits, restricted review) that can alter remedies and the practical ability of parties to vindicate rights.

shared_topics.topic: market and institutional drivers behind the expansion or reform of arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Both papers situate arbitration changes in broader market and institutional contexts: Paper A links the proliferation of mandatory arbitration to the spread of contracts of adhesion and commercial incentives to reduce dispute costs, while Paper B describes Delaware's legislative innovations as competitive moves to attract commercial and international dispute business and to reshape the arbitration market.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nclrev1091!!Article: JUDGING-LITE: HOW ARBITRATORS USE AND CREATE PRECEDENT*
compared_to.partner_title: Article: JUDGING-LITE: HOW ARBITRATORS USE AND CREATE PRECEDENT*

shared_topics.topic: arbitration's effect on enforcement of individual statutory and consumer/employee rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that mandatory consumer arbitration clauses and recent Supreme Court doctrine can undermine judicial policing doctrines (e.g., unconscionability, duress) that protect weaker parties, while Paper B empirically examines whether arbitrators actually vindicate statutory and employment rights and whether arbitration produces ad hoc outcomes that threaten enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of judicial oversight of arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how the FAA and Supreme Court decisions have constrained courts' ability to police arbitration agreements and protect assent-based contract doctrines, and Paper B interrogates the formal limits on judicial review of awards and proposes more informal judicial engagement with arbitral decisions as a corrective or dialogue.

shared_topics.topic: how arbitration changes the development and availability of legal precedent and private law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A claims the expansion of arbitration risks elevating arbitral processes over the precedent-driven moral foundations of contract law, reducing public law development, while Paper B studies whether and when arbitrators cite and create precedent and assesses the extent to which arbitral decisionmaking contributes to or diminishes the body of authoritative law.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of assent/consent and power imbalances in enforcing arbitration clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes how adhesion contracts and unequal bargaining power render assent suspect and yet are increasingly enforced by courts, and Paper B considers how arbitrators apply rules the parties (or the more powerful party) select and how mandatory regimes affect arbitrators' treatment of non-waivable statutory claims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 21nevlj1223!!ARTICLE: HIDING SEXUAL HARASSMENT: MYTHS AND REALITIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HIDING SEXUAL HARASSMENT: MYTHS AND REALITIES

shared_topics.topic: legal mechanisms that systematically impede effective remedies for vulnerable parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how sexual harassment complainants are disadvantaged at every stage of reporting and resolution, producing quasi-immunity for wrongdoers and employers; Paper B shows how mandatory arbitration and recent Supreme Court doctrines channel consumers away from judicial forums and dilute judicial policing, reducing meaningful remedies for contract counterparties in weaker positions.

shared_topics.topic: the centrality of power imbalances and systemic inequality in producing and sustaining private harms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A ties ongoing sexual harassment to entrenched gender inequality and workplace hierarchies that enable harassers, while Paper B analyzes how contracts of adhesion and disparate bargaining power create systemic disadvantages for consumers and individuals confronted with take-it-or-leave-it terms.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and legal doctrines in either perpetuating or addressing injustices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques institutional responses and legal processes that leave complainants frustrated and unredressed, and Paper B traces how judicial doctrines (e.g., separability, pro‑arbitration precedent) have reshaped dispute-resolution law in ways that can undermine the moral and remedial foundations of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: calls for reform (legislative, judicial, or institutional) to restore fairness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concludes with proposals aimed at transforming myths into realities through affirmative corrective measures, and Paper B ends with recommendations for legislative, judicial, and strategic responses to recent appellate and Supreme Court arbitration decisions to protect contracting parties in weak positions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58bclrev1355!!ARTICLE: SHARING ECONOMY INEQUALITY: HOW THE ADOPTION OF CLASS ACTION WAIVERS IN THE SHARING ECONOMY PRESENTS A THREAT TO RACIAL DISCRIMINATION CLAIMS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SHARING ECONOMY INEQUALITY: HOW THE ADOPTION OF CLASS ACTION WAIVERS IN THE SHARING ECONOMY PRESENTS A THREAT TO RACIAL DISCRIMINATION CLAIMS

shared_topics.topic: how mandatory arbitration clauses and class-action waivers impede the vindication of substantive rights (especially systemic civil‑rights/discrimination claims)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses Airbnb and Selden's failed racial‑discrimination class action to show that individual arbitration clauses and class‑action waivers block systemic civil‑rights litigation, while Paper B analyzes how the broad judicial enforcement of consumer arbitration agreements has elevated arbitration at the expense of litigated protections, undermining the ability of disadvantaged parties to obtain collective relief.

shared_topics.topic: the consequences of adhesion contracting and unequal bargaining power for fairness in consumer/platform markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how sharing‑economy platforms impose take‑it‑or‑leave‑it terms that prevent aggregated claims by minorities, and Paper B theorizes more broadly that proliferation of contracts of adhesion and diminished meaningful assent call for judicial policing (unconscionability, duress, etc.) to protect parties in inferior bargaining positions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the Federal Arbitration Act and judicial precedent in expanding arbitration's reach and limiting judicial policing
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents courts compelling arbitration under platform terms of service (foreclosing court scrutiny of discrimination claims), and Paper B traces the FAA and key Supreme Court doctrines (Prima Paint, Buckeye) showing how federal precedent has constrained courts' ability to police unfair contracting practices.

shared_topics.topic: the need for legislative or regulatory responses to mitigate arbitration's harms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for Congress or a federal agency to ban class‑action waivers in civil‑rights contexts, and Paper B concludes with recommendations for legislative, judicial, and strategic responses to Supreme Court arbitration doctrine to preserve contract law values and protections for consumers.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93nwulrev453!!ARTICLE:THE RISKS AND VIRTUES OF LAWLESSNESS: A "SECOND LOOK"AT INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE RISKS AND VIRTUES OF LAWLESSNESS: A "SECOND LOOK"AT INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION

shared_topics.topic: judicial policing and scope of court review over arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the need for a meaningful 'second look' by courts (and proposes differentiated, exacting review for arbitrations implicating mandatory law) and Paper B analyzes how doctrines like separability and recent Supreme Court rulings (e.g., Buckeye) limit courts' ability to police arbitration agreements and results in consumer disputes.

shared_topics.topic: whether arbitration clauses can displace mandatory legal protections or public-policy rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the arbitrability and potential displacement of mandatory U.S. economic legislation by private arbitration, while Paper B addresses how mandatory arbitration clauses in adhesion consumer contracts can oust contract-law protections (unconscionability, fraud, capacity) and undermine substantive safeguards for weaker parties.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of Supreme Court precedent in expanding arbitration's reach and transforming adjudicatory power
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Supreme Court and circuit decisions (Scherk, Mitsubishi, M/V Sky Reefer and displacement cases) that shift adjudicatory functions to private arbitrators, and Paper B critiques Supreme Court precedents (Prima Paint, Buckeye) that strengthen the enforceability of arbitration clauses and constrain judicial oversight.

shared_topics.topic: proposals and institutional responses to mitigate harms from arbitration's expansion
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys and critiques reform proposals (greater transparency, uniform procedures, institutional rule changes, differentiated review under the New York Convention) to preserve arbitration's virtues while protecting mandatory laws, and Paper B offers legislative, judicial, and strategic remedies to respond to pro-arbitration rulings and protect consumer-contract policing doctrines.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52bclrev137!!ARTICLE: ARE ARBITRATORS ABOVE THE LAW? THE "MANIFEST DISREGARD OF THE LAW" STANDARD
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ARE ARBITRATORS ABOVE THE LAW? THE "MANIFEST DISREGARD OF THE LAW" STANDARD

shared_topics.topic: how Supreme Court interpretations of the Federal Arbitration Act have constrained judicial oversight of arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how high‑court precedents (Paper A: Prima Paint, Buckeye; Paper B: Wilko, Hall Street and related line‑items) have reshaped the FAA to narrow courts' ability to review or refuse arbitration, and they trace the doctrinal effects of those decisions on lower‑court policing of arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: the rise of mandatory arbitration and its consequences for enforcing substantive legal protections
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the spread of mandatory arbitration clauses (Paper A in consumer adhesion contracts; Paper B in employment and statutory claims) and the resulting risks to individuals' ability to vindicate legal rights and to have courts police unfair or illegal conduct.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between arbitration finality and judicial policing of legal error or unfairness (e.g., manifest disregard, unconscionability)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the core conflict between deference to arbitrators (finality) and the need for courts to correct egregious legal errors or address unfair bargaining outcomes—Paper A through contract doctrines that police assent and fairness, Paper B through the manifest‑disregard/vacatur framework.

shared_topics.topic: who decides gateway questions of contract validity and arbitrability (separability and allocation of jurisdictional issues)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with whether challenges to contract validity or statutory claims belong to courts or arbitrators (Paper A via the separability doctrine and Buckeye; Paper B via analysis of Wilko/Hall Street and whether non‑statutory standards like manifest disregard survive), and the implications of allocating those gateway issues away from judicial review.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93kylj423!!ARTICLE: At the Crossroads of Federalism and Arbitration: The Application of Prima Paint to Purportedly Void Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: At the Crossroads of Federalism and Arbitration: The Application of Prima Paint to Purportedly Void Contracts

shared_topics.topic: the Prima Paint separability (severability) doctrine and its consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze Prima Paint's rule that an arbitration clause is separable from the underlying contract, assessing how that doctrine has been applied by courts and the doctrinal confusion and consequences that follow from treating the arbitration clause independently.

papers.node_id: 56galrev299!!ARTICLE: THE GIG ECONOMY'S SHORT REACH: AN ANALYSIS OF THE SCOPE OF THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT'S "TRANSPORTATION WORKER" EXEMPTION
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE GIG ECONOMY'S SHORT REACH: AN ANALYSIS OF THE SCOPE OF THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT'S "TRANSPORTATION WORKER" EXEMPTION
papers.abstract:
The gig economy is a lucrative industry in the United States: in 2017, approximately 57 million people--or a third of the entire workforce--engaged in some form of gig work.By 2021, estimates project that the gig economy will contribute over $ 1 trillion to the U.S. economy.Referred to by various names, including the "sharing" or "1099 economy,"the gig economy often involves "economic transactions that are facilitated by online platforms that match customers with providers."The transportation services sector represents one major component of the gig economy that employs this online platform system.Within the transportation services sector, last-mile delivery drivers form one subsect of gig economy workers.These drivers transport people and deliver goodsor prepared restaurant meals to customers' homes or offices.While some platform companies offer only one type of service, generally either some form of ride-sharing or food delivery, other companies are expanding their range of services, meaning drivers can participate in transporting both goods and people through the same platform.
Regardless of the platform, there are benefits of working as a gig economy delivery driver, including a flexible self-created work schedule,the opportunity to gain supplemental or part-time income,and the ability to work seamlessly for multiple platforms simultaneously.
To become a driver for one of these platform-based companies, applicants must accept the terms of use that create a contractual relationship between the company and the driver.An agreement to arbitrate a dispute, which precludes a driver from bringing a collective or representative action against the company,is common in these contracts.Despite this requirement to arbitrate disputes, there has been an uptick in suits brought by drivers against their respective platform employers for employment contract violations.Litigation brought against these companies conflicts with a recent trend in the United States to view arbitration, including employment arbitration, favorably.In bringing these suits, drivers argue that they are exempt from arbitration based on a carveout in the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA).Section 1 of the FAA exempts certain classes of workers from mandatory arbitration, including "workers engaged in foreignor interstate commerce,"which the U.S. Supreme Court has ambiguously classified as "transportation workers."
Without guidance from either the statutory language or Supreme Court jurisprudence, it is unclear which workers are "transportation workers" for purposes of the Section 1 exemption.The influx of these suits forces lower courts to determine whether gig economy drivers are transportation workers under Section 1 of the FAA; if so, Section 1 would exempt them from mandatory arbitration.A recent circuit split involving a range of gig-based companies and their drivers considers whether gig economy drivers are transportation workers "engaged in foreign or interstate commerce," thereby exempting these drivers from having to arbitrate their claims.Recent cases illustrate that courts diverge widely in their treatment of gig economy drivers based on a variety of Section 1 interpretations.The Supreme Court has declined to rule on this issue,which will invariably result in lower courts furthering the patchwork of interpretations.
This Note argues that a narrow interpretation of the Section 1 exemption is the appropriate reading, under which gig economy delivery drivers are not entitled to the arbitration exemption. Part II examines the contours of the FAA, Section 1, and the recent extension of Section 1 to employment disputes within the scope of Supreme Court caselaw. Part III surveys the current circuit split and the varied approaches taken by three circuit courts of appeals. Part IV then illustrates why the Section 1 exemption should not extend to gig economy delivery drivers and offers a defense of arbitration in employment dispute contexts.

questions.question: Whether gig-economy last-mile delivery drivers qualify as transportation workers engaged in interstate or foreign commerce such that they are exempt from mandatory arbitration agreements.

What interpretive approach courts should adopt to define the scope of the transportation-worker exemption, and how a narrow versus broad interpretation would affect the use of arbitration in employment disputes involving gig workers.

papers.abstract:
Taking the Supreme Court's 1991 decision inas his starting point, Professor Gorman discusses the scope of arbitration agreements in public-law disputes. He begins by sketching the background of arbitration proceedings as developed in labor arbitration. He then discusses the need for formal procedural standards to ensure the fairness of the public-law arbitration. These standards should be derived fromGilmer,the Federal Arbitration Act, and other sources. The result should be a hybrid system that builds upon the virtues of grievance and commercial arbitration, but selectively incorporates elements of fair procedure from civil courts.
Taking the Supreme Court's 1991 decision inas his starting point, Professor Gorman discusses the scope of arbitration agreements in public-law disputes. He begins by sketching the background of arbitration proceedings as developed in labor arbitration. He then discusses the need for formal procedural standards to ensure the fairness of the public-law arbitration. These standards should be derived fromGilmer,the Federal Arbitration Act, and other sources. The result should be a hybrid system that builds upon the virtues of grievance and commercial arbitration, but selectively incorporates elements of fair procedure from civil courts.
In 1991, the Supreme Court decided, inGilmer v. Interstate/Johnson Lane Corp.,that a sixty-two-year-old stock broker, who believed that his employment had been terminated in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA), could be required to drop his federal court action and to proceed instead before an arbitrator, as he had agreed to do when he secured employment six years before. With this decision, the Supreme Court ushered in a new era in labor arbitration, in which employees working in nonunion workplaces will be arbitrating claims of violation of public laws, both federal and state, and based on statutory and regulatory enactments as well as upon judicial precedent. Emerging now, alongside the traditional and tested techniques of grievance arbitration under collective bargaining agreements, will be what could be referred to as public-law arbitration by individual employees under the negotiated, or in many instancesdictated, terms of an employment contract or personnel handbook.
When Mr. Gilmer began to work for Interstate, he was required to register as a securities representative with several stock exchanges, including the New York Stock Exchange, which in turn required, through standard forms, that he abide by its Rule 347, which provides for arbitration of "any controversy . . . arising out of the employment or termination of employment of [any] registered representative."The district court in which Gilmer brought his ADEA action rejected Interstate's motion to compel arbitration, but the court of appeals reversed, concluding that nothing in that civil rights statute precluded enforcement of Gilmer's promise to arbitrate. The Supreme Court agreed with the court of appeals, and rested its decision upon the 1925 Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)which, among other things, provides for specific performance of agreements to arbitrate disputes relating to interstate commerce.
The FAA -- shaped by commercial lawyers within the American Bar Association -- had as its principal focus the enforcement of arbitration promises contained in commercial contracts, when parties have a dispute that requires interpreting and applying the terms of those contracts.The purpose of the statute was to overturn centuries, going back to the English common law, of hostility to arbitration, which was viewed by the courts as a system of private justice which displaced the jurisdiction of the civil courts.The FAA was intended to make arbitration promises equally enforceable in courts as other contract promises, and in particular to provide for specific performance of such promises.
What is most significant about the Supreme Court decision inGilmeris its conclusion that an employee's promise to arbitrate all disputes "arising out of the employment or termination of employment" is, in effect, presumed to embrace more than disputes about private contractual understandings in the workplace. It also covers claims of violation of protective workplace legislation, including federal (and state) laws barring employment discrimination on the basis of race, religion, gender, age, and disability. As the Court forcefully stated inGilmer:It is by now clear that statutory claims may be the subject of an arbitration agreement, enforceable pursuant to the FAA. . . . The burden is on Gilmer to show that Congress intended to preclude a waiver of a judicial forum for ADEA claims. . . . If such an intention exists, it will be discoverable in the text of the ADEA, its legislative history, or an "inherent conflict" between arbitration and the ADEA's underlying purposes.Mr. Gilmer had attempted in particular to show that the standard elements of arbitration procedure provide so little protection for a victim of discrimination who is a member of a statutorily protected class, such as himself, that such procedure is incompatible with the ADEA. The Court, however, gave his arguments short shrift.
It is by now clear that statutory claims may be the subject of an arbitration agreement, enforceable pursuant to the FAA. . . . The burden is on Gilmer to show that Congress intended to preclude a waiver of a judicial forum for ADEA claims. . . . If such an intention exists, it will be discoverable in the text of the ADEA, its legislative history, or an "inherent conflict" between arbitration and the ADEA's underlying purposes.
Mr. Gilmer cited bias in the panels from which arbitrators were chosen, the unavailability of adequate discovery, the lack of written and published arbitral decisions, the customary limitations upon arbitral remedies, and the near nonexistence of judicial review of arbitration decisions.He also claimed that arbitration promises covering civil rights claims are suspect from the outset, given the inequality of bargaining power between the employer and the protected employee.Many of these criticisms of arbitration should have sounded familiar to the Court, because they were based in large measure upon the Court's 1974 decision inAlexander v. Gardner-Denver Co.,which allowed an individual to bring a Title VII race discrimination action in federal court after having unsuccessfully pressed a just-cause grievance to an arbitrator under a collective bargaining agreement. The Court rejected each of Gilmer's attacks, distinguished and narrowedGardner-Denver, and concluded that he had "not met his burden of showing that Congress, in enacting the ADEA, intended to preclude arbitration of claims under that Act."
The holding inGilmerwas by no means surprising, because the Court, for nearly a decade before, had been giving ever-wider berth to the substantive reach of the Federal Arbitration Act so as to embrace agreements to arbitrate disputes arising under important and complex federal statutes: the Sherman Act in the Court's 1985 decision inMitsubishi Motors Corp. v. Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc.,both the Securities Exchange Act and the federal RICO statute in the Court's 1987 decision inShearson/American Express Inc. v. McMahon,and the Securities Act of 1933 in its 1989 decision inRodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/American Express, Inc.
My purpose is not so much to assess the soundness of theGilmerdecision, for that has already been done by many scholars and other commentators.Rather, I would like to reflect on the implications ofbringing court-enforced arbitration to the world of public-law employment claims. Among the questions to be explored are these: Will arbitration of public-law disputes be suitable and successful? Will it prove to be fair to the worker, in its procedures and in its outcomes? What sources of law and what legal institutions -- Congress, the courts, administrative agencies, arbitrators themselves -- will be called upon to guarantee such fairness? To what extent will it be appropriate to transfer structures and procedures used in grievance arbitration, under collectively bargained agreements, to the new forum of public-law arbitration?
Some of my more general conclusions about these questions are as follows:
-- To make public-law arbitration effective and acceptable, arbitration of public-law disputes must incorporate several important procedural and substantive protections that will redound to the benefit of both parties. A code of "due process of arbitration" must therefore be articulated by the courts through a "common law" type of evolutionary development.
-- The source of those protections can be found in part in the Federal Arbitration Act, in part in the inherent powers of the arbitrator, and in part in the underlying policies of the various substantive worker-protection laws.
-- TheGilmerdecision itself invites, indeed requires, the establishment of such a code of due process, for the Court emphasized that arbitration promises are to be enforced only if not in "inherent conflict" with such laws; this requires that arbitration provide a full and fair opportunity for the trial of statutory claims.
-- The format and procedures of public-law arbitration should look significantly different from the familiar format and procedures of grievance arbitration, which are rooted in the context of unionization and collective bargaining and which must thus not be mechanically transferred to public-law arbitration. A hybrid or amalgam will develop that builds upon the virtues of grievance (and commercial) arbitration and that selectively incorporates elements of fair procedure from the civil courts.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how arbitration should resolve statutory/public-law employment claims (e.g., ADEA, Title VII)

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights critics' concerns about the near nonexistence of judicial review in arbitration and how that affects vindication of statutory rights; Paper B centers on whether courts should adopt broader substantive review (including contracted review or manifest-disregard doctrines) or instead preserve the FAA's narrow grounds, arguing the consequences of changing review standards.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for articulating a code of 'due process of arbitration' (discovery, neutral panels, remedies, published decisions) for public-law disputes; Paper B develops a 'process characteristics and values' framework to assess innovations and warns that mixing processes or expanding review can undermine core procedural attributes that give arbitration legitimacy.

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE IMPROBABLE BIRTH AND CONCEIVABLE DEATH OF THE SECURITIES ARBITRATION CLINIC
papers.abstract:
Americans have unprecedented access to global debt and equity markets to purchase investment and income-producing products. While individual stock ownership peaked in the late 2000s with the 2008 financial crisis, at least half of Americans still own stocks.The Revenue Act of 1978 created the 401(k) plan that, in turn, opened up the world of mutual fund investing to the average American employee.According to the Investment Company Institute, as of September 2012, 401(k) plans held about $ 3.5 trillion in assets, representing about 18% of the U.S. retirement market, "which includes employer-sponsored retirement plans, individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and annuities."Additionally, therapid expansion of online trading in the 1990s provided Americans with convenient access to brokerage accounts and the ability to implement self-directed trading strategies.This increase in investing naturally has led to an explosion of disputes between investors on the one side and individual brokersand their employer firms (broker-dealers)on the other.
For more than twenty-five years, arbitration in forums sponsored by the securities industryhas been the primary mechanismfor the resolution of disputes among investors, broker-dealers, and associated persons.In the late 1980s, the U.S. Supreme Court overruled prior lawand held that brokerage firms could enforce pre-dispute arbitration agreements in customer agreements, thus forcing customers to arbitrate their federal securities law claims.Virtually all broker-dealers--and many investment advisors--now include a pre-dispute arbitration clause in their retail customers'account agreements.Brokerage customers who allege, for example, that their broker recommended unsuitable investments or strategies, placed unauthorized trades, or committed fraudmust, because of the ubiquitous arbitration clause in their customer agreements,arbitrate those claims in the FINRA arbitration forum. Moreover, even if the customer agreement does not contain a pre-dispute arbitration clause, FINRA rules require broker-dealers and their associated persons to submit to arbitration upon the demand of a customer.
However, many investors, particularly if they are unsophisticated or of modest means, are unfamiliar with the arbitration processand thus cannot navigate the forum without legal representation. Several studies show that disputants fare better in a dispute resolution process when represented by counsel.Yet it is not economically feasible for those customers with low-dollar-value claims to retain counsel because legal fees would dwarf any possible recovery. Similarly, investors with larger claims but with few remaining disposable assets (precisely because of the monetary losses stemming from the alleged misconduct) may not be able to afford to retain private counsel or pay for upfront costs such as filing fees, forum fees, and expert witness fees.
One means available to investors who have low-dollar-value disputes with their brokers to obtain assistance in the securities arbitration process is to retain the services of a law school securities arbitration clinic (SAC).Generally, SAC is a clinical law program in which students, for academic credit and under the supervision of law faculty who act as supervising attorneys, provide free legal assistance to eligible investors who have disputes with their securities brokerage firms that must be resolved in arbitration, but who are unable to obtain private legal representation because of the low dollar value of their claims. While SACs did not exist at law schools until the late 1990s, as of early 2014, eighteen such programs are open in the United States.Resort to a SAC may be the best option available to an investor seeking legal representation in low-dollar-value arbitration disputes. Indeed, SACs have helped many investors since the first clinic opened at Pace Law School in 1997.
However, a few SACs recently have closed and several of the existing ones are currently in jeopardy of closing due to lack of funding.Many law schools will not commit to support them long-term.Other law schools have declined to open SACs because the faculty or the administration does not believe they are the type of clinic a law school should offer. Unless dollars flow in the general direction of law school clinics, and in particular to this type of clinic, the SAC may not make it to its twentieth anniversary.
This Article explores the birth, life, and possible death of SACs in the United States. Part II of this Article describes the history of the securities arbitration clinic in the United States. Part III describes how a SAC operates and how SAC students help investors. Part IV reviews the pedagogical advantages and disadvantages of a SAC, and addresses the reluctance of many law schools to embrace this type of clinic. Part V concludes by predicting whether these clinics have a future in light of the modern challenges to clinical legal education.

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE INTERACTION BETWEEN THE EMPLOYMENT-AT-WILL DOCTRINE AND EMPLOYER-EMPLOYEE AGREEMENTS TO ARBITRATE STATUTORY FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES CLAIMS: DIFFICULT CHOICES FOR AT-WILL EMPLOYERS
papers.authors: Stephen L. Hayford; Michael J. Evers
papers.abstract:
In 1991, the Supreme Court signalled a change in its attitude toward the enforcement of agreements between employers and individual employees to arbitrate statutory fair employment practice claims. Although Gilmer v. Interstate Johnson/Lane Corp. approved the arbitration of claims arising under just one of the several existing fair employment practice statutes, the rationale and result of Gilmer are likely to apply to claims brought under other fair employment practice statutes. This Article explores the potential impact of the post-Gilmer proliferation of these employer-employee agreements on the continued viability of the employment-at-will doctrine.
Combining existing limitations on the employment-at-will doctrine with employer-employee agreements to arbitrate statutory fair employment practice claims will produce results on two distinct levels. First, the authors identify those effects resulting directly from the interaction of the at-will doctrine with agreements to arbitrate - those flowing from the implied covenant of good faith doctrine, the implied-infact/enforceable promises doctrine, and the public policy exception to the employment-at-will doctrine.
The authors foresee a second level of interaction that may ultimately have a profound impact on the discretion of at-will employers. They posit that when arbitration of statutory fair employment practice claims becomes commonplace, employers will be obligated to arbitrate virtually all challenged discharges of traditional protected-group members under an emergent de facto just cause standard, a standard that will greatly constrain the at-will employer's right to discharge protected group members for reasons other than those proscribed by statute. Moreover, employers may also be compelled to arbitrate the discharges of nonprotected-group members. Thus, by agreeing to arbitrate employee statutory fair employment practice claims, employers may inadvertently limit or surrender their remaining discretion under the employment-at-will doctrine.

papers.node_id: 87indljsupp31!!ARTICLE: The Irony of AT&T v. Concepcion
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Irony of AT&T v. Concepcion
papers.abstract:
Irony is defined as "the use of words to express something other than and especially the opposite of the literal meaning."Though many other definitions of the word exist, in light of the Supreme Court's majority opinion inAT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion, this definition comes to mind. Read broadly, the decision strikes a blow to the ability of consumers to bring suits against companies, both inside and outside of arbitration. But that was not the intent behind the federal act that the Court relied upon to justify its decision.
In 1925, when Congress passed the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), its intended purpose was to promote enforcement of arbitration clauses.Congress did not sweep away all state-created defenses to contract, however; quite the contrary, Congress inserted a savings clause that arbitration provisions, like any other contract, could be stricken "upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity . . . ."It was upon this basis that the Ninth Circuit upheld a decision to strike down a clause in an agreement between AT&T and the Concepcions that required not only that the Concepcions submit all disputes to arbitration, but also forbade them from forming a class within that arbitration. The Ninth Circuit held that under California law, such clauses in take it or leave it contracts, as the one presented to the Concepcions, are unconscionable and unenforceable.
On appeal to the Supreme Court, AT&T argued that the FAA preempted the unconscionability finding despite the savings clause, as California law discriminated against arbitration clauses in violation of the FAA.Justice Scalia, writing for the majority, agreed that the unconscionability finding under California law was preempted by the FAA.In overruling the Ninth Circuit, he repeated the theme of needing to promote arbitration. Throughout the majority opinion, he introduced, as a corollary, the desire to promote expedited resolution of disputes.
However, the majority opinion is itself open to multiple interpretations. Read narrowly, the opinion may do nothing more than restate the already established principle that states cannot strike down arbitration clauses simply by virtue of their existence. If this is true, then unconscionability may still offer parties a way to avoid arbitration clauses. But the decision can also be read much more broadly. A broad reading of the opinion suggests that any attempt by a court or state legislature to limit the method and means of arbitration in a way inconsistent with what Congress envisioned is preempted by the FAA. InConcepcion, this meant that an attempt by the California courts to force parties to permit class action arbitrations despite contractual provisions to the contrary was in violation of the FAA because Congress intended to promote bilateral arbitrations.Thus, according to the majority opinion, Congress's desire to promote bilateral arbitrations preempted the California courts' rulings that clauses limiting the ability to form class actions are unconscionable.

papers.node_id: 21cardozojconflictresol1!!ARTICLE: THE LIFE OF ARBITRATION LAW HAS BEEN EXPERIENCE, NOT LOGIC: GORSUCH, KAVANAUGH, AND THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE LIFE OF ARBITRATION LAW HAS BEEN EXPERIENCE, NOT LOGIC: GORSUCH, KAVANAUGH, AND THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT
papers.abstract:
The U.S. Supreme Court (hereinafter the "Supreme Court" or the "Court") is the main architect for developing the arbitration doctrine in the United States. Many of the Court's decisions have been so doctrinally powerful that it has had a major impact on international arbitration as well. Put a bit differently, it is no understatement to say that the doctrine and practice of arbitration has thrived because of the Court's willingness to re-evaluate and re-formulate the law on arbitration. While an extremely important statute, the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)provides mainly a framework, indeed only a skeleton for arbitration practice. The Court has effectively re-written the content of the FAA in its decisional law. It has done so in order to accommodate policy objectivesand redress political concerns that the Act, on its face, simply does not address. Therefore, the understanding of the FAA is buried in decisional law and arbitration doctrine is centered on purpose-oriented pragmatism. Rather than anchoring their decisions in analytical and logical statutory interpretation, the Court gives arbitration-related cases a reading, and subsequently a decision, in light of a "strong federal policy favoring arbitration."These days, the FAA is mainly effectuated through judicial opinions and not legislative changes.
However, the Court's consistent favoring of arbitration in its decisions does not meet with the approval of all scholars, lawyers, judges, and courts. There have, of course, been some relatively unsuccessful challenges to this line of cases. There have always been adversaries of arbitration who eagerly await any opportunity to dismantle arbitration in favor of judicial recourse: either by limiting the arbitral tribunal's jurisdictional powers at the front-end of the procedure, by pushing the court to elaborate a doctrine oninarbitrability that excludes, among other things, statutory and regulatory matters, and by eliminating the "hands-off" judicial deference at the back-end of the procedure. Any opening will be enough to a wage war on arbitration, which has already been in the making - intentionally and unintentionally - for several years now. Therefore, it is important that the United States Supreme Court gives arbitration its unconditional and unqualified support, which, thus far, it has. The already-settled arbitration issues enjoy a large degree of immunity due tostare decisis, and should therefore, in principle, be irreversible and irrevocable.
However, as the Supreme Court bench changes, we must re-evaluate the main policy objectives and political concerns of the "new court" in order to develop some predictive techniques for anticipating subsequent decisions. There are a number of unsettled issues that may be in the danger-zone. Further, the Court mightdecide to pour new wine in old bottles andtotallyre-evaluate even settled issues. Up until today, arbitration has beenrelativelyfree from ideological battles, and perhaps still is. But certain considerations of social engineering may steer the Court toward comprehensive "judicial consistency" in order to push their main agenda. Any departure from a strong, pragmatic interpretation of the FAA will be seized upon by the adversaries of arbitration. Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh's constitutional agenda, wrapped in "consistency" clothing, will inevitably lead to an "originalist" interpretation (wrapped in "textualism") that can lead to results that are absolutely unwelcomed in the arbitration community. Thus far, the Court has beenagainstjudicial recourse as opposed toforarbitration, primarily motivated bydeeply rooted legal need.
The constitutional landscape in the United States is facing significant disruption due to methodological differences in constitutional and statutory interpretation - primarily motivated by differences in ideology. These spill-over burdens will likely affect statutory interpretation in various settings. We will be justly-criticized, indeed idle, bystanders if we silently accept the methodological approach to crucial federal legislation that has defined, promoted, enabled, and fostered commerce, trade, and investment - including arbitration law. It is our duty, as scholars and citizens of the world, to make the case that ideologically motivated dogma cannot and must not define the destiny of a twenty-first century citizenry.
In, the late Justice Antonin Scalia, writing for the majority, criticized "judge-made" law with respect to the applicability of extraterritoriality in § 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act 1934. InMorrison, the Court elaborated on a new doctrine anchored in originalism but sold as textualism.Justices Stevens' concurring opinion pointed out that Scalia's criticism of applying judge-made rules is misplaced and that Congress had in fact invited an expansive role for judicial elaboration in the open-ended statute.The Court elaborated a doctrine with the tacit approval of Congress but the lack of "permissive" language paved the way for a new future for § 10(b). The fundamental question we pose in this article is, what disruption to the normal order of things Justices Gorsuch andKavanaugh will risk in order to engineer their new ideas into the fabric of Supreme Court jurisprudence? Constitutional agendas aside, will their deep philosophical convictions, that clearly shape their approach to statutory interpretation, affect U.S. arbitration law?
We worry that they may have such an impact. We seeNew Prime Inc. v. OliveiraandHenry Schein v. Archer & White Salesas striking illustrations of a Court either surreptitiously or unintentionally reintroducing judicial hostility towards arbitration in the name of methodological consistency. Both cases are pro-arbitration in nature, but only as the decisions deal with the low-hanging fruit of arbitration doctrine. The two holdings standing alone will not significantly harm the current scope and understanding of the FAA, but both cases include language and reasoning that potentially can be used by adversaries of arbitration to cause serious and long-term damage to U.S. arbitration law. Both cases represent a possible doctrinal basis for striking down a substantial amount of the judge-made law that has grown out of arbitration law and practice.
InNew Prime, the Court (re)introduced an "intent-based" and "actual language" approach to the reading of the FAA. InSchein, the Court downsized its own role in elaborating upon the content of the Act. In the hands of arbitration's adversaries, who would like to dismantle much of our current arbitration jurisprudence, the pragmatic, purpose-oriented approach of these two cases could grow into outright hostility toward arbitration. It appears clear to the authors that the Court, in bothNew PrimeandHenry Schein, focused on the text, precedent, history, and architecture of the FAA (and much less so the accompanying decisional law). But the decisions did not rely on ethics or prudence. It is probably in the latter two aspects that purposivism or consequentialism has grown. The "strong federal policy favoring arbitration" is anchored in the latter approach to statutory interpretation. The judicial policy favoring arbitration has long been the sole canon of interpretation with respect to the FAA. Perhaps a better approach would be to recognize this proposition formally.This very likely does not representthe view of the entire Court, but the remaining justices may find their hands tied by this new constitutional agenda. This approach plays right into the hands of those who wish to reinstate the judicial supremacy (or hegemony) of the courts. In other words, the reasoning in these cases may well lead us into a fatal misunderstanding of U.S. arbitration law.
It can be alleged that arbitrators are empowered withde factolaw - making capacity without public responsibility or accountability. We concede that this argument has substance. It stands on a base of logic and reason and has captured the attention of many. The criticism has had such an impact that even proponents of arbitration are of the opinion that arbitration should be "judicialized,"partly due to the exponential growth in subject-matter arbitrability. A number of different schools of thought have emerged in both the domestic and international arbitration community.One school of thought gives arbitrators a quasi-judge like role. Similarly, many argue with deep conviction that the default "arbitral trial" must include, among other things, pre-trial discovery, cross-examination, and back-end scrutiny.The war on arbitration can be full-blown, piece-meal, creeping, or unintentional.
Sometimes, the answers to contemporary debates are to be found in old wisdom; as Justice Holmes said, the life of law has not been logic, but experience.Many answers lie in the hidden truthsof judicial and arbitral evolution and history. They all culminate in the same thing: a deeply rooted legal need and an aspiration for adjudicatory efficiency and effectiveness. History has taught us that functionality can be perfection in and of itself. The bottom line is this: The U.S. law on arbitration has evolved to recognize the superior role of the judicial decisions, in particular those of the Supreme Court and the much less important role of the FAA text. In the absence of continued legislative modification, the FAA has become a "living statute" through the work of the federal courts.
II. The Evolution of United States Arbitration Law - Case Law Has Rewritten the Federal Arbitration Act
The evolution of U.S. law on arbitration can best be described by human and legal experience, in general, and by pragmatic thinking, in particular. As we earlier quoted, Justice Oliver Wendall Holmes has written: "The life of the law has not been logic; it has been experience ... The law embodies the story of a nation's development through many centuries, and it cannot be dealt with as if it contained only the axioms and corollaries of a book of mathematics."Arbitration is not perfect. It does not promote justice and fairness in the same manner that (supposedly) litigation within the judicial system does. But experience tells us that, because arbitration is workable, it is still needed. Continuing in echoing Holmes, one could say that, "practicality is the primary reason for creation of law; the observance and application of logical propositionsshould not prevent the application of functional legal rules for the regulation of social conduct."Briefly stated, the Court's logic and analytical reasoning in support of arbitration is often based on flawed reasoning and serious shortcomings in its justifications. The bottom line is this: arbitration experience rests, in fact, on a sound method that justifies "legal madness," - a method nonetheless anchored in policy objectives and political concerns.
The federal law on arbitration - commonly referred to as the Federal Arbitration Act ("FAA") - was enacted in 1925.It was "special interest legislation" enacted to promote consistent determinations between state and federal courts. At the time the FAA was enacted, the courts were hostile towards arbitration. The hostility rendered the procedure a less desired venue for redressing commercial grievances.
It is true that the FAA is archaic and perhaps in need of updating; despite the fact that the U.S. law of arbitration is not fully visible in the FAA's text and that it is the oldest arbitration statute, it is still functioning because judges have elaborated on its scope and meaning.In fact, the act itself is not as "favorable" to arbitration as it has sometimes been made out to be. This was understood by the Court subsequent to the Act's inception. Initially, the Court was more hostile and rendered a series of cases that were adverse to a pro-arbitration doctrine.
However, the early hostility began to change about fifty years ago. The FAA's continuing legitimacy and landmark status lies at the feet of the U.S. Supreme Court, not of Congress. The legislative history of the FAA and the historical context in which it was enacted stands in stark contrast to the current U.S. law on arbitration. The Court has indeed transformed the content and purpose of the statute. One of us described this evolution:
Simply reciting the act's provisions conceals many of the major contributions made by the statute to the arbitration process in general. First, note that the statute was enacted in 1924, long before the alternative dispute bandwagon began rolling. Second, it minimizes - at least in theory - the manner in which a court may interrupt or interfere with the arbitration process.
The Supreme Court's "interruption" or "interference" with the original intent or actual language of the FAA has caused the pendulum in the U.S. law of arbitration to swing to maximum apogee from the initial position of hostility.Through its decisional law, the Court has effectively rewritten the content of the FAA to accommodate policy objectives, political concerns, and global commercial realities. Statutory methodology and ideological convictions have been cast aside. There is now a well-settled judicial doctrine on arbitration. The Court is superior, and the text is inferior. Functionally, civil dispute resolution has trumped deeply rooted issues of pride, ego, and philosophical convictions. The currency and standing of arbitration are at an all-time high. In particular, the role arbitration plays in promoting, fostering, and enabling trans-border commerce, trade, and investments makes it a vital mechanism transnationally as well. Arbitration has taken on an almost religious standing in both domestic and international applications. So far there has been no legal fundamentalism in the Court's case law on arbitration. The ideological battle has been manifested elsewhere but not in the area of arbitration. The Court has filled the necessary gaps of the legislation in order to foster an adjudicatory framework that responds to the constitutional need of access to justice.
The Supreme Court has emphasized that it has had congressional approval (at least by way of Congress' silence and inaction) in establishing the doctrinal framework of arbitration. The Court can ground almost any case favoring arbitration in an analysis of the core objectives of the FAA that grow out of Section 2 of the Act. But a great deal of the Supreme Court's arbitration jurisprudence has gone well beyond Section 2's express language. Through the Court's liberal reading of the FAA, the justices have unquestionably reformulated and effectively re-written the FAA.
Thus, the application of the FAA reads differently than its content. Put a bit differently, the presumption of validity of arbitration agreements and arbitral awards is rooted less in statutory language and more in pragmatic reasoning. This is the better approach and the Court is to be commended for its sensitive approach to the immediate needs of the business community. At least in this area of its case law, the Court has not genuflected toward philosophical convictions or ideological preferences. Instead it has provided almost total judicial deference prior to, during, and subsequent to the arbitral procedure.Judicial intervention in the arbitral procedure is now very rare, with only a few "common law exceptions." But even so, to a certain extent arbitral procedure is becoming "judicialized" (or as is sometimes discussed in the context of international commercial arbitration, it is becoming "Americanized"). We believe this represents a major danger to arbitral autonomy, in particular, and to functional, effective civil dispute resolution, in general.
Perhaps the most significant judge-made contribution to U.S. arbitration law has been what is normally referred to as "federalization." The concept grows out of the Supreme Court's articulation of the now-virtually unquestioned "strong federal policy favoring arbitration." The policy has served as the bedrock of current understanding and interpretation of the FAA. Federalization made the FAAde factothe only law on arbitration in the United States. Federalism has allowed the Court to eradicate any opposition to the pro-arbitration policy. The policy is emphatic, unequivocal, and clear. Born described the work of the Court in the following manner:
The U.S. Supreme Court has held that the domestic FAA "contains no express preemptive provision, nor does it reflect a congressional intent to occupy the entire field of arbitration." At the same time, the Court has also repeatedly declared that the FAA creates a body of substantive federal rules relating to arbitration: in enacting the FAA, "Congress declared a national policy favoring arbitration and withdrew the power of the states to require a judicial forum for the resolution of claims which the contracting parties agreed to resolve by arbitration." As a consequence, it is well settled that U.S. state law rules which single out and purport to render inter-state and international arbitration agreements invalid, illegal, or revocable are preempted bythe FAA. As noted above, it is also settled, in both domestic and international contexts, that the FAA and federal law establish the presumptive separability of the arbitration agreement, provide the exclusive standards for interpreting arbitration agreements and for confirming and vacating arbitral awards.
Grounded in freedom of contract, arbitration is promoted as an effective, efficient procedure used to remedy private grievances through a privatized system of justice. Individual liberty is at the core of American identity, and is perhaps the reason why arbitration, clothed in contractual freedom, has resonated so well with political groups, the business community, and the American citizenry in general. Freedom of contract paves the way for a liberal and positive understanding of arbitration, allowing the courts to construe the FAA liberally which in turn adds important content to the Act. But examined closely, there are other motivations to be found at the intermediate level of arbitration. For example, one major accomplishment of arbitration has been to develop a functional, workable, and effective system of dispute resolution domestically and internationally. Most importantly, it is an adjudicatory system that is not hampered by backlog. Quite the opposite, it assists overly burdened courts so that litigants in judicial recourse can enjoy constitutional guarantees. The integration of freedom of contract into the framework of arbitration jurisprudence requires the lower courts to give unqualified and unconditional judicial deference to arbitration. The Courts need to embrace a "hands-off" approach.Thus, we have the coming together of three separate concepts: (a) the evolution of a concept of freedom of contract that favors private justice; (b) policy objectives that promote the idea of arbitration; and (c) important political concerns. This is the basis for the Supreme Court's crafting the "strong federal policy favoring arbitration." The policy has allowed the Court to elaborate a doctrine on adjudication that rewrites the litigation landscape in the United States. All of this is done with Congress' tacit approval. The deference applied by all courts is so unqualified and unconditionedthat the policy could be rebranded as an "emphatic deferral policy favoring arbitration."
Prior to the FAA and the Court's liberal, purpose-oriented and pragmatic approach to its vague language, a judge would be hostile toward the arbitral procedure. For example, "a judge would not issue an injunction ordering a party to proceed with arbitration and appoint an arbitrator or arbitrators in good faith, on penalty of being found in contempt of court."The pro-arbitration policy goes beyond merely redressing judicial bias or hostility. It is now more compelling than merely fulfilling a statutory duty. When the Court confronts the FAA, the policy favoring arbitration is now an interpretative tool in and of itself. The doctrine can be comfortably used as a canon of construction: in comes an arbitration-related dispute and out goes a pro-arbitration decision that is anchored in policy rather than in analytical and logical statutory interpretation. In resolving cases, the courts should ask themselves one simple and direct question: Do the facts and circumstances of this case resonate with the "strong federal policy favoring arbitration?"
