papers.node_id: 93nwulrev453!!ARTICLE:THE RISKS AND VIRTUES OF LAWLESSNESS: A "SECOND LOOK"AT INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION
papers.title: ARTICLE:THE RISKS AND VIRTUES OF LAWLESSNESS: A "SECOND LOOK"AT INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION
papers.abstract:
One reasonably might inquire with respect to international commercial arbitration whether a more complete separation from national courts and national laws even is possible. The divorce seems complete. International commercial arbitrations today are virtually lawless, or at least they can be, at the election of the parties or the private arbitrators who serve them. It is entirely possible today for parties to conduct an international arbitration in a nation that imposes no requirements or review whatsoever on the procedure or outcome of the arbitration. It is possible for the parties to elect, or for the arbitrators to decide, that the "law" governing the merits of the arbitration isbasically no law at all. Further, it is possible for the parties to escape meaningful review of their resulting arbitral award and to secure the award's judicial enforcement in virtually all developed nations of the world.All but the last of these events, moreover, may occur in complete secrecy.
As unsettling as these developments may seem, the lawlessness of international commercial arbitration is consistent with its traditional scope: the resolution of claims and disputes within the contractual prerogative of the parties. If the arbitral issue was one about which the parties lawfully could have substituted a contractual term had they only anticipated the issue, the matter was arbitrable. If the dispute concerned a matter over which the parties did not enjoy contractual prerogative, such as conduct regulated by competition or consumer welfare laws around which parties are not allowed to contract, the dispute generally was not arbitrable but rather was the province of national courts. This divide reflected the twin constraints traditionally imposed by mandatory national laws on the contractual autonomy of private parties conducting cross-border commercial affairs. First, party autonomy with respect to contractual choice of law traditionally did not exclude or displace otherwise applicable mandatory national laws. Second, party autonomy to arbitrate privately contractual disputes traditionally did not extend to the arbitration of claims arising under mandatory national laws.
In fact, international arbitration's lawlessness - its secrecy, its procedural irregularity, its essential divorce from national laws and national courts - presupposes these mandatory law constraints and was allowed to emerge because of them.Precisely because matters of important national interest, as typically expressed in mandatory laws, rarely were implicated in international commercial arbitrations, national legislatures and national courts simply saw no need to impose their parochial notions of procedure or justice on international arbitrations. If arbitral lawlessness occasionally resulted in unjust outcomes, the consequences of the injustice ordinarily were confined to the parties to the dispute and were not significant to the state. An unjust arbitral outcome was not unlike a bad business deal; both remained within the sphere of private contractual prerogative.
A fundamental issue confronting international commercial arbitration today concerns the substantial erosion of these foundational mandatory law constraints, principally as a result of decisions by United States courts. In Scherk v. Alberto-Culver Company,Mitsubishi v. Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc.,and Vimar Seguros Y Reaseguros, S.A. v. M/V Sky Reefer,the Supreme Court authorized the international arbitration of claims under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, the Sherman Act, and the Carriage ofGoods by Sea Act, respectively, and the logic of those decisions suggests that few, if any, hurdles remain to the arbitrability of all mandatory U.S. economic legislation.
The erosion of the mandatory law constraint on contractual choice of law has occurred at the courts of appeals level. In Riley v. Kingsley Underwriting Agencies, Ltd.,Roby v. Corporation of Lloyd's,Bonny v. The Society of Lloyd's,Allen v. Lloyd's of London,Haynsworth v. Lloyd's of London,Richards v. Lloyd's of London,and Lipcon v. Underwriters at Lloyd's,the,,,,,, andCircuit Courts of Appeals held that parties to international commercial transactions effectively may elect out of applicable mandatory national law (in these cases the Securities Acts of 1933 and 1934), so long as the "law" they substitute for mandatory national law "vindicates" similar rights and does "not subvert" the general policy of the displaced law.I will refer to these cases throughout the Article as the "displacement cases."
Even more than the arbitrability of mandatory law claims, the notion of contractual choice of law as a jurisdictional limit on otherwise applicable mandatory law represents a radical departure from prior jurisprudence. Traditionally, contractual choice of law has been confined to private law, such as the main body of contract law, which serves principally in a default capacity and applies only in the absence of private party agreement concerning the subject matter at issue. Questions concerning the reach or applicability of mandatory law, in contrast, normally present issues of prescriptive or legislative jurisdiction. Contractual choice of law reflects primarily the intent of private parties; prescriptive or legislative jurisdiction reflects the intent of Congress. The Riley, Roby, Bonny, Allen, Haynsworth, Richards and Lipcon courts may have been correct in their assessments that the parties to the international transactions in those cases had agreed to avoid the application of mandatory U.S. law, but they failed completely to analyze whether Congress had granted private parties the power to make that election. In this respect, those cases reflect a specious assumption that private parties to international transactions somehow are entitled to haveonly a single nation's mandatory law apply to their multinational conduct. The Supreme Court's decision in Hartford Fire Insurance v. California,suggests exactly the opposite: considerations of private burden and international comity are not permissible constraints on the jurisdictional reach of mandatory national law (in that case, the Sherman Act), and private parties to international transactions, consequently, must often contend with overlapping regulation by several different national jurisdictions. It would be an odd twist of jurisprudence indeed if private contractual choice-of-law clauses could serve as vehicles for imposing precisely the sorts of constraints on the jurisdictional reach of mandatory law forbidden by Hartford Fire.
The holdings of Scherk, Mitsubishi, and M/V Sky Reefer, of course, are very different from those of Riley, Roby, Bonny, Allen, Haynsworth and Richards, and Lipcon. Permitting the arbitration of mandatory law claims, as did the Supreme Court in Scherk, Mitsubishi, and M/V Sky Reefer, changes procedure but not necessarily substance. Permitting the displacement of otherwise applicable mandatory law, as did the courts of appeals in Riley, Roby, Bonny, Allen, Haynsworth, Richards, and Lipcon, assumes a difference of substance.
Nonetheless, the Scherk, Mitsubishi, and M/V Sky Reefer and Riley, Roby, Bonny, Allen, Haynsworth, Richards, and Lipcon decisions are very much alike insofar as they all reflect a similar and radical change of philosophy with respect to the assumed jurisdictional basis of international commercial arbitration. These decisions transform international arbitration from a consensual exercise of contractual autonomy into essentially an exercise of the state's adjudicatory power. Significantly, however, none of the decisions suggests that this delegation of adjudicatory power was accompanied by anyof the requirements that customarily attend its exercise - established rules of evidence and procedure rather than no rules of evidence and irregular procedure, openness and public scrutiny rather than privacy and secrecy, and judges sworn to serve the public interest rather than private arbitrators beholden only to private parties. Consequently, private arbitral decisions resolving mandatory law claims, or resolving claims according to principles that do not subvert those of displaced mandatory law, are far less likely than public judicial decisions to effectuate the purposes of the mandatory laws. The same presumably is true of the voluntary settlement of mandatory law claims in arbitral rather than judicial contexts, because settlements achieved in the shadow of arbitral lawlessness are far less likely to approximate actual mandatory law requirements than are settlements achieved in the shadow of judicial lawfulness.
The Supreme Court, in fact, has acknowledged these risks, and perhaps sought to reduce them, by expressly warning in Scherk, Mitsubishi, and M/V Sky Reefer that if mandatory U.S. law claims are not adjudicated properly or fairly by private international arbitrators, U.S. courts might refuse on grounds of public policy to enforce the resulting arbitral award. "Having permitted the arbitration to go forward, the national courts of the United States will have the opportunity at the award enforcement stage to ensure that the legitimate interest in the enforcement of the antitrust laws has been addressed."These warnings have come to be known as the "second look doctrine,"a promised review by the Supreme Court of the consequences of its decisions permitting the private arbitration of mandatory law claims. The Court's "second look" has not yet occurred.
Leading commentators, however, have taken a "second look" at international arbitration, and they have expressed their concern over its potential for lawlessness by urging dramatic procedural reforms designed to increase the probability of international arbitrations achieving proper legal results. The proposed reforms extend to mandatory and nonmandatory law cases alike. Among the proposals are calls for greater transparency of the arbitral process, more uniform rules of procedure, standard rules of evidence, reasoned arbitral opinions, and the publication of opinions and awards. Some commentators even have proposed the creation of a single neutral international institution that would administer all international commercial arbitrations pursuant to a system of adjudication incorporating the foregoing reforms. All of the reform proposals assume that the principal desire of parties to international arbitrations is a neutral adjudicatory process; otherwise, as one professor has asserted, parties to international commercial arbitrations are "not opting for the abandonment of legal rules."Thus, whether with respect to the arbitration of mandatory law claims or simply the arbitration of claims within the parties' contractual prerogative, the proposed reforms seek uniformly to restore lawfulness to the arbitral process. The reformers thereby seek to address what Martin Domke long ago called the "principal challenge" facing commercial arbitration: achieving "predictability of result."
The goal of "legal predictability" in the outcomes of international commercial arbitrations, however, is uniquely Western. It assumes, as do Western common- and civil-law traditions, that commercial disputes arise when one party or another to a transaction arguably departs from some preordained, codified, or contractual standard of conduct, and that the appropriate way to resolve such disputes is to compare the conduct in question to the relevant legal standard for the purpose of determining and attributing breach, blame and fault. The proposed reforms of international arbitration thus would achieve legal predictability by replicating in international commercial arbitration those features of Western adjudicatory systems intended to ensure the accuracy of such comparisons; that is, uniform rules of procedure, standard rules of evidence, and published reasoned opinions.
But Western assumptions regarding the role of codes and contracts in commercial relationships are not shared throughout most of Asia and much of the developing world, regions that are home to increasing numbers of participants in major international transactions.The traditions in these regions subordinate the role of "law" and "contracts" in the ordering of commercial relationships, and in fact attribute to those concepts meanings that are substantially different from the meanings of those terms in the West. Asian and Western parties to a commercial transaction may clearly understand the terms of their business agreement, yet differ radically in their respective conceptions of their contract and its legal consequences. For the Asian party, the relationship giving rise to the contract and the actual circumstances of its performance likely will have far greater significance than the contract itself. In fact, the Asian party likely will assume, just as the Western party will resist, that the business relationship will adjust responsively to future contingencies ignored or even contradicted in the contract or codified law. The Western assumption that the consequences of commercial conduct are to be prescribed long before the conduct's occurrence is essentially alien to Asian commercial traditions.
Moreover, commercial customs in Asia and much of the developing world typically value nonconfrontational resolutions of commercial disputes far more highly than they value "properly legal" resolutions. This preference is consistent with the emphasis given in these regions to relationships and their preservation. This tradition values "predictability," but in terms of the fact of resolution, not in terms of result. Commercial parties from these regions tend to shy from public civil conflict and efforts to attribute breach and blame. For them, publicly adjudicated dispute resolutioncan be deeply embarrassing; not because, as Western commentators often assume, of the risk that public adjudication will expose improper conduct, but because public adjudication communicates to the world that their opponents lack sufficient respect for them to settle their differences privately. Public adjudication thus causes a loss of stature, a loss of "face." As a result, the success of commercial dispute resolution for participants from these areas of the world often turns on the availability of precisely those features of arbitral "lawlessness" that proponents of arbitral reform seek to displace: carefully guarded secrecy, complete flexibility of procedure and evidence, and the absence of reasoned opinions and published awards attributing breach, blame and fault. To borrow a phrase from the eminent French scholar RenJ David, the purpose of arbitration for parties from these regions is "not to apply law, but to function as a remedy against its insufficiency."
"Lawlessness" in international commercial arbitration, consequently, has virtues as well as risks, thus complicating the Supreme Court's promised "second look." Particularly in light of the ever-expanding role of Asian and other non-Western nations in international commerce, the lawless features of international commercial arbitration seem worth preserving. Indeed, it would be the height of parochialism for the Supreme Court not to endeavor to respect and preserve features so accommodating of established dispute resolution traditions in much of the non-Western world. Yet it is precisely these features that most jeopardize the important public interests inherent in the private arbitration of U.S. mandatory law claims. If the Supreme Court shies from meaningful review of mandatory law arbitrations, there is a great risk that international businesses will escape the regulatory dictates of U.S. law, perhaps to the substantial detriment of nonparticipating third parties or the public. On the other hand, if the Supreme Court's "second look" involves an appropriately searching review of arbitrations including mandatory law claims, the resulting procedural adjustments to the arbitral process necessary to enable such a review likely would threaten arbitration's continuing utility for the resolution of important cross-cultural nonmandatory law claims, which form the heart of most international arbitrations. This result would expose a paradox of the Supreme Court's Scherk, Mitsubishi, and M/V Sky Reefer decisions: instead of promoting and facilitating international arbitration, as the Court presumably intended, those decisions will have discouraged it.
Thus, absent the restoration of international commercial arbitration to its original intended scope, the Supreme Court will be confronted in its "second look" with the difficult task of promoting proper legal results in the arbitration of U.S. mandatory law claims while avoiding the imposition ofthat value-laden concept in the arbitration of other cross-cultural claims. My purpose in this Article is to examine the tension inherent in these contradictory goals. Part I describes international arbitration's current lawlessness, Part II the mandatory law constraints on arbitrability and contractual choice of law that underlay the emergency of arbitral lawlessness, and Part III the recent erosion of those mandatory law constraints. Part IV then examines the risks of arbitral lawlessness when applied to international arbitration's new mandatory law responsibilities, and Part V explores the inevitable reactive proposals for arbitral reform and their common assumption that the principal goal of international commercial arbitration is not national-neutral decisionmaking, but properly legal results. Part VI questions this assumption and the appropriateness of arbitral reform by suggesting their inconsistency with the commercial traditions and dispute resolution goals and traditions on non-Western participants in international arbitrations, particularly participants from East Asia. I suggest that these non-Western commercial traditions and dispute resolution goals demand maintenance of precisely those features of international arbitration most reform proposals seek to displace. Finally, Part VII discusses the implications of these competing considerations for the Supreme Court's "second look" at international commercial arbitration.
conclude in Part VII that the contradictory goals the Court will confront are largely irreconcilable. No model of international commercial arbitration is flexible and accommodating enough to fully and fairly consider contractual claims implicating non-Western interests also is capable of predictably achieving legally correct results in the adjudication of important mandatory U.S. law claims. No model capable of accomplishing the latter would fail to Westernize a process whose raison d'etre is precisely the avoidance of that result. The private ordering of international commerce clearly is advanced by the arbitrability of mandatory law claims but at the likely expense of many of the rules designed to ensure its integrity. Ensuring appropriate international arbitral results of mandatory law claims, on the other hand, necessarily renders the arbitral process inhospitable, if not uninhabitable, for those whose notions of dispute resolution and commercial justice do not comport with those of the West. Mandatory law claims belong in the courts of the nation supplying the mandatory law and not in private commercial arbitration.
Scherk, Mitsubishi, and M/V Sky Reefer, however, seem so firmly entrenched in Supreme Court jurisprudence that proposing their abandonment is not a realistic means of addressing this problem. Those decisions also effectively preclude the judicial interpretation of contractual arbitration clauses to exclude mandatory law claims, which would have been the "next best" solution. Some hope remains following Hartford Fire v. California that the Supreme Court will reject the displacement case holdings that private contractual choice of law is a jurisdictional constraint on otherwise applicable mandatory law. Even assuming that appropriate outcome,however, the problem remains of securing exacting judicial review of mandatory law arbitrations without destroying the usefulness of arbitration for the resolution of cross-cultural nonmandatory law claims. My suggested solutions for this intractable problem are only partial at best.
My first suggestion is that the Supreme Court endeavor in its "second look" at international commercial arbitration to establish rules of judicial review that clearly differentiate between arbitrations that include mandatory law claims and those that do not. The former require exacting merits review, the latter virtually no review. Although perhaps not contemplated by the 1958 United Nations Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (the "New York Convention"), which governs the standards by which U.S. courts must review most international awards, such a difference clearly is consistent with Article V(II)(a) of that Convention. I also suggest that Article V(1)(e) of the New York Convention can be read to authorize a similarly exacting judicial review of arbitrated mandatory law claims by courts of the nation supplying the mandatory law even if the resulting arbitral award is not presented in that nation for recognition or enforcement. This suggestion is contrary to the few commentators and lower federal courts that have considered the issue,andacknowledge concern for the extent to which adoption of this suggestion could undercut a major purpose of the New York Convention. Nonetheless, the language and history of Article V(1)(e) permits this reading.Finally, I suggest that international arbitral institutionsmight help reduce the spillover effect of exacting judicial review in mixed-claim arbitrations - arbitrations including both mandatory and nonmandatory law claims - by amending their rules in ways that will both reduce the likelihood of mixed-claim arbitrations and help preserve the virtues of lawlessness when such arbitrations occur.
Although not nearly as preferable an outcome as the restoration of international commercial arbitration to its original scope and purpose, these proposals at least would help preserve the virtues of international arbitration's lawlessness without imposing its risks on the resolution of important mandatory law issues.

Whether distinct standards of judicial review or institutional rule changes can be designed to protect public interests in arbitrated mandatory-law claims while preserving the informal, flexible features of arbitration valued by non-Western parties.

papers.node_id: 2001wislrev831!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:CONTRACT AND CONFLICT MANAGEMENT
papers.title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:CONTRACT AND CONFLICT MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract:
We live in the era of the made-to-order issue resolution clause. A quarter century after Macaulay, Macneil, and others first explored systems of governance for contractual relationships,bargains have plumbed the breadth and depth of that universe. Agreements to arbitrate future disputes are broadly enforceable under federal and state statutes;a series of U.S. Supreme Court decisions have transformed the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)into a source of burgeoning substantive arbitration law that preempts state initiatives aimed at restricting the enforceability of agreements to arbitrate.A quiet revolution in court and agency "ADR" - alternative or "appropriate" dispute resolution - has given official imprimatur to mediation, early neutral evaluation and other conflict resolution approaches and stimulated their use in the realm of private transactions.Taken together, these events are reshaping the way many people think about managing and resolving disputes.
As contract planners, lawyers do not simply respond to conflict; they have the opportunity to limit or manage problems prospectively throughnegotiation and drafting. They may tackle prospective conflict at its roots by encouraging clear and concise contract language, realistic risk assessment and allocation, and suitable issue and conflict resolution mechanisms for contractual relationships.For many businesses, for example, tailoring of dispute resolution approaches most appropriate to resolving particular issues "is an integral part of corporate policy" and an important measure for achieving corporate objectives.These include: saving time and money, adapting a problem solving approach to fit the problem and thereby assuring control and reducing uncertainty and risk, maintaining privacy and confidentiality, and preserving business relationships. In some cases, carefully crafted approaches may serve even higher values for individuals.In light of the great flexibility parties enjoy in adapting ADR approaches to their specific goals, there is considerable room for creativity in planning the process.
Much time and energy is now devoted to the design and implementation of multi-step contract-based conflict management programs to resolve disputes effectively, early, and informally, with relatively minor diversion of financial and human resources.Today,garden-variety arrangements for binding arbitration are increasingly joined by more exotic specimens reflecting the imaginativeness of the drafters and the need to fit procedures to specific needs, ends and contingencies. These include specialized variants (such as "Biblically based mediation"), complex mechanisms to "filter" disputes through a progression of discrete ADR processes, often culminating in binding arbitration,and even judgments by public "spectacle" in the form of a televised courtroom.
The spectrum will soon encompass a full range of "virtual" options made possible by the current revolution in information technology.A harbinger of these developments is SquareTrade's innovative multi-step voluntary dispute resolution process for parties to transactions on the E-Bay web site.In a little over a year, the online program for negotiation and mediation of buyer/seller disputes handled more than 20,000 cases involving parties from eighty countries.
Because each of these schemes is a creature of contract, its essential character and legal ramifications depend upon the expressed, implied, or presumed intent of the parties. Sometimes the latter convey their procedural intentions with great specificity; at other times they make do with the sketchiest of integrations. Well-counseled parties may make the most of the opportunity to craft their own dispute resolution procedure, weaving their way between the Scylla of ambiguity and the Charybdis of too-tight drafting.
Unfortunately, despite the current widespread use of mediation and other ADR processes in the United States today,many members of the bench and bar - including those responsible for the drafting, interpretation and implementation of consensual ADR provisions - still lack a fundamental grasp of the process choices available to contracting parties.More often than not, their information is fragmentary, their perceptions framed by anecdote and hearsay in lieu of personal experience. Transactional lawyers, those in the best position to offer advice and counsel in the structuring of contractual conflict management options, tend to be less well informed than colleagues in what are traditionally know as litigation departments.Opportunities may be squandered or abused, and clients and third parties ill-served. Venturing into a complex and changing landscape of evolving statutory and case law, moreover, even sophisticated scriveners may face unwelcome surprises when their hothouse variety ADR provisions are unveiled in court. Lacking a clear road map, courts often rely on the tools at hand. This frequently means resorting to the relatively well-trodden highways and byways of federal and state arbitration law, perhaps without thoughtful consideration of the nature and purposes of the statute and the inherent differences between binding arbitration - the intended focus of such legislation - and other intervention strategies now enshrined in contract. Although the quiet revolution in conflict resolution, public and private, has spawned a vast body of commentary, including treatises,practical tomes for lawyers and judges,academic journals,andnumerous web sites,no systematic, comprehensive treatment of contractual ADR approaches and relevant legal issues has yet been published. More significantly, there is relatively little hard information regarding contract-based dispute resolution experiences and perceptions of users. Through the years, there have been few empirical studies of binding arbitration and other ADR processes,due in part to the transaction costs associated with acquiring information about processes that, if not purely ad hoc, are administered by many different organizations in an atmosphere of relative privacy. Although these realities are beginning to change, thanks in part to the transparency affordable through online communications,much of the current literature still relies heavily on anecdote; some is animated by little more than the personal or professional agenda of the writer. Contracts classes are taught as if the appellate judicial decision is the normal method of resolving contracts disputes, despite the fact that the vast majority of issues and disputes never result in a complaint, and the vast majority of filed cases are dismissed or settled without trial.
It is critical for legal practitioners, judges and contracts scholars to better understand these alternatives, especially arrangements involving third party "interveners" - mediators, arbitrators, and others assigned to help manage or resolve issues or disputes. The subject of consensualdispute resolution should be woven into first-year courses in contracts, encouraging law students to consider key questions such as:
. What forms of agreement now exist for out-of-court issue resolution and conflict management?
. To what extent are particular kinds of agreements given legal effect, and on what basis?
. What roles are played by third party "interveners"? What constraints, if , are placed upon their selection?
. What are the legal "results" of issue resolution? In other words, how do courts treat decisions/evaluations by interveners or settlement agreements facilitated by interveners?
These issues will be addressed in Parts I-IV. An important subtext of the discussion is the abiding tension between the need for judicial intervention and the desire for party autonomy implicit in private conflict resolution provisions. Indeed, from the flourishing of international merchant fairs, to the dawn of chancery jurisdiction, and to the present day, a recurring theme in the history of Anglo-American conflict resolution is the search for alternatives to the formalities and perceived limitations of traditional court adjudication. The norms of public law and procedural due process often give way to other priorities in bargaining; going to court is often precisely what parties are trying to avoid.Mindful of these realities, modern courts tend to afford wide berth to private conflict management arrangements.
That said, we must carve out for special treatment the growing universe of agreements that implicate significant disparities in bargaining power, including the power of information. Highly publicized cases such as a computer purchase contract which required consumers to arbitrate under the rules and fee structure of the Paris-based International Chamberof Commerce (ICC),and an HMO's in-house arbitration program that entailed more than two years of delay of a malpractice claimhave drawn public attention to the abuses that can occur in private dispute resolution programs. It is fair to say that consumers, employees, and others may benefit from meaningful access to prompt, inexpensive, and effective out-of-court dispute resolution. On the other hand, non-dickered boilerplate making general reference to an arcane set of dispute resolution procedures may produce an unwelcome surprise to non-drafting parties, particularly where a clause purports to substitute binding arbitration for the right to go to court. Such concerns have spurred action or calls for action on many levels: policing by industry, association, or quasi-public groups or associations, legislative action, judicial oversight, or agency regulation. Part V analyzes the special concerns associated with private justice under adhesion contracts and treats the range of existing and suggested options for addressing these approaches.
A thorough treatment of all of the issues implicated by the growing use of private governance mechanisms would require a lengthy treatise.The intent of this article is to stimulate awareness and understanding of such issues, encourage more thoughtful, helpful classroom dialogue, and identify new opportunities for scholarship.

questions.question: Do contractually specified dispute-resolution procedures (including multi-step, tailored ADR processes) produce faster, less costly, and more relationship-preserving outcomes than resolving disputes through traditional court litigation?

How do courts and other enforcement actors interpret and give legal effect to parties' chosen contractual dispute-resolution processes, and to what extent does that enforcement reflect or frustrate the parties' procedural autonomy?

Do non-negotiated, boilerplate dispute-resolution clauses in standard-form contracts systematically disadvantage weaker parties (e.g., consumers or employees), and what contractual or institutional safeguards reduce any such harms?

shared_topics.topic: the Supreme Court's role in shaping arbitration doctrine and statutory interpretation of the FAA
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the Supreme Court's decisions have effectively rewritten the FAA and emphasizes concerns about methodological shifts under new justices, while Paper B documents the 'quiet revolution' in which Supreme Court case law transformed the FAA into a substantive source that preempts state limits and guides how courts treat contract-based ADR.

shared_topics.topic: party autonomy and the drafting/design of bespoke dispute-resolution clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on 'made-to-order' clauses, multi-step and hybrid ADR designs, and the transaction-cost tradeoffs of specific drafting choices, and Paper A situates those drafting freedoms within a broader legal regime that treats freedom of contract as a core justification for enforcing arbitration agreements.

shared_topics.topic: tension between privatized dispute resolution and public accountability/access to justice (including concerns over adhesion contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B interrogates abuses and fairness problems where disparities in bargaining power make private dispute systems problematic for consumers and employees, while Paper A addresses critiques that arbitration grants arbitrators de facto lawmaking power, raises concerns about loss of public accountability, and notes calls for judicial oversight or 'judicialization' of arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: federalization, preemption of state law, and uniformity of arbitration rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the Court-driven 'federalization' of arbitration and the strong federal policy favoring arbitration that displaces state rules, and Paper B similarly notes that Supreme Court decisions have made the FAA a bulwark against state initiatives and that courts often apply federal arbitration principles when interpreting contract-based ADR provisions.

shared_topics.topic: the evolution and practical consequences of ADR proliferation (multi-step processes, mediation, technological innovations) for dispute management
shared_topics.justification: Paper B surveys the expanding landscape of ADR—mediation, early neutral evaluation, multi-stage filtering, and online platforms—and emphasizes practical implications for contract planners, while Paper A situates the evolution of arbitration law in pragmatic, experience-based judicial developments that responded to commercial needs and shaped how ADR practices function in practice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ARBITRATION AGREEMENTS AND NURSING HOMES: A REGULATORY COMPROMISE

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and legal consequences of arbitration clauses (including FAA preemption)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how federal and state law—particularly the Federal Arbitration Act and Supreme Court decisions—have transformed the enforceability and legal treatment of arbitration provisions; Paper B documents how mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses in nursing home admission contracts are being enforced to bar residents from Article III courts and discusses related judicial and regulatory responses.

shared_topics.topic: mandatory pre-dispute arbitration in adhesion contracts and power disparities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the risks posed by boilerplate dispute-resolution provisions and the special concerns when parties face significant disparities in bargaining power; Paper B focuses on mandatory arbitration in nursing home admission contracts as a paradigmatic adhesion setting where vulnerable residents lack meaningful bargaining power.

shared_topics.topic: effects of arbitration on public accountability, transparency, and access to remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns that private ADR can reduce public scrutiny, obscure outcomes, and substitute private justice for public adjudication; Paper B shows empirically that arbitration clauses can shield nursing homes from public accountability and impede access to publicly recorded court remedies for abuse and neglect.

shared_topics.topic: regulatory and policy responses to arbitration (judicial, legislative, and agency roles)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys possible forms of oversight—from judicial scrutiny to legislative and agency regulation—to address abusive ADR clauses and protect disadvantaged parties; Paper B traces efforts by the legislative, judicial, and executive branches and focuses on CMS's attempts and possible regulatory approaches to govern nursing home arbitration agreements.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE DAMAGES IN ARBITRATION: CONTRACTING OUT OF GOVERNMENT'S ROLE IN PUNISHMENT AND FEDERAL PREEMPTION OF STATE LAW

shared_topics.topic: the Federal Arbitration Act's role in enforcing arbitration agreements and preempting state law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the FAA requires enforcement of arbitration clauses, creates a default federal rule preempting contrary state arbitration law (while allowing parties to incorporate state law by contract), and uses that preemption to justify permitting arbitral punitive damages; Paper B documents the transformation of the FAA into a source of substantive arbitration law that preempts state efforts to limit enforceability of ADR clauses and discusses the practical consequences for contract drafters and courts.

shared_topics.topic: party autonomy / freedom of contract to design dispute-resolution procedures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that parties, through freedom of contract, can allocate the power to award punitive damages (or exclude it) and even choose whether federal or state arbitration law governs; Paper B emphasizes the broad contractual flexibility to craft multi-step ADR regimes, the benefits of tailoring dispute processes to parties' goals, and the legal significance of those private design choices.

shared_topics.topic: scope of arbitrators' authority and the enforceability of arbitral remedies (including punitive damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on when arbitrators may award punitive damages—whether that power flows from the arbitration agreement and what default rules courts should apply—while Paper B addresses how contracting parties define the legal effect of third‑party interveners' decisions and how courts treat outcomes of ADR processes, including binding arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: limits of private dispute resolution and the need for judicial oversight / due process concerns (especially where bargaining power is unequal)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether enforcement of arbitral punitive awards implicates state action or constitutional due process and whether parties waive those protections by agreeing to arbitration; Paper B highlights the tension between private conflict management and public law/due process norms, warning of abuses in adhesion settings and calling for special scrutiny or remedies where significant power imbalances exist.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between arbitration agreements and governing law (FAA, state law, and preemption)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between the Federal Arbitration Act and state law or other governing-law choices: Paper A surveys how the FAA has reshaped arbitration enforcement and preemption issues, and Paper B analyzes FAA case law (e.g., Volt) and circuit approaches to whether federal policy displaces state limitations on remedies.

shared_topics.topic: role of courts in interpreting and enforcing contractual ADR provisions
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss judicial oversight and interpretation of private dispute-resolution clauses — Paper A warns that courts often default to arbitration doctrines when confronted with diverse ADR schemes, and Paper B examines how courts resolve conflicts over arbitrators' authority and whether to apply rules like Garrity when reviewing awards.

shared_topics.topic: problems created by ambiguous or self-contradictory dispute-resolution clauses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers highlight drafting-induced disputes: Paper A emphasizes the varied specificity parties use and the litigation that can follow bespoke ADR mechanisms, while Paper B gives concrete examples of self-contradictory clauses (e.g., choice-of-law forbidding punitive damages versus rules allowing them) that generate judicial confusion.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CLASS ACTION LITIGATION AFTER DUKES: IN SEARCH OF A REMEDY FOR GENDER DISCRIMINATION IN EMPLOYMENT+

shared_topics.topic: restriction of access to courts through ADR and judicial decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Wal‑Mart v. Dukes and recent decisions as shrinking plaintiffs' access to class adjudication and court oversight, and Paper B explores how the proliferation of contract‑based ADR and judicial deference to arbitration shifts disputes out of courts, altering access to public adjudication and remedies.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how arbitration and class‑certification rulings disproportionately burden individual employees (often with limited resources), and Paper B focuses on adhesion contexts where boilerplate ADR clauses and information asymmetries produce unfair surprises—both papers engage the problem of unequal bargaining power and the need for careful clause design or limits on boilerplate arbitration.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CLAIM PRECLUSION AND REFORMATION OF CONTRACTS: NEW YORK CPLR 3002(d)

shared_topics.topic: the impact of procedural costs and fee allocation on access to remedies and effective dispute resolution

papers.node_id: 92notredamelrev1977!!FEDERAL COURTS, PRACTICE & PROCEDURE SYMPOSIUM: JUSTICE SCALIA AND THE FEDERAL COURT: JUSTICE SCALIA AND CLASS ACTIONS: A LOVING CRITIQUE
papers.title: FEDERAL COURTS, PRACTICE & PROCEDURE SYMPOSIUM: JUSTICE SCALIA AND THE FEDERAL COURT: JUSTICE SCALIA AND CLASS ACTIONS: A LOVING CRITIQUE
papers.abstract:
I have been asked to write an essay on Justice Scalia's class action jurisprudence and although I suspect many readers will find this surprising because the Justice is so often linked to constitutional law, I actually think that his class action jurisprudence may be where his opinions leave some of the biggest marks. To be as blunt about it as the Justice himself would have been: for better or for worse, I am not sure any other Justice of the Supreme Court in American history has done more to hinder the class action lawsuit than Justice Scalia did.
The Justice did his damage not so much in his opinions interpreting the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure - there, his opinions gave both sides of the class action divide something to like - but in his opinions interpreting the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA). Under the auspices of the FAA, the Justice authored two majority opinions giving a green light to corporations that want to opt out of class-wide liability entirely so long as they do so using arbitration contracts.
one of the Justice's biggest fans. But his FAA opinions are not my favorites of his opinions. As many commentators have noted, it is very hard to square these opinions with either the text or the history of the FAA.
For these reasons, many commentators have assumed that Justice Scalia was more animated by his conservative ideological preferences in these casesthan to his fidelity to the original understanding of the text. That may be - although the Justice tried very hard to separate his personal views from his jurisprudential views, he was not superhuman - but, if it is what motivated these decisions, I am not sure the Justice got it right on this point either. On a superficial level, of course, conservatives tend to side with the interests of corporations and liberals with the interests of plaintiffs' lawyers. But not always. There are plenty of times when conservative principles deviate from corporate interests. As I explain, I wonder if class action waivers should be one of these times. In my view, it is hard to see how the conservative (and, often, libertarian) free market principles that Justice Scalia and I shared suggest that corporations should be allowed to opt out of class action lawsuits.
In Part I of this Essay, I review the Justice's class action opinions; I give special emphasis to his opinions interpreting the FAA and explain why I think it is hard to square those decisions with either text or history. In Part II, I explain why I think even conservative and libertarian ideology may not be consistent with the Justice's FAA opinions.

papers.title: INSTITUTE FOR LAW AND ECONOMIC POLICY 22ND ANNUAL SYMPOSIUM: VINDICATING VIRTUOUS CLAIMS (IN HONOR OF JAMES D. COX): ARTICLE: USING THE FALSE CLAIMS ACT TO REMEDY TAX-EXPENDITURE FRAUD
papers.abstract:
The government can create incentives for private action by either granting subsidies or reducing taxes on desired behaviors.Thegovernment "spends" money when it gives individuals and entities tax credits and deductions for taking particular actions, because it foregoes tax revenue. These so-called "tax expenditures" by the federal government have been estimated to cost over one trillion dollars annually - an amount that rivals all discretionary direct spending.
This Article argues that tax expenditures, like direct expenditures, should be protected against false and fraudulent claims. If a health-care provider's fraud inflates employer contributions for medical insurance premiums - which are not taxed - the government's interest is injured just as much as it would be in a run-of-the-mill federal False Claims Act (FCA) case involving a more traditional form of fraud.Historically, the FCA has been used to protect the public fisc by creating liability against anyone who makes a false or fraudulent claim relating to a direct expenditure of federal funds. But we argue that the FCA might also be used to combat fraud that targets government spending in the form of tax expenditures.
Although taxpayers themselves may defraud the government by making false claims for tax credits or deductions, this Article focuses on fraud committed against taxpayers by third parties who target the government-subsidized funds in the hands of those taxpayers. Such "third-party" fraud against taxpayers in their capacity as claimants or recipients of government tax expenditures does not just harm those taxpayers. It also undermines the government's programmatic goal in granting the tax expenditure in the first place, whether that goal is to encourage employer spending on health plans, to promote home ownership, or some other public policy purpose. These third-party frauds against taxpayers are economically indistinguishable from third-party frauds against contractors, grantees, and other direct recipients of government money.In 1986, when Congress enacted the modernversion of the law, it clearly made third-party fraud against contractors, grantees, and "other recipients" of federal funds a target of the FCA.Accordingly, we argue that fraud against taxpayer-claimants - who, being economically indistinguishable from direct recipients of government money, are properly deemed "other recipients" - should also be actionable under the FCA.
This Article explores how the FCA might be invoked to combat fraud that targets government spending in the form of tax expenditures, as well as doctrinal counterarguments to such an application. We touch on the potential breadth of the FCA's reach insofar as it encompasses such claims, as well as the prospect of amending the FCA or using other whistleblower mechanisms to achieve similar results.
The Article is organized in three parts. Part I introduces the FCA. Part II explains the concept of a tax expenditure. Part III argues that claims under the FCA should include fraud relating to government spending in the form of tax expenditures. There, we analyze two cases that appear to reject the application of the FCA to tax-expenditure fraud, use our analysis of the case law to refute concerns relating to our tax-expenditure theory, and describe some areas where the tax-expenditure theory may be used. Finally, we conclude that our approach could allow the federal government to extend the anti-fraud protections of the FCA to cover for the first time more than one trillion dollars of spending that is accomplished through the tax code.

papers.node_id: 12cardozojconflictresol665!!N0TE: THE DEMISE OF CLASS ACTIONS WILL NOT BE TELEVISED
papers.title: N0TE: THE DEMISE OF CLASS ACTIONS WILL NOT BE TELEVISED
papers.abstract:
As evidenced by two recent Cardozo Journal of Conflict Resolution articles, class action waivers in arbitration clauses are currently a hot topic in the field of conflict resolution.With increasing frequency, arbitrators and courts are presented with class action waivers in compulsory arbitration agreements prohibiting the aggregation of claims.This Note argues that some courts have reversed course in their treatment of class action waivers contained in arbitration clauses. There is a new movement to find class waivers, and the arbitration clauses that harbor them, unenforceable.This Note further argues that while plaintiffs uniformly oppose class action waivers, defendants widely oppose class arbitration, preferring instead to defend class actions in court. Finally, this Note contends that these recent decisions present a serious problem for arbitration as a forum because they represent a widening judicial recognition that arbitration clauses in adhesive consumer contracts are being used in an unjust manner.
The majority of court decisions finding class waivers unenforceable have relied on unconscionability theory.However, some state courts have also based their decisions on public policy favoring the right to aggregate claims.By finding more class waivers unenforceable, the courts have provided a remedy for plaintiffs when arbitrators either could not or would not do the same.While decisions finding class action waivers unenforceable on unconscionability grounds have been rendered as early as 2000, the number of decisions finding class waivers unconscionable or against public policy has increased tremendously since 2006.This Note argues that this trend evidences that courts are now becoming less willing to trust arbitration to provide just and consistent resolutions in high stakes class litigation.
Two significant and interesting cases to find a class waiver unenforceable were decided in 2009: Feeney v. Dell Inc.and In re American Express Merchants' Litigation.This Note will parse the language of both opinions, and discuss the implications of the reasoning employed by each court in reaching its decision. The two opinions take different routes to the same conclusion: that class action waivers are substantively unfair and bad for the public. The Feeney court arrived at its decision relying on state public policy grounds,while the Second Circuit used unconscionability.Both cases represent mile markers in the evolution of jurisprudence on class waivers. Feeneycould be construed to offer many state courts, and possibly federal courts,an easier route to finding the waivers unenforceable. In In re American Express,by adopting an unconscionability rule in the Second Circuit similar to that in place for a number of years in the Ninth Circuit,the court greatly expanded the number of cases brought annually in jurisdictions with strong law against class waivers. Further, Feeney and In re American Express are especially noteworthy for the strong language they employ in expressing the courts' unwillingness to trust arbitration to adjudicate litigation by consumers involving entire classes of plaintiffs.
In 2009, a vast array of consumer contracts were governed by mandatory arbitration clauses usually including a class action waiver: movie tickets, cell phone agreements, gym memberships, and software agreements. The frustration evidenced by the trend and voiced in the wording of Feeney and In re American Express may represent a canary in the mineshaft for the arbitration industry, seeming to add to increasing discomfort with the results of arbitration in the commercial context that is shared by defendants and plaintiffs, as well as the courts.The commercial arbitration community should conduct a deep inquiry into the place of compulsory arbitration clauses in adhesive consumer contracts, as courts seem to increasingly acknowledge the clauses can be a device for depriving citizens of their remedy against corporate wrong-doing.
In Section I, this Note will discuss the social and historical background that gave rise to the current prevalence of compulsory arbitration clauses and class waivers in consumer contracts. In Section II, this Note explores major Supreme Court cases that paved the way for the current dynamic between the courts, arbitrators and the law in cases implicating class waivers. The argument section, Section III, will contend that: (1) there is a trend in some jurisdictions of courts finding class waivers unenforceable; (2) Feeney and In re American Express have expanded on this trend in important ways; (3) this trend is evidence that the failure of arbitration to act as an instrument of justice in connection with consumer class action waivers may be creating a judicial backlash; and (4) in light of the foregoing, the ability of arbitration to justly and fairly resolve major disputes is in question.

papers.node_id: 65ucinlrev43!!NINTH ANNUAL CORPORATE LAW SYMPOSIUM: SECURITIES REGULATION: ARTICLE: FEDERAL VERSUS STATE LAW IN THE INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS CONTAINING ARBITRATION CLAUSES: REFLECTIONS ON MASTROBUONO
papers.title: NINTH ANNUAL CORPORATE LAW SYMPOSIUM: SECURITIES REGULATION: ARTICLE: FEDERAL VERSUS STATE LAW IN THE INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS CONTAINING ARBITRATION CLAUSES: REFLECTIONS ON MASTROBUONO
papers.abstract:
As a result of a series of United States Supreme Court cases handed down in the 1980s that interpreted the Federal Arbitration Act(FAA), industry-sponsored arbitration has become the primary forum in which securities customers resolve legal disputes with their brokers.However, the transition from judicial to arbitral dispute resolution for securities disputes has not been smooth.
Customers have fought at every turn for the right to rely on courts and juries for a variety of claims. Meanwhile, securities firms have become increasingly disenchanted with the legalization of arbitration procedures and have sought restrictions on customers' arbitral rights and remedies. Most recently, firms have become alarmed by the tendency of some arbitrators to award punitive damages against them in customer-broker cases.
It was within the context of industry concern over punitive damage claims that the United States Supreme Court in Mastrobuono v. Shearson Lehman Hutton, Inc.upheld a $ 400,000 punitive damage award in favor of Antonio Mastrobuono, a University of Illinois professor of medieval literature. Although the result gratified Professor Mastrobuono, Justice Stevens's majority opinion caused considerable confusion among commentators.
Instead of tackling the broad policy issue of whether arbitrators have the power to award punitive damages, the Court rested its decision on a painstaking examination of contractual language in the customer-broker contract that the Court acknowledged Professor Mastrobuono had probably neither read nor understood. The pivotal points of reference in the Court's analysis were not statutory terms or even prior cases, but rather two provisions in the agreement: a standard New York choice-of-law clause, which was relevant because New York's highest court has held that arbitrators may not award punitive damages in any case, and an obscure reference to unenumerated "rules" of a securities self-regulatory organization (SRO) -- the National Association of Securities Dealers, Inc. (NASD).The narrow question addressed by the Court was whether, under state contract law, the New York choice-of-law clause constituted a contractual agreement by Mastrobuono to adopt New York's idiosyncratic restriction on the remedial powers of arbitrators.
In his lone dissent, Justice Thomas observed that the majority opinion represented "only the understanding of a single federal court regarding the requirements imposed by state law. As such, the majority's opinion has applicability only to this specific contract and to no other."If Thomas was correct, and this Articlewill argue that he was, the interesting question about Mastrobuono is not the specific result reached by the Court, but the reasons why the Court addressed this very important policy issue using such ill-suited analytic tools.
This Article explores why the Mastrobuono Court decided the case as it did and how the arbitration field in general and the securities industry in particular have been affected by the decision. It is a story about the interaction of state contract law, state and federal arbitration law, and the regulatory system that governs the securities industry. It is also a story of considerable importance to the overall regulation of fraud within the securities industry because the possibility of punitive damages surely acts as one of the more significant deterrents to widespread commission of such fraud in commercial life.
Finally, as we shall see, it is a story that is still being written. The punitive damages question is part of a larger discussion about reforms to the entire securities arbitration process. Securities regulators, customers, and firms are now in the throes of an important debate over how best to structure the "privatized" system of dispute resolution that governs the nation's securities markets.
The Article is organized as follows. In Part I, I give needed background on securities industry arbitration and examine the Supreme Court's treatment of the FAA. The Court has tried to implement two primary policies in its FAA cases: the promotion of arbitration as an alternative to court litigation and advancement of "freedom of contract" norms under state common-law rules of contract interpretation. With these two points of reference, I look, in Part II, at the punitive damages controversy and examine the Mastrobuono opinion in detail. Part II closes with a critique of Mastrobuono and points out the gaps that the opinion leaves in arbitration law and practice.
In Part III, I place Mastrobuono within the context of the Court's overall treatment of contracts, demonstrate the shortcomings of the Court's contracts jurisprudence, and discuss how these short-comings explain what has happened in the aftermathof the case. Part III concludes with a call for legislative action by Congress to clarify the federal interest in all contracts that contain arbitration clauses that fall within the scope of the FAA. I argue that the failure of the Supreme Court to fully resolve the punitive damages question in Mastrobuono reveals that it has reached a jurisprudential impasse that Congress must remedy by bringing all matters of contractual interpretation related to implementing the FAA within the ambit of federal law.

questions.question: Should federal arbitration policy or state contract law govern how courts interpret contracts that contain arbitration clauses?

Can contractual provisions (including choice-of-law or references to industry rules) be interpreted to limit arbitrators' authority to award punitive damages, and how would such limits affect deterrence of misconduct in the securities context?
Do divergent judicial approaches to interpreting arbitration-related contract terms create legal uncertainty that requires legislative clarification at the federal level?
