shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes party autonomy in selecting arbitration procedures and choice-of-law as a mechanism that sidelines state laws, while Paper B interrogates the legal consequences of parties' written contracts (and a party's failure to read/sign) for plaintiffs' ability to reform contracts and obtain remedies.

shared_topics.topic: state versus federal allocation of authority to regulate contracts and dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques Supreme Court interpretations of the Federal Arbitration Act for subordinating state arbitration laws and federalism values; Paper B focuses on a New York statutory rule creating a state-law exception to preclusion—both engage with how statutory and judicial choices allocate regulatory power over contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: tension between finality of dispute resolution and exceptions permitting re-litigation or reformation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses doctrines (e.g., arbitrability and preemption) that produce conclusive outcomes outside state court control, while Paper B addresses the narrowness of preclusion rules that prevent reformation after an adverse judgment and critiques the statutory carve-out meant to allow reconsideration on equitable grounds.

papers.node_id: 8nevlj1!!SYMPOSIUM - RETHINKING THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT: AN EXAMINATION OF WHETHER AND HOW THE STATUTE SHOULD BE AMENDED: INTRODUCTION: Dreaming About Arbitration Reform
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM - RETHINKING THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT: AN EXAMINATION OF WHETHER AND HOW THE STATUTE SHOULD BE AMENDED: INTRODUCTION: Dreaming About Arbitration Reform
papers.abstract:
Some peoples' dreams are really great, or at least really exotic. Reverend Martin Luther King had a history-changing dream, of the end of discrimination.Me, I had a dream about a really great conference on arbitration, and how it might ultimately help lead to legal reform of arbitration. While the dream may not have been the most exotic, thanks to the participants in this Symposium, and many others,at least the first part of my dream has come true. We did host a very good conference. Perhaps this Symposium issue will even impact the nature of the law on arbitration in this country.
The Federal Arbitration Act ("FAA") is now eighty-two years old.Thus, its age, alone, raises the question as to whether the statute is in need of reform. Beyond such ageism, the Act of late has become quite controversial. Originally adopted to allow businesses to knowingly choose a potentially quicker, cheaper, more expert arbitration process over litigation,for many years the Act initially received little criticism or even attention. However, a series of Supreme Court decisions commencing in the mid-1980s made clear that the Act could be used not only in business-to-business settings, but also in contexts involving disputes between a business and a "little guy" consumer, employee, or franchisee.When companies began to rely on these Supreme Court decisions to mandate that "little guys" resolve future disputes through private arbitrationrather than litigation, many commentators and even some courts condemned the practice and, at least indirectly, the FAA for permitting the practice.Of course, the Court's decisions permitting mandatory arbitration also have their defenders,which is what makes for a controversy.
Apart from the disputes over mandatory arbitration, other aspects of the Federal Arbitration Act have recently engendered increased controversy as well. Whereas it once was assumed that disputants who chose arbitration would prefer a quick, inexpensive, informal, and private process, today some disputants and some commentators are seeking to create more complex hybrids between traditional arbitration and litigation.For example, some disputants have written clauses seeking to replace the very limited review mechanisms, described in the FAA, with a far more extensive appellate process.Also, the seemingly arcane question of whether arbitrators or courts should make certain arbitration-related decisions has recently received a great deal of attention from both courts and commentators.The existence of mandatory arbitration has a substantial impact on discussion of these issues as well, in that the nature of appellate review and division of jurisdictional powers can affect both the extent and impact of mandatory arbitration.
Although academics have spent a great deal of time and pages bashing the Supreme Court's recent interpretation of the Federal Arbitration Act, they have devoted far less energy to the more positive mission of trying to reform the statute, assuming reform is needed. In an attempt to take some positive steps towards reform, co-authors Edward Brunet, Richard Speidel, Stephen Ware, and I decided to write a book discussing what if any reforms of the FAA are needed.While we did not agree amongst ourselves as to what reforms were needed,we all found that the process of thinking through possible legislative reform, and debating it amongst ourselves, was very rewarding.
This Symposium is an outgrowth of the book project. As Director of the Saltman Center for Conflict Resolution, I have the luxury of being able to host conferences related to the topic of conflict resolution. I decided to invite some of the best-known and respected arbitration scholars in the country to come to Las Vegas and opine on how if at all the Federal Arbitration Act should be revised. To my delight (and a bit of shock), every single invitation I extended was accepted, and this terrific group of articles is the result.
Those of us who participated in the Symposium know that it was a great deal of fun.But, I believe I speak for the entire group of scholars when I say that we fervently hope that this Symposium will prove to be valuable not only to us, but to policy makers as well. The potential for reform of the Federal Arbitration Act is real. For example, on July 12, 2007, the Arbitration Fairness Act of 2007 was introduced before both the House and Senate.This bill, if passed, would amend the FAA to prohibit the use of mandatory arbitration with respect to consumers, employees, or franchisees.Similarly, on June 12, 2007, the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law for the House Judiciary Committee held a hearing on whether mandatory binding arbitrationagreements are fair to consumers.Thus, it is clear that there is interest, in Congress, in considering potential reform of the FAA.
In organizing the Symposium, I basically asked each invitee to write about whatever aspect of FAA potential reform they found most compelling. Yet, notwithstanding this libertarian approach, the panelists' remarks divided themselves fairly neatly into five panels, as discussed below.
Participants in the first panel all examine the question of whether and when agreements to arbitrate ought to be enforceable. Professor Richard Bales and co-author Christopher Kippley present an argument regarding the type of consent that ought to be required before pre-dispute arbitration agreements would be enforceable with respect to consumers and employees.They urge that just as workers are protected, by statute, from waiving their rights to benefits, so too should all consumers and employees be protected from agreeing, unwittingly, to resolve future disputes through binding arbitration rather than through litigation. Next, Professor Amy Schmitz also examines the dangers of enforcing small-print contracts of adhesion mandating arbitration.However, rather than urging the outright ban of pre-dispute arbitration clauses in the consumer and employment settings, she instead suggests that Congress impose minimum standards of fairness with respect to such clauses. Then Professor Michael Green examines the question of what if any steps Congress might take to encourage post-dispute agreements to arbitrate.Green asserts that if opponents to mandatory employment arbitration are successful in banning pre-dispute agreements to arbitrate employment disputes, it is critically important simultaneously to find means to encourage post-dispute agreements to arbitrate. Otherwise, urges Green, the many potential benefits of arbitration over litigation for both employees and employers will be lost.Finally, as the last participant in the first panel, I seek to turn matters a bit on their head. As a longtime opponent of the imposition of mandatory arbitration on "little guys," Ihave frequently urged Congress, states, or courts to ban the practice.In this presentation, for a change of pace, I decided to defend the practice of mandatory arbitration but only if imposed on the company, rather than on the little guy.From both a policy and a constitutional perspective, I consider why it might be acceptable for Congress to impose arbitration on companies, even if it is not acceptable in my view for private companies to impose arbitration on little guys.
The second panel of the Symposium focuses on issues pertaining to how responsibilities and legal issues should be divided between arbitrators and courts. As the commentators recognize, these issues of "separability" and jurisdiction are often seen as the most complex in arbitration. In Prima Paint Corp. v. Flood & Conklin Manufacturing Co.,the Supreme Court explained that arbitration clauses and the contracts in which they are contained are "separable," and that arbitrators rather than courts should typically determine the validity of the container contract. Professor Stephen Ware, first, focuses on the Supreme Court's most recent foray into this morass: Buckeye Check Cashing Inc. v. Cardegna.Considering how Buckeye might be reconciled with such prior Supreme Court decisions as Prima Paint,First Options of Chicago, Inc. v. Kaplan,and Howsam v. Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc.,Ware boldly calls for a repeal of the separability doctrine in order to better honor parties' contractual intentions.Professor William Park, next, addresses doctrines of separability and jurisdiction from the perspective of one deeply versed in international as well as domestic arbitration. Showing that the Supreme Court's approach is closely analogous to the way other countries have approached these jurisdictional issues, Park concludes: "While not entirely free from doubt, the American cases are probably getting things more right than wrong."Finally Professor Alan Rau provides his rationale for why the Federal Arbitration Actshould not be revised with respect to separability (or any other matter).As to separability, Rau has previously explained that while the doctrine is often misunderstood, he for one finds it "unproblematical."Defending that notion as well as courts' generally superior abilities as compared to legislators, Rau colorfully proclaims: "The power of Congress over the practice of arbitration should, I think, be precisely equivalent to that of the Czar over the far-flung peasant villages of Russia - absolute, but exercised at an inconceivably remote distance."
The third panel focuses on the terms under which courts should be able to vacate arbitral awards. Several of the panelists favor amending the FAA to allow for more expansive review than currently permitted by section 10 of the Act, although they differ substantially on the specifics. For example Professor Sarah Cole, espousing the virtues of freedom of contract, urges that the FAA be amended to "permit parties to agree to expanded judicial review, so long as the court's review of the award does not compromise the institutional integrity of the courts."Professor Christopher Drahozal focuses on "manifest disregard" as a basis for vacating arbitral awards, rather than on contractual expansions of section 10.As Drahozal notes, although courts generally allow arbitral awards to be vacated due to their manifest disregard of the law, this doctrine lacks good support as a matter of either doctrine or case law.He advocates that the doctrine ought to be codified to support the integrity of the court system.Professor Jeffrey Stempel focuses on the implications of mandatory or "mass" arbitration for determination of an appropriate vacatur standard.As a prudential matter, Stempel urges that opponents of mandatory arbitration are better off seeking an improved vacatur standard, which would help ensure that arbitrators apply the law, than opposing the enforcement of mandatory arbitration provisions altogether.
However, not all the presenters favor the use of expanded review. Professor Richard Reuben instead states: "The displacement of finality with substantive judicial review, if codified, will greatly undermine the arbitration process, its attractiveness as an alternative to public adjudication or negotiated settlement, and its utility as an aid to the judiciary as a forum for the expeditious resolution of disputes."Thus, Reuben urges that "rather than requiring or permitting substantive judicial review … the FAA should maintain itscurrent narrow grounds for substantive review and be amended to resolve a split in the lower courts, to make clear that parties cannot contract for substantive judicial review … ."
Finally, switching gears to consider the international context, Professor Richard Speidel considers how contractually expanded review, such as that discussed by Professor Cole,might be treated in an international contract.Speidel is concerned with the potential for lack of parity between the treatment afforded to domestic and foreign arbitral awards. He urges that it ought not to be permissible, in the international setting, to expand the scope of review beyond that permitted by treaty, and that the relevant laws ought to be revised to ensure that result.
The fourth panel focuses on multi-jurisdictional issues brought into play by the Federal Arbitration Act and its interpretation. Professor Edward Brunet discusses what he sees as the anomalous fact that "federal law has been permitted to run roughshod over the subtleties of state efforts to regulate aspects of arbitration."One might have expected that states rather than the federal government would play a major role in regulating arbitration, says Brunet, given that contractual and consumer matters are typically left to states' police powers, given that states are typically allowed to provide their own procedural rules, and given the Supreme Court's current supposed devotion to federalism values.To correct this situation, Brunet urges that the FAA be amended to specify no intent to preempt the field of arbitration regulation.Turning, then to the international setting, Professor Catherine Rogers considers how the arrival of "have-nots" into the world of international arbitration will and should affect the nature of arbitration that crosses international boundaries.Specifically, whereas international arbitration has traditionally been premised on the supposition that two sophisticated parties with relatively equal bargaining power voluntarily agreed to arbitrate rather than litigate their disputes, Rogers explains that globalization and increased reliance on the Internet have now brought both consumers and employees into the world of international arbitration. Looking at the effect these new arrivals may have on the system of international arbitration, Rogers concludes that such arbitration has the potential to "operate as an instrument for … mediating conflicting national laws and policies, for securing effective transnational regulation, and for generating international public policy norms."She believes that other countries' protection of consumers and employees from unfair processes may ensure that international arbitration involving "have-nots" will be fairer than its domestic counterpart.
The fifth panel of the Symposium looks at the FAA through a wide-angle lens, rather than focusing on particular narrow aspects that might be in need of reform. Professor Maureen Weston traces the history of the Act and argues that whereas the Act was "ostensibly designed to provide for the voluntary private adjudication of disputes, [it] generates thousands of lawsuits, is vociferously challenged by consumer protection groups, widely criticized in scholarly articles, and is judicially determined to preempt and thus substantially restrict states' ability to enact legislation responsive to constituent concerns."Therefore, urges Weston, Congress ought to pass legislation that returns the FAA to its roots by limiting its preemptive scope and either exempting consumer and employment disputes altogether or, at minimum, providing extra protections for consumers or employees who are contractually mandated to take claims to arbitration.Next Professor David Schwartz, a long-time critic of the Supreme Court's arbitration jurisprudence,sounds similar themes when he contends that "we are nearing the quarter-century mark in the Supreme Court's misguided reinterpretation of the Federal Arbitration Act."He targets the Court's decisions permitting the growth of mandatory arbitration and urges that these decisions are bad not only because they support unfair policy,but also because "the forcing of employment and consumer cases into the mandatory arbitration system has created inexorable pressures to judicialize arbitration."Thus, addressing himself to those who love arbitration as it was, Schwartz urges that the FAA be amended to exempt consumer and employment disputes from pre-dispute arbitration.Finally, Professor Thomas Stipanowich ends the Symposium by examining how the law of binding arbitration is affecting the law of other dispute resolution processes.Stipanowich explains that binding arbitration is no longer the main game in town, and that contracts are increasingly calling for the use of other informal processes such as non-binding arbitration and mediation. Also, contracts increasingly include step-dispute resolution clauses that anticipate the potential use of multiple processes.Yet, courts are not quite sure how to handle these non-arbitration clauses and are inconsistent as to whether they apply the Federal Arbitration Act to processes other than binding arbitration.Stipanowich urges that "the burden generally outweighs whatever benefits may be achieved by viewing ADR processesthrough the lens of arbitration law," and instead suggests that courts needed to be provided with other guidance, perhaps through a Restatement of Dispute Resolution.
Maybe it's just "Nevada Dreamin'"but I truly hope that this conference, and this Symposium issue, can help influence debate in this country regarding arbitration. Having brought together some of the best arbitration scholars in the country, it would be a real shame if this conference was only a good time for us and had no impact in the real world.

questions.question: Whether pre-dispute mandatory arbitration clauses should be enforceable against consumers, employees, or franchisees.
How decisionmaking authority and standards of judicial review should be allocated between private arbitrators and public courts in resolving contractual disputes.

Whether the federal arbitration framework should be revised to limit federal preemption, provide additional protections for weaker parties, and address multi-jurisdictional and international arbitration issues.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45yalejintll227!!ARTICLE: The Adjudication Business
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Adjudication Business

shared_topics.topic: competition and convergence between arbitration and litigation (including hybrid forums)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and debates the growing hybridization of arbitration and litigation—clauses creating appellate review, non‑binding ADR, and courts unsure how to treat non‑arbitral processes—while Paper B analyzes the rise of international commercial courts that intentionally combine litigation and arbitration features and compete with arbitration for international commercial cases.

shared_topics.topic: how institutional design affects parties' preferences and access to dispute resolution (including effects on consumers/employees)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how mandatory pre‑dispute arbitration, appellate rules, and vacatur standards affect the bargaining power and remedies available to 'little guys' and whether protections or inducements for post‑dispute arbitration are needed, while Paper B interrogates whether parties actually prefer arbitration or new international commercial courts and how court design choices influence forum selection and perceived accessibility.

shared_topics.topic: internationalization, forum shopping, and multi‑jurisdictional dynamics in commercial dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses cross‑border concerns such as parity in review of foreign awards, the impact of globalization on bringing consumers/employees into international arbitration, and federal preemption of state regulation, whereas Paper B surveys the global proliferation of international commercial courts, their roles in attracting cases (e.g., Belt and Road disputes), and how their emergence reshapes forum selection for transnational disputes.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of adjudicatory authority and standards of review between courts and arbitrators
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on doctrinal questions like separability (who decides arbitrability), standards for vacating awards (manifest disregard, expanded review), and the proper division of jurisdiction between judges and arbitrators; Paper B engages this theme more institutionally by showing how international commercial courts borrow party‑driven and confidential procedures from arbitration and by challenging the strict litigation–arbitration dichotomy that underpins how authority and procedural roles are allocated.

shared_topics.topic: policy and regulatory choices shaping the market for adjudication services
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates statutory reform of the Federal Arbitration Act, possible exemptions for consumers/employees, and federalism/preemption issues that would reshape dispute‑resolution markets, while Paper B analyzes how state policy goals and political‑economic incentives (e.g., creating legal hubs, special economic zones, or strategic influence) drive the creation and funding of international commercial courts and thereby alter the supply side of adjudication.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62brooklynlrev1335!!SYMPOSIUM: SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A DECADE AFTER McMAHON: CONTRACT THEORY AND SECURITIES ARBITRATION: WHITHER CONSENT? (c) 1996 Richard E. Speidel. All Rights Reserved.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: SECURITIES ARBITRATION: A DECADE AFTER McMAHON: CONTRACT THEORY AND SECURITIES ARBITRATION: WHITHER CONSENT? (c) 1996 Richard E. Speidel. All Rights Reserved.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of consent in pre-dispute arbitration agreements (contracts of adhesion)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A features multiple contributions debating whether consumers and employees truly consent to pre-dispute arbitration clauses and whether such clauses should be banned or subject to minimum fairness standards; Paper B analyzes consent as the doctrinal and practical underpinning of securities arbitration, characterizing many broker-customer clauses as adhesion contracts and questioning whether consent is meaningful or a legal fiction.

shared_topics.topic: whether statutory and regulatory claims are properly subject to arbitration (scope of arbitrability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the expansion of mandatory arbitration into consumer and employment statutory claims and the implications of Supreme Court decisions permitting such enforcement; Paper B centers on McMahon and related case law that treats securities Act and other regulatory claims as arbitrable under broad clauses and interrogates that shift.

shared_topics.topic: the allocation of decision‑making between courts and arbitrators (who decides arbitrability/separability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A devotes a full panel to separability and jurisdictional allocation, debating whether courts or arbitrators should decide threshold issues and whether separability should be repealed; Paper B explicates the Supreme Court framework that generally reserves questions of arbitrability (and enforcement) to courts unless parties clearly agreed otherwise.

shared_topics.topic: federal preemption and the role of the FAA in limiting state regulation of arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A includes criticism that federal arbitration law has preempted state efforts to regulate arbitration and urges possible statutory clarification or limits on preemption; Paper B analyzes the Court's preemption doctrine under the FAA, explaining how state laws that discriminate against arbitration are preempted and how that shapes consent and regulation in securities arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope of judicial review and vacatur of arbitral awards (manifest disregard / section 10)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's third panel debates expanding judicial review, codifying 'manifest disregard', or preserving narrow FAA section 10 standards in light of mandatory arbitration; Paper B summarizes the limited scope of review under section 10, the uncertainty around 'manifest disregard', and how narrow review affects enforcement of statutory/regulatory claims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 8nevlj314!!SYMPOSIUM - RETHINKING THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT: AN EXAMINATION OF WHETHER AND HOW THE STATUTE SHOULD BE AMENDED: ARTICLE:Parties' Power to Vary Standards for Review of International Commercial Arbitration Awards
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM - RETHINKING THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT: AN EXAMINATION OF WHETHER AND HOW THE STATUTE SHOULD BE AMENDED: ARTICLE:Parties' Power to Vary Standards for Review of International Commercial Arbitration Awards

shared_topics.topic: whether parties can contractually expand judicial review / vacatur grounds for arbitral awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly asks whether parties may agree to broaden judicial review (e.g., for errors of fact or law) and treats the FAA as potentially containing default rather than mandatory rules; Paper B summarizes symposium contributions that debate amending the FAA to permit or prohibit party‑agreed expanded review and describes specific authors advocating for or against such contractual expansions.

shared_topics.topic: the status and role of the 'manifest disregard' doctrine as a basis for vacatur
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the judicially created 'manifest disregard of law' ground and questions its doctrinal solidity and incentives, while Paper B highlights panel discussion on manifest disregard (including calls to codify, clarify, or reform it) as central to how courts should vacate awards.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract and public/mandatory rules (including mandatory arbitration concerns)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the debate as whether arbitration law should enforce party autonomy or impose mandatory rules to protect public interests like finality and efficiency, and Paper B repeatedly addresses that same tension in the context of mandatory pre‑dispute arbitration for consumers and employees and whether the FAA should be reformed to limit or regulate such impositions.

shared_topics.topic: limits imposed by international law and treaty parity on expanding review of foreign arbitral awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the international dimension—questioning whether parties can expand review in international commercial arbitration and how treaties constrain that power—while Paper B reports symposium contributions (e.g., Speidel, Rogers, Park) that analyze treaty limits, parity between domestic and foreign awards, and the impact of international arbitration involving 'have‑nots.'

shared_topics.topic: who decides threshold questions (separability / definition of 'arbitration') and the allocation of jurisdiction between courts and arbitrators
shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes the definitional issue of when a transaction qualifies as arbitration for statute/treaty purposes and whether parties can alter finality, implicating who should decide such questions, and Paper B devotes a panel to separability and jurisdictional allocation (discussing Prima Paint, Buckeye, and calls to reassess the separability doctrine).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18nevlj427!!SYMPOSIUM: RE-INVENTING ARBITRATION: Arbitration's Dark Shadow
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: RE-INVENTING ARBITRATION: Arbitration's Dark Shadow

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy and fairness of mandatory pre‑dispute arbitration for consumers and employees
shared_topics.justification: Paper A devotes multiple panels to whether pre‑dispute mandatory arbitration should be enforceable (including proposals to ban or impose minimum fairness standards and the Arbitration Fairness Act), while Paper B centers on the harms produced by the growth of mandatory arbitration and its effects on vulnerable parties.

shared_topics.topic: the private/secrecy of arbitration and its impact on public information and reputational incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes the historical promise of arbitration's privacy and the contemporary concern that secrecy undermines oversight, and Paper B frames secrecy as arbitration's 'dark shadow' that hides industry practices and reduces reputational penalties for abusive behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the scope of judicial review and vacatur standards (and the consequences of limited review)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A extensively analyzes section 10, manifest disregard, and proposals to expand or preserve narrow vacatur standards, whereas Paper B highlights the practical problem created by the absence of judicial review and argues that that absence contributes to arbitral lawlessness and may justify federal corrective action.

shared_topics.topic: the need for statutory or federal legislative reform of the Federal Arbitration Act to address arbitration's expansion
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is explicitly organized around potential amendments to the FAA (e.g., exemptions, preemption limits, Arbitration Fairness Act), and Paper B likewise argues that federal intervention or reform may be necessary to restore consumer protections and public accountability.

shared_topics.topic: the judicialization and hybridization of arbitration (arbitration evolving toward litigation‑like procedures and costs)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents trends toward more complex, appellate‑style procedures and hybrid ADR clauses and debates whether that judicialization should be encouraged or restrained, while Paper B observes that arbitration has adopted litigation‑like processes which have increased cost and undermined many traditional arbitration benefits.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49arizlrev69!!ARTICLE:Arbitration and the Individuation Critique
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Arbitration and the Individuation Critique

shared_topics.topic: the fairness and enforceability of pre‑dispute mandatory arbitration clauses for consumers and employees
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the 'individuation critique' as a core objection to pre‑dispute arbitration clauses that force one‑shot consumers and employees into individualized proceedings, questioning whether such clauses are fair; Paper B organizes multiple symposium contributions that directly evaluate when pre‑dispute arbitration should be enforceable (consent standards, adhesion contracts) and canvasses legislative proposals (e.g., the Arbitration Fairness Act) to restrict or condition mandatory clauses.

shared_topics.topic: aggregation versus individuation (class arbitration and other collective mechanisms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that class arbitration and informal aggregative practices may counter the individuation critique and explores how arbitrators and ADR institutions can enable collective relief; Paper B engages the problem of 'mass' and class arbitration across panels—discussing the implications of multi‑claim proceedings, how vacatur standards and procedural rules should handle mass arbitration, and the pressures that mandatory arbitration places on aggregate dispute resolution.

shared_topics.topic: judicial review, vacatur standards, and the separability doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that class arbitration awards are subject only to limited judicial review and raises empirical and doctrinal questions about how much court oversight occurs in practice; Paper B contains extensive discussion of whether and how to expand or restrict judicial review of arbitral awards (section 10 vacatur, 'manifest disregard'), debates over appellate review, and the separability/competence division between courts and arbitrators.

shared_topics.topic: institutional and regulatory design of arbitration (role of ADR providers, the FAA, and preemption/state regulation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the role of arbitration providers (AAA, JAMS) and their due‑process standards and suggests provider policy reforms to improve fairness and aggregation; Paper B surveys potential statutory reforms to the Federal Arbitration Act, federal preemption of state regulation, international implications, and broader calls for institutional guidance (including possible Restatement or legislative adjustments) shaping how arbitration is administered and regulated.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18nevlj437!!SYMPOSIUM: RE-INVENTING ARBITRATION: Evolution Of The Arbitration Forum As A Response To Mandatory Arbitration
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: RE-INVENTING ARBITRATION: Evolution Of The Arbitration Forum As A Response To Mandatory Arbitration

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and spread of pre‑dispute mandatory arbitration agreements (PDAAs) in consumer and employment settings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally interrogates the Supreme Court-enabled expansion of PDAAs under the FAA and the controversies about enforcing small‑print adhesion clauses against consumers and employees; Paper B documents the ubiquity of PDAAs (clickwraps, account agreements) and the practical lack of knowing consent in consumer, employment, investor and civil‑rights contexts.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how to reform the Federal Arbitration Act or arbitral forums in response to mandatory arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a symposium devoted to potential legislative and doctrinal amendments to the FAA (e.g., Arbitration Fairness Act, preemption, separability, vacatur standards); Paper B likewise argues the need to realign domestic arbitration (via legislation) and/or to evolve arbitration forums and rules (e.g., FINRA) as a pragmatic response to mandatory arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: the need for enhanced procedural protections, due‑process safeguards, transparency and expanded review for parties forced into arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A features debate over permitting expanded judicial review, codifying 'manifest disregard', and appropriate vacatur standards to protect the integrity of adjudication; Paper B describes how arbitral forums are incorporating judicial‑style due‑process protections and procedural reforms (and highlights FINRA’s rule changes) to increase fairness, transparency, and access for forced participants.

shared_topics.topic: impact of mandatory arbitration and class‑action waivers on access to justice and public‑policy disputes (especially for 'little guys' and small claims)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A repeatedly raises how mandatory arbitration and mass arbitration affect consumers/employees, the judicialization pressure, and how international arbitration now reaches 'have‑nots'; Paper B emphasizes that class‑action waivers and PDAAs channel small claims and public‑policy disputes out of courts, preventing aggregation of small claims and undermining public enforcement and access to justice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 14lewisclarklrev905!!SYMPOSIUM: THE SUPREME COURT AND ARBITRATION: THE SUPREME COURT AND ARBITRATION: CONTRACTING AROUND HALL STREET
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE SUPREME COURT AND ARBITRATION: THE SUPREME COURT AND ARBITRATION: CONTRACTING AROUND HALL STREET

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of contractual provisions that expand judicial review of arbitration awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether and how parties can contract for expanded court review of arbitral awards after Hall Street, focusing on enforceability in federal versus state court; Paper B collects symposium arguments about whether the FAA should be amended to permit or prohibit party-agreed expanded judicial review and presents competing scholarly views on allowing contractual appellate review of awards.

shared_topics.topic: scope and standards for vacating arbitration awards under the FAA (section 10 / manifest disregard)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the Hall Street holding that section 10 supplies the exclusive statutory vacatur grounds and examines alternative legal theories for expanded vacatur; Paper B devotes a panel to vacatur standards, debating codification or repeal of doctrines like 'manifest disregard' and whether broader substantive review should be authorized by statute.

shared_topics.topic: federal preemption and the interaction between the FAA and state arbitration law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates the prospects for enforcing expanded-review clauses under state law and highlights uncertainty about FAA preemption of state-law-based review or confirmation procedures; Paper B addresses multi-jurisdictional concerns, including critiques that the FAA has preempted state regulatory nuance and proposals to amend the Act to limit federal preemption of state arbitration regulation.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and implications of pre‑dispute arbitration agreements and mandatory arbitration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames its analysis assuming pre-dispute arbitration agreements and considers the legal constraints on contracting for different review regimes in that context; Paper B's opening panel extensively examines when pre-dispute arbitration clauses should be enforceable (especially for consumers and employees), the politics of mandatory arbitration, and the downstream effects such enforcement has on review standards and judicialization.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71valrev1305!!ARTICLE: THE SECOND ARBITRATION TRILOGY: THE FEDERALIZATION OF ARBITRATION LAW.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SECOND ARBITRATION TRILOGY: THE FEDERALIZATION OF ARBITRATION LAW.

shared_topics.topic: the Supreme Court-driven federalization and expanded scope of the Federal Arbitration Act
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames recent Supreme Court decisions (since the mid-1980s) as having dramatically changed the FAA and motivates thinking about statutory reform, while Paper B traces that same expansion (Prima Paint and the Trilogy) and analyzes how the Court converted the FAA into a body of federal substantive law applicable in state courts.

papers.node_id: 39houslrev693!!SYMPOSIUM 2002:THE FUTURE OF PATENT LAW: "MAYBE WE SHOULDN'T ARBITRATE": SOME ASPECTS OF THE RISK/BENEFIT CALCULUS OF AGREEING TO BINDING ARBITRATION OF PATENT DISPUTES
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM 2002:THE FUTURE OF PATENT LAW: "MAYBE WE SHOULDN'T ARBITRATE": SOME ASPECTS OF THE RISK/BENEFIT CALCULUS OF AGREEING TO BINDING ARBITRATION OF PATENT DISPUTES
papers.abstract:
It is not my purpose here to bless or condemn the wisdom of submitting patent law disputes to arbitration. A number of observers have pointed out the advantages of arbitration over conventional litigation in general, especially where the dispute possesses international characteristics.Others have pointed to similar advantages in resolving intellectual property disputes in particular.I do propose herein some grounds for caution. I very much doubt the wisdom of any general proposition that it is better for a patent license agreement to provide that all disputes regarding the agreement will be resolved by arbitration, especially where no risk-limiting provisions are included.I think the view of Chief Judge Judith Kaye of the New York Court of Appeals regarding pre-agreement to arbitrate complex matters has force for patent cases:
A crystal ball of course would be useful. It would be nice to know, for example, just what the nature of the dispute will be; how and where it will erupt; whether your client will bethe wronged party or the wrongdoer; whether your client will want vengeance, vindication or just a quick and very private settlement; whether your counterparts, when they become your adversaries, will want to eat the orange or cook the peel - in other words, their desires and objectives and how they will relate to yours. Sad to say, crystal balls are not readily available - and as with much else in this world of uncertainties, in the end the only reliable tools will be the judgment and experience of counsel.
Confining ourselves to the present subject of patent disputes, the uncertainties observed by Judge Kaye are often present in large degree. A division needs to be made based on whether we are dealing with a decision to arbitrate an already-ripened patent dispute, or with a contractual covenant to arbitrate all unknown future disputes that could arise in connection with a patent. The existing dispute is, of course, the easier case to deal with. Each disputant typically knows the answers to the following important questions: (1) Who is claiming and who is defending? (2) What are the likely stakes? (3) For the likely controlling issues, who would have the better chance of winning in court? (4) How long is the litigation apt to take and how disruptive will it be to business? (5) What will be the other costs, notably counsel fees? (6) How do we think the other side is assessing the dispute? Against this backdrop, the parties may decide to submit the dispute to arbitration. They will do so if each party believes the procedure does not pose unacceptable risks and is likely to have lower costs.
When deciding whether to arbitrate all future disputes the risk calculus goal is the same, but far less can be concretely known in advance. If one party is the patent owner and the other is the licensee, and the license is a simple patent license, the most likely future dispute will place the patent owner as claimant and the licensee as respondent. The licensee's goal in resolving the dispute will be to avoid or minimize royaltypayments by contending either that a particular product is not covered by the licensed patents, or that any applicable patents are invalid.It is relatively unlikely that the licensee will be a claimant in the simple case,although in more complex license arrangements - such as where trade secrets are also being conveyed, joint development is provided for, policing of the patents is assured, and other covenants beyond the simple patent license are in place - the likelihood of finding the licensee as the claimant increases.
Even in the simple case, the answer to query two above, assessing the stakes, is difficult to come by in advance. With a running-royalty license that contains no quantity restrictions and no royalty caps, the amount of money moving pursuant to the license is generally variable throughout the license term.Question three, estimating the chances of success, is alsoproblematic because at the time the agreement is signed, validity and scope have seldom been the subjects of comprehensive study or evidentiary development. Questions four and five, relating to likely costs, can be partially answered based on the normal procedural savings inherent in a well-structured arbitration, as compared with litigation.Question six, guessing the adversary's assessment of the dispute, is wholly out of the realm of meaningful prediction until the contours of a particular dispute emerge.
Considerations like these have led commentators to caution against allowing over-enthusiasm for the frequently mentioned advantages of arbitration to cloud the parties' judgment at the time of contracting.Benefits of arbitration can seldom be posited as absolutes or desirables at that time. Experience is, as Judge Kaye puts it, the only anchor in this sea of uncertainty.Among the many factors to be considered when deciding whether to agree to arbitration in patent law situations, three will be addressed here: (1) To what extent do courts in the United States and other countries order arbitration to proceed and recognize arbitral awards that include or are based on a determination of the central issues of patent validity and patent scope?(2) To the extent a party may need injunctive relief against ongoing patent infringement or breach of a license covenant, will she be able to obtain that relief by arbitration?(3) To what extent are arbitral awards deemed preclusive in later arbitral or judicial proceedings, as to either general contentions (claim preclusion) or particular issues resolved (issue preclusion)?In the literature on arbitration of patent disputes, these topics are not often addressed, yet they are important to understanding the ramifications of submitting patent disputes to resolution by arbitration.

questions.question: Whether agreeing in advance to resolve all future patent-related disputes by binding arbitration is generally advisable compared with leaving disputes for court resolution, given uncertainty about future facts, stakes, and parties' positions.

To what extent will courts (domestic and foreign) compel arbitration and recognize/enforce arbitral awards that decide core patent matters - for example, whether a patent is valid or whether a product falls within the patent's scope?

Whether arbitration can provide effective remedies for ongoing patent infringement or license breaches (including injunctive relief) and whether arbitral awards prevent relitigation of the same issues in later arbitral or judicial proceedings.

papers.node_id: 54arklrev285!!SYMPOSIUM CASE NOTE: Walton v. Lewis: Chipping Away at the Policy and Precedent in Favor of Mandatory Arbitration
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM CASE NOTE: Walton v. Lewis: Chipping Away at the Policy and Precedent in Favor of Mandatory Arbitration
papers.abstract:
Over the past decade, the concept of alternative dispute resolution ("ADR") has become a hot topic within jurisprudential circles. The Arkansas General Assembly has taken an especially active role in encouraging the use of ADR by enacting statutes concerning the use of mediation and arbitration.Contract clauses mandating the use of arbitration and mediation have begun to surface in contracts in a variety of areas, including the securities, retail, restaurant and hotel, health care, and broadcasting industries.However, the widespread use of such clauses has caused many to fear the potentially unfair consequences of mandating the use of such a forum.
In particular, arbitration clauses have begun to dominate the securities industry. The National Association of Securities Dealers ("NASD"), the governing body for the securities industry, mandates that certain disputes involving its membersorthose associated with its membersbe resolved through arbitration.This arbitration requirement has received more than its fair share of criticism. Courts in many jurisdictions have held that mandatory arbitration in securities disputes provides an unfair advantage for large securities and brokerage firms.However, other courts have held that the requirement of arbitration in securities disputes is in accordance with the Unites States Supreme Court's policy in favor of arbitration.
Recently, the Arkansas Supreme Court encountered the issue of securities arbitration in Walton v. Lewis.In Walton, the court, in resolving a dispute involving a securities firm's alleged failure to pay a bonus due an employee, declined to effectuate an arbitration clause embodied in a NASD registration application completed by the employee.Although the court based its opinion on tenuous factual determinations, the Walton court's holding seems to show a disfavor for contractual clauses mandating arbitration. This case note will analyze the Walton opinion by examining the plethora of case law concerning mandatory arbitration.

papers.node_id: 27iowajcorpl537!!SYMPOSIUM IN MEMORY OF DAVID H. VERNON:Nonmutual Agreements To Arbitrate
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM IN MEMORY OF DAVID H. VERNON:Nonmutual Agreements To Arbitrate
papers.abstract:
Some find the law of contracts to be "characterized by a comforting symmetry."It is easy to see why. Both parties must manifest assent for a contract to be formed.Consideration requires a "bargained-for exchange,"in which the "root of the whole matter is the relation of reciprocal conventional inducement, each for the other, between consideration and promise."The common law doctrine of "mutuality of obligation" - that "either both must be bound, or neither is bound"- and the equitable doctrine of "mutuality of remedy" - that "a contract will not be specifically enforced … unless both parties at the time it is executed have the right to resort to equity for its specific enforcement"- have long historical roots (albeit the former longer than the latter). Indeed, whether based in a norm of fairness,an anti-speculation principle,or something else,symmetry in contract law, as with symmetry in the rest of the law, seems to be "of the essence of the American way of life."
But on closer examination, the symmetry of contract law breaks down.While both parties must manifest assent for a contract to be formed, that manifestation need not be symmetric in time, place, or form.Mutuality of consideration is not necessary for apromise to be enforceable.The doctrine of mutuality of obligation has been "thoroughly discredited,"and the doctrine of mutuality of remedy has been "quite generally repudiated, especially as the exceptions gradually swallowed it."
Moreover, contract law has never required that the precise terms of the exchange be symmetrical,beyond some minimum requirement of value being given on each side.Buyers and sellers do not exchange identical promises. Buyers promise to pay and sellers promise to sell.In complex corporate deals, the parties make different representations and warranties.Liquidated damages clausesand covenants not to competeoften are asymmetrical - ordinarily only one party to the contract is subject to such a clause - yet are enforceable so long as reasonable.
Indeed, the nature of exchange belies any such term-by-term requirement of symmetry. The economic theory of comparative advantage is premised on the asymmetry of exchange: each party specializes in what it is best at producing, and then makes a trade that both parties prefer- precisely because each gets something other than what it gave up.If the law required the terms of the deal to be symmetrical - such that the partiesmerely traded the same thing, one for the other - no legally enforceable exchange would take place.
Nonetheless, "the ghost of mutuality still walks," and until laid to rest, "will continue to haunt our law."A "growing number of courts"- albeit still a minority - refuse to enforce arbitration clauses with asymmetric obligations to arbitrate, either on the ground that the clause is unconscionable or that it lacks mutuality of obligation.Such "nonmutual arbitration clauses," as part of an underlying contract between the parties, take various forms:
The arbitration clause itself may create an option in one of the parties to arbitrate, but not in one or more of the other parties. Or the arbitration clause may appear to bind both parties, but a different superseding provision in the contract may grant one of the parties a unilateral right to a judicial forum in the event of the breach with rights to obtain damages or specific performance, thus eliminating the first party's right to arbitrate. The lack of mutuality may also be partial, in that it applies to only some arbitrable issues.
Although nonmutual arbitration clauses are used in contracts between sophisticated businesses,the current controversy is the result of their increasing use in contracts between businesses and consumers, and employers and employees.Courts invalidating such clauses,and critics of predispute arbitration clauses in consumer and employment contracts,take the view that nonmutual arbitration clauses are unfair to such "little guys."
This Article challenges that view. Certainly to the extent market forces constrain business (mis)behavior, nonmutual arbitration clauses may make consumers better off.Commentators who criticize (and courts that invalidate) nonmutual arbitration clauses, however, are skeptical of markets and question the effectiveness of market constraints.This Article shows that even accepting - for the sake of argument - the skeptical view of markets and business behavior held by critics of predispute consumer arbitration clauses, a requirement that arbitration clauses contain mutual promises to arbitrate may actually make consumers worse off, not better off. Moreover, such a mutuality requirement may result in arbitration proceedings that are less fair, rather than more fair, to consumers. Thus, while a poorly functioning market is a necessary condition for a mutuality requirement to make sense as a policy matter, it is not a sufficient condition. Courts that refuse to enforce nonmutual agreements to arbitrate may be harming consumers rather than helping them.
Part II of the Article provides an overview of the current state of the law. With one principal exception, courts have refused to invalidate nonmutual arbitration clauses as lacking mutuality of obligation. Instead, those courts that have invalidated nonmutual arbitration clauses (an increasing number but still a minority) rely instead on the doctrine of unconscionability to impose a requirement of mutuality.
Part III presents possible business justifications for nonmutual arbitration clauses. For various reasons, such clauses may reduce a business's dispute resolution costs. Even if consumers' dispute resolution costs do not go down as well, consumers will benefit to the extent the business passes on its costs savings in the form of lower prices.
Part IV is the heart of the Article. It argues that even under the assumptions about markets and business behavior usually made by critics of predispute consumer arbitration clauses, it is not necessarily the case that invalidating nonmutual arbitration clauses will make consumers better off. Instead, whether consumers benefit depends on how a business responds to the mutuality requirement. If the business responds by requiring arbitration of all claims, both those brought by the consumer and by the business - certainly a plausible response - the consumer may actually be worse off with a mutuality requirement.
Part V considers whether a business subject to a mutuality requirement will modify the arbitration process to make it more fair to consumers. Again, under the usual assumptions of critics of predispute consumer arbitration clauses, the answer is that it likely will not. If anything, the greater amount at stake in arbitration under a mutual arbitration clause gives the business a greater incentive to structure the process in ways that favor the business than under a nonmutual arbitration clause.

papers.abstract: This Article analyzes current arbitration trends in the United States. The arbitrability of non-statutorily created claims is no longer disputed, as long as the underlying contractual agreement embraces arbitration of the dispute. Likewise, the result appears to be the same for most statutorily created claims, with the result that United States courts will enforce almost all agreements to arbitrate disputes, regardless of the claim's genesis. This Article initially discusses the law governing arbitrabilityand then explores current trends in the arbitrability of specific types of disputes.

papers.node_id: 59alblrev831!!SYMPOSIUM ON BUSINESS DISPUTE RESOLUTION: ADR AND BEYOND: FOREWORD
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM ON BUSINESS DISPUTE RESOLUTION: ADR AND BEYOND: FOREWORD
papers.abstract:
Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) concepts have been with us for approximately 15 years. In the beginning, practitioners, particularly trial lawyers and judges, scorned ADR as a waste of time, talent, and money. One of the reasons for such mutual scorn and skepticism may have been the fact that ADR was not conceived by lawyers, legislators, or courts. It grew out of litigants' increasing frustration with the way our civil justice system, both state and federal, works. As the following papers written from several perspectives suggest, times have changed.
It did not take long for users or putative users of ADR to realize that if properly structured, it could save significant amounts of time and money. Still later, people began to realize that the flexibility of ADR processes is extremely important and attractive to most parties in civil disputes. Lawyers, including trial lawyers, were finally persuaded that not all clients are convinced that unlimited discovery in our state and federal courts is the best way to resolve a civil controversy. Lawyers and litigants gradually came to realize that ADR procedures permit them to choose their "neutral." Experience teaches that most litigants and their lawyers love to "pick their own judge" whenever possible, or at least have a voice in the selection of a good neutral.
Some years ago, well-meaning people in academe and private practice began writing articles claiming there should be specific rules for the handling and disposition of ADR proceedings.Furthermore, some advocated the requirement of "full disclosure" by neutrals before they were hired. This was the first effort to adopt a form of procedural rules for ADR. Fortunately, this has not happened. Such rules are not necessarily helpful; worse, constraining creative ADR techniques by specific rules may render ADR processes less flexible. The history of procedural rules in our courts illustrates that they grow increasingly complex and assume an importance beyond that of simplicity and speed of resolution of the merits.
No litigant needs rules to understand that retention of a neutral with a bias or conflict of interest is undesirable. Thanks to the efforts of organizations like Center for Public Resources and Endispute-Jams, resources now exist to alleviate this concern. Model agreements to structure ADR procedures, lists of qualifiedneutrals in various fields and suggested questions to ask potential neutrals are all currently available to aid in the ADR process. Law firms are beginning to build up repositories of such information in order to assist clients who wish to pursue some type of ADR process.
Eighteen years ago, a young assistant professor at the University of Texas Law School had the courage to publish an article in which he pointed out that most civil litigation has now reduced itself to endless discovery, mostly depositions, with a result that there are almost no trials, all in the quest of a "complete record."The irony here is that trials, even long ones, do not take as long as the depositions which are encouraged in the federal system and in the courts of most large commercial states. Few lawyers, also ironically, really want to try civil cases. Professor Schwartz posed the question of whether or not there must be a "complete record" in every civil trial in order to achieve a correct result. His point infuriated all parts of the legal profession, judges, academics, and litigators. Each of these groups had its own reasons for wanting to have a "complete record." If you think about it, however, most ADR procedures do not require a "complete record" by any stretch. There is, in fact, a growing practice of submitting to ADR processes an issue or a defense in an existing civil case which, if resolved by someone the parties trust, will tend to lead to resolution of the entire case or controversy.
It was not until the late 1980s that the United States Senate Judiciary Committee began to think of ways to cut down burgeoningcivil case loads. Someone explained the device of ADR techniques to the Committee. That inquiry led to what is called the Civil Justice Reform Act.This Act required all 94 federal district courts to establish procedures encouraging litigants to at least consider mediation, arbitration, or some other form of non-judicial intervention to resolve cases. In New York, as far as I know, the courts have generally been reluctant to push ADR, although certain individual judges have had the good sense to suggest ADR techniques rather than a full trial. Soon, however, New York will almost certainly encourage ADR techniques on a unified basis in appropriate cases in our civil courts. As you will see hereinafter, the main thrust for encouraging ADR comes from litigants and those lawyers who have learned that they can still make money representing clients outside of a courtroom. There will always be cases which should or must be resolved by a court of record. But most civil disputes do not need to be recorded in the case reports of our court systems. Hence, as you will see from the papers that follow, more and more people are creatively resorting to new and varied ADR techniques even though mediation, dating back to the Greeks and the Romans, is still very much favored. Creativity comes about when lawyers and litigants decide to focus on key issues in their dispute which, if resolved, will probably clear the way for a settlement. Another creative approach is to use several forms of ADR (i.e. nonbinding mediation and binding arbitration) in the same case.The ideas and approaches described in the following papers will be used increasingly, thereby leading to new ways of fairly resolving civil controversies - unless legislatures or courts are persuaded to create "civil rules" and mandate their application to various ADR procedures.

Does encouraging or mandating consideration of ADR in court systems reduce judicial caseloads while still producing satisfactory and just resolutions for parties?
